en: *Rājanighaṇṭu*,
Maṅgalācaraṇa:
With cool sprays of water falling from clouds held aloft by the tips of his tusks— mistaken for a great elephant encircling the girdle of the Śrīkaṇṭha mountain— [the Lord protects us].

May the illustrious Vighnarāja, who is delighted by the fever of intoxication in Nirvāṇa, grant you incessant joy—he who spreads the splendor of a parasol. I meditate incessantly upon that Lord known as Amṛteśa, who is white as camphor powder, who bears tawny matted locks, has three eyes, and a moon upon his crest; who holds a conch, a vessel, the nectar-moon, and a boon-granting gesture along with the gesture of fearlessness in his four arms; and who carries on his left lap Śarvāṇī, whose limbs are radiant and adorned with various clusters of jewels, and who is worthy of him.
May the illustrious Maheśa, Nārāyaṇa, and Indra, the lords of the gods; then the two Aśvins, and thereafter the son of the three bodies (Agni);
Dhanvantari, Caraka, Suśruta, and the foremost of sages—may all those who established the tradition of Ayurveda be victorious!
Having bowed my head to Śambhu, having worshipped my own gurus, and having prostrated with devotion at the pair of lotus-feet of my parents;
Having approached Vighneśvara and Sarasvatī, the *Rājanighaṇṭu*, the king of lexicons, was commenced for the benefit of medical practitioners.
Having examined the works of Dhanvantari, Madanapāla, Halāyudha, and others, as well as the Viśvaprakāśa, the Amarakośa, the Śeṣanāmamālā, and the Rājanighaṇṭu,
and having reflected upon words well-known in the world, this compendium of substances, names, and groups has been composed.
It is an incomparable benefactor for the sciences of medicine and grammar, following the principles of the treatises of Dhanvantari.

We shall proclaim this collection of names, which bears the characteristics of diagnostic signs and dispels all diseases. He who is devoted to the investigation of various medicinal substances through the determination of definitions, characteristics, and examinations—by studying this entire work, he understands everything; therefore, this *Sarvanighaṇṭu* reigns supreme.

Even one whose intellect is expert in introducing, resolving, and mastering the names, potencies, and post-digestive transformations of various medicinal herbs will certainly become bewildered if they do not consult this glossary (nighaṇṭu). Therefore, it has been composed for the benefit of physicians. Without a glossary, a physician is like a learned man without grammar.
Through lack of practice, these three [types of people] become objects of derision for the archer.

(Rājñī-Garuḍapurāṇa 5) Since there is no counting by name—whether *saṃskṛta*, *prākṛta*, *apabhraṃśa*, or otherwise—due to the influence of various regional dialects when expressing a collection of substances, I therefore accept here only that which provides assistance. Is all the water of the ocean drunk by the clouds? (Rājñī-Garuḍapurāṇa 6)

Having examined Ābhīras, cowherds, Pulindas, ascetics, travelers, and others who have mastered the forest lore, one should then employ [the remedies] from them according to the characteristics of the various medicinal herbs, their names, juices, and extracts. Furthermore, that which has various designations— such as the names Śivā, Samaṅgā, Śyāmā, and so forth— established in the Vedic scriptures;

Having reflected upon this with one's intellect according to its introductory context, potency, taste, and combination, the physician must exercise firm resolve. (Rājani-Guṇapradīpa 8) The names of medicinal substances are stated here as being certainly of seven kinds: in some cases by convention, in some by their natural state, in some by regional usage, by their characteristic marks, by comparison, by their potency, and in some by another name or region. (Rājani-Guṇapradīpa 9)

In this work, while discussing the enumeration of the names and qualities of various medicinal herbs, other subjects— such as lands, mountains, rivers, gems, animals, and so forth— have been described with great detail due to their utility in that context. If even a single quality in this discourse might bring joy to those possessed of discernment, then other virtuous men will themselves extend their high regard for it without being asked.

Having drunk the lunar nectar that moistened even the rocks upon the mountain peaks, by what affliction are the oceans and the eyes of the worlds now gladdened by the night-lotuses? (Rājñī-Garuḍapurāṇa 11) Furthermore, regarding the medicinal substances mentioned here whose names are not well-known, there shall be a discernment of their designations in the determination of their single or multiple meanings. (Rājñī-Garuḍapurāṇa 12)
Those meanings such as "Rambhā," "Śyāmā," and so forth, as well as "celestial woman" and "young tree," which are taught in the *Nānārthatantra*, have been omitted here as they are irrelevant. Here,
the explanation has been rendered in the Karṇāṭaka and Mahārāṣṭrī languages.

The dialects of Āndhra, Lāṭa, and others, which are based on those two [Sanskrit and Prākṛt], should also be known. May this string of necklaces, consisting of a collection of wish-fulfilling gems named after the abode of all cessation (*nivṛti*), bring delight to the throats of the virtuous— this string enriched with pearls in the form of meters whose syllables are permeated by qualities multiplied by the three eyes (nine), and which possesses the essence of a multitude of white pearls.

Herein, first is the *anūpa* group and others; from this, the *avanī* group, then the two groups beginning with *guḍūcī* and *śatāhvā*; at the end of that, the *parpaṭa* group and others are recited; above that is the group beginning with *pippalīmūla*; following that is the *śālmali* group, then the *prabhadraka* group; then the *karavīra* group, another is the *āmra* group; before that [last one] is the *candana* group; after that is declared the *komala* group beginning with *kāñcana*. Then the *pānīya* group is mentioned, followed by the *kṣīra* and *śāli* groups; then the *māṃsa* and *mānuṣyaka* groups; then there is the *siṃha* group, then the *gada* group; thereafter follows the *sattvādhika* group, and another is the *miśraka* group.

Let the learned physician, having reached this section on the manifestation of intuitive insight through these groups of three-fold familiarized topics beginning with "having the same meaning," reach a definitive conclusion within the heart of his own system. This pedestal, brilliantly adorned with a range of golden plates, has been joyfully established by the illustrious Narasiṃha— the scholar whose path of glory, fortune, fame, and power was acquired through the worship of the pair of lotus feet of the Kashmiri Kapardi— and which serves as the foundation for the science of royal physicians.
Because they exist elsewhere, because their utility was not considered,
and for fear of excessive prolixity, I have not stated the multitude of their qualities. (Rājanighaṇṭu 19)

The *anūpa* region consists of land abounding in rice and other crops, which is very extensive, cool, and non-saline; it is inhabited by various people of the earth, water-dwelling creatures, and wild animals; it is cooled by clusters of mountain torrents, strewn with hills, and adorned by birds such as the *kurara* and others; its soil is copper-colored. (Rajni 1.1)

If that [land] possesses the full range of its own characteristics as previously described, with abundant shade covering the interior and flowing with much water, and if the water is slightly visible, it is considered middling; and if the water is not very deep, it is the lowest. Where there is a reversal of the marshy conditions, where the earth is covered with sparse grass, greyish in color, yielding crops such as mung beans, rice, barley, and other grains, and possessing intense heat—that is the best.

Generally, bile is increased [in this region], and living beings possess exalted strength; cows and goats yield much milk, and the water in its wells is of the *jāṅgala* type. (RājN 1.3) This is declared to be the primary [type of *jāṅgala*] when it is complete in its own qualities; if it possesses only a few trees, it is considered middling.
That in which water is easily obtained by digging a well is to be known as the lowest; thus the *jāṅgala* land is of three forms. (RājN 1.4)
Where prosperity blossoms slightly in both the *jāṅgala* and *anūpa* regions, and where there is the production of grains such as wheat, barley, and mung beans flourishing in abundance;

where the land possesses various colors and grants happiness to all beings—the wise know that region to be "Middle" (*madhyama*), characterized by the presence of both the arising of defects and their pacification, and they call it "Ordinary" (*sādhāraṇa*). And that "Ordinary" [land] is further divided into two types: derived from the *anūpa* and the *jāṅgala*. (RājN 1.5)
Wherever there is an abundance of qualities, one should partake of those qualities;
for due to the diversity of regions, that which is primary is not found everywhere in common.
Because of its subtlety, the characteristic of reality is perceived by those who know it through the Veda.
I shall now declare, exactly as it was proclaimed by Śiva, the classification of the fields:
namely, the Brāhma, the Kṣātra, the Vaiśyīya, and the Śaudra, in their proper order.
Among them, the field rich with trees of the Brahma-land is abundant in water and strewn with sprouts of *kuśa* grass.
"That which is delightful and endowed with white clay is called Brāhma," so says the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva).
"That region which possesses a copper-colored circle of earth, is supported by mountains, is crowded with lions,
and is filled with the terrible roar of the *khadira* and other impenetrable forests— this is declared by the wielder of the Pināka bow to be Kṣatriya."
The Moon-crested Lord described this region as Vaiśya— resplendent with a ground shining like gold, strewn with golden dust according to the ordinances, and frequented by Siddhas, Kiṃnaras, and gods;
a land abounding in dark soil, yielding abundant harvests, and where lush grasses and Babūla trees flourish.
The bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) spoke of the Śūdra-born [mercury] as that which brings joy to the world of farmers through the production of grain.

O sinless one, the substance arising from the field is Brāhma; it bestows success. That which arises from the Kṣatriya conquers wrinkles and grey hair and removes all diseases of the world. That born from the Vaiśya is exceedingly powerful for the accomplishment of minerals, metals, and the like. That produced from the Śūdra instantly drives away all maladies.
Brahmā, Śakra, the Lord of the Kinnaras, and likewise Bhū—these are the presiding deities for these [elements] in sequence.
Having been thus declared there by the beloved of Umā, I shall now describe those five elements individually.
That which is yellow, possessing shimmering bracelets, delightful with sugary stones, golden, and having the excellent deer as its emblem, is the square earth element.
Generally, that earthly [terrain] is hard, rising up entirely with creepers and the like adorned with yellow flowers;
however, that watery field is said to be white, shaped like a half-moon, shining like a lotus, paved with stone, and strewn with the waters of rivers and streams.
Abounding with *khadira* and other trees, filled with many variegated bamboos,
triangular, and consisting of red stone— this is the supreme fiery field (*taijasa-kṣetra*).
Dhūmrasthala is surrounded by smoky rocks, hexagonal, and quickly strewn with wild beasts.
This enclosure, indeed, is made of wind, consisting of grasses and trees that are sparse and withered.
That which is multicolored, circular, highly praised, mostly white, and filled with lofty mountains—
the place that is sacred to the deities— the Three-eyed One has declared to be the celestial field (*kṣetra*) of the atmosphere.

Earthen substances remove disease, bestow great strength, and are sweet and stable; those of water are pungent and astringent, entirely cold, and destroy bile (*pitta*). That which is bitter, salty, digestive, wind-dispelling, and hot is fiery (*taijasa*); that which is both cold and hot, sour, weak, and insipid belongs to the wind (*vāyavya*); and that which is ethereal (*nābhasa*) is devoid of taste.
From this [earth] arise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.

Thus, these five are the presiding deities of the fields in their respective order. In ancient times, having conquered the army of the Ajas with his speed in battle, the hero Garuḍa brought away the jar of nectar here;
indeed, by the fragments of nectar scattered upon the earth at that time, all things such as trees became [sweet] for him, and the Moon became its lord.
Those who were born there in the highest portion of the field, wherever they were as drops,
having attained the state of substances such as the earth-born [plants], they subsequently bore those various designations.
Thus, according to the suitability of the field, those born therein came to belong to the castes of Brahmins and so forth.
Or rather, I shall describe the characteristics for the sake of the non-delusion of the wise:
"They declare these [trees] to be a Brahmin when their sprouts and flowers are pure;
a Kṣatriya when they are very red; a Vaiśya when they resemble gold; and a Śūdra when they are other than white. (Rājñī 1.24–25)
One should employ those born of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes among the Brāhmaṇas and others respectively;
one should not practice the reverse order even with trees and the like, though they may be rich in qualities.
A Brāhmaṇa [should be employed] among the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, a Kṣatriya among the Kṣatriyas and others, and a Vaiśya among the principal Vaiśyas.

For a Śūdra, among those beginning with the Śūdra, wealth rich in qualities is recommended; nothing at all [is recommended] by way of inverse order (prātilomya). (RājNī 1.27) That which the noble ones call "plant-born" wealth, they further declare to be of five kinds: the tree (vanaspati), the forest-tree (vānaspatya), the shrub (kṣupa), the creeper (vīrudh), and the medicinal herb (oṣadhī). (RājNī 1.28)
In this context, that which bears fruit without flowers is to be known as a *vanaspati*; that which is remembered as a *vānaspatya* is a small, short shrub (*kṣupa*).

That which creeps by virtue of taking refuge upon trees and the like is considered a *vallī* (creeper). Furthermore, *oṣadhi* refers to rice and similar plants, characterized by having their existence terminate with the ripening of the fruit.
Even among stationary beings, there is a threefold division according to female, male, and neuter.
Listen, O Queen; I shall describe their characteristics clearly and in due order.

Sugarcane, bamboo, trees, creepers, and the like—those women who possess the delightful qualities of thick, long, thin, or slender stems, trunks, fruits, flowers, and shoots are indeed considered [excellent] by the wise. (Rajñī 1.30–1.31)
Where the flowers, sprouts, and so forth are neither too long nor too short,
and are thick rather than coarse— this, the wise have declared, is a male tree.
Where the characteristics of both sexes appear together on the branches, fruits, and other parts, [it is known as a hermaphrodite].
O wise ones, they say that which causes doubt and cannot be determined as either one or the other is the neuter (napuṃsaka).
A male substance brings health to every living being and increases his strength;
a woman is weak and possesses few qualities, yet among women alone there may be those rich in virtues, whereas a neuter person is never found to be so anywhere.

Some say that if women possess qualities [begetting] women, and those possessing eunuch bodies possess eunuch qualities, then a man, when employed at all times and in all places, brings about qualities; yet others say this. Hunger, thirst, and sleep are observed even in trees and other such things.
"From the taking up of earth and water, however, the first [element] is present; the last [element] is indicated by the contraction of the leaves.

That which possesses hardness is the earth; that from which moisture arises is water; that whose heat increases is fire; that which is the void is space; and that which is the movement is air. Thus, these stationary beings consist of the five elements. (Rajni 1.36–37)

Having studied this section, which follows the sequence of describing the nature of the qualities of the country and the properties of substances found in the lovely forest regions, a man quickly attains— like a physician— the skill in the art of medicine that makes him an "unconquerable healer" (agadaṅkāra) in the assembly of the gods, reaching the further shore of proficiency in the sphere of medical practice. (Rajni 1.38) The Lord Śrutayaśas, whose intellect had reached the far shore of the ocean of the eighteenfold varieties of the branches of learning, begot a son...
This first section, concerning the earth and other elements, has been completed in this excellent *Sadabhidhānacūḍāmaṇi* by that eminent author, the lord Nṛhari.
Now, Dharaṇī, Dharitrī, Bhūtadhātrī, Dharā, Bhūḥ, Kṣiti, Mahī, Dharaṇī, Īḍā, Kṣmā,
Vanī, Medinī, Jyā, Avani, Udadhivastṛā, Gauḥ, Kṣamā, Kṣauṇi, Urvī, Kurapi, Vasumatī,
Rā, Kāśyapī, Ratnagarbhā— this earth is Kṣamā, Ilā, Vasundharā, Varā, Dhātrī, Vasudhā, Acalorvarā.
Viśvaṃbharā, jagatī, kṣiti, rasā, pṛthvī, gotrā, pṛthivī, pṛthu, mahī,
kṣauṇī, sarvasahā, anantā, bhūtamātā, niścalā, bhūmi, bījaprasū, śyāmā, and kroḍakāntā are proclaimed as synonyms for the earth. (Rajñi 2.2–3)

That ground which provides the growth of all crops is called *urvarā*; because it is the source of all things, this earth is named *urvarā*. (Rājñī 2.4) That which is excellent soil is *mṛd*, *mṛttikā*, *mṛtsā*, or *mṛtsnā*. (Rājñī 2.5)

A region with saline and soft saline soil is called *iraṇa* or *ūṣara*; they say that uncultivated land is *khila*, while *dhanva* is said to be a desert (*maru*). A region that consists mostly of desert is called by the name *jāṅgala*.
Black earth is *kṛṣṇamṛt*, while pale earth is *pāṇḍumṛt*. A region that is full of gravel is *śārkara* or *śārkarila*;
it is *saikata*, *sikatila*, or *sikatāvān* if it is sandy.
*Deśa*, *janapada*, *nīvṛt*, *viṣaya*, and *upavartana* denote a country;
*pradeśa*, *sthāna*, *ākhyā*, *bhū*, *avakāśa*, *sthiti*, and *pada* denote a location or region. A territory filled with rivers, lotuses, and grain is called a *nadīmātraka*.
But by means of those waters produced by rain, this region would be "god-mothered" (devamātṛka).
(Rājñī 2.10) Filled with various grains produced from the waters of rivers and rain, a region is called "dual-mothered" (dvaimātṛka) because it follows both [sources]. (Rājñī 2.11)
That which produces a field of mung beans and the like is called *maudgīna*; likewise, that for kodrava is *kodravīṇa*, and so too for others.
One should know that for rice it is *vrīheya* or *śāleya*, and similarly for *buddha* and *aṇu* it is *buddhāṇavya* and *āṇavīna*.
Furthermore, for black gram it is *māṣya* or *māṣīṇa*; for hemp, *bhaṅgya* or *bhāṅgīna*; and for flax, *umya* or *aumīna*.
*Tilya* and *tailīna* refer to [land] for sesamum; likewise, *ṣaṣṭikya* and *yavya* refer to [land] for sixty-day rice and barley.
Where vegetables and the like are produced, that is called *śākaśākaṭa*, *śākaśākinam*, or similarly *vāstūkaśākaṭa*. (Rājñī 2.13–14)

Then there were the mountain, the earth-supporter, the lineage-holder, the king of mountains, the peak, the mass of rocks, the crag, the one with ridges, the earth-bearer, the goat-eater, the goer, the earth-holder, the mountain, the firm one, the great mountain, the earth-sustainer, and the supporter;
the unshakable, the mountain, the rock, the one with peaks, and the one with plateaus. (Rājñī 2.15)
*Śṛṅgin*, *vṛkṣavān*, and other such words denote a mountain (*śaila*). The middle part [of a mountain] is called the *nitamba*; it is also known as the *kaṭaka* or *mekhalā*.
The slope is the *taṭa* or *taṭī*; the precipice is the *prapāta*. The level plateau is the *prastha*; the ridge is the *snu* or *sānu*. (Rājñī 2.16–17)

*Śṛṅga*, *śikhara*, and *kūṭa* denote a peak; *kandara* and *kandarā* denote a cave or chasm; *vila* and *guhā* denote a cavern; *gahvara* denotes a mountain cleft or a natural excavation made by the gods (*devakhāta*);
the term *pāda* refers to the foothills of a mountain; and *gaṇḍaśaila* refers to large boulders that have fallen from the cliffs. (Rājñī 2.18)
A mine is called an *ākara* or a *khani*; the minerals are *gairika* and so forth.
A rock is a *prastara*, a *pāṣāṇa*, a *dṛṣad*, an *aśman*, an *upala*, or a *śilā*.
Various metals may be designated by such terms as *aśmasāra* (iron) and the like.
*Kānana*, *gahana*, *satra*, *kāntāra*, *vipina*, *vana*,
*araṇya*, *aṭavī*, *dāva*, and *dava* are synonyms for forest (*vana*). Furthermore, *udyāna* and *ākrīḍa* refer to a pleasure garden where those with passion (*rāgin*) sport.
In royal palaces, there is a pleasure grove suitable for the inner apartments.
A great forest is called *araṇyānī*, *mahāraṇya*, or *mahāṭavī*.
Furthermore, that which is a forest on the outskirts of a city is called an *upavana* or an *ārāma*.
*Kuja*, *kṣitiruha*, *aṅghripa*, *śikharin*, *pādapa*, *viṣṭara*, *kuṭha*, *taru*,

*anokaha*, *kuruba*, *bhūruha*, *drudruma*, *aga*, *naga*, *vanaspati*, *viṭapi*, *śākhi*, *bhūjāga*, *mā*, *mahīja*, *dharaṇīruha*, *kṣitija*, *vṛkṣa*, *śāla*, and so forth, are synonyms for a tree. Furthermore, *phalita*, *phalavān*, *phalina*, and *phalī* likewise denote that which bears fruit.
*Phalegrahi* is that which is not barren, being one from which fruitful results arise;
*athāva-keśī* is barren, fruitless, seedless, and unproductive.
The terms *vānaspatya* and *vanaspati*, though previously stated to be distinct in their own right, [are thus differentiated].
The root is called *netra*, *pāda*, *aṅghri*, and also *caraṇa*.
A sprout is to be known as *udbheda* and *aṅkura*; *praroha* is also a term for a sprout. Its front part is the *budhna*, while the broad part is the *nitamba*.
From the *skandha* (trunk) upward, it is called the *prakāṇḍa*; the *kāṇḍa* and *daṇḍa* are also so designated.
Its creepers, equal in measure to the trunk, are the branches (*śākhā*); the branches arising from the trunk are the *śālā*s.
Its *jaṭā*s are its veins (*sirā*), and its downward-growing roots are the *avaroha*s; the branch-roots are the *śiphā*s, and they say the pith is in the marrow (*majjan*).
*Niṣkuṭa* and *koṭara* are said to mean a hollow; *valka*, *valkala*, and *tvac* denote the bark. *Vallarī* and *mañjarī* refer to a cluster of new flowers at the tip of a branch.
*Parṇa*, *patra*, *dala*, *barha*, *palāśa*, *chadana*, and *chada* all signify a leaf.
Pallava, kiśalaya, and pravāla denote a sprout; pallava also refers to a new leaf.
Viṭapa is said to mean a branch or extension, while śikhara and śiras refer to the tip or summit.
Māḍhi should be known as the midrib of a leaf, and vṛnta is the stalk that attaches the flower or fruit.
The terms *kulakṣāraka*, *jālaka*, and *kalikā* are said to denote a bud (*kuḍmala*).
A flower (*kusuma*) may be called *sumanas*, *prasūna*, *prasava*, *suma*, *sūnu*, *phulla*, or *puṣpa*.
*Makaranda* and *maranda* are synonyms for honey (*madhu*), which is also termed the nectar of flowers (*puṣparasa*).
The pollen of flowers is called *parāga*; it is also known as *madhulī* and *dhūlikā*. A cluster of blossoms is a *guccha*, *guluncha*, *stavaka*, or *gucchaka*, as well as a *kusumoccaya*.
*Parimala*, *āmoda*, *gandha*, *saurabhya*, and *saugandhya* are synonymous terms for fragrance.

Ujjṛmbhita, ujjṛmbha, smita, unmiṣita, vinidra, unnidra, unmīlita, vijṛmbhita, udbuddha, udbhidura, bhinna, and udbhinna; likewise vikasita, hasita, vikasvara, vikaca, vyākośa, phulla, and samphulla. (Rājñī 2.36)
*Sphuṭa*, *udita*, *dalita*, *dīrṇa*, *sphuṭita*, *utphulla*, and *praphulla* have the same meaning. *Nidrāṇa*, *mudrita*, *supta*, *milita*, *mīlita*, *nata*,
*nikūṇita*, *saṅkucita*, *sanidra*, *alasa*, and *sama* [are synonyms].
They say that among trees, the fruit here is the grain; when raw, it is indeed called *śalāṭu*.
When dried, they call it *vāna*; a shrub (*gulma*) and a thicket (*stamba*) are plants growing from the earth that lack trunks (*prakāṇḍa*).
A creeping plant (*ulapa*) is a shrubby vine (*gulminī*); a spreading creeper (*vīrud*) is a climbing vine (*vallī*), which is also called a spreading creeper (*pratāninī*).
This creeper, spreading and extensive, is called a *vīrud*. Now I shall describe the trees associated with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), as identified in the Āgamas;
they are worthy of worship, bestow long life, and grant prosperity through both cultivation and protection.
Viṣadra, rudrātrī, the golden-milked tree, jambū, as well as khadira,
black bamboo, aśvattha, nāga, vaṭa, palāśa, plakṣa, and the ambaṣṭha tree in sequence;
bilva, arjuna, vikaṅkata, then kesara, śambara, sarja, and vañjula.
The *sapānasārkas*, the *śamī* and *kadamba*, as well as the *āmra*, *nimba*, and *madhuka* trees, in due order—
these twenty-seven trees have the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) as their presiding deities;
this is the sequence of the mansions for them, beginning with Aśvinī.

But that mortal, blinded by intoxication, who should administer medicines and the like to these [planets] when they occupy the natal asterism of one's self—his longevity, his prosperity, his wife, and his son perish; yet this [condition] increases through propitiatory rites and the like. Thus it is clearly stated in the *Ācāryokta*, the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*, the *Nāradīya*, the *Nārāyaṇīya*, and likewise in other treatises (*tantrāntara*).
Although this has been clearly established by renowned physicians, we have not explained it here out of respect [for tradition] and fear of increasing the bulk of the book.
(RājN 2.46) All the species beginning with *tāla*, as well as *kramuka*, *ketakī*, *kharjūrī*, *nārikela*, and others, are proclaimed to be the *tara* trees. (RājN 2.47)

The wise say that all these fresh herbs are full of great potency; however, those that are dry are middling, while those that are withered and old are fruitless. [These include] vāstūka, kuṭaja, guḍūcī, vāsā, kuṣmāṇḍaka, and śatapatrī. *Rājñī* 2.48.
The above-mentioned items remain eternally fresh and possess their full qualities; however, when they become dry, they are then doubled in measure.
Viḍaṅga, honey, māgadhī, pomegranate, long pepper, jujube, betel leaf, induvallī, śāli rice, and other such grains are best when old and reddish-brown. (Rajni 2.49)
Hardness, moderate hardness, and softness—
these three are said by the wise to be the fundamental nature of all substances here.
All substances possess these three qualities mentioned by the ancients.
Their taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation should be understood with great care.
Taste consists of sweet and the rest; potency is the capacity for action;
and that which possesses excellence in its final state is designated as post-digestive transformation (vipāka).
Cold, hot, dry, unctuous, sharp, as well as soft,
slimy, and clear— thus potency is said to be eightfold.
Even this substance would be devoid of its qualities in places such as gardens and pleasure groves.
Whether from hearing false words in some place, or from associating with unchaste women and the like,
a substance produced in a cremation ground, in an anthill, or in a place defiled by urine and such, is of no use whatsoever to physicians. (Rājñī 2.54–55)
They say that the bulbous root (*kanda*) is beneficial in the winter and early spring, the root in the late winter, the flower in the spring,
the tender shoots and leaves in the summer, and those born from the mud (the lotus) when used in the autumn.
Neem, *udumbara*, *jambu*, and other such trees are increasingly superior in quality according to their respective seasons.
Now, regarding all [medicinal substances] such as tubers and the rest, their tastes and other qualities are distinct for each:
some are in the tuber, some in the roots, some in the leaves, some in the flowers, and some in the fruits;
others are in the bark, and still others in the inner rind—thus the multitude of substances is enriched by various and diverse qualities.
In every region, at intervals of twelve *yojanas*, they say the names of substances differ in the world;
moreover, among these, the complexion, speech, gestures, and shadows of living beings appear in diverse forms.
In cases where the application is not specified, the root should be taken from among the bark and other parts.
When a general statement is made, they say that "water" should be understood as water from the sky (rainwater).
Where the proportions for powders, pastes, and decoctions have not been specified,
one should apply them according to the quantity of the substance itself, using one's own intelligence.
Among all wines, *mādhvīka* is the best; likewise, among honeys, *mākṣika* is the best.
Among oils, that produced from sesame is the best; and among minerals, those originating from the bladder are the best.
O Queen, among *śāli* rice, *raktaśāli* is the best; and among pulses, *mudga* is indeed the best.
Among roots, the root of *pippalī*; among fruits, the fruit of *madana*. Among aromatic substances, bark; among leaves, *gandhapattraka*.
Among pot-herbs, *jīvantī*; and among salts, *saindhava*.

Because of the general instruction regarding flowers, one should cast a *mālatī* blossom; in this manner, other applications characterized by their specific properties (*yoga*) are also to be understood. Whatever substance removes wind (*vāta*), all of that is an excellent digestive stimulant (*dīpana*).

That which is said to be equal [in its action] removes phlegm, subdues bile, and mildly stimulates digestion. (Rajni 2.66) That substance which is cold in potency, heavy, and removes bile is said to increase wind in men;
whereas that which is hot in potency, light, removes wind, and destroys phlegm would increase bile. (Rajni 2.67)

Having thus described in detail the names, qualities, and common characteristics of various countries, mountains, trees, forests, shrubs, and creepers— including their specific distinctions— I shall now describe them further. Thus, this [work], which is mature in its exposition of the multitude of names for lands, forests, regions, fields, lineages, and so forth, and in its description of their qualities and classifications—

"Having understood the category [of diseases], the physician should treat those whose intellects are illuminated by the light of accumulated, unimpeded, and extremely subtle wisdom, as if they were sovereign kings. Thus ends this [section] from the *Rājanighaṇṭu*, the crest-jewel of the methods for the classification and diagnosis of medical treatments, composed by one who has reached the further shore of the supreme scriptures of Śiva.
The group beginning with *guḍūcī*:
*guḍūcī*, then *mūrvā*, wild *paṭola*, and *kākolī* which is said to be of two kinds, as well as *māṣaparṇī* and others. (Rajni 3.1)
Mudgaparṇī, jīvantī, the three kinds of liṅginī,
kaṭukośātakī, kapikacchu, and others;
as well as khalatā, kaṭutumbī, and devadālī are thus recorded.
Vandhyākarkoṭakī is called Kaṭutuṇḍī and Ākhukarṇikā; Indravāruṇī is of two kinds here, as are Yavatiktā and Iśvarī;
Jyotiṣmatī is likewise of two kinds, and Girikarṇikā is also of two kinds.
Then there are moraṭa, and if it is indīvarā, it is also called vastāntrikā;
likewise somavallī, vatsādanī, and gopālakarkaṭī;
kākatuṇḍī is of two kinds, as well as guñjā and vṛddhadāru, which is also twofold.
Kaivartī, tāmravallī, kāṇḍīrī, and jantukā;
likewise amlaparṇī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and avartakī;
as well as karṇasphoṭā, kaṭvī, latā, and amṛtasravā.

*Putradā*, *palāśī*, and *vijñeyā*—these nine names should be understood here. (RājN 3.7) These creepers, though not explicitly mentioned by the wise in this manner, are to be understood in their proper order;
they are celebrated in this section on creepers according to their names and qualities. (RājN 3.8)
Even the enumeration of the names of all these medicinal herbs, which is otherwise unknown because they lack well-known designations, has been stated here up to the number one hundred.

That enumeration is expressed clearly by their actual names in some places, while in others it is stated through sophisticated poetic devices; yet even where it was not explicitly stated, it is found within the cryptic numerical verses (*naṣṭāṅkavākya*).
Therefore, in this work, there is no place where the construction of the names' numerical values has not been explained.
In each of those cases, the number eight alone is to be understood everywhere by the wise.
Even if, in some instances, a restriction regarding the number of missing limbs is observed,
one should understand that the number was not explicitly stated there simply because it was self-evident.

Others have declared that the potency (*vīrya*) of substances is determined by their classification, reputation, and application; however, the ancient sages did not state that the medical procedure prescribed in the *Nigamas* (Vedic texts) depends upon those factors.
Therefore, we have not spoken here according to the consensus of those who know the collection of *Naigama* applications, but rather each of these [substances] is described individually.
Guḍūcī is known as Amṛtavallī, Amṛtā, Jvarāri, Śyāmā, Varā, Surakṛtā, and Madhuparṇikā.
Chinnodbhavā, amṛtalatā, rasāyanī, chinnā, somalatikā, and amṛtasambhavā;
vatsādanī, chinnaruhā, viśalyā, bhiṣakpriyā, kuṇḍalinī, vayaḥsthā, jīvantikā, nāgakumārikā, chadmikā, and caṇḍahāsā are synonyms for the same plant. (Rājñī 3.13–14)
Another is *kandodbhavā*, *kandāmṛtā*, *piṇḍaguḍūcikā*,
*bahucchinnā*, *bahuruhā*, *piṇḍālu*, and *kandarohiṇī*.
The former is called *vārdhikarā* and the latter is known as *lokasaṃjñikā*.
Thus, there are thirty-one names for the two types of *guḍūcī* here.

*Guḍūcī* should be known as heavy, hot in potency, bitter, and astringent; it destroys fever and removes burning sensations, pain, thirst, vomiting, blood disorders, wind disorders, urinary disorders, anemia, and vertigo. (Rajni 3.16–17)

Guḍūcī, which originates from a bulb, is pungent and hot; it destroys the *saṃnipāta* disorder, neutralizes poison, subdues fever and malevolent spirits, and eliminates wrinkles and graying hair. (Rajni 3.18) Mūrvā, Divyalatā, Mirā, Madhurasā, Devī, Triparṇī, Madhuśreṇī, Bhinnadalā, Amarī, Madhumatī, Tiktā, Pṛthakparṇikā, Gokarṇī, Laghuparṇikā, Dahanī, Tejasvinī, Moraṭā, Devaśreṇī, Madhūlikā, Madhudalā, Pīlunī, and Raktalā are synonyms. (Rajni 3.19)
Sukhoṣitā, Snigdhaparṇī, Pīluparṇī, Madhusravā, Jvalanī, and Gopavallī—these are the twenty-eight names [of the plant].
Mūrvā is bitter, astringent, and hot; it removes heart disease, phlegm, and wind.
It destroys vomiting, urinary disorders, skin diseases, and irregular fevers. *Rājñī* 3.21.
*Paṭola* is known as *kaṭuphala*, *kulaka*, *karkaśacchada*, *rājanāma*, *amṛtaphala*, *pāṇḍu*, and *pāṇḍuphala*. *Rājñī* 3.22.
Bījagarbha, nāgaphala, kuṣṭhāri, kāsamardana, pañcarājiphala, jyotsnī, kuṣṭhaghna—these are the sixteen names [of nāgabalā].
Paṭola is pungent, bitter, and hot; it conquers blood-bile and phlegm.

It destroys phlegm, itching, skin diseases, blood disorders, fever, and the pain of burning sensations. Kākolī is sweet; it is called kākī, kālikā, vāyasolikā, kṣīrā, dhvāṅkṣikā, vīrā, śuklā, dhīrā, and medurā.
Dhvāṅkṣolī, Svādumāṃsī, Vayaḥsthā, and Jīvinī—
this Kākolī is indeed known by these fifteen names.
(Rājñī 3.26) Kākolī is sweet, unctuous, and removes the afflictions of wasting, pitta, and vāta.

It destroys blood-burn and fever, and increases phlegm and semen. (Rajni 3.27) The second is Kṣīrakākolī, also known as Kṣīraśuklā, Payasvinī, Payasyā, Kṣīramadhurā, Vīrā, and Kṣīraviṣāṇikā. (Rajni 3.28)
Jīvavallī and jīvaśuklā—thus this plant has nine names;
and it is similar to kākolī in its taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation (vipāka).
Māṣaparṇī, however, is known as kāmbojī, kṛṣṇavṛntā, and mahāsahā.
Ārdramāṣā, māṃsamāṣā, maṅgalyā, hayapucchikā, haṃsamāṣā,
aśvapucchā, pāṇḍurā, māṣapattrikā,
kalyāṇī, vajramūlī, śāliparṇī, and visāriṇī.
"Born from itself, yielding many fruits, self-existent, easily obtained, and dense"—
thus is this *māṣaparṇī* known by twenty-one names.
(Rajñī 3.32) *Māṣaparṇī* is bitter in taste, aphrodisiac, and removes burning sensations and fever.
It increases semen, is strengthening, cooling, and promotes nourishment.
Mudgaparṇī, Kṣudrasahā, Śimbī, Mārjāragandhikā, Vanajā, Riṅgiṇī, Hrasvā, Sūryaparṇī, and Kuraṅgikā [are synonyms]. (Rajñī 3.33–3.34)
Kāṃsikā, kākamudgā, vanamudgā, vanodbhavā,
araṇyamudgā, and vanyā— these are known as the fifteen names [of this plant].
Mudgaparṇī is cooling and removes cough, vātarakta, and consumption.
It destroys bile, burning sensations, and fever; it is beneficial for the eyes and increases semen.
(3.36) Jīvantī is known as jīvanī, jīvanīyā, jīvā, jīvyā, jīvadā, and jīvadātrī.
It is the best of greens, called jīvabhadrā, bhadra, maṅgalyā, kṣudrajīvā, and yaśasyā. (3.37)
Śṛṅgāṭī, jīvapṛṣṭhā, kāñjikā, śaśaśimbikā,
and supiṅgalā— jīvantī is known by these eighteen names.
Jīvantī is sweet, cooling, and removes blood-bile and wind.

It destroys wasting diseases, burning sensations, and fevers, and increases phlegm and virility. Jīvantī is another [variety] preceded by *bṛhat* (bṛhajjīvantī); it is called putrabhadrā, priyaṃkarī, madhurā, jīvapṛṣṭhā, bṛhajjīvā, and yaśaskarī.
In this very way, Bṛhatpūrvā is known to be endowed with juice, potency, and strength;
she is the dispeller of spirits and, by her force, the regulator of fluids.
Hemā, Hemavatī, Saumyā, Tṛṇagranthi, and Himāśrayā [are likewise].
Svarṇaparṇī, sujīvantī, svarṇajīvā, suvarṇikā, hemapuṣpī, svarṇalatā, svarṇajīvantikā,
hemavallī, and hemalatā— these are its fourteen names. (Rājñī 3.42–43)

Svarṇajīvantikā is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, sweet, cooling, a conqueror of wind, bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations, and it increases strength. Liṅginī is also called bahupattrā, īśvarī, and śaivamallikā.
Svayambhū, Liṅgasambhūtā, Liṅginī, Citraphalā, Amṛtā, Paṇḍolī,
Liṅgajā, Devī, Caṇḍā, Apastambhinī, Śivajā, and Śivavallī— these should be known as the sixteen names. (Rājñī 3.45–46)

Liṅginī is pungent, hot, foul-smelling, and an elixir; it is divine, bestows all accomplishments, brings things under control, and regulates the flow of fluids. Koṣātakī, Kṛtacchidrā, Jālinī, and Kṛtavedhanā [are synonyms].
Kṣveḍā, sutiktā, ghaṇṭālī, mṛdaṅgaphalinī,
and kośātakī are cooling, pungent, and slightly astringent;
they destroy pitta, vāta, and kapha, and cleanse the impurities and flatulence.
Kapikacchu, ātmaguptā, svayaṃguptā, maharṣabhī, lāṅgūlī, kuṇḍalī, caṇḍā, markaṭī, durabhigrahā,
kapiromaphalā, guptā, duḥsparśā, kacchurā, and jayā.
Prāvṛṣeṇyā, śūkaśimbī, badarī, gurur-ārṣabhī, śimbī, varāhikā,
tīkṣṇā, romālur, vanaśūkarī, kīśaromā, and romavallī— this plant has twenty-six names. (Rājñī 3.51–52)
*Kapikacchū* is sweet-tasting, aphrodisiac, and removes the depletion of *vāta*;
it destroys cold-pitta and blood disorders, and when processed, it destroys wounds. *Khavallī*, *ākāśavallī*, and *asparśā* are synonyms for *vyomavallikā*.
That creeper, known by the name Ākāśa, is recorded as having synonyms such as Vallī.
Ākāśavallī is pungent and sweet, it destroys bile, is aphrodisiac,
an elixir, strengthening, and is considered the supreme among divine medicinal herbs.
Kaṭutumbī, kaṭuphalā, tumbinī,
kaṭutumbinī, bṛhatphalā, rājaputrī, tiktabījā, and tumbikā are synonyms for the bitter gourd.
Kaṭutumbī is pungent, sharp, emetic, and it conquers asthma and wind disorders.

Kāsaghnī purifies and removes swelling, wounds, and poisons. Jīmūtaka, kaṇṭaphalā, garāgarī, veṇī, sahā, krośaphalā, kaṭphalā, ghorā, kadambā, viṣahā, karkaṭī, devadālī, and sāramūṣikā are indeed synonyms.
Vṛttakośā, viṣaghnī, dālī, lomaśapattrikā,
turaṅgikā, and tarkārī— these are the nineteen names [of the plant].
Devadālī is bitter and hot, pungent, and it removes jaundice and phlegm.
It destroys bad names, asthma, and cough; it destroys jaundice and malevolent spirits.
The goddess Vandhyā is Vandhyakarkoṭakā, Nāgārāti, and Nāgahantrī;
she is Manojñā, Pathyā, Divyā, Putradātrī, Sukandā, Śrīkandā, and Kandavallīśvarī.
Sugandhā, sarpadamanī, viṣakaṇṭakinī, varā, kumārī, and bhūtahantrī—these are its nineteen names.
Vandhyākarkoṭakī is bitter, pungent, and hot; it removes phlegm (kapha).
It is praised as a destroyer of poisons from stationary sources (plants/minerals) and is recommended for rejuvenation therapy (*rasāyana*).
*Tiktatuṇḍī* is called *tikta*, while *kaṭukā* and *kaṭutuṇḍikā* are synonyms;
*bimbī* is also included among the synonyms for *kaṭutiktādi-tuṇḍī*.
Kaṭutuṇḍī is pungent and bitter; it removes phlegm, induces vomiting, and destroys poisons.
It cures anorexia and blood-bile (raktapitta), is always wholesome, and improves the appetite. Ākhukarṇī is also known as kṛṣikā, dravantī, citrā, sukarṇī, and undurukarṇikā.
Nyagrodhikā, mūṣikanāgakarṇī, syād, vṛścikarṇī, and bahukarṇikā;
mātā, bhūmicarī, caṇḍā, śambarī, and bahupādikā; pratyakśreṇī, vṛṣā, putraśreṇī, and the one called adribhū. (Rājñī 3.66–67)

Ākhukarṇī is pungent and hot; it always removes phlegm and bile, destroys the pain of abdominal distension, fever, and colic, and is a supreme digestive. Aindrī, indravāruṇī, aruṇā, mṛgādanī, gavādanī, kṣudrasahā, indrā, and cirbhiṭā—[these are synonyms]. Rajni 3.68.
Sūryā, Viṣaghnī, Guṇakarṇikā, Amarā, Mātā, Suvarṇā, Suphalā, and Tārakā; Vṛṣabhākṣī, Gavākṣī, Pītapuṣpī,
Indravallarī, Hemapuṣpī, Kṣudraphalā, Vāruṇī, and Bālakapriyā.
Rakta-indravāruṇī, aru-viṣalatā, śakravallī, viṣāpahā, amṛtā, and viṣavallī are known by these twenty-nine names. Indravāruṇikā is bitter, pungent, cooling, and clarifying.
It cures abdominal tumors, bile disorders, enlargement of the abdomen, phlegm, worms, skin diseases, and fever.
Mahendravāruṇī is delightful, Citravallī, and Mahāphalā;
it is also called Māhendrī, Citraphalā, Trapusī, and Trapusā.
Ātmarakṣā, viśālā, dīrghavallī, bṛhatphalā,
bṛhadvāruṇī, and saumyā— these are its fourteen names.
Mahendravāruṇī should be known as possessing the qualities previously mentioned.
In terms of taste, potency, and post-digestive effect, some of these possess superior qualities.
*Rajani* 3.75–3.76: *Yavatikta*, *mahātiktā*, *dṛḍhapādā*, *visarpiṇī*, *nākulī*, *netramīlā*, *śaṅkhinī*, and *patrataṇḍulī*.

Taṇḍulī, akṣapīḍā, sūkṣmapuṣpī, yaśasvinī, māheśvarī, tiktayavā, and yāvī— these sixteen are known as *tikta*. Yava-tikta is slightly bitter and sour, a digestive stimulant (*dīpanī*), and highly effective for improving the appetite.

It destroys worms, skin diseases, and poisons; it cures disorders of undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and acts as a purgative. Raudrī, jaṭā, rudrajaṭā, rudrā, saumyā, sugandhā, suhatā, ghanā, īśvarī, rudralatā, supattrā, sugandhapatrā, surabhi, and śivāhvā are synonyms for this plant.
Pattravallī, Jaṭāvallī, Rudrāṇī, Netrapuṣkarā, Mahājaṭā, and Jaṭārudrā— these twenty names have been declared. Jaṭā has a pungent taste and destroys asthma, cough, and heart disease.
It is the dispeller of demons and the destroyer of Rākṣasas.
Jyotiṣmatī, Svarṇalatā, Analaprabhā, Jyotirlatā, Kaṭabhī, Supiṅgalā,
Dīptā, Medhyā, Matidā, Durjarā, Sarasvatī, and Amṛtā— these are the names [of the plant] according to the number twelve (the sun).
*Tejovatī*, *bahurasā*, *kanakaprabhā*, another is *tīkṣṇā*; *suvarṇanakulī* is salty and kindles the fire.
*Tejasvinī*, *suralatā*, *agniphalā*, and *agnigarbhā* are synonyms; thereafter, *kaṅgaṇī* is known as *śailasutā* and *sutailā*.
*Suvegā*, *vāyasī*, *tīvrā*, *kākāṇḍī*, and *vāyasādanī* [are names for the same plant].
Gīrlatā, śrīphalī, saumyā, brāhmī, lavaṇakiṃśukā, pārāvatapadī, pītā, pītatailā, yaśasvinī, medhyā,
medhāvinī, and dhīrā— this plant has thirty-one names. (Rajñī 3.84–85)
Jyotiṣmatī is bitter in taste, dry, slightly pungent, and it subdues vāta and kapha;
it causes a burning sensation, stimulates digestion, promotes mental clarity, and likewise nourishes wisdom.
Aśvakṣurā, Adrikarṇī, Kaṭabhī, and Dadhipuṣpikā are [similar]. Rajñi 3.86.
Gardabhī, sitapuṣpī, śvetaspandā, aparājitā,
śvetā, bhadrā, supuṣpī, and viṣahantrī are each synonyms for the same plant.
Nāgaparyāyakarṇī is known as aśvāhvā and kṣurī.
Girikarṇī is cooling, bitter, and destroys complications caused by pitta;
it is beneficial for the eyes, removes the defects of poison, and pacifies the three doṣas.
Nīlapuṣpī, mahānīlā, nīlā, and girikarṇikā are synonyms for it.
Gavādanī has a distinct fragrance, flows blue, and is known by six names.
It is cooling, slightly bitter, and destroys red dysentery, fever, and burning sensations;
it also removes vomiting, insanity, intoxication, dizziness, distress, asthma, and chronic cough.
Moraṭa, kīrṇapuṣpa, pīlupattra, madhusrava, ghanamūla,
dīrghamūla, puruṣa, and kṣīramoraṭa [are synonyms].
Moraṭa is rich in latex, sweet, and slightly astringent.
It destroys bile-born burning sensations and fever; it is aphrodisiac and increases strength.
Indīvarā, Yugmaphalā, Dīrghavṛttā, Uttamāraṇī, Puṣpamañjarikā, Droṇī, Karambhā, and Nalikā are synonyms for it.

Indīvarā is pungent and cold; it removes pitta and phlegm, is beneficial for the eyes, destroys the defects of cough, and is supreme in curing wounds and worms. Vastāntrī is also known as vṛṣagandhā, meṣāntrī, and vṛttapattrikā.
The *ajāntrī* and the *vokaḍī* constitute this group known by six names.
The *vastāntrī* has a pungent taste and destroys the disorders of cough;
it is proclaimed by the best of physicians to be a giver of seeds and a producer of conception.
Somavallī, Mahāgulmā, Yajñaśreṣṭhā, Dhanurlatā, Somārhā,
Gulmavallī, Yajñavallī,
Dvijapriyā, Somakṣīrā, and Somā— these eleven are the limbs of sacrifice, equal in number to Rudra.
Somavallī is pungent, cooling, and sweet; it alleviates bile and burning sensations, pacifies thirst and dryness, is purifying, and serves as a means for sacrifice.
Saumyā, Mahiṣavallī, Pratisomā, and Antravallikā [are also known by these names].
Apattravallikā is said to have six names, including Kāṇḍaśākhā;
it is considered equal to Somavallī in its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect (rasa-vīrya-vipāka).
Vatsādanī, Somavallī, Vikrāntā, and Mecakā are its designations.
Pātālagaruḍī, Tārkṣī, Sauparṇī, Gāruḍī, Vāsanī, Dīrghakāṇḍā, Dṛḍhakāṇḍā, Mahābalā,
Dīrghavallī, and Dṛḍhalatā— these are its fourteen names. (Rajñī 3.101–102)

Vatsādanī is sweet, it removes the disorders of pitta, burning sensations, and blood; it is aphrodisiac, nourishing, appetizing, and a destroyer of the effects of poison. Gopālakarkaṭī, vanyā, and likewise gopakarkaṭikā [share these qualities]. Rajni 3.103.
Kṣudravāru, kṣudraphalā, gopālī, and kṣudracirbhaṭā— also known as gopālakarkaṭī—
are cooling and sweet; they destroy pitta and alleviate dysuria,
urinary calculi, urinary disorders, burning sensations, and wasting.
Kākanāsā, Dhvāṅkṣanāsā, Kākatuṇḍā, and Vāyasī;
Suruṅgī, Taskarasnāyu, Dhvāṅkṣatuṇḍā, and Sunāsikā;
Vāyasāhvā, Dhvāṅkṣanakhī, Kākākṣā, and Dhvāṅkṣanāsikā.
It should be known as *kākaprāṇā*, and it has thirteen names. *Kākanāsā* is sweet, cooling, and removes bile;
it is an elixir (*rasāyana*), provides firmness, and especially removes gray hair.
Kākādanī, kākapīlu, kākaśimbī, raktalā,
dhvāṅkṣādanī, vaktraśalyā, durmohā, vāyasādanī, kākatuṇḍī,
dhvāṅkṣanakhī, vāyasī, and kākadantikā.
It should be known by thirteen names, including *dhvāṅkṣadantī*.
*Kākādanī* is pungent, hot, and bitter; it is a divine elixir (*rasāyana*), removes disorders of wind (*vātadoṣa*), improves the appetite, and is supreme for arresting premature graying of the hair.
Guñjā, cūḍāmaṇi, saumyā, śikhaṇḍī, kṛṣṇalāruṇā, tāmrikā, śītapākī, uccaṭā, and kṛṣṇacūḍikā;
as well as raktā, raktikā, kāmbhojī, and bhillibhūṣaṇā. (Rajni 3.112)
Vanyā, āsyā, mānacūḍā, and vijñeyā are to be known as the sixteen names [of the first].
The second has six names: śvetakāmbhojī, śvetaguñjā, bhiriṇṭikā, kākādanī, kākapīlu, and vaktraśalyā. (Rajni 3.113–114)

The two types of *guñjā* are bitter and hot; the seed induces vomiting, while the root cures colic. The leaf is a poison-remover, and the white variety is recommended for subjugation (*vaśya*). *Vṛddhadāruka*, *āvegī*, *juṅgaka*, and *dīrghabāluka* [are synonyms].
Vṛddhā is known as Koṭarapuṣpī; Ajāntrī is Chāgalāntrikā.
Jīrṇadāru is the second [name], while Jīrṇā, Phaṇjī, Supuṣpikā, Ajarā, and Sūkṣmapattrā are to be understood as its six names.
The two types of *vṛddhadāru* are sweet, slimy, and remove phlegm and wind;
they are strengthening and cure cough and the disorders of *āmadoṣa*, though the second variety provides little potency.
*Kaivartikā*, *suraṅgā*, *latā*, *vallī*, and *drumāruhā* [are synonyms].

Riṅgiṇī, vastraraṅgā, and bhagā—these are the eightfold designations [of the plant]. Kaivartikā is light, aphrodisiac, astringent, and destroys phlegm; it removes cough and asthma, and likewise cures the disorder of weak digestion.
Tālī, tamālī, tāmrā, tāmravallī,
tamālikā, sūkṣmavallī, sulomā, śodhanī, and tālikā— these are the nine [varieties].
Tāmravallī is astringent and destroys the disorder of phlegm (kapha).
It destroys the humors arising from the mouth and throat, and is supreme for purifying phlegm. Kāṇḍīra, kāṇḍakaṭuka, nāsāsaṃvedana, paṭu, ugrakāṇḍa,
toyavallī, kāravallī, and sukāṇḍaka [are its synonyms].
Kāṇḍīra is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is laxative and removes pain from malignant ulcers.
It destroys spider-bites, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the spleen, colic, and weak digestion.
Jantukā, jantukārī, jananī, and cakravartinī [are synonyms].
Tiryakphalā, niśāndhā, bahupattrā, supattrikā, rājakṛṣṇā, janeṣṭā, kapikacchuphalopamā,
rañjanī, sūkṣmavallī, bhramarī, and kṛṣṇavallikā. (Rajni 3.125–126)
Vijjullikā, vṛkṣaruhā, granthiparṇī, suvallikā, taruvallī,
and dīrghaphalā— these are the twenty-one names [of this plant].
It is cooling and bitter, and it removes blood-bile (raktapitta) and phlegm (kapha).
It destroys burning sensations and thirst, provides relish, and is a supreme digestive stimulant.
Atyamlaparṇī is sharp, causes itching, and is a climbing root (vallīsūraṇa);
it is a creeper (vallī) such as karavaḍā and others, growing wild in forests and inhabited by forest-dwellers.

*Atyamlaparṇī* is pungent and sour; it destroys splenic pain, removes wind from the heart, stimulates digestion, improves appetite, and cures abdominal tumors and diseases of phlegm. (Rajni 3.130) *Śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *Supuṣpī*, *Śaṅkhāhvā*, and *Kambumālinī* [are synonyms].
Sita-puṣpī, Kambu-puṣpī, Medhyā, Vanavilāsinī, Ciriṇṭī,
Śaṅkhakusumā, Bhūlagnā, and Śaṅkhamālinī—
thus this Śaṅkhapuṣpī is said to have twelve names.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī is cooling, bitter, a promoter of intelligence, and a restorer of the voice;
it destroys the afflictions caused by planetary influences and spirits, and grants success in the practice of subjugation.
Vartakī, Tindukinī, Vibhāṇḍī, Viṣāṇikā, Raṅgalatā, and Manojñā [are likewise].
That *raktapuṣpī* is a great net-like plant; it is also *pītakīlā* and *carmaraṅgā*.
When combined with a leftward whorl, it is joined with the number of the earth [one] and the moon [one], making two.
It is *āvartakī*, astringent and sour, cooling, and a remover of bile.
Karṇasphoṭā, Śrutisphoṭā, Tripuṭā, Kṛṣṇataṇḍulā, Citraparṇī, Sphoṭalatā, Candrikā, and Ardhacandrikā.
Karṇasphoṭā is pungent, bitter, and cooling; it removes all poisons.
It destroys the afflictions caused by planets and spirits, and it eradicates all diseases.
Kaṭvī, Kaṭukavallī, Sukāṣṭhā, Kāṣṭhavallikā,
Suvallī, Mahāvallī, Paśumohanikā, and Kaṭu [are its names].

Kaṭvī, however, is pungent and cooling; it destroys the afflictions of phlegm and asthma, removes various fevers, improves the appetite, and wards off pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman). It should be known as amṛtasravā, vṛttāruha, and toyavallikā. (Rajni 3.139)
Ghanavallī, śītalatā, and other names—these fifteen [plants] have been mentioned.
Known as amṛtasravā, they are wholesome (pathyā), slightly bitter, and an elixir (rasāyana).
They destroy poison and conquer wounds, leprosy (kuṣṭha) and the like, jaundice (kāmalā), and swelling (śvayathu).
Putradātrī, vātāri, bhramarī, śvetapuṣpikā, vṛttapattrā, atigandhālū, vaiśijātā, and suvallarī [are synonyms]. Putradātrī destroys wind, is pungent and hot, and removes phlegm.
*Surabhi* is always wholesome and destroys the defects of sterility.
*Palāśī*, *pattravallī*, *parṇavallī*, and *palāśikā* are synonyms.
*Khuraparṇī*, *suparṇī*, *dīrghavallī*, and *viṣādanī* are also names for it.
Amlapattrī, dīrghapattrī, rasāmlā, amlakā, amlātakī, and kāñjikā—this [plant] has fourteen names. Rajni 3.145: Palāśī, laghuramyā, and mukhadoṣavināśanī [are its names].
"It cures loss of appetite, yet it aggravates bile.

(Rajni 3.146) Thus, may the physician, like Vyāsa, expound this work—which is filled with the accurate description of the names and qualities of a multitude of various creepers, composed of verses with elegant phrasing, and arranged according to groups of names—with great charm in the assembly. (Rajni 3.147)

Like the blazing rays of the sun for the destruction of blinding darkness, these plants spread their own power to conquer disease; they possess a virile potency that triumphs even over adversaries. This peerless class of creepers is renowned as the "Vīrud-varga" (the group of creepers), celebrated for its innate qualities and serving as the very playground of their splendor.
Having become the possession of him who is the unique crest-jewel of the three kinds of noble heroes, these potent herbs suddenly discharge their fierce potencies, as if from an inexhaustible source.
This group, beginning with *guḍūcī*, has found its place within the work of that Nṛhari; it is proclaimed as the third section in this crest-jewel of lexical compositions, the *Rājanighaṇṭu*.
(Rājanighaṇṭu, Parpaṭādivarga 3.149)
Parpaṭa, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, the two kinds of śrāvaṇī,
the two types of medā, ṛddhi, vṛddhi, dhūmrapattrā,
prasāraṇī, catuṣpā, pāṣāṇabheda, kanyā, and likewise barhiśikhā.
The two types of *kṣīriṇī*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *rudantikā*;
the two kinds of *brāhmī*, *vandāka*, *kulatthā*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*;
*civillo*, *nāgaśuṇḍī*, *kuṭumbī*, and *sthalapadminī*.
Jambū, nāgadantī, viṣṇukrāntā,
kuṇañjara, bhūmyāmalī, gorakṣī, golomī, dugdhaphenikā, kṣudrāmlikā, lajjāhvī, haṃsapādī, and kātharā.
Three types of *punarnavā* are proclaimed, and *vasuka* is remembered as being of two kinds.
*Sarpiṇī*, *āli*, *matsyākṣī*, *guṇḍālā*,
*avanipāṭalī*, *pāṇḍuraphalī*, *śvetā*, *brahmadaṇḍī*, and *dravantikā* [are synonyms].
The two types of *droṇapuṣpī*, *jhaṇḍū*, and *gorakṣadugdhikā*—
these nine are declared to be small shrubs (*kṣudrakṣupa*) in their respective order.
*Parpaṭa*, *caraka*, *reṇu*, *tṛṣṇāri*, *kharaka*, and *rajaḥ*.
Śīta, Śītapriya, Pāṃśu, Kalpāṅgī, Varma, Kaṇṭaka, Kṛśaśākha, Parpaṭaka, Sutikta, Raktapuṣpaka,
Pittāri, Kaṭupattra, and Kavaca— these are the eighteen names [of the plant].

Parpaṭa is cooling and bitter; it removes bile, phlegm, and fever, and destroys blood-burning sensations, loss of appetite, exhaustion, intoxication, and vertigo. Jīvaka is life-sustaining, vitalizing, nourishing, known as Śṛṅgāhva, bestower of breath, and dear [to the wise].
Long-lived, sweet, auspicious, and with a beard upon his head;
short-limbed, bestowing growth, long-lived, living, likewise possessing longevity, and strength-bestowing— these are the sixteen names.

Jīvaka is sweet and cooling; it conquers the afflictions of blood-bile (rakta-pitta) and wind (anila), destroys consumption, burning sensations, and fever, and increases semen and phlegm (kapha). Ṛṣabha, gopati, dhīra, viṣāṇin, dhūrdhara, and vṛṣa [are synonyms for the bull].
Kakudmān, puṅgava, voḍhā, śṛṅgī, dhurya, and bhūpati;
kāmī, ṛkṣapriya, cokṣā, lāṅgulī, gau, and bandhura;
gorakṣa, and vanavāsī—these are to be known as the twenty names [of the bull].
Ṛṣabha is sweet, cooling, and removes the purging of pitta and blood;
it generates semen and phlegm, and it alleviates burning sensations and wasting fevers.
Śrāvaṇī is known as muṇḍitikā, bhikṣu, and śravaṇaśīrṣikā.

Śravaṇā is a female renunciant, a wandering mendicant rich in asceticism. Śrāvaṇī, however, is astringent, pungent, and hot; it subdues phlegm and bile, destroys undigested matter, dysentery, and cough, and eliminates poison and vomiting.
There is Mahāśrāvaṇikā, as well as Mahāmuṇḍī and Locanī;
Kadambapuṣpī, Vikacā, Kroḍacūḍā, and Palaṅkaṣā;
Nadīkadamba, Muṇḍākhyā, and Mahāmuṇḍanikā.
Chinnā, Granthinikā, Mātā, Sthavirā, Lobhanī, Bhūkadamba, and Alambuṣā— these are its seventeen names.
Mahāmuṇḍī is hot and bitter, slightly sweet, and a destroyer of wind (vāta).
It improves the voice, is clarifying, cures urinary disorders, and acts as an elixir. Medā, vasā, maṇicchidrā, jīvanī, śalyaparṇikā, nakhacchedyā, himā, and raṅgā grow in the Middle Country.
Medasārā, Snehavatī, Medinī, Madhurā, Varā, Snigdhā, Medodravā, Sādhvī, Śalyadā, Bahurandhrikā—
known by these nineteen names, she is considered Pūruṣadantikā. (Rājñī 4.23)

Medā is sweet and cooling; it removes the pain of burning sensations caused by pitta, cures consumption (rājayakṣman), fever, and wind disorders (vātadoṣa).
