Deveṣṭā, suramedā, divyā, and likewise devamaṇi;
devagandhā, mahācchidrā, ṛkṣārhā, and rudrasaṃmitā;
the bulb known as mahāmedā, which grows on a creeper and is very pale white.

Medā may also be the white-knotted plant (śuklakanda), which exudes a secretion like the fat-element (medas). Mahāmedā is cooling and appetizing; it increases phlegm and semen, and it destroys burning sensations, hemorrhagic disorders, consumption, and vāta-fever.
R̥ddhi, Siddhi, Prāṇadā, Jīvadātrī, Siddhā, Yogyā, Cetanīyā, Rathāṅgī, Maṅgalyā,
Lokakāntā, Yaśasyā, and Jīvaśreṣṭhā— these are the twelve names in sequence.
Vṛddhi, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭidā, Vṛddhidātrī, Maṅgalyā, Śrī, Sampad, and Āśīr are beloved by the people.
Lakṣmī, Bhūti, Mut, Sukha, and Jīvabhadra—these are the names for the bulb in sequence according to worldly convention.
Ṛddhi and Vṛddhi are the two types of bulbs found in the Kośa and Yāmala varieties;
the Ṛddhi bulb is covered with white hair, grows from a creeper, and possesses pores.
Prosperity is like a knot of cotton, and its fruit is said by the great seers to be a counter-clockwise turn;
whereas growth has a clockwise turn as its fruit.
Prosperity and growth are sweet, very unctuous, bitter, and cool.
It stimulates the appetite and intellect, and is supreme in removing phlegm, worms, and skin diseases.
(4.32) One should employ one or the other of these two in practical applications according to availability; where both are available, one should employ both. (4.33)

Dhūmrapattrā is called Dhūmrāhvā; it is easily obtained and was produced by Svayambhū. It is also known as Gṛdhrapattrā and Gṛdhrāṇī; it destroys worms and removes the impurities of women. Dhūmrapattrā is bitter in taste, cures swelling, and destroys worms.
It is hot, cures cough, improves the appetite, and stimulates digestion. Prasāraṇī, suprasarā, sāraṇī, saraṇī, sarā,
cāruparṇī, rājabalā, bhadraparṇī, and pratānikā [are synonyms].
Prabalā, rājaparṇī, balyā, bhadrabalā, candravallī, and prabhadrā are known by these fifteen names.
Prasāraṇī is heavy, hot, bitter, and a destroyer of wind (vāta).
It destroys hemorrhoids and swelling, and removes the obstruction of waste. Pāṣāṇabheda, aśmaghna, śilābheda, aśmabhedaka,
śvetā, upalabhedī, nagajit, and śilagarbhajā [are synonyms].
Pāṣāṇabheda is sweet and bitter;
it destroys urinary disorders (meha), removes thirst, burning sensations, and dysuria, is cooling, and cures calculi (aśmarī).
Another variety is called Vaṭapattrī, and another is Erāvatī.
Godhāvatī, rāvatī, śyāmā, and that named khaṭvāṅgā;
vaṭapattrī, himā, and gaulyā destroy urinary disorders and strangury.
They bestow strength, heal wounds, and slightly stimulate the digestive fire.
Another is *śvetā*, *śilāvalkā*, *śilājā*,
*śailavalkalā*, *valkalā*, *śailagarbhāhvā*, *śilātvak*— it has seven names.
*Śilāvalka* is cooling, sweet, and a destroyer of urinary disorders and gravel.

It removes urinary obstruction, urinary calculi, colic, consumption, and bile disorders. *Kṣudrapāṣāṇabheda* is also known as *catuṣpatrī*, *pārvatī*, *nāgabhū*, *aśmaketu*, *giribhū*, and *kandarodbhavā*.
Śailodbhavā, Girijā, Nagajā, and Daśāhvayā;
Kṣudrapāṣāṇabhedā removes wounds, urinary distress, and stones. Gṛhakanyā, Kumārī, Kanyakā, and Dīrghapattra are synonyms.
The *sthaleruhā* is soft; the maiden has many petals and is the queen of the gods (*amarājarā*).
The *vīrā* is covered in thorns, is desired by bees (*bhṛṅgeṣṭā*), and has abundant flow.
The *brahmaghnī* is young and beautiful (*rāmā*), tawny (*kapilā*), and flows from the ocean (*ambudhisravā*).
Sukaṇṭakā and Sthūladalā are its twenty-one names.
Gṛhakanyā is cold, bitter, has the scent of rut, and removes phlegm;
it destroys bile, cough, poison, asthma, and leprosy, and is an elixir (rasāyana).
*Barhicūḍā*, *śikhinī*, *śikhālu*, *suśikhā*, *śikhā*,
*śikhābalā*, *kekiśikhā*, and names such as *mayūra* (peacock) refer to the *śikhā* plant.
*Barhicūḍā* is sweet in taste and destroys dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*).
It destroys the afflictions caused by child-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*) and others, and is recommended for rites of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*). *Kṣīriṇī*, *kāñcanakṣīrī*,
*karṣaṇī*, *kaṭuparṇikā*, *tiktadugdhā*, *haimavatī*, *himadugdhā*, and *himāvatī* [are synonyms].

Himādrijā, Pītadugdhā, Yavaciñcā, Himodbhavā, Haimī, and Himajā—these six names denote a single substance possessing four qualities. It is known as Kṣīriṇī; it is pungent and bitter, acts as a purgative, and removes swelling and fever.
It destroys worms, defects, and phlegm, and it removes fever caused by pitta. Svarṇakṣīrī, svarṇadugdhā, svarṇāhvā, rukmiṇī, suvarṇā, hemadugdhī, hemakṣīrī, and kāñcanī are its synonyms.

Svarṇakṣīrī is cooling and bitter; it removes worms, bile, and phlegm, and is supreme for curing dysuria, urinary calculi, swelling, burning sensations, and fever. (Rajani 4.56) Trāyamāṇā is so called because she provides protection; she is also known as Trāyantī and Trāyamāṇikā.
Balabhadrā, Sukāmā, Vārṣikī, Girijānujā, Maṅgalyāhvā, Devabalā, Pālanī, Bhayanāśinī,
Avanī, Rakṣaṇī, and Trāṇā— these are to be known as her sixteen names. (Rajñī 4.57–58)
Trāyantī is cool and sweet; it cures abdominal tumors, fever, phlegm, and asthma, and it destroys vertigo, thirst, consumption, exhaustion, poison, and vomiting.
Rudantī is that which exudes water; it is Saṃjīvanī and Amṛtasravā.
Romāñcikā, mahāmāṃsī, caṇapattrī, and sudhāsravā— known as rudantī—
are pungent, bitter, and hot; they destroy wasting diseases and worms,
remove blood-bile, phlegm, asthma, and urinary disorders, and act as a rejuvenative elixir.
The *caṇapattrasama*, the *pattraka*, the *kṣupa*, and likewise the *amlaka*—
these are called *rudantikā* because they exude drops of water during the cold season.
*Brāhmī*, *sarasvatī*, *saumyā*, *suraśreṣṭhā*, and *suvarcalā* [are synonyms].
Kapotavegā, Vaidhātrī, Divyatejas, Mahauṣadhī,
Svāyambhuvī, Somalatā, Surejyā, Brahmakanyā, Maṇḍūkamātā, Matsyākṣī, Maṇḍūkī, and likewise Surasā. (Rajñī 4.63–64)
Medhyā, Vīrā, Bhāratī, Varā, Parameṣṭhinī, Divyā, and Śāradī—these are its twenty-four names.
Brāhmī is cooling, astringent, and bitter; it conquers disorders of wind, blood, and bile.
It produces intellect, wisdom, and memory, and increases longevity.
Brāhmī has small leaves; another is the small-leaved Laghubrāhmī, which grows in water.
Brāhmī is bitter in taste and hot, is laxative, and conquers wind, fever, and swelling.
Vandāka, pādaparuhā, śikharī, tarurohiṇī,
vṛkṣādanī, vṛkṣaruhā, kāmavṛkṣa, and śekharī;
[also] keśarūpā, taruruhā, tarusthā, and gandhamedinī.
Kāminī, taruruṭ, śyāmā, drupadī, and ṣoḍaśā are its six names.
Vandāka is bitter and cooling; it removes phlegm, bile, and fatigue.
It grants success in subjugation and other rites, is aphrodisiac, astringent, and an elixir (rasāyana).
*Kulatthā* and *dṛkprasādā* are known as wild *kulatthikā*;
*kulālī*, *locanahitā*, *cakṣuṣyā*, and *kumbhakārikā* are synonyms for it.
*Kulatthikā* is pungent and bitter, and it destroys hemorrhoids and colic.

It pacifies constipation and flatulence, is beneficial for the eyes, and promotes the healing of wounds. Taṇḍulīya is called bhaṇḍīra, taṇḍulī, taṇḍulīyaka, granthila, bahuvīrya, meghanāda, and ghanasvana.
Suśāka, pathyaśāka, sphūrjathu,
svanitāhvaya, vīra, and taṇḍulanāman are the fourteen synonyms.
Taṇḍulīya is cooling, sweet, and a destroyer of poison.
It is palatable, digestive, wholesome, and removes bile, burning sensations, and vertigo.
*Civillikā*—also known as *raktadalā*, *kharacchadā*, *kṣudragholī*, and *madhumālapattrikā*—is pungent and astringent;
it is beneficial in fever and diarrhea and acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
Hastiśuṇḍī, mahāśuṇḍī, śuṇḍī, and ghūsarapattrikā—
hastiśuṇḍī is pungent and hot, and it removes fevers caused by the combination of all three humors (saṃnipāta).
Kuṭumbinī, payasyā, kṣīriṇī, and jalakāmukā are [synonyms].
Vakraśalyā, Durādharṣā, Krūrakarmā,
Jhiriṇṭikā, Śītā, Prahara-jāyā, Śītalā, and Jaleruhā—
she is indeed renowned by the learned under these twelve names.
Kuṭumbinī is sweet, astringent, and subdues kapha and pitta;
it destroys wounds, blood disorders, defects, and itching, and is a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
Sthalapadmī, Padmāhvā, Cāraṭī, and Padmacāriṇī [are synonyms].
Sugandhamūlā, Amburuhā, Lakṣmīśreṣṭhā, Supuṣkarā, Ramyā,
Padmavatī, Aticarā, Sthūlaruhā, Puṣkariṇī, Puṣkarādyā, and Parṇikā are known as the varieties beginning with Puṣkara. Rajñī 4.81.

The channel (nāḍī) known as Puṣkarādi is said to have fifteen names. Rajñī is a lotus-like plant growing on dry land; it is sweet, bitter, and cooling, and it cures vomiting, blood-bile disorders, urinary diseases, and destroys spirits and dysentery.
Jambū, jāmbavatī, vṛttā, vṛttapuṣpā,
jāmbavī, madaghnī, nāgadamanī, durdharṣā, and duḥsahā— these nine are known as jambū. They destroy the three doṣas and are sharp, hot, pungent, and bitter.

Nāgadantī destroys the disorder of abdominal distension and acts as a purifier of the internal organs (koṣṭha). It is also known as Śvetaghaṇṭā, Madhupuṣpā, Viśodhanī, Nāgasphotā, Viśālākṣī, Nāgacchatrā, and Vicakṣaṇā. (Rajni 4.85–86)
Sarpapuṣpī, śuklapuṣpī, svādukā, śītadantikā, sitapuṣpī,
sarpadantī, nāginī, and bāṇabhūmitā— these are synonyms for nāgadantī. It is pungent, bitter, dry, and it removes wind and phlegm.

Viṣṇukrāntā—also known as Harikrāntā and Aparājitā with blue flowers—is a promoter of intelligence, a destroyer of the defects of poison, a digestive stimulant, and a bestower of auspiciousness; it cuts through abdominal tumors, colic, diseases of the abdomen, and disorders of the throat. (Rājñī 4.88)
Nīlakrāntā, satīnā, vikrāntā, and chardikā—these are synonyms for viṣṇukrāntā. It is pungent and bitter, and it removes diseases caused by phlegm and wind.
Kuṇañjara, kuṇañjī, and kuṇañja are names for araṇyavāstuka (wild spinach).
Kuṇañja is sweet, pleasant, digestive, carminative, and wholesome.
Bhūmyāmalī, tamālī, tālī, tamālikā, uccaṭā, dṛḍhapādī, vitunnā, and vitunnikā [are likewise].
Bhūdhātrī, cāruṭā, vṛṣyā, viṣaghnī, bahupatrikā,
bahuvīryā, ahibhayadā, viśvaparṇī, himālayā, jaṭā, and vīrā— these constitute its nineteen names. (Rājñī 4.92)

Bhūdhātrī is astringent and sour; it destroys pitta-type urinary disorders (pittameha), is cooling, alleviates the pain of urinary diseases, and removes burning sensations. Gorakṣī, sarpadaṇḍī, dīrghadaṇḍī, and sudaṇḍikā [are likewise].

Citralā, gandhabahulā, gopālī, and pañcaparṇikā—these are known as gorakṣī. They are sweet and bitter, cooling, and they alleviate burning sensations and pitta; they destroy the disorders of eruptive boils, vomiting, dysentery, and fever.
Golomikā, godhūmī, gojā, kroṣṭukapucchikā,
gosambhavā, and prastariṇī— these are known as its six names.
Golomikā is pungent, bitter, pacifies the three doṣas, and is cooling.

It destroys root diseases, blood disorders, and humoral imbalances; it is astringent and stimulates the digestive fire. It is known by seven names: dugdhaphenī, payaḥphenī, phenadugdhā, payasvinī, lūtāri, vraṇaketu, and gojāparṇī.
Dugdhaphenī is pungent, bitter, cooling, and destroys poison;
it heals wounds, improves the appetite, and when used appropriately, acts as an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Kṣudrāmlikā, however, is also known as cāṅgerī, cukrāhvā, and cukrikā.
Loṇāmlā, catuṣparṇī, loṇā, loḍāmlapatrikā, ambaṣṭhā,
amlavatī, amlā, dantaśaṭhā, śastrāṅgā, and amlapatrī— these are known by fifteen names. (RājNī 4.100–101)

Kṣudrāmlī is sour in taste; it is acidic and hot, and it increases the digestive fire (*vahni*). It improves the appetite, cures disorders of the *grahaṇī*, destroys intestinal worms (*durnāman*), and removes phlegm (*kapha*). (Rajni 4.102) Raktapādī, Śamīpatrā, Spṛkkā, and Khadirapatrikā [are synonyms].
*Saṅkocanī*, *samaṅgā*, *namaskārī*, and *prasāriṇī*;
*lajjālu*, *saptaparṇī*, *khadirī*, and *gaṇḍamālikā*;
as well as *lajjā*, *lajjikā*, *sparśalajjā*, and *asarodhanī*.

*Raktamūlā*, *tāmramūlā*, *svaguptā*, and *añjalikārikā*—these twenty names have been declared for *lajjā* (the sensitive plant) by the best of physicians. It has red roots, is pungent, and is cooling; it destroys *pitta* and diarrhea.
It cures swelling, burning sensations, fatigue, dyspnea, ulcers, leprosy, phlegm, and hemorrhoids.
(Rajni 4.106) The *lajjālu* plant has small leaves, while the other variety, *vaiparītyā*, has large leaves;
one should employ the *vaiparītyā* when referring to the *lajjālu*. (Rajni 4.107)

The *rasa* known as *vaiparītyāhvā* is astringent, pungent, and hot; it subdues phlegm and wind, acts as a digestive regulator (*niyāmaka*), and produces various types of consciousness. Another variety is called *raktapādī*, while the three-footed one is known as *haṃsapādikā*.
Ghṛtamaṇḍalikā is to be known as Viśvagranthi and Tripādikā.
Vipādī, Kīṭamārī, Hemapādī, Madhusravā, Karṇāṭī, Tāmrapatrī, Vikrāntā, and likewise Suvahā [are synonyms]. (RājNī 4.109–110)
Brahmādanī, Padāṅgī, Śītāṅgī, Sutapādukā, Saṃcāriṇī, Padikā, Prahlādī,
Kīlapādikā, Godhāpadī, Haṃsāṅghri, and likewise Dhārttarāṣṭrapadī.

It should be known as Haṃsapādī, and it is also called Śarākṣidhā. Haṃsapādī is pungent and hot; it destroys poison and spirits, cures the defects of vertigo and epilepsy, and is known to be a rejuvenative elixir.
Kātharā is proclaimed by its synonyms as kātharāntā;
it is known as aśvakātharikā, and is bitter, a destroyer of wind (vāta), and an excellent digestive stimulant.
Punarnavā, viśākha, kaṭhilla, and śaśivāṭikā [are its names].
Pṛthvī, sitavarṣābhū, dīrghapatra, and kaṭhillaka are synonyms for śvetā punarnavā. It is heating, bitter, and removes phlegm and poison;
it cures cough, heart disease, colic, hemorrhage, anemia, edema, and the afflictions of wind (vāta).
Furthermore, there is *punarnavā* known as *raktā*, also called *krūrā*, *maṇḍalapatrikā*, *raktakāṇḍā*,
*varṣaketu*, *lohitā*, *raktapatrikā*, *vaiśākhī*, *raktavarṣābhū*, *śophaghnī*, and *raktapuṣpikā*. (Rājñī 4.117)
Vikasvarā, viṣaghnī, prāvṛṣeṇyā, and sāriṇī;
varṣābhava, śoṇapatra, śoṇa, and saṃmīlitadruma;
punarnavā, nava, and navya—these are the twenty-two names [of the plant].
Red *punarnavā* is bitter, laxative, and a destroyer of swelling;
it removes the defects of *darada* (mercury) and suppresses anemia and bile. Blue *punarnavā* is blue, dark, and known as *nīlapunarnavā*.

Known as *kṛṣṇā*, *nīlavarṣābhū*, and by its own name *nīlinī*, it is also called *nīlā* and *punarnavā*. It is bitter and pungent, hot in potency, and an elixir (*rasāyana*). It cures heart disease, anemia, edema, asthma, wind disorders, and phlegm.
Vasuko, then Vasu, Śaiva, Vasa, then Śivamallikā, Pāśupata, Śivamata, Sureṣṭa, and Śivaśekhara;
he is declared to be twofold— white and red— and should be known by these nine names.
Vasuka is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is cooling in its post-digestive effect (pāka) and stimulates the digestive fire.
It destroys indigestion and abdominal tumors caused by vāta, while the white variety is a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
Sarpiṇī, bhujagī, bhogī, kuṇḍalī, pannagī, and phaṇī [are synonyms for the snake].

*Ṣaḍabhidhā*, *sarpiṇī*, *viṣaghnī*, and *kucavardhanī* are six names for the same plant. *Vṛścikā*, *nakhaparṇī*, *picchilā*, and *alipatrikā* are synonyms; *vṛścikā* is also called *picchalāmlā*, and it cures disorders such as hernia (*antravṛddhi*).
Brāhmī, Vayasyā, Matsyākṣī, Mīnākṣī, and Somavallarī are synonyms.
Matsyākṣī is cooling, palatable, and it removes wounds, disorders, and consumption.
Guṇḍālā, however, is water-born, has a cluster of roots, and dwells in reservoirs.

Guṇḍālā is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys swelling and wounds. Bhūpāṭalī, kumbhī, bhūtālī, and raktapuṣpikā—of these, bhūpāṭalī is pungent and hot, and is very useful for the extraction of mercury.
Pāṭalī has six names: pāṇḍuraphalī, dhūsarā, vṛttabījakā, bhūriphalī, pāṇḍuphalī, and [pāṭalī] itself (Rājñī 4.130).
Pāṇḍuraphalī is cooling, sweet, and removes the afflictions caused by urinary disorders and imbalances of the bodily humors.
It is strengthening, pacifies pitta, is aphrodisiac, and cures urinary obstruction.
(4.131) The white variety, known as *churikāpatrī* or *parvamūlā*, is also called *avipriyā*. It is extremely sweet, cooling, increases breast milk, and is highly beneficial for the appetite. (4.132)
Brahmadaṇḍī is also known as ajalādaṇḍī and kaṇṭapatraphalā.
Brahmadaṇḍī is pungent and hot; it destroys phlegm, swelling, and wind. Dravantī, śāmbarī, citrā, nyagrodhī, and śatamūlikā [are synonyms].
Pratyakśreṇī, vṛṣā, and caṇḍā; patraśreṇī and ākhukarṇikā;
mūṣakāhvādikā, karṇī, pratiparṇī, śiphā, sahasramūlī, and vikrāntā—these should be known as the four types of ekadhā. (RājNī 4.134–135)
*Dravantī* is sweet, cooling, and supreme for binding the bodily fluids (*rasa*);
it destroys fever, kills worms, pacifies colic, and acts as a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).
*Droṇapuṣpī*, *dīrghapatrā*, *kumbhayoni*, and *kutumbikā* [are synonyms].
Citrākṣupa, Kutumbā, Supuṣpā, Citrapattrikā,
and Droṇapuṣpī are pungent and hot; they stimulate the appetite, alleviate wind and phlegm,
cure sluggish digestion, are wholesome, and remove wind disorders.

There is another, the Mahādroṇā, also called Kurumbā, Devapūrvakā, Divyapuṣpā, Mahādroṇī, Devīkāṇḍā, and Ṣaḍāhvayā. It is known as Devadroṇī; it is pungent, bitter, purifies the intellect, and cures afflictions caused by wind and spirits.
It removes the dullness of phlegm when used appropriately for the purification of mercury. Jhaṇḍū has large flowers; it is also called jhaṇḍūka and jheṇḍuka.
Jhaṇḍū is pungent and astringent, and it destroys fever, spirits, and planetary influences.
Gorakṣadugdhī, gorakṣī, tāmradugdhī, rasāyanī, bahupatrā,
mṛtājīvī, mṛtasaṃjīvanī, and muni are synonyms.
Gorakṣadugdhī is sweet, aphrodisiac, constipating, and cold.
It is indeed a subduer of all things and bestows the qualities of perfection in alchemy (*rasa*).

(Rājñī 4.143) Having thus extensively arranged this section—which provides liberation through the excellence of the various minor medicinal herbs whose names and properties are being clarified—the physician, who is the lord capable of performing eradication (*uccāṭana*) and [healing] diseases, should employ this "face-ornament" (*mukhamaṇḍana*). Because they bring great relief (*rānti*) from hunger (*kṣudh*) to people, these are therefore proclaimed as "minor" (*kṣudra*).

This group of medicinal herbs is said to belong to the verbal root *dhā* (to take) in the sense of "taking up. In this work by the skillful Nṛsiṃha, this fifth great section on *parpaṭa* and other herbs—which serves as the crest-jewel of the chapter on names—extends forth; it is that group which, through the power of constant practice in meditative concentration, truly bestows the hand of its own immortal nectar, ever-life-restoring, offered with love by the Lord worshipped with devotion.
In the *Rājanighaṇṭu*,
in the section on the *Pippalyādivarga*,
it is stated that long pepper (*pippalī*) is said to be fourfold, as is its root (*tanmūla*) and ginger (*nāgara*).
Fresh ginger, the two types of black pepper, coriander, and *yavānikā*; *cavya*, the two types of *citraka*, *viḍaṅga*, the two types of *vacā*;
*kulañja*, the five types of cumin, *methikā*, and *hiṅgupatrikā*.
The two types of asafoetida, agnijāra, rāsnā, the two types of cardamom,
śiva, sauvarcala, kāca, viḍa, and that which is named gaḍa;
likewise, sāmudra, drauṇika, auṣara, and romaka.
Nine types of salt have been described, as well as ajamodā and reṇukā;
bola, karcūraka, pāṭhā, vṛkṣāmla, and amlavetasa;
kaṭukā, ativiṣā, mustā (in two varieties), and the two types of yaṣṭīmadhu.
Bhārgī, puṣkaramūla, śṛṅgī, and the two kinds of dantī;
jaipāla, the two types of trivṛt, bark, leaf, and nāgakeśara; tālakṣīra, that which is called tālīsapatra, and vaṃśarocanā.
Mañjiṣṭhā is considered to be of four kinds, and the two types of haridrā are likewise recognized.
Lākṣā, alaktaka, lodhra, dhātakī, and abdhiphala;
then nirviṣā, the pair of poisons (viṣadvandva), and the two types of amlaharidrakā.
Abdhiphena, aphena, the two types of ṭaṅkaṇa, along with akuruṇḍaka;
himāvalī, elephant ichor, svarjika, and likewise loṇaka;
vajraka, yavaja, then sarvakṣāra, and māyikā.
The medicinal herbs are designated by the number six parts:
*pippalī*, *kṛkarā*, *śauṇḍī*, *capalā*, *māgadhī*, and *kaṇā*;
also *kaṭubījā*, *koraṅgī*, *vaidehī*, and *tiktataṇḍulā*.
Śyāmā, dantaphalā, kṛṣṇā, kolā, and that which originates from Magadha;
uṣaṇā, upakulyā, smṛtyāhvā, and tīkṣṇataṇḍulā—these are synonyms for pippalī. It destroys fever, is aphrodisiac, unctuous, hot, pungent, and bitter.
It is digestive, and it removes wind, dyspnea, cough, phlegm, and consumption. Gajoṣaṇā, cavyaphalā, cavyajā, gajapippalī, śreyasī,
chidravaidehī, dīrghagranthi, and taijasī [are synonyms].
The round, thick Videhī is also to be known; thus, these are the ten designations.
Gajoṣaṇā is pungent and hot, dry, and it dries up impurities;
it destroys phlegm and wind, and increases breast milk and complexion.
Saiṃhalī, Sarpadaṇḍā, Sarpāṅgī born in Brahmabhūmi,
Pārvatī, Śailajā, Tāmrā, Lambabījā, as well as Utkaṭā,
Adrijā, Siṃhalasthā, Lambadantā, and Jīvalā.

Jīvālī, Jīvanetrā, and Kuravī are known by sixteen names. Saiṃhalī is pungent and hot; it is a supreme destroyer of worms, a digestive stimulant, and a pacifier of phlegm, asthma, and wind-pain, as well as a cleanser of the internal organs.
This [term] "vanādi-pippalī" is designated as "sūkṣmādi-pippalī";
it is fit to be designated as "kṣudrādi-pippalī," preceded by the designation "vana" and followed by the designation "kaṇā.
Vanapippalikā is hot, sharp, appetizing, and digestive.
When fresh, it is rich in qualities, but when dried, it is considered to have very few qualities.
Granthika, pippalīmūla, cavikāśira, kolamūla, kaṭugranthi, kaṭumūla, and kaṭūṣaṇa; (these are the names for various types of long pepper roots).
*Sarvagranthi*, *patrāḍhya*, *virūpa*, *śoṇasambhava*, *sugranthi*, and *granthila*—these are the fourteen synonyms. The root of *pippalī* is pungent and hot; it destroys phlegm and worms.
It is digestive, destroys wind diseases, improves the appetite, and aggravates bile.
Ginger is known as *śuṇṭhī*, *mahauṣadha*, *viśva*, *nāgara*,
*viśvabheṣaja*, *viśvauṣadha*, *kaṭugranthi*, *kaṭubhadra*, and *kaṭūṣaṇa*.
Sauparṇa, śṛṅgavera, kaphāri, ārdrika, śoṣaṇa, and nāgarāhva—these sixteen names are known for [the plant] ginger (śuṇṭhī).
Ginger is pungent, hot, and unctuous; it removes phlegm, swelling, and wind.
It removes pain from the spear-like piercing sensation, abdominal distension, flatulence, dyspnea, and elephantiasis.
Fresh ginger, *gulmamūla*, the excellent root-born *kandalī*, *śṛṅgavera*, and that which grows in the earth—preferably on sandy soil—and that which grows in marshy lands; [these are the best].
Apākaśāka, Ārdra, Rāhucchatra, Suśāka, Śārṅga, Ārdraśāka, Sacchāka, and the one called Ṛtubhū;
ginger (ārdraka) is pungent and hot, beneficial for the heart, cooling in its post-digestive effect, and light.

It is illuminating, provides relish, and removes swelling, phlegm, and diseases of the throat. Black pepper (marica), palita, śyāma, kola, vallīja, ūṣaṇa, yavaneṣṭa, vṛttaphala, śākāṅga, and dharmapattana [are its varieties]. 5.30–5.30½ The fruit of pippalī is beneficial for the heart, the digestive fire, and the eyes; it cures consumption, cough, piles, and wind-disorders. It is astringent, pungent, and bitter, and it destroys phlegm and wind. 5.31–5.31½ The fruit of pippalīmūla is similar to that of pippalī, but it is especially beneficial for the stomach. The fruit of cavya is like that of pippalī, but it is superior in its power to stimulate digestion. 5.32–5.32½ Citraka is heating, pungent, and bitter, and it destroys wind and phlegm. It is beneficial for the eyes, the digestive fire, and the skin, and it cures piles, abdominal tumors, and worms. 5.33–5.33½ Vaca is heating, pungent, and bitter, and it destroys wind and phlegm. It is beneficial for the voice, the ears, and the memory, and it cures fainting, poison, and worms. 5.34–5.34½ Śuṇṭhī is heating, pungent, and bitter, and it destroys wind and phlegm. It is beneficial for the voice, the ears, and the memory, and it cures fainting, poison, and worms. 5.35–5.35½ Pippalīmūla is like pippalī, but it is especially beneficial for the stomach. It is beneficial for the voice, the ears, and the memory, and it cures fainting, poison, and worms. 5.62–5.62½ Śuṇṭhī is heating, pungent, and bitter,
Black pepper (marica) is pungent, bitter, hot, light, and a destroyer of phlegm;
it is drying, beneficial for all [the bodily constituents], and is declared to be the foremost among the seven types of black substances.
Rajni_5.31 It is pungent, bitter, hot, light, and a destroyer of phlegm.
It removes wind disorders, worms, and heart disease, and stimulates the appetite. White pepper (sitamarica), also known as sita, produced from the white creeper (sitavallī),
bālaka, bahula, dhavala, and candraka— these are named after sages and are superior in quality, acting as aphrodisiacs.
White pepper is pungent and hot; it destroys poison and subdues malevolent spirits.
It is non-aphrodisiac, cures diseases of the eyes, and when used with proper method, serves as an elixir (*rasāyana*).
(Rajñī 5.34) Dhānyaka, dhānyaja, dhānya, dhāneya, and likewise dhanika—these are synonyms for coriander.
Kustumburu, āvalikā, chatradhānya,
vitunnaka, sugandhi, śākayogya, sūkṣmapatra, janapriya, dhānyabīja, bījadhānya, and vedhaka— these are the sixteen names [of this plant]. (Rājñī 5.35–36)
Coriander is sweet, cooling, astringent, and a destroyer of pitta;
it removes fever, cough, thirst, vomiting, and phlegm, and is a digestive stimulant. (Rajni 5.37) Ajwain is called dīpyaka, dīpya, yavasāhva, and yavāgraja.
Dīpanī, cogragandhā, vātāri, and bhūkadambaka;
yavaja, dīpanīya, śūlahantrī, and yavānikā; ugrā and tīvragandhā—these are known by fifteen names. (Rājani 5.38–39)
Yavānī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys wind-type hemorrhoids and phlegm, alleviates colic, flatulence, worms, and vomiting, and is a supreme digestive stimulant.
Cavyaka, cavikā, cavya, vaśira, and gandhanākulī—these are synonyms for cavya.
Vallī and kolavallī; kola is kuṭalamastaka. Tīkṣṇā, kariṇikā, vallī, kṛkara, and netrabhū are synonyms. Cavya is hot, pungent, light, appetizing, and digestive.
It removes an excess of worms and cuts through the pain of cough, asthma, and colic.
Citraka is also known as Agni, Śārdūla, Citrapālī, Kaṭu, Śikhin, Kṛśānu,
Dahana, Vyāla, Jyotiṣka, and likewise Pālaka.

Anala, dāruṇa, vahni, pāvaka, śabala, pāṭhī, dvīpī, citrāṅga, and śūra—these twenty are to be known [as varieties of fire]. Citraka is equal to fire in its digestive power; it is pungent in taste and removes swelling and phlegm.

It destroys wind-disorders, abdominal dropsy, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), worms, and itching. Kāla, Vyāla, Kālamūla, Atidīpya, Mārjāra, Agni, Dāhaka, and Pāvaka—this Citrāṅga is red-spotted and large-bodied. Another variety called Rudrāhvaya is known as Citraka, which is rich in medicinal qualities.

Red *citraka* produces a robust body, is pleasing, destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), acts as a regulator for mercury, is a penetrator (*vedhaka*) for metals, and is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). *Viḍaṅga* is called *krimihā*, *caitrā*, *taṇḍula*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*. It destroys worms.
Vātārī, taṇḍulā, jantughnī, mṛgagāminī,
kairalī, gahvarā, amoghā, kapālī, citrataṇḍulā,
varā, sucitrabījā, and jantuhantrī are said to be the sixteen [species]. (Rājñī 5.48–49)

Viḍaṅga is pungent, hot, and light; it removes afflictions caused by vāta and kapha, and destroys weak digestion, loss of appetite, dizziness, and disorders of worms. Vacā, ugragandhā, golomī, jaṭilā, ugrā, and lomaśā [are synonyms].
Vaca has ten names: Rakṣoghnī, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Maṅgalyā, and others.
It is sharp, pungent, and hot; it destroys phlegm, tumors caused by undigested food (āmagraṇthi), and swellings.
It cures Vāta-fever and diarrhea, induces vomiting, and removes intoxication.
Medhyā, śvetavacā, and another known as ṣaḍgranthā or dīrghapatrikā,
which is pungent-smelling, originating from the Himalayas, auspicious, and called vijayā—
this śvetavacā is exceedingly rich in qualities, bestowing intelligence, memory, and longevity, and subduing phlegm.
Vaca is aphrodisiac, destroys disorders caused by wind, spirits, and worms, and is a digestive stimulant.
Kulañja, also known as Gandhamūla, Tīkṣṇamūla, and Kulañjana;
Kulañja is pungent, bitter, and hot, it stimulates digestion, and removes defects of the mouth.
Jīraka, jaraṇa, jīra, jīrṇa, dīpya, dīpaka, ajājika, vahni, śaṅkha, and māgadha are the nine names [of cumin].
Cumin is pungent and hot; it removes wind and is an excellent digestive stimulant.
It is supreme for destroying abdominal tumors, flatulence, and diarrhea, and for removing disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*) and worms.
*Gaurādijīraka* is another [variety]; *ajājī* is white cumin (*śvetajīraka*).
*Kaṇāhvā*, *kaṇajīrṇā*, and *kaṇā* refer to black cumin; it is also called *dīpya* and begins with the word "white" (*sita*).
Dīrghakaṇā and sitājājī are known by ten names.
Gaurājājī is cooling, appetizing, pungent, sweet, and digestive;
it destroys worms, neutralizes poison, is beneficial for the eyes, and cures flatulence.
Kṛṣṇā, jaraṇā, kālī, bahugandhā, bhedinī,
kaṭubhedinikā, rucyā, nīlā, and nīlakaṇā are recorded as synonyms for pippalī.
Kāśmīra, jīrakā, varṣā, kālī, and dantaśodhanī are synonyms for jīraka.

Kālameṣī and Sugandhā are known by the names Bāṇa and Bhūhvayā. Jaraṇā is pungent and hot; it destroys phlegm and swelling, improves the appetite, cures chronic fever, is beneficial for the eyes, and alleviates disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
Dīpyā, upakuñcikā, kālī, pṛthvī, sthūlakaṇā,
pṛthu, manojñā, jaraṇī, jīrṇā, taruṇī, sthūlajīraka, suṣavī, kāravī, pṛthvīkā, and caturdaśa— these are known as the fourteen names for black cumin.
Pṛthvīkā is pungent, bitter, and hot; it removes wind, abdominal tumors, and disorders of the humors.
When digested, it cures phlegm and flatulence, kills parasites, and is an excellent stimulant of digestion.
Bṛhatpālī, kṣudrapatra, araṇyajīra, and kaṇā are likewise [described].
Vanajīra is pungent, cooling, heals wounds, and has five names.
Jīrakas are pungent in digestion, destroy worms, kindle the digestive fire,
cure chronic fever, improve appetite, heal wounds, and eliminate flatulence.
Methikā, methinī, methī, dīpanī, bahupatrikā,
vedhanī, gandhabījā, and likewise jyotirgandhaphalā;
vallarī, candrikā, methā, miśrapuṣpā, and kairavī.

Kuñcikā, bahuparṇī, pītabījā, and munīndudhā; methikā is pungent and hot, it aggravates blood-bile (raktapitta), removes loss of appetite, stimulates the digestive fire, subdues wind (vāta), and acts as a carminative.
Pṛthvīkā, hiṅgupatrī, kavarī, dīrghikā, pṛthu, tanvī, dārupatrī, bilvī, bāṣpī, and navāhvayā are its nine names.
Hiṅgupatrī is pungent, sharp, bitter, and hot; it subdues phlegm and wind.
It destroys raw parasites, is appetizing, wholesome, and stimulates digestion and the digestive fire.
Hingu (Asafoetida) has a pungent smell; it is the enemy of malevolent spirits, known as Vāhlīka, and is a destroyer of worms.
It cures colic, abdominal tumors, and other ailments, wards off demons, possesses fierce potency, and is called Rāmaṭha.
It is known by fifteen names: *agūḍhagandha*, *jaraṇa*, *bhedana*, *sūpadhūpana*, *dīpta*, and *sahasravedhin*.
Hingu is pleasing to the heart, pungent, and hot; it destroys worms, wind, and phlegm.

It destroys constipation, flatulence, and colic; it is beneficial for the eyes and cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*). Nāḍīhiṅgu is also called palāśā, jantukā, rāmaṭhī, vaṃśapatrī, piṇḍāhvā, and suvīryā; it is indeed *hiṅgunāḍikā*.

Nāḍīhiṅgu is pungent and hot; it pacifies the afflictions of phlegm and wind, removes the defects of constipation and obstruction, and cures diseases of abdominal distension. Agnijāra, agniniryāsa, agnigarbha, and agnija are known as synonyms for this substance.
The impurity of the *vaḍavāgni* (submarine fire) is to be known as *jarāyu*, which originates from fire.
*Agnijāra* is pungent and hot in potency; it cures diseases of the mouth, wind, and phlegm.
It increases bile and destroys excessive *saṃnipāta*, colic pain, and diseases caused by cold.

Jārābha is burning to the touch; Bhava is found in the ocean and is slimy. Jarāyu is four-colored, and among these, the one with red is the best. Rāsnā, Yuktarasā, Ramyā, Śreyasī, Rasanā, and Rasā [are synonyms].

Sugandhimūlā, surasā, rasāḍhyā, and atirasā—these ten [are the varieties]. Rāsnā is said to be of three kinds: patra, tṛṇa, and likewise dala; among these, dala is known as the best, while tṛṇarāsnā is considered middling.
Rāsnā is heavy, bitter, and hot; it conquers poison, wind-disorders, blood-disorders, and cough.
It pacifies swelling, tremors, abdominal enlargements, and phlegm, and it is a digestive stimulant.
Sthūlailā, bṛhadelā, tripuṭā, tridivodbhavā, and bhadrailā [are synonyms].

Surabhitvak, mahailā, pṛthvī, kanyā, kumārikā, aindrī, kāyasthā, gopuṭā, kāntā, ghṛtācī, garbhasambhavā, indrāṇī, and divyagandhā— these should be known as the eighteen names [of the plant]. (Rājñī 5.83–84)
Elā, bahulagandha, indrī, drāviḍī, niṣkuṭī, truṭi, kapotavarṇī, gaurāṅgī, bālā, balavatī, himā, candrikā,
upakuñcī, sūkṣmā, and sāgaragāminī. (Rājñī 5.85)
Garbhāri, gandhaphalikā, and kāyasthā have eighteen names.
The two types of *elā* (cardamom) are said to be cooling and bitter, fragrant, and they remove the affliction of *pitta* and eliminate *kapha*.
They cure heart disease, ailments of the impurities (*mala*), and pain in the bladder; among these, the *sthavirā* variety is rich in qualities.

Saindhava is known as śītaśiva, nādeya, sindhuja, śiva, śuddha, śivātmaja, pathya, and maṇimantha— thus it has nine names. Saindhava salt is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and a stimulator of appetite.
It pacifies the three *doṣas*, is pure, and overcomes the defects of wounds and constipation.
Saindhava salt is known to be of two kinds, white and red respectively;
the fresh variety is auspicious and rich in qualities regarding its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect.
Sauvarcala, rucaka, tilaka, hṛdyagandhaka, akṣa, kṛṣṇalavaṇa, rucya, and likewise kaudravika—
sauvarcala is light, alkaline, pungent, hot, and it conquers abdominal tumors and parasites.
It overcomes upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), abdominal pain, colic, constipation,
and loss of appetite. Blue glass-born salt,
glass-born salt, sesame-salt, glass-born black salt, Sauvarcala salt, and Pākya salt are thus remembered.
Glass-born, heart-pleasing fragrance,
black salt, kuruvinda, glass-dirt, and artificial— these are the fourteen [types].
Glass and the other salts are appetizing, slightly alkaline, and increase bile.
It is burning, it subdues phlegm and wind, it is digestive, and it removes abdominal tumors and colic. Viḍa, Drāviḍaka, Khaṇḍa, Kṛtaka, Kṣāra, Āsura, Supākya,
Khaṇḍalavaṇa, Dhūrta, and Kṛtrimaka— these are the ten [types of] salt.
Viḍa salt is hot, salty, digestive, and a destroyer of wind;
it is appetizing, cures indigestion and colic, and destroys abdominal tumors and urinary disorders. Gāḍha-lavaṇa is bright white, born of the earth, and produced in the Gaḍa region.
[There are] that produced from salt-impregnated soil (*gaḍottha*), that of great undertaking (*mahārambha*), that from *sāmbara* [salt], and that originating from *saṃbhara*.
Salt produced from salt-impregnated soil (*gaḍottha*) is saline, slightly sour, and removes impurities;
it stimulates digestion, subdues phlegm and wind, cures hemorrhoids, and cleanses the digestive tract.

Sāmudraka, however, is known as sāmudra and samudralavaṇa; it is auspicious (śiva), called vaṃśira and sāgarottha, and is cooling (śiśira) as it is born from the salt ocean. Sāmudra is light, beneficial for the heart, and it removes gray hair, blood disorders, and pitta.
It causes a burning sensation, destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, stimulates digestion, and is highly beneficial for the appetite.
(5.101) Drauṇeya, vārdheya, droṇīja, vārija, vārdhibhava, droṇīlavaṇa, droṇa, trikaṭulavaṇa, and vasusaṃjñaka are synonyms for this salt. (5.102)
The salt produced from saline soil (*drauṇeya-lavaṇa*) is not excessively hot when cooked,
does not cause a burning sensation, is laxative, unctuous, slightly [pungent], destroys colic, and produces little bile.
The salt born of saline soil (*auṣaraka*) possesses all qualities, contains all tastes, and comprises all types of salt.

Sāmbhāra, bahulavaṇa, melakalavaṇa, and miśraka—these are the nine types [of salt]. Auṣara salt is pungent, alkaline, and bitter; it subdues vāta and kapha, causes a burning sensation, increases pitta, is constipating, and dries up the urine.
Romaka is said to be *audbhida*, as well as *vasuka*, *vasu*, *pāṃśulavaṇa*, and *ūṣaraja*;
it is also called *pāṃśava*, *auṣara*, *airiṇa*, *aurva*, *sārvasaha*, and *rudra*.
Romaka is sharp, very hot, pungent, bitter, and digestive.
It causes burning and dryness, is constipating, and is highly provocative of pitta.
Ajamodā, kharāhvā, bastamodā, markaṭī, modā, gandhadalā, hastikāravī, and gandhapatrikā [are synonyms]. (Rajni 5.107–108)
Māyūrī, Śikhimodā, Modāḍhyā, Vahnidīpikā, Brahmakośī, Viśālī, Hṛdyagandhā, Ugragandhikā,
Modinī, Phalamukhyā, and she who is known as Vasucandrā are considered [the ten]. (Rājñī 5.109)
Ajamodā is pungent, hot, dry, and removes phlegm and wind;
it stimulates the appetite and destroys colic, flatulence, loss of appetite, and abdominal diseases.
Reṇukā is also known as Kapilā, Kāntā, Nandinī, Mahilā, and Dvijā.
Rājaputrī, himā, reṇu, pāṇḍupatrī, hareṇukā, suparṇī, śiśirā, śāntā, kauntī, vṛttā, dharmiṇī, kapilomā,
haimavatī, and pāṇḍupatrī— these are the twenty.
Reṇukā is pungent and cooling;
it removes itching caused by *kharju* and destroys thirst, burning sensations, and poisons, while also bringing clarity to the mouth.
Bola removes blood [disorders], as do Muṇḍa, Surasa, Piṇḍaka, and Viṣa.
Nirloha, barbarapiṇḍa, saurabha, raktagandhaka,
rasagandha, mahāgandha, viśva, śubhagandhaka, viśvagandha, gandharasa, vraṇāri, and vasubhū— these are its names. (Rajñī 5.114–115)
Bola is pungent, bitter, hot, and astringent; it removes blood disorders, destroys diseases of *kapha* and *pitta*, and alleviates ailments such as menorrhagia.
Karcūra, Drāviḍa, Kārśa, Durlabha, and Gandhamūlaka are synonyms for it.

Vedhamukhya, Gandhasāra, Jaṭila, and Aṣṭanāmaka—these are the eight names of Karcūra. It is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys phlegm and cough, produces clarity of the mouth, and removes disorders such as goiter.
Pāṭhā, ambaṣṭhā, ambaṣṭhikā, prācīnā,
pāpacelikā, pāṭhikā, sthāpanī, śreyasī, vṛddhikarṇikā,
ekāṣṭhīlā, kucailī, dīpanī, and varatiktakā are synonyms. (Rājñī 5.119)
Tiktapuṣpā, bṛhattiktā, dīpanī, triśirā,
vṛkī, mālavī, varā, devī, and vṛttaparṇī are the twelve [names] for pāṭhā;
it is bitter, heavy, and hot, and it removes wind, bile, and fever.
It heals broken joints and removes bile, burning sensations, diarrhea, and colic. Vṛkṣāmla is sour vegetable; cukrāmla is the fruit of the tittiḍī;
śākāmla is amlapūra; pūrāmla is red pūrakā. (RājN 5.121–122)
Cūḍāmla, bījāmla, āmlaka, vṛkṣāmla, phala, rasāmla,
śreṣṭhāmla, atyamlam, amlabīja, and the fruit of cukra and others— these are eighteen in number.
Vṛkṣāmla is sour, pungent, astringent, hot, and is said to destroy phlegm and hemorrhoids.

It destroys thirst, abdominal diseases, heart ailments, and disorders such as gulma, diarrhea, and wounds. Amlavetasa is sour, penetrating, and has a sour taste; it is also called vīravetasa, vetasāmla, amlasāra, śatavedhī, and vedhaka.
Bhīma, Bhedana, Bhedin, Rājāmla, Amlabhedana, Amlāṅkuśa, Raktasāra, Phalāmla,
Amlanāyaka, Sahasravedhī, Vīrāmla, Gulmaketu, and Dharākṣidhā.

Amlavetasa is of two kinds: that which dissolves conch shells, meat, and the like, and the other. Amlavetasa is extremely sour, astringent, and hot; it conquers wind (vāta), destroys phlegm, hemorrhoids, fatigue, and abdominal tumors (gulma), and is supreme for curing loss of appetite.
Kaṭukā, jananī, tiktā, rohiṇī, tiktarohiṇī,
cakrāṅgī, matsyapittā, bakulā, and śukulādanī;
sādanī and śataparvā are synonyms for cakrāṅgī and matsyabhedinī.
Aśokarohiṇī, Kṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇamedā, Mahauṣadhī, Kaṭvī, Añjanī, Kāṇḍaruhā, Kaṭu,
Kaṭurohiṇī, Kedārakaṭukā, Ariṣṭā, and Āmaghnī— these are the twenty-five [synonyms].
Kaṭukā is extremely pungent and bitter; it conquers the disorders of śītapitta and blood, as well as phlegm, loss of appetite, asthma, and fever, and it is a purgative.
Ativiṣā has white tubers; it is also called viśvā, śṛṅgī, and bhaṅgurā.
Virūpā, Śyāmakandā, Viśvarūpā, Mahauṣadhī,
Vīrā, Prativiṣā, Cāndrī, Viṣā, and Śvetavacā are recorded;
Aruṇā and Upaviṣā are likewise to be known— these constitute the sixteen.

Ativiṣā is pungent, hot, and bitter; it removes fever caused by kapha and pitta, destroys undigested matter (āma), diarrhea, and cough, and is a destroyer of poison and vomiting. Ativiṣā is known to be of three types: white, black, and reddish-brown.
And it possesses qualities that are indistinguishable in terms of taste, potency, and post-digestive effect.
Then, one should cook ativiṣā in a swing over a decoction of cow dung;
once dried in the heat of the sun, the excellent physician should employ it.
Mustā, bhadrā, vārida, ambhoda, megha, jīmūta, abda, nīrada, abbhra, and ghana are synonyms for *mustā*.
Gāṅgeya is another name for *bhadramustā*. Varāhī, guñjā, granthi, bhadrakāsī, and kaseru are synonyms for *kaseru*. It is also known as kroḍeṣṭā, kuruvinda, sugandhi, granthilā, and himā.
The wild rājakaseru and that which grows in marshy places—these twenty-five [types] are as follows:
*bhadramustā* is an astringent, bitter, and cooling;
it is known to be digestive, a destroyer of bile-fever and phlegm, and astringent.
The other [names] are nāgara-mustā, nāgarotthā, and the name nāgarādi-ghana;
also cakrāṅkā, nādeyī, cūḍālā, piṇḍa-mustā, śiśirā, vṛṣadhvāṅkṣī, kaccharuhā, cārukesarā, and uccaṭā. (Rajni 5.141)
That plant known as *pūrṇakoṣṭha* is a *kalāpinī*, measured by the number of the oceans and the moon (one hundred and four).
It is bitter, pungent, and astringent, and it is cooling;
it subdues *kapha* and destroys *pitta*-fever, dysentery, loss of appetite, thirst, and burning sensations, while also removing fatigue.
Yaṣṭīmadhu, madhuyaṣṭī, madhuvallī, madhusravā, madhuka,
madhukā, yaṣṭī, yaṣṭyāhva, and vasusaṃmita are synonyms for licorice.
Madhura-yaṣṭimadhuka is sweet, slightly bitter, and cooling.
It is beneficial for the eyes, removes bile, promotes relish, and cures consumption, thirst, and wounds.
(Rajni 5.145) Another is called *klītanam*, *klītanakam*, *klītanīyakam*, *madhukam*, *madhuvallī*, *madhūlī*, *madhuralatā*, and *madhurasātirasā*. (Rajni 5.146)
It is a destroyer of wasting diseases, gentle, and exists in two forms—growing on land and growing in water.
This single plant is generally recognized by those of great wisdom under eleven names.
*Klītaka* is sweet, appetizing, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and a healer of wounds.
It is cooling, heavy for the eyes, and an excellent remedy for hemorrhaging and bilious disorders (asrapitta).
Padmā, yaṣṭi, bhāraṅgī, vātāri, kāsajit, surūpā, bhramareṣṭā, and śakramātā—these are the sixteen [synonyms]. Bhāraṅgī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys cough and asthma.
It destroys swelling, wounds, and worms, and wards off burning sensations and fever.
(Rajñī 5.151) The root is *puṣkaramūla*, *puṣkara*, and *padmapatraka*;
it is the lotus (*padma*), the seed born of the lotus (*puṣkaraja*), *pauṣkara*, and named after the lotus (*puṣkarāhvaya*). (Rajñī 5.152)

Kāśmīra, Brahmatīrtha, Śvāsāri, Mūlapuṣkara, and Pañcadaśāhva—these are to be known as the varieties of Puṣkara and the others, including Jaṭā and Śiphā. (Rajni 5.153) Puṣkara is pungent, bitter, and hot; it removes phlegm, wind, and fever.

It destroys dyspnea, anorexia, and cough; it cures swelling and eliminates anemia. Śṛṅgī, kulīraśṛṅgī, ghoṣā, vanamūrdhajā, candrā, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, mahāghoṣā, and śṛṅgikā are synonyms for [the plant] Śṛṅgī.
Kālikā, indukhaṇḍā, latāṅgī, viṣāṇikā,
cakrā, śikhara, and karkaṭāhvā— thus it is fivefold.
Karkaṭaśṛṅgī is bitter, heavy, hot, and dispels wind.
It destroys hiccup, diarrhea, and cough, and it cures asthma and hemorrhaging from bile (pitta). Dantī, Śīghrā, Śyenaghaṇṭā, Nikumbhī, Nāgasphotā, Dantinī, Upacitrā,
Bhadrā, Rūkṣā, Rocanī, Anukūlā, Niḥśalyā, Vakradantā, and Viśalyā are synonyms for the plant [Dantī].
Madhupuṣpī, aṇḍaphalā, bhadrā, eraṇḍapatrikā, udumbaradalā, taruṇī, cāṇurevatī,
viśodhanī, kumbhī, and agnikarāhvayā are to be known [as synonyms]. (Rajñī 5.159)
Dantī is pungent and hot; it pacifies colic, indigestion, and skin diseases.
It cleanses hemorrhoids, ulcers, urinary stones, and foreign bodies, and is a supreme digestive stimulant. Another variety of Dantī is known as Keśaruhā, Viṣabhadrā, and Jayāvahā.
Āvartakī, Varāṅgī, Jayāhvā, and Bhadradantikā—
these others are known as Dantī; they are pungent and hot, purgative, destroyers of worms,
and they cure colic, leprosy, intoxication, and skin diseases.
Recaka, Jayapāla, Sāraka, Tittirīphala, and Dantībīja—
which causes the expulsion of impurities— should be known as *bījarecanī*.
Kumbhībīja is known by the name Kumbhinībīja, and Ghaṇṭābīja is said to be Dantinībīja.

The seed known as *bījānta* is a purifier; the seeds of *cakradantī* and *nikumbhī* are called "moon of the Vedas" (*vedendu*). Jaipāla is pungent and hot, it destroys worms, acts as a purgative, stimulates digestion, subdues phlegm and wind, and cleanses abdominal diseases.

The three types of *trivṛt*—namely *mālavikā*, *masūrā*, and *śyāmārdhacandrā*—as well as *vidalā*, *suṣeṇī*, *kālindikā*, *kālameṣī*, *kālī*, *trivelā*, *avanicandrasaṃjñā*, and *saiva* [the same] are mentioned. *Trivṛt* is bitter, pungent, and hot; it conquers worms, phlegm, abdominal diseases, and pain.
It destroys skin diseases, itching, and ulcers, and is highly recommended for purgation. *Rajñī* 5.167.
Furthermore, *raktā*, *kālindī*, *tripuṭā*, *tāmrapuṣpikā*, *kulavarṇā*, *masūrī*, *amṛtā*, and *kākanāsikā* [are also used]. *Rajñī* 5.168.
Red Trivṛt is bitter in taste, pungent and hot;
it is a purgative that removes disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), impurities, and constipation, and is beneficial. Bark, bark-skin, Bhṛṅga, and Varāṅga are cleansers of the mouth.
Śakala, saiṃhala, vanya, surasa, rāmavallabha,
utkaṭa, bahugandha, vijjula, vanapriya,
lāṭaparṇa, gandhavalka, vara, śīta, and grahakṣitī. (Rājñī 5.170–171)

The bark (tvacā), however, is pungent and cooling; it destroys phlegm and cough, pacifies semen and vomiting, cleanses the throat, and is light. Tamālapattra, patraka, chadana, and dala are synonyms for the leaf.
Palāśa, aṃśuka, vāsas, tāpasa, sukumāraka, vastra, tamālaka, rāma, gopana, vasana, tamāla,
and surabhigandha— these are to be known as the seventeen names [of the tree]. (Rajñī 5.173–174)

Patraka is light, bitter, and hot; it removes phlegm, wind, and poison, cures bladder itching and disorders, and cleanses the mouth and head. Kiñjalka, kanakāhva, kesaraka, and nāgakeśara [are synonyms].
Cāmpeya, nāgakiñjalka, nāgīya, and likewise kāñcana;
suvarṇa, hemakiñjalka, rukma, hema, and piñjara; phaṇi, punnāga, yogādi, kesaraka, and the one named after the five elements (pañcabhū). Rajni 5.176–177.
Nāgakeśara is slightly heating, light, bitter, and dispels phlegm;
it cures diseases of the bladder and wind, and relieves pain in the throat and head.
Tavakṣīra, payaḥkṣīra, yavaja, and that produced from the gavaya [are also mentioned].
One [type] is produced from wheat, and another arises from ground rice;
another is derived from palm [juice], known by such names as *tālakṣīra* (palm-milk).
That which is produced from wild cow's milk is the best; in its absence, another is prescribed.
Your milk is sweet, cooling, and removes burning sensations and pitta;
it destroys consumption, cough, phlegm, and asthma, and alleviates blood disorders.
Tālīsapatra, tālīśa, patrākhya, and śukodara—these are synonyms for tālīśapatra.
Dhātrīpattra, arkavedha, karipatra,
ghanacchada, nīla, nīlāmbara, tāla, tālīpatra, talāhvaya, and tālīsapatraka— these are said to be the thirteen names [of this plant]. (Rajñī 5.182–183)

Tālīsapatra is bitter and hot, yet sweet; it subdues *kapha* and *vāta*, and acts as a destroyer of cough, hiccup, consumption, asthma, vomiting, and the [three] *doṣas*. (Rajni 5.184) Vaṃśarocanā, vāṃśī, tuṅgakṣīrī, and tugā are synonyms for the auspicious [bamboo manna].
Tvakkṣīrī, vaṃśagā, śukrā, vaṃśakṣīrī, and vaiṇavī;
tvaksārā, karmarī, śvetā, vaṃśakarpūra, and rocanā; tuṅgā, rocanikā, piṅgā, navendu, and vaṃśaśarkarā. (RājNī 5.185–186)
Vaṃśarocanā may be dry, astringent, sweet, and cooling;
it purifies the blood, removes fever and excess bile, and is auspicious.
That which is produced from *tavakṣīra*, *yavakṣīra*, and [ordinary] milk possesses superior qualities.
It is said to be equal to bamboo-milk; in its absence, it may be produced from other substances.
Milk derived from the *gavaya* (wild ox) is very unctuous, cooling, light, fragrant, liquefying, and pure; other types are considered to possess only minor qualities.
Mañjiṣṭhā, hariṇī, raktā, gaurī, yojanavallikā, samaṅgā, vikasā, padmā, rohiṇī, kālameṣikā,
bhaṇḍī, citralatā, citrā, citrāṅgī, and she is also called jananī. (Rājñī 5.190)
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, Vijayā, Mañjūṣā, Raktayaṣṭikā, Kṣetriṇī, Rāgāḍhyā, Bhaṇḍīrī, Kālabhāṇḍikā,
Aruṇā, Jvarahantrī, Chadmā, and Nāgakumārikā. (Rajñī 5.191–192)
Bhāṇḍīralatikā, Rāgāṅgī, Vastrabhūṣaṇā,
Triṃśāhvayā, and Mañjiṣṭhā are thus declared by the best of physicians. Mañjiṣṭhā is sweet in taste, astringent, hot, and heavy.
It removes wounds, urinary disorders, fever, phlegm, poison, and diseases of the eyes. The fourfold *colā*—namely *yojanī*, *kauñjī*, *siṃhilī*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*—is thus described;
among these, *mañjiṣṭhā* is said to be the most excellent of all.
Haridrā, haridrañjanī, svarṇavarṇā, suvarṇā, śivā, varṇinī, dīrgharāgā,
haridrī, pītā, varāṅgī, gaurī, janiṣṭhā, varā, varṇadātrī, and pavitrā;
Haritā is known by the name rajanī, she is the destroyer of poison and possesses excellent color.
Piṅgalā, Varṇadā, Maṅgalyā, and Maṅgalā;
Lakṣmī, Bhadrā, Śiphā, Śophā, Śobhanā, and she who is called Subhagā;
Śyāmā and Jayantikā—these two are the thirty playful names.
Turmeric (haridrā) is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys phlegm, wind, blood disorders, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
It cures urinary disorders, itching, and wounds, and it restores the complexion of the body.
Another variety is Dāruharidrā, also known as Dārvī, Pītadru, and Pītikā.
Kāleyaka, pītadāru, and sthirarāgā are synonyms for kāminī.
Kaṭaṅkaṭerī, parjanyā, pītā, and dāruniśā are recorded as names for dāruniśā.
Kālīyaka, kāmavatī, dārupītā, and pacampacā are synonyms for kālīyaka.
It should be known as *karkaṭakī*, which is said to have seventeen names.

*Dāruharidrā* is bitter, pungent, and hot; it cures wounds and urinary disorders, and destroys itching, erysipelas (*visarpa*), skin diseases, poisons, and ailments of the ears and eyes. (RājN 5.201–202)
Lākṣā, khadirakā, raktā, raṅgamātā,
palaṅkaṣā, jatu, krimijā, drumavyādhi, and alaktaka; palāśī, mudraṇī, dīpti, jantukā, and gandhamādanī.
Lākṣā is blue and liquid in taste; it is the enemy of pitta, and its name consists of the numbers for sage (seven) and earth (one).
It is bitter and astringent, and it removes the afflictions caused by phlegm and bile.
It pacifies poison and blood disorders and destroys irregular fevers.
Alaktaka is the essence of insects, a dye, and likewise a stern reproach;
Jananī is the maker of living beings, while Saṃdharṣā is the crusher of the wheel. Alaktaka is very bitter and hot, and it removes disorders caused by phlegm and wind.
It soothes throat ailments, is pleasing to the taste, and destroys the pain caused by the defects of wounds.
Lodhra, rodhra, bhillataru, cillaka,
kāṇḍakīlaka, tirīṭa, lodhraka-vṛkṣa, śambara, and hastirodhraka [are its synonyms].
Tilvaka, kāṇḍahīna, śāvara, hemapuṣpaka, bhillī, and śāvaraka— these are known as the fifteen names [of the tree].
Kramuka, paṭṭikārodhra, valkarodhra, and bṛhaddala [are synonyms].
Jīrṇabudhna, bṛhadvalka, jīrṇapatra, akṣibheṣaja, śāvara, śvetarodhra, mārjana, bahalatvak, paṭṭī, lākṣāprasāda, valkala, and bāṇabhū— these are its names. (RājN 5.210–211)

The decoction of the two types of *lodhra* is cooling, cures wind, phlegm, and hemorrhaging, is beneficial for the eyes, and destroys poison; among these, the bark of *rodhra* is particularly distinguished. *Dhātakī*, *vahnipuṣpī*, and *tāmrapuṣpī* are purgatives.
Agnijvālā, Subhikṣā, Pārvatī, Bahupuṣpikā,
Kumudā, Sīdhupuṣpī, Kuñjarā, Madyavāsinī,
and those ending with Gucchasaṅghādipuṣpā should be known as Lodhrapuṣpiṇī. (Rājñī 5.213)
The *dhātakī* flower, which possesses intense flames like the crest of fire and is equal to the lord of liquors (*madya*), is pungent and hot;
it induces intoxication, destroys poison, cures dysentery and diarrhea, and heals erysipelas and wounds. (Rajni 5.214–215)
One should first state the name "samudra" (ocean) and afterwards mention the fruit;
thus the name "samudraphala" (ocean-fruit) and so forth should be uttered by the best of physicians.
The fruit of the ocean is pungent and hot, dispels wind, and suppresses malevolent spirits.

It removes the defects of the forest fire of the three humors (*tridoṣa*), and it causes the cessation of the delusions of phlegm diseases (*kaphāmaya*). It is the poisonless, the remover of poison, the one possessing various poisons, the supreme destroyer of poison, the slayer of poison, the absence of poison, the poisonless, and the enemy of poison.
The *nirviṣā* plant is pungent and cold; it removes the disorders of phlegm (*kapha*), wind (*vāta*), and blood (*āsṛj*).

It destroys many types of poison and disease, and it heals wounds. Poison (*viṣa*) is of two kinds: that which comes from snakes (*āheya*) and that which is not (*amṛta*). It is also called *garala*, *dārada*, and *gara*.
Kālakūṭa, Kālakūṭa, Haridra,
Raktaśṛṅgaka, Nīla, Garada, Kṣveḍa, Ghora,
Hālāhala, Hara, Mara, Halāhala, Śṛṅgī, and Bhūgara— these are the twenty-one [types of poison].
Amṛta, vatsanābha, viṣa, ugra, mahauṣadha, garala,
maraṇa, nāga, stokaka, and prāṇahāraka—
these eleven names are said to be for poison (garala), such as that which is stationary (sthāvara) and so forth. (Rajni 5.222)
Vatsanābha is extremely sweet, hot, and subdues wind and phlegm;
it cures throat pain and disorders of the three humors (saṃnipāta), yet it causes heat in the bile (pitta).
Among the varieties of stationary poisons, Nāga and Ugraśṛṅga are the best.

The *nāga* is the best among those that produce bodily [poisons], while the *ugraśṛṅgaka* is the best among metals. Regarding the eighteen varieties of poison and the four groups which are distinct, we have not mentioned them here, being afraid of making the book too voluminous.
Śaṭī, śaṭhī, palāśa, ṣaḍgranthā, suvratā, vadhū, sugandhamūlā, gandhālī, śaṭikā,
palāśikā, subhadrā, tṛṇī, dūrvā, gandhā, and pṛthupalāśikā.
The *saumyā* (gentle), *himodbhavā* (born from snow), and *gandhavadhū* (fragrant woman) are synonyms for *śaṭī*, numbering eighty-one [according to the Nāgas].
*Śaṭī* is slightly bitter and sour in taste, light, hot in potency, and provides relish;
it removes fever, destroys phlegm, blood disorders, itching, wounds, and defects, and is said to eliminate diseases of the mouth. (Rajñī 5.227–228)
But another is *gandhapattrā*, which has a thick mouth and bitter tubers;
it is wild (*vanajā*), *śaṭikā*, forest-born (*vanyā*), *stavakṣīrī*, and *ekapattrikā*.
It is yellowish-scented (*gandhapītā*), ending in leaves (*palāśāntā*), rich in fragrance (*gandhāḍhyā*), and *gandhapattrikā*.
Dīrghapattrā, Gandhaniśā, Śarabhūhvā, Supākinī,
Gandhapattrā, Kaṭu, Svādu, Tīkṣṇa, and Uṣṇā conquer phlegm and wind;
they destroy cough, vomiting, and fever, yet they provoke the bile.
Samudraphena, phena, vārdhiphena, payodhija, suphena, abdhihiṇḍīra, and sāmudra are the seven names for sea-foam. Samudraphena is cooling, astringent, and cures eye diseases.
It destroys phlegm and diseases of the throat, stimulates the appetite, and removes ear diseases.
(Rājñī 5.233) Phenless *khaskhasa* juice, as well as *niphena* and *ahiphenaka*—the phenless variety destroys the *saṃnipāta* fever, is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and induces stupor. (Rājñī 5.234)
The fourfold [process] shall be without froth: digestion (*jāraṇa*), killing (*māraṇa*), retention (*dhāraṇa*), and extraction (*sāraṇa*). I shall now describe their characteristics in order:
that which is white is said to be digestion, and that which is black in color is killing.
Retention (*dhāraṇa*) is yellow in color, while *sāraṇa* is variegated (*karbura*). *Jāraṇa* causes food to be digested, and *māraṇa* bestows death.
Furthermore, retention stabilizes youth, and *sāraṇa* extracts impurities.
Ṭaṅgaṇa is ṭaṅkaṇakṣāra, raṅga, kṣāra, rasādhika, lohadrāvī,
rasaghna, subhaga, and raṅgada;
it is also called vartula, kanakakṣāra, malina, and dhātuvallabha.

This is called by the name Trayodaśa by the best of physicians. Ṭaṅkaṇakṣāra (borax) is described as pungent and hot; it destroys phlegm, neutralizes the poisons of stationary organisms and the like, and removes cough and asthma.
The second is ṭaṅgaṇa, also known as śveta, śvetaka, and śvetaṭaṅgaṇa;
it purifies metals, originates from the banks of the Mālatī river in Sindhu, and is called śiva and drāvaka; this white alkali is said to have ten names. (Rajni 5.241)
Sulphate of soda (ṭaṅkaṇa) is very white, unctuous, cooling, and it subdues phlegm and wind;
it removes undigested matter (āma) and consumption, and it destroys asthma, poison, cough, and impurities.
It is also known as *sākuruṇḍa*, *granthiphala*, *vikaṭa*, and *vastrabhūṣaṇa*.
Kuruṇḍa has variegated fruit and is of seven types, including sakuruṇḍa.
It is astringent, highly appetizing, and digestive;
it removes phlegm and wind, serves as a dye for cloth, and is light.
Himāvalī is the nourisher of the heart; Gārakuṣṭhaka destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha).
Aṅgāragranthika, Granthi, Granthila, and Munisaṃjñaka are synonyms [for it].
Himāvalī is laxative and bitter, and it removes splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen.
It removes worms, skin diseases, severe anal itching, and the irritation of scratching.
Elephant-ichor—known as *gajamada*, *gajadāna*, *mada*, *kumbhimada*, *dantimada*, and *dvīpimada*—is of eight kinds, including *dāna*. (RājNī 5.247)
Elephant ichor (*hastimada*) is unctuous, bitter, beneficial for the hair, and a destroyer of epilepsy;
it removes poison and cures leprosy, itching, ulcers, ringworm, and erysipelas.
Svarjikṣāra, svarjika, kṣārasvarjī, and sukhārjika are synonyms for the alkali of *svarjika*.
Suvarcikā, suvarcī, sukhavarcā, and muni—these are its names.

Svarjika is pungent, hot, and sharp; it removes afflictions caused by vāta and kapha, destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), flatulence, and worms, and cures disorders of the wounds and the digestive tract.

Lavaṇāra, lavaṇottha, and that which is born from the asura Lavaṇa are varieties of salt; there is also the water-born lavaṇakṣāra, as well as lavaṇa and kṣāralavaṇa. Loṇārakṣāra is extremely hot and sharp, and it increases pitta.

Alkali (kṣāra) and salt slightly alleviate disorders such as wind-born abdominal tumors (vātagulma). O elephants, vajraka, vajrakakṣāra, vidāraka—the best of alkalis—and candanasāra—the essence—are produced from smoke; they are known as *dhūmottha* and *dhūmaja*.

Vajraka is an intensely hot, sharp alkali that acts as a purgative; it pacifies abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, constipation, and colic, and is laxative. Yavakṣāra is known as pākya, yavaja, and yavasūcaka. It is derived from barley. Rajni 5.254.
Yavaśūka, yavāhva, yavāpatya, and yavāgraja are synonyms for barley-alkali (yavakṣāra).
It is pungent and hot, and it relieves the pain of phlegm, wind, and abdominal enlargement;
it removes the defects of undigested matter (āma), colic, stones, urinary distress, and poison, and it is laxative.
Sarvakṣāra, Bahukṣāra,
Samūhakṣāraka, Stomakṣāra, Mahākṣāra, Malāri,
Kṣāramelaka, Sarvakṣāra, and Atikṣāra are indeed beneficial for the eyes and purify the bladder.
It destroys worms in the rectum and cleanses the impurities of the clothing. (RājNī 5.258) Māyāphala, māyiphala, māyikā, chidrāphala, and māyi are its five names.
Māyāphala removes wind, is pungent and hot, and bestows laxity, contraction, and blackness of the hair. (RājNī 5.259)

Thus, having understood this chapter— which begins with the explanation of the names and qualities of the collection of various medicinal substances and which destroys the onset of diseases through its potency— the physician shall attain a state of being honored by the whole world. (Rajni 5.260) Indeed,

those [medicines] which have come from the far reaches of the wilderness for the sake of making one's birth fruitful, and which occupy the center of the marketplace for the purpose of examining the vessels of their own potency;

This group, consisting of the *pippalika* and others, which possesses a praiseworthy nature, belongs here to that Lord of Men; it has been described by the wise, who are skilled in denoting the qualities of substances, as the "Section on Commercial Medicines" (*paṇyauṣadhivarga*), being the foundational ground for those medicinal drugs, categorized under the heading of the "Commercial Section" (*paṇyavarga*). This group, through its gentle disposition, quickly dispels the miserable states of those who have reached [heaven], manifesting the majesty of the divine scriptures—which is difficult for people to grasp—by means of a virtuous intention.
Indeed, when it was made the crest-jewel of the collection of names, the sixth [chapter] attained its established place. (Rājanighaṇṭu,
Śatāhvādivarga 5.262)
Śatāhvā, miśreyā, śāliparṇī, samaṣṭhilā,
bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārī, and pṛśniparṇikā— each of these exists in two varieties. Gokṣuraka also exists in two varieties, as do yāsa, vāsā, and śatāvarī.
Dhanvayāsā (two types), agnidamanī, vākucī, śaṇapuṣpī (two types), śarapuṅkhikā (three types),
śaṇa, ambaṣṭhā (two types), nīlī (two types), and gojihvikā are recorded [as medicinal plants].
Two types of *apāmārga*, five kinds of *balā*, *rāṣṭrī*, *mahādi*,
*hayagandhā*, *hapuṣā*, and two varieties of *śatāvarī* are recognized;
as well as *elavāluka*, *tairaṇya*, *kalikārī*, and *jayantikā*.

*Kākamācī*, *śrutaśreṇī*, and *bhṛṅgarāja* are considered to be of three kinds each. *Kākajaṅghā* is of three kinds, as is *cuñcu*; *sinduvāraka* is likewise of three types. *Bheṇḍā* is also called *putradā*, and *takrā* is known by the name *svarṇulikā*.
*Khaskhasa* and *śimṛḍī* should be known as wild safflower (*vanyakusumbhaka*).
*Dvayāhulya*, *kāsamarda*, and *ravipattrī* are the two types of *amlikā*. *Ajagandhā*, *ādityabhaktā*, and *viṣamuṣṭi* are the other two [types].
Kālāñjanī, the two types of Kārpāsī, the two kinds of Kokilākṣaka,
Sātalā, Kāmavṛddhi, Cakramarda, and Jhiñjhirā—
these shrubs, beginning with Śatāhvā, have been described in order according to their qualities.
Śatāhvā, śatapuṣpā, misī, ghoṣā,
potikā, ahicchatrā, avākpuṣpī, mādhavī,
kāravī, śiphā, saṅghātapattrikā, chattrā, vajrapuṣpā, and supuṣpikā.
Śataprasūnā, Bahalā, Puṣpāhvā, and Śatapatrī; Vanapuṣpā,
Bhūripuṣpā, Sugandhā, Sūkṣmapattrikā, Gandhārikā,
and Aticchatrā— these are its twenty-four names.
Śatāhvā is pungent, bitter, unctuous, and cures phlegmatic diarrhea;
it destroys fever and eye ulcers, and is recommended for enema therapy. Miśreyā, tālaparṇī, tālapatrā, and likewise miśi—these are synonyms.
Śāleyā is known as śītaśivā, śālīnā, and vanajā.
Avākpuṣpī, madhurikā, chattrā, saṃhitapuṣpikā, supuṣpā, and surasā are to be known as the wild variety (vanyā); thus it has fifteen names.
Miśreyā is sweet, unctuous, pungent, and excels as a destroyer of phlegm;
it subdues disorders arising from wind and bile and destroys splenic enlargement and parasites.
Śāliparṇī is also known as Sudalā, Supattrikā, Sthirā, Saumyā, Kumudā, Guhā, and Dhruvā.
Vidārigandhā, aṃśumatī, suparṇikā, dīrghamūlā, and dīrghapattrikā; vātaghnī, pītinī, tanvī, sudhā, and sarvānukāriṇī;
śophaghnī, subhagā, devī, niścalā, and vrīhiparṇikā. (Rājñī 6.17–18)
Sumūlā, surūpā, supattrā, śubhapattrikā, śāliparṇī, and śālidalā—this plant has twenty-nine names.
Śāliparṇī is bitter in taste, heavy, and hot; it alleviates disorders of the wind (vāta).
It destroys irregular fevers, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, swellings, and burning sensations. *Samaṣṭhilā*, *bhaṇḍīra*, *nadyāmra*, *āmragandhadhṛk*,
*kākāmra*, *kaṇṭakiphala*, *upadaṃśa*, and *munihvaya* are its names.

The *nadyāmra* is pungent and hot; it is appetizing, cleanses the mouth, pacifies *kapha* and *vāta*, produces a burning sensation, and is an excellent digestive stimulant. *Bṛhatī*, *mahatikrāntā*, *vārttākī*, *siṃhikā*, and *kulī* [are similar].
Rāṣṭrikā, sthalakaṇṭā, bhaṇṭākī, mahoṭikā, bahupattrī,
kaṇṭatanu, kaṇṭālu, kaṭphalā, ḍoralī, and vanavṛntākī— these are its fourteen names. (Rājñī 6.23–24)
Bṛhatī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it conquers wind (vāta), removes fever, destroys anorexia, cough, and asthma, and cures heart disease.
Another variety of Bṛhatī is known as sarpatanu, kṣavikā, and pītataṇḍulā.

Known by six names—putrapradā, bahuphalā, and godhinī—it is pungent, large, bitter, and hot, possessing qualities similar to those [of the preceding]. When combined with specific substances through proper application, it bestows the power to arrest the flow [of blood]. (Rajñī 6.26–27)
Śvetānyā, śvetabṛhatī, śvetamahotikā, śvetasiṃhī, śvetaphalā, and śvetavārtākinī—these six are to be known as śvetabṛhatī; it destroys wind and phlegm. (Rajni 6.28)

When used as an ointment with *añjana*, it removes various eye diseases. *Kaṇṭakārī*—also known as *kaṇṭakinī*, *duḥsparśā*, *duṣpradharṣiṇī*, *kṣudrā*, *vyāghrī*, *nidigdhā*, *dhāvinī*, and *kṣudrakaṇṭikā*. (Rajni 6.29–30)
It is known as *bahukaṇṭā*, *kṣudrakaṇṭā*, and *kṣudraphalā*;
it is also called *kaṇṭārikā* and *citraphalā*. Thus, it has fourteen names.
*Kaṇṭakārī* is pungent, hot, digestive, and a conqueror of asthma and cough.
It destroys the afflictions caused by catarrh and the humors, and relieves the suffering of phlegm, wind, and fever.
Sita-kaṇṭārikā, śvetā, kṣetradūtī, lakṣmaṇā, sitasiṃhī, sitakṣudrā, kṣudravārtākinī, and sitā are synonyms for it. (Rajni 6.32–33)
Klinnā, kaṭuvārtākī, kṣetrajā, kapaṭeśvarī,
niḥsnehaphalā, rāmā, sitakaṇṭā, and mahauṣadhī; gardabhī, candrikā, cāndrī, candrapuṣpā, and priyaṃkarī.

Nākulī and rāsnā are difficult to obtain; these two together have twelve names. Śvetakaṇṭārikā is known to be appetizing, pungent, and hot; it subdues phlegm and wind, is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, and is said to regulate the taste.
Pṛśniparṇī may be called Kalasī, Mahāguhā, Śṛgālavinnā, Dhamanī, and Mekhalā;
likewise, Lāṅgalikā, Kroṣṭukapucchikā, Guhā, Śṛgālikā, and Siṃhapucchikā are synonyms for the same plant.
Pṛthakparṇī, Dīrghaparṇī, and Dīrghā are names for Kroṣṭukamekhalā.
Citraparṇī and Upacitrā are known by eighteen names, including Śvapucchā (Rājñī 6.38).
Pṛśniparṇī is pungent, hot, and sour; it conquers bitter diarrhea and cough, and destroys wind-diseases, fever, insanity, ulcers, and burning sensations (Rājñī 6.39).

Gokṣura may be called gokṣuraka, kṣurāṅga, śvadaṃṣṭraka, kaṇṭaka, bhadrakaṇṭaka, vyāladaṃṣṭra, kṣuraka, mahāṅga, duścakrama, and krama; thus it has ten names in succession. Another, smaller variety of gokṣuraka is known as trikaṇṭaka, kaṇṭī, ṣaḍaṅga, bahukaṇṭaka, and kṣura.
Gokaṇṭaka, kaṇṭaphala, palaṃkaṣa, kṣudrakṣura, bhakṣaṭaka, caṇadruma, sthalaśṛṅgāṭaka,
vanaśṛṅgāṭaka, ikṣugandha, and svādukaṇṭa are recorded as the sixteen synonyms. (RājNī 6.41–42)

Both types of *gokṣuraka* are very cooling, strength-giving, sweet, nourishing, and destroyers of dysuria, urinary calculi, urinary disorders, and burning sensations; they are rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), among which the larger variety possesses superior qualities. *Yāsa*, *yavāsa*, *bahukaṇṭaka*, *alpaka*, *kṣudreṅgudī*, *rodanikā*, and *kacchurā* [are also included].
It may be the *bālapattra*, the *adhikakaṇṭaka*, the *khara*, the *sudūramūlī*, or even the *viṣakaṇṭaka*.
There is also the *ananta*, the *tīkṣṇakaṇṭa*, the *samudrānta*, the *marūdbhava*,
the *dīrghamūla*, the *sūkṣmapattra*, and the *viṣaghna* known as *kaṇṭakāluka*.

Triparṇikā and Gāndhārī are known by twenty-one names. Yāsa is sweet and bitter; it is cooling and conquers the afflictions of pitta, burning sensations, thirst, phlegm, vomiting, and erysipelas (visarpa), while promoting strength and stimulating the digestive fire.
Vāsaka, siṃhikā, vāsā, bhiṣaṅmātā, vasādanī, āṭarūṣa,
siṃhamukhī, siṃhī, kaṇṭhīravī, and vṛṣa;
likewise śitaparṇī, vājidantā, nāsā, and pañcamukhī.

Siṃhaparṇī has sixteen names, including Mṛgendrāṇī. Vāsā is bitter, pungent, and cooling; it cures cough, overcomes blood-bile (raktapitta), and removes jaundice, disorders of phlegm, fever, asthma, and consumption.
Śitāvarī, śitāvara, sūcyāhva, sūcipattraka,
śrīvāraka, śikhī, babhru, svastika, suniṣaṇṇaka,
kuruṭa, kukkuṭa, sūcīdala, and he is also called śvetāmbara.
It should be known as having fifteen names, including *medhākṛt* (intellect-promoting) and *grāhaka* (astringent).
*Śitāvara*, however, is astringent, decoctive, hot, and a conqueror of the three *doṣas*;
it bestows intellect and appetite, removes burning fever, and is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
Dhanvayāsa, durālambhā, tāmramūlī, and kacchurā;
durālabhā, duḥsparśā, dhanvī, and dhanvayavāsaka;
prabodhanī, sūkṣmadalā, virūpā, and durabhigrahā.
It is difficult to obtain, invincible, and known by fourteen names.
It is hard to grasp, pungent, bitter, hot, alkaline, and sour;
it is also sweet, subdues wind and bile, and conquers fever, abdominal tumors, and urinary disorders.
Another is the *kṣudradurālambhā*, which grows in deserts and originates in arid lands;
it is called *viśāradā* when eaten by goats, and *ajādany* when eaten by camels.
It is astringent (*kaṣāyā*), removes phlegm (*kaphahṛt*), is constipating (*grāhiṇī*), and is dear to young camels (*karabhapriyā*).

And Karabhādanikā—these are to be known as the twelve names [of the plant]. Durālambhā is the second; it removes jaundice, acidity, fever, and leprosy, destroys asthma, cough, and vertigo, and effects purification in mercury.
Now, *agnidamanī*, *vahnidamanī*, *bahukaṇṭakā*,
*vallikaṇṭārikā*, *gucchaphalā*, and *kṣudraphalā*—
these are to be known as *kṣudraduḥsparśā* and likewise *kṣudrakaṇṭārikā*. (Rājñī 6.59)
The mother of the lord of mortals (Indrāṇī) is *damanī*; this plant is known by ten names.

It is pungent and hot, subdues fire, is dry, and removes wind and phlegm. It creates relish, stimulates digestion, is beneficial for the heart, and destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and splenic disorders (*plīha*).
Vākucī, somarājī, somavallī, suvallikā,
sitā, sitāvarī, candralekhā, cāndrī, suprabhā, kuṣṭhahantrī, kāmbojī, pratigandhā, and valgujā.
The plant known as *candrābhidhā* is also called *rajī*, *kālmāṣī*, and *aindavī*.
It removes the defects of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), bestows beauty, and is likewise *valgujā*.
Thus, *candrābhidhā* possesses radiance and has twenty names.

Vākucī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys worms, skin diseases, and phlegm, and it pacifies skin disorders, poisons, itching, and scabies. Śaṇapuṣpī, bṛhatpuṣpī, śaṇikā, and śaṇaghaṇṭikā [are synonyms].
Pītapuṣpī, Sthūlaphalā, Lomaśā, and Mālyapuṣpikā;
Śaṇapuṣpī is bitter in taste and astringent, it conquers phlegm and wind,
destroys indigestion, fever, and deranged humors, acts as an emetic, and removes blood disorders.
The second variety is *sūkṣmapuṣpā*, also known as *kṣudraśaṇapuṣpikā*, *viṣṭikā*, *sūkṣmaparṇī*, *bāṇāhvā*, and *sūkṣmaghaṇṭikā*.
It is called *śaṇapuṣpī* and *kṣudratiktā*; it is emetic and regulates the bodily fluids (*rasa*).
Another third variety is *vṛttaparṇī*, which has white flowers and is called *mahāsitā*;
it is also known as *mahāśvetaghaṇṭī* and *mahāśaṇapuṣpikā*.
*Mahāśvetā* is astringent and hot, and is recommended for regulating the bodily fluids (*rasa*).
And she is proclaimed among curiosities, such as those for delusion, immobilization, and so forth. Śarapuṅkhā, kāṇḍapuṅkhā, bāṇapuṅkha, iṣupuṅkhikā,
sāyakapuṅkhā, and iṣupuṅkhā— she is to be known as sixfold.
Śarābhidhā, puṅkhā, śvetāḍhyā, sitasāyakā, sitapuṅkhā, śvetapuṅkhā, and śubhrapuṅkhā—thus it is fivefold.
Śarapuṅkhā is pungent and hot; it destroys worms and diseases caused by vāta.
This white variety, however, is rich in qualities and is highly praised for its use as an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Another plant is *kaṇṭapuṅkhā*, also known as *kaṇṭālu* and *kaṇṭapuṅkhikā*;
this *kaṇṭapuṅkhā* is pungent, hot, and destroys worms and colic.
The *śaṇa* tree is known as *mālyapuṣpa*, *vamana*, *kaṭutiktaka*, *niśāvana*, *dīrghaśākha*, *tvaksāra*, and *dīrghapallava*.
The *śaṇa* is sour and astringent; it expels impurities from the womb and causes the discharge of blood.
It induces vomiting, subdues wind and phlegm, and should be known as a conqueror of intense body aches.
Ambaṣṭhā, ambālikā, ambālā, śaṭhā, ambā, ambaṣṭhikā,
ambikā, ambā, mācikā, dṛḍhavalkā, and mayūrikā [are synonyms].
Gandhapattrī, Citrapuṣpī, Śreyasī, Mukhavācikā, Chinnapattrā, and Bhūrimallī—this plant known by sixteen names should be understood as such.
This Ambaṣṭhā is astringent and sour; it cures disorders of phlegm and diseases of the throat.
It destroys diseases of wind and *balāsa*, promotes relish, and is a supreme digestive stimulant.
*Nīlī*, *nīlā*, *nīlinī*, *nīlapattrī*, *tutthā*, *rājñī*,
*nīlikā*, *nīlapuṣpī*, *kālī*, *śyāmā*, *śodhanī*, *śrīphalā*, *grāmyā*, *bhadrā*, *bhāravāhī*, and *mocā* [are synonyms].
Kṛṣṇā, Vyañjanakeśī, Rañjanī, Mahāphalā, Asitā, Klītanī, Nīlakeśī, and Cāraṭikā are considered [synonyms]. Gandhapuṣpā, Śyāmalikā, Raṅgapattrī, and Mahābalā [are also synonyms]. Rajni 6.80.
Sthiraraṅgā and raṅgapuṣpī are names for this plant, which has thirty synonyms. Nīlī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is beneficial for the hair and cures cough, phlegm, and vomiting.
It removes wind-disorders, abdominal diseases, gulma, parasites, and fever.
Furthermore, there is the mahānīlī, the pure rājanīlikā, the tutthā, the śrīphalikā,
the melā, the keśārhā, and the bhṛśapattrikā. The mahānīlī is rich in qualities, the best for dyeing, and a giver of great potency.
The previously mentioned *nīlikā*-like plant is endowed with qualities for all ritual acts.
*Gojihvā*, *kharapattrī*, *pratanā*, *dārvikā*, *adhomukhā*, *dhenujihvā*, and *adhaḥpuṣpī*—thus it is sevenfold. (Rajñī 6.84–85)
Gojihvā is pungent, sharp, cooling, and a destroyer of bile;
it heals wounds and overcomes all toothaches and the afflictions of poison.
Apāmārga, however, is also known as śikharī, kiṇihī, and kharamañjarī.
Durgraha, adhaḥśalya, pratyakpuṣpī, and mayūraka;
kāṇḍakaṇṭa, śaikharika, markaṭī, and durabhigraha;
vaśira, parākpuṣpī, kaṇṭī, and markaṭapippalī.
Kaṭu, māñjarika, nandī, kṣavaka, paṅktikaṇṭaka,
mālākaṇṭa, and kubja— these are its twenty-three names.
Apāmārga, moreover, is bitter and hot, pungent, and a destroyer of phlegm.

It destroys hemorrhoids, itching, abdominal diseases, and ulcers; it is astringent, heart-tonic, and causes vomiting. (Rajñī 6.90) There is another red variety of Apāmārga, known as Kṣudrāpāmārgaka, Āghaṭṭaka, Dugdhaniṅkā, Raktabindu, and Alpapattrikā. (Rajñī 6.91)
The red apāmārga is cooling, pungent, and subdues phlegm and wind;
it destroys wounds, itching, and poisons, is astringent, and is an excellent emetic.
Balā, samaṅgā, udakikā, bhadrā, bhadrodanī, and kharakāṣṭhikā are [synonyms].
Kalyāṇinī, Bhadrabalā, Moṭā, Vāṭī, and Balāḍhyā are the names for Rudra-balā.
It is extremely bitter, sweet, and destroys bile and dysentery;
it bestows strength and virility, promotes nourishment, and purifies diseases of the phlegm.
Mahāsamaṅgodanikā, balāhvayā, vṛkṣāruhā, vṛddhibalā, akṣataṇḍulā,
bhujaṃgajihvā, śītapākinī, śītā, balā, śītavarā, balottarā,
khirihiṭṭī, balyā, and lalajjihvā— these are the fifteen kinds [of balā].

Mahāsamaṅgā is sweet and sour; it destroys the three doṣas and, when administered by the wise according to the proper method, it is a destroyer of fever and burning sensations. Mahābalā, Jyeṣṭhabalā, Kaṭaṃbharā, Keśāruhā, Kesarikā, and Mṛgādanī—[these are synonyms for Mahābalā].
It may also be known by seventeen names: *varṣapuṣpā*, *keśavardhanī*, *purāsaṇī*, *devasahā*, *sāriṇī*, *sahadevī*, *pītapuṣpī*, *devārhā*, *gandhavallarī*, *mṛgā*, and *mṛgarasā*. (Rājñī 6.97–98)

Mahābalā destroys heart disease, wind disorders, hemorrhoids, and swellings; it increases semen, is strengthening, and removes irregular fevers. Balikā, Atibalā, Balyā, Vikaṅkatā, Vāṭyapuṣpikā, and Ghaṇṭā [are likewise].

Śītā, śītapuṣpā, bhūribalā, vṛṣyagandhikā—these are the ten types [of atibalā]. Atibalā is bitter and pungent; it subdues wind, destroys worms, and is supreme for alleviating burning sensations, thirst, poison, vomiting, and moisture.
Bhadrodanī, nāgabalā, kharagandhā, catuṣphalā,
mahodayā, mahāśākhā, mahāpattrā, mahāphalā, viśvadevā, as well as ariṣṭā, kharvā, hrasvā, and gavedhukā.
Devadaṇḍā, mahādaṇḍā, and ghāṭā—these are the sixteen names [of the plant].
It is known to be sweet and sour, possessed of strength, astringent, hot, and heavy;
it destroys itching, skin diseases, and wind disorders, and conquers wounds and ailments of bile.
Mahārāṣṭrī is said to be the same as śāradī and toyapippalī;
it is also known as macchādanī, macchagandhā, lāṅgalī, śakulādanī, agnijvālā, citrapattrī, prāṇadā, and jalapippalī. (Rajni 6.105)

Tṛṇaśītā has many spikes; thus, this [group] consists of thirteen [plants]. Mahārāṣṭrī is pungent, sharp, and astringent; it cleanses the mouth and destroys defects such as wounds and worms, and it eliminates disorders of the bodily fluids.
Aśvagandhā, vājigandhā, kambukāṣṭhā, varāhikā,
varāhakarṇī, turagī, vanajā,
vājinī, hayī, puṣṭidā, baladā, puṇyā, hayagandhā, and pīvarā. (Rajñī 6.108)
Palāśaparṇī, vātaghnī, śyāmalā,
kāmarūpiṇī, kālapriyakarī, balyā, gandhapattrī, hayapriyā, and varāhapattrī— these are known as the twenty-three names [of this plant]. (Rajni 6.109–110)
Aśvagandhā is pungent and hot, and it is bitter and has the scent of intoxication;
it is strengthening, removes wind, and destroys cough, dyspnea, consumption, and ulcers.
Hapuṣā is also known as vipuṣā, visrā, visragandhā, and vigandhikā.

This other variety yields little fruit; it is known as *kacchūghnī*, *dhvāṅkṣanāśanī*, *plīhaśatru*, *viṣaghnī*, *kaphaghnī*, and *aparājitā*. The former has five names, while the latter has seven designations.

Hapuṣā is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is heavy and conquers phlegm and balāsa. It removes menorrhagia, abdominal enlargement, constipation, colic, gulma, and hemorrhoids. (Rajni 6.114) Śatāvarī is also known as śatapadī, pīvarī, indīvarī, and varī.
Bhīru, dvīpyā, dvīpiśatru, dvīpikā,
amarakaṇṭikā, sūkṣmapattrā, supattrā, bahumūlā, śatāhvayā, nārāyaṇī, svādurasā, śatāhvā, and laghuparṇikā.
Ātmaśalyā, Jaṭāmūlā, Śatavīryā, Mahaudanī, Madhurā, Śatamūlā, Keśikā,
Śatanetrikā, Viśvākhyā, Vaiṣṇavī, Kārṣṇī, Vāsudevī, and Varīyasī. (Rajñī 6.117)
Durmarā, Tejavallī, and Syāt are its thirty-three names.
Mahāśatāvarī, Vīrā, Tuṅginī, Bahupattrikā,
Sahasravīryā, Surasā, and Mahāpuruṣadantikā [are synonyms].
Ūrdhvakaṇṭā, Mahāvīryā, Phaṇijihvā,
