Mahāśatā, Śatavīryā, and Suvīryā— these are its thirteen names.
The two types of Śatāvarī are cooling, aphrodisiac, sweet, and supreme subduers of pitta.
The two types of *śatāvarī* remove *kapha* and *vāta*, are bitter, highly excellent, and act as rejuvenatives (*rasāyana*). They are aphrodisiacs, sweet, alleviate *pitta*, and are heating.
The larger variety destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, is bitter, and is preeminent as a rejuvenative.
Its sprouts are known to be bitter and they remove phlegm and bile.
Elavāluka, ālūka, vāluka, harivāluka,
elvāluka, kapittha, durvarṇa, prasara, and dṛḍha— [these are its varieties].

Elāgandhika, elāhva, guptagandhi, sugandhika, and elāphala are to be known as synonyms for cardamom; it is said to have fourteen names. Elavāluka is extremely pungent, astringent, and subdues phlegm and wind.
It destroys fainting, pain, fever, and burning sensations, and is an excellent appetizer.
Tairiṇī, teraṇa, tera, and kunīlī are its four names.
Teraṇa is cooling, bitter, a destroyer of wounds, and it imparts a reddish hue.
*Kalikārī*, *lāṅgalinī*, *halinī*, *garbhapātinī*, *dīpti*, *viśalyā*, *agnimukhī*, *halī*, *naktendupuṣpikā*, *vidyujjvālā*,
*agnijihvā*, *vraṇahṛt*, and *puṣpasaurabhā*.
Svarṇapuṣpā is Vahniśikhā; it has sixteen names. It is pungent and hot, a destroyer of phlegm and wind, a means for extracting foreign objects from within the womb, and an excellent purgative.
Jayantī, balāmoṭā, haritā, jayā,
vijayā, sūkṣmamūlā, vikrāntā, and aparājitā are known as jayantī. It cures goiter, is bitter, pungent, and hot, and it destroys Vāta.
Black [Kṛṣṇā] removes the elements from the body, cleanses the throat, and serves as an elixir (*rasāyana*) there.
Kākamācī, Dhvāṅkṣamācī, Vāyasāhvā, and Vāyasī are all synonyms;
it is Sarvatiktā, Bahuphalā, and Kaṭphalā, and it is an elixir.
Gucchaphalā, kākamātā, svādupākā, sundarī, varā, candrāviṇī, matsyākṣī, kuṣṭhanāśanī, tiktikā, and bahutiktā— these are remembered as its eighteen names. (Rajñī 6.133)

Kākamācī is pungent, bitter, hot in potency, and destroys phlegm; it cures colic, hemorrhoids, swelling, and disorders, and removes skin diseases and itching. Śrutaśreṇī, Dravantī, Nyagrodhī, and Mūṣikāhvayā [are also known by these names].
Citrā, mūṣakamārī, pratyakśreṇī, and śambarī; śrutaśreṇī, cakṣuṣyā, kaṭu, and ākhuviṣāpahā;
as well as vraṇadoṣaharā and netrāmayanikṛntanī. (Rājñī 6.135–136)
Mārkava, bhṛṅgarāja, bhṛṅgāhva, keśarañjana,
pitṛpriya, raṅgaka, keśya, and kuntalavardhana [are synonyms for the black bee-tree]. Another variety is yellow (pīta), known as svarṇabhṛṅgāra, harivāsa, and haripriya.
Devapriya, vandanīya, and pavana constitute the six names [of one plant].
Nīla, bhṛṅgarāja, mahānīla, nīlaka,
mahābhṛṅga, nīlapuṣpa, and śyāmala constitute the six names [of another].
The *bhṛṅgarāja* plants are beneficial for the eyes, bitter and hot, and they dye the hair;
they destroy phlegm, swelling, and poisons, among which the blue variety is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
*Kākajaṅghā*, *dhvāṅkṣajaṅghā*, *kākāhvā*, and *vāyasī* are synonyms for it.

Pārāvatapadī is a female servant-like plant; it is river-favored and possesses abundant hair. Kākajaṅghā is bitter and hot; it removes worms, ulcers, and phlegm, conquers deafness and indigestion, and is a destroyer of chronic and irregular fevers.

*Cuñcu*, *vijalā*, *cañcu*, *kalabhī*, *vīrapattrikā*, *cuñcura*, and *cuñcupattra*—these are excellent vegetables grown in cultivated fields (*kṣetrasambhava*). *Cuñcu* is sweet, pungent, and astringent; it dries up impurities.
It cures abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, constipation, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
There are seven varieties: *bṛhaccuñcu*, *viṣāri*, *mahācuñcu*, *sucuñcukā*, *sthūlacuñcu*, *dīrghapattrī*, and *divyagandhā*.
The *mahācuñcu* is pungent and hot, astringent, and an obstructor of the channels;
it destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), colic, abdominal diseases, hemorrhoids, and the pain of poisons, and it is an elixir (*rasāyana*).
The *kṣudracuñcu*, *sucuñcu*, *cuñcu*, and *śunakacuñcukā* are synonyms for the small *cuñcu*.

*Tvaksārabhedinī*, *kṣudrā*, *kaṭukā*, and *cirapattrikā* are synonyms for *kṣudracuñcu*. It is sweet, pungent, hot, and astringent; it stimulates digestion, pacifies colic, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids, yet causes constipation.

The seed of *cuñcu* is pungent and hot; it overcomes abdominal tumors, colic, and pain in the stomach, and it removes poison, skin diseases, itching, *kharju*, leprosy, and toxins. (Rajni 6.149) *Sinduvāra*, *śvetapuṣpa*, *sinduka*, and *sinduvāraka* [are synonyms].
Sūrasādhana, Netā, Siddhaka, and Arthasiddhaka;
Sinduvāra is pungent and bitter, it removes phlegm, wind, and consumption, pacifies leprosy and itching, relieves colic, and brings success in treating cough. (Rājani 6.150–151)
Sugandhā, śītasahā, nirguṇḍī, nīlasinduka, sindūka, capikā, bhūtakeśī, indrāṇī, and nīlikā [are the names of this plant].
Blue nirguṇḍī is pungent, hot, bitter, and dry; it conquers cough.
It removes phlegm, swellings, wind-pain, menorrhagia, and flatulence. (6.153) Śephālikā is called suvahā, śuklāṅgī, and śītamañjarī;
it is also known as aparājitā, vijayā, vātāri, and bhūtakeśī. (6.154)
Śephālī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is dry and cures wind and wasting diseases.
It destroys wind in the joints of the limbs and removes disorders such as flatulence in the rectum.
Bheṇḍā, bhiṇḍātikā, bhiṇḍa, and bhiṇḍaka are names for the plant produced in cultivated fields.
Catuṣpada, catuṣpuṇḍra, suśāka, amlapattraka, karaparṇa, vṛttabīja—these are the eleven names [of this plant]. Bheṇḍā, however, has a sour taste; it is heating, constipating, and appetizing.
She bestows sons, she is the giver of conception, the giver of progeny, and the giver of offspring;
she is the bestower of creation, the mother of living beings, resembling a tree for ascetics.
She is the giver of sons, sweet, cooling, and a destroyer of defects such as those caused by women's menses.
It removes bile, burning sensations, and fatigue, and bestows the production of offspring.
*Takrāhvā*, *takrabhakṣā*, and *takraparyāyavācakā* are synonyms for it.
*Pañcāṅgulī* has a white luster; this plant is known by these five names.
*Takrā* is pungent, destroys worms, and eradicates ulcers.
*Svarṇulī* is also known as *hemapuṣpī*, *svarṇapuṣpī*, and *dhvajā*;
it is pungent, cooling, astringent, and removes ulcers.
Khaskhasa is a fine seed; it is also called subīja and sūkṣmataṇḍula.
Khaskhasa is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka) and bestows luster, virility, and strength.
Śimṛḍī is said to bestow intelligence, be strengthening, and remove lameness.
*Dravatpatrī*, *vātaghnī*, and *gucchapuṣpī*—thus it is sevenfold.
*Śimṛḍī* is pungent and hot; it removes wind (*vāta*) and cures pain in the back.
When used appropriately, it is suitable for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*) and brings firmness to the body.
*Jñeya* is known as *araṇyakusumbha*, while *kausumbha* is produced from fire (*agnisambhava*).
That *kausumbha* is pungent in digestion, it removes phlegm (*śleṣman*), and it is digestive (*dīpana*). *Āhulya*, *halurākhya*, *karaṃ*, and likewise *taravaṭa*—these are its names.
Śimbīphala, Supuṣpa, Arbara, and Dantakāṣṭhaka;
Hemapuṣpa, Pītapuṣpa, Kāñcanapuṣpaka, Nṛpamaṅgalyaka, and Śaratpuṣpa—these are the three names for each [of these plants]. (Rajñī 6.166–167)
Āhulya is bitter and cold; it is beneficial for the eyes and removes the disorder of pitta.
It cures diseases of the mouth, skin eruptions (kuṣṭha), itching, parasites, pain, and wounds.
Āhulya is also known as kuṣṭhaketu, mārkaṇḍīya, and mahauṣadha.

Āhulya has a bitter taste and cures fever, leprosy, consumption, and vitiligo. Kāsamarda, arimarda, kāsāri, and kāsamardaka are synonyms; it is also called kāla and kanaka, and is known as jāraṇa and dīpaka.
Kāsamarda is bitter and hot, yet sweet; it subdues phlegm and wind, destroys indigestion, cough, and bile, acts as a digestive, and cleanses the throat.
(Rajni 6.171) Ādityapattra, arkadala, arkapattra, sūkṣmapattra, and tapanacchada are synonyms for the same plant.
Kuṣṭhāri, arka, viṭapa, supattra, ravipriya, raśmipati, and rudra are synonyms for the plant [arka].
It has sun-like leaves (ādityapattra), is pungent, possesses a hot potency, removes phlegm, and cures diseases caused by wind.
It is digestive, destroys abdominal tumors, and should be known as a destroyer of loss of appetite.
Śvetāmlī is called Ambikā, Piṣṭauṇḍī, and Piṇḍikā;
Śvetāmlī is sweet, aphrodisiac, a destroyer of pitta, and a giver of strength. Nīlāmlī, Nīlapiṣṭauṇḍī, Śyāmāmlī, and Dīrghaśākhikā [are synonyms].
Nīlāmlī is sweet, appetizing, and an excellent remover of phlegm and wind. Ajagandhā, bastagandhā, surapuṣpā, avigandhikā,
ugragandhā, brahmagarbhā, brāhmī, and pūtimayūrikā [are synonyms].
Ajagandhā is pungent and hot; it removes wind-disorders, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen.

It destroys ear ulcers, pain, and colic. When drunk, it is beneficial, and when used as an ointment, it is likewise wholesome. Ādityabhaktā, varadā, arkabhaktā, suvarcalā, sūryalatā, and arkakāntā [are synonyms].
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, surasaṃbhavā, saurī, sutejā, arkahitā, and ravīṣṭā;
maṇḍūkī, satyanāmnī, devī, mārtaṇḍavallabhā, vikrāntā, and bhāskareṣṭā—it has eighteen names. (Rajñī 6.178–179)

Ādityabhaktā is cooling, slightly bitter, and pungent; it is fierce, subdues *kapha*, and destroys skin diseases, itching, ulcers, leprosy, spirits, planetary afflictions, and severe cold fevers. Viṣamuṣṭi, Keśamuṣṭi, Sumuṣṭi, and Aṇumuṣṭika [are its synonyms].

The fist (muṣṭi) is known to have five names when combined with kṣupa and doḍī. Viṣamuṣṭi is pungent and bitter; it stimulates digestion, removes phlegm and wind, cures diseases of the throat, improves the appetite, and causes pain and burning in blood-bile disorders.

Another *ḍoḍī* is indeed *jīvantī*, the best of greens, known as *sukhālukā*, *bahuparṇī*, *dīrghapatrā*, *sūkṣmapattrā*, and *jīvanī*. *Ḍoḍī* is pungent, bitter, and hot; it stimulates digestion and conquers *kapha* and *vāta*.
It removes throat ailments, is appetizing, and alleviates the pain of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) and burning sensations.
*Kālāñjanī*, *añjanī*, *recanī*, *asitāñjanī*, *nīlāñjanī*, *kṛṣṇābhā*, *kālī*, and *kṛṣṇāñjanī* are its names. (6.184–185)

Kālāñjanī is pungent and hot; it cleanses acidity, worms, and parasites, pacifies the upward movement of the downward wind (apānavāyu), and removes diseases of the stomach. Kārpāsī, Sāriṇī, Cavyā, Sthūlā, and Picu are likewise [described].
Badarī, bādara, guṇasu, tuṇḍikerikā, marūdbhavā, and samudrāntā are known as the eleven names [of the jujube].
Kārpāsī is sweet and cooling; it increases breast milk and removes pitta and kapha.
It relieves thirst, burning sensations, fatigue, dizziness, and fainting, and it bestows strength upon the heart.

(Rajni 6.188) The wild cotton plant (*vanajāraṇyakārpāsī*), known as *bhāradvājī* when grown in the forest, is cooling, appetizing, and removes the pain of wounds and injuries from weapons. (Rajni 6.189)
Kokilākṣa, Śṛgālī, Śṛṅkhalā,
Rakaṇa, Śṛṅgālaghaṇṭī, Vajrāsthiśṛṅkhalā,
Vajrakaṇṭaka, Ikṣura, Kṣuraka, Vajra, Śṛṅkhalikā, and Pikekṣaṇa.
Picchilā and Ikṣugandhā should be known as equal to the earth [in number].
Kokilākṣa is sweet, cooling, and cures bile and diarrhea;
it is aphrodisiac, removes phlegm, strengthening, appetizing, and supremely nourishing.
Sātalā, saptalā, sārī, vidulā, vimalā, amalā,
bahuphenā, carmakaṣā, phenā, dīptā,
viṣāṇikā, svarṇapuṣpī, and citraghanā— these are its thirteen names.
Sātalā destroys phlegm and bile; it is light, bitter, and astringent.
It cuts away erysipelas, leprosy, eruptions, ulcers, and swellings.
Kāmavṛddhi is known as Smaravṛddhi, Manojavṛddhi, and Madanāyudha.
Kandarpajīva, Jitendriyāhva, Kāmopajīva, and he known as Jīva;
the seed of Kāmavṛddhi is sweet, strength-increasing, an enhancer of desire, appetizing, and a provider of great increase to the senses. (Rājñī 6.195–196)
Cakramarda, aṇḍagaja, gajākhya, meṣāhvaya, eḍagaja, aṇḍahastī, vyāvartaka,
cakragaja, cakrī, puṃnāḍa, puṃnāṭa, vimardaka,
dadrughna, tarvaṭa, cakrāhva, and śukanāśana are synonyms for the same plant.
Dṛḍhabīja, prapunnāṭa, and kharjūghna—these nineteen [plants] are as follows:
Cakramarda is pungent and sharp; it removes fat, wind, and phlegm, and cures wounds, itching, leprosy, pain, ringworm, scabies, and other such disorders.
Jhiñjhirīṭā, kaṇṭaphalī, pītapuṣpā, jhiñjhirā,
huḍaromāśrayaphalā, and vṛttā— these are its six names.
Jhiñjhirīṭā is pungent, cooling, astringent, and a conqueror of diarrhea.
The milk of the buffalo increases virility, is nourishing, strengthening, and promotes the growth of the *mahiṣī* plant.

(6.201) Having thus clearly studied this section—preceded by the detailed description of the names and groups of broad-leaved plants and the determination of their qualities—a student shall immediately acquire excellent proficiency in the investigation of divine medicine. (6.202)

By their own great vigor, these men—who in a single moment are like the sun—forcefully cast away diseases by altering the very nature of their limbs through their intensity; and because they bring about the reversal of the arising of deformities even at the mention of their own names, this class of shrubs is exceedingly dense. Having seen his majesty now, which forcibly overcomes the distress of the learned in assembly and the swelling power of his enemies, one marvels at both his splendor and his destruction of the forest.

The group of herbs beginning with *śatāhvā*, which, when applied, reportedly dispel diseases by their own power as if through rivalry, constitute the fourth division of the *Narahari* [classification] in this work.
Radish is said to be of five kinds; the śigru is said to be of four kinds;
bamboo is of two kinds; likewise, there is the mākandī, the wild turmeric, and the śṛṅgāṭa, the bhramaracchallī, and furthermore, the wild ginger.
Garlic is said to be of two kinds, and the onion is considered to be of two kinds as well. Twenty-one root vegetables are declared to be the refuge [of those who avoid meat],
along with the seven types of *ālūka* and the forest tubers (*āraṇyakandaka*).
Mahiṣī, hastikolā, vārāhī, viṣṇudhāriṇī,
the two kinds of nākulī, mālā, the two kinds of vidārī,
śālmalī, caṇḍāla, tailakanda, triparṇī, and likewise puṣkara.
Musalī is of two kinds, and likewise the gucchas are of three kinds.
Among these is the one called Nāgakara; now the leaf-vegetables (pattraśāka) are described:
vāstuka, cukraka, cillī, and the three types of śigru leaves.
Pālakyā, Rājaśākinī, and four types of Upodakī in sequence;
Kuṇañjara, that which is called Kusumbha, Śatāhvā, and Patrataṇḍulī;
the two types of Rājikā, Cāṅgerī, and Gholikā are considered to be of three kinds.
Jīvaśāka, as well as that called gaurasuvarṇa, punarnavā, vasuka,
phañjikā and others, miśraka, and that named aṅkakarā;
after this, there are kuṣmāṇḍī, kumbhatumbī, and alābukā.
Bhūtumbikā, kaliṅga, the two kinds of kośātakī,
paṭolī, madhurādyā, mṛgākṣī, dadhipuṣpikā,
śimbī, kāravallī, karkoṭī, and svādutumbikā.
Niṣpāvī, dvayavārttākī, ḍaṅgarī, kharbujā, as well as karkaṭī, trapusa, ervāru, vālukī,
cīnakarkaṭī, cirbhiṭā, śaśāṇḍūlī, kuḍuhuñcī, and munīkṣaṇa. (RājNī 7.11)
The divisions of the Vedas, consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, and fruits respectively,
are described here among the vegetable group as possessing enchanting qualities.
Thus, there are four types of substances, numbering fifty-one (five times ten plus one).
Mūlaka, nīlakaṇṭha, mūlāhva, and dīrghamūlaka;
bhūkṣāra, kandamūla, hastidanta, and likewise sita;
śaṅkhamūla, haritparṇa, rucira, and dīrghakandaka.

And the root of *kuñjarakṣāra*—these are the thirteen roots. Root ginger (*mūlaka*) is sharp, hot, pungent and heating, constipating, and a digestive stimulant; it destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, heart disease, and wind disorders, provides relish, and is heavy.
The nine varieties to be known are: that called *cāṇākhyamūlaka*, another called *śāleya* or *viṣṇuguptaka*, *sthūlamūla*, *mahākanda*, *kauṭilya*, *marusambhava*, and *śālāmarkaṭaka*. Rajni 7.17.
The root known as *cāṇākhya* is warm, pungent, appetizing, and digestive;
it destroys phlegm, wind, worms, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*), while being constipating and heavy.
The *gṛñjana*, the root of the *śikhī*, the *yavaneṣṭa*, and the *vartula* [are similar].
Granthimūla, śikhākanda, kanda, ḍiṇḍīra, modaka,
and gṛñjana are pungent and hot; they alleviate diseases caused by *kapha* and *vāta*,
improve the appetite, stimulate digestion, are beneficial for the heart, counteract foul odors, and destroy abdominal tumors (*gulma*).

Piṇḍamūla, gajāṇḍa, piṇḍaka, and piṇḍamūlaka—piṇḍamūla is pungent and hot, and it removes disorders such as abdominal tumors (gulma) and wind (vāta). It is warm, sharp, bitter, and possesses sweet and pungent tastes; it cures urinary disorders, and destroys asthma, hemorrhoids, cough, abdominal tumors, consumption, eye diseases, and pain in the navel.

Young radish (*mūlaka*) is beneficial for the throat, strengthening, appetizing, and it removes impurities and disorders; however, when mature, it is said to be heating, causes emaciation, and produces burning sensations, bile, and blood.

(Rajni 7.22) Raw radish is constipating, appetizing, and subdues *kapha* and *vāta*; when cooked, it is pungent and heating. If eaten before a meal, it immediately provokes bile, burning, and blood disorders. But if eaten together with the meal, or if cooked with minced meat (*veśavāra*), it is wholesome, strength-giving, and is said to pacify heart disease and colic, acting as a root-remedy for the pain of colic. (Rajni 7.23)
Garjara, piṅgamūla, pītaka, sumūlaka,
svādumūla, supīta, nāraṅga, and pītamūlaka—
garjara is sweet, appetizing, slightly pungent, and it removes phlegm.

It destroys flatulence, worms, and colic, and removes burning sensations, bile disorders, and thirst. (Rajni 7.25) The *śigru* is a green vegetable; it is known as *śākapattra*, *supattraka*, *upadaṃśa*, *kṣamādaṃśa*, and *komalapattraka*.
Bahumūla, daṃśamūla, tīkṣṇamūla, and daśāhvaya;
and śigru is pungent, bitter, and hot, sharp, and it removes wind and phlegm. It cures numbness of the mouth, is appetizing, stimulates digestion, and alleviates defects of wounds.
Śobhāñjana, nīlaśigru, tīkṣṇagandha, janapriya, mukhāmoda, kṛṣṇaśigru, cakṣuṣya, and rucirañjana are synonyms for the black variety of śigru. Śobhāñjana is pungent, bitter, sweet, hot, and slimy.
It destroys worms, wind-disorders, and colic; it is beneficial for the eyes and highly appetizing. White *śigru* is very sharp, causes facial contortions, and is called "white-named.
It has excellent roots, is known as white pepper, is appetizing, and is called honey-*śigru*.

The white *śigru* is pungent and sharp; it destroys swelling and wind, relieves pain in the limbs, improves the appetite, stimulates digestion, and removes numbness of the mouth. The red *śigru*, known as *raktaka*, is sweet and possesses many leaves.
Sugandhakesara is celebrated as a lion and the enemy of deer. Raktaśigru is of great potency, sweet, and an elixir; it removes swelling, flatulence, wind-pain, bile, and phlegm.
Vaṃśa, yavaphala, veṇu, karmāra, tṛṇaketuka, maskara,
śataparvan, kaṇṭālu, and likewise kaṇṭakī;
mahābala, dṛḍhagranthi, dṛḍhapattra, and dhanudruma.
The *dhanuṣya* should be known as having firm joints and originating from the region of Bāṇa.
The two types of bamboo (*vaṃśa*) are sour and astringent, slightly bitter and cooling;
they destroy dysuria, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, bile, burning sensations, and bleeding.

But another is the *randhravaṃśa* (hollow bamboo), known as *tvaksāra*, *kīcaka*, *maskara*, *vādanīya*, and by the name *suṣira*; thus it has six names. The specific *randhravaṃśa* is stimulating and destroys indigestion.
It is appetizing, digestive, heart-tonic, a destroyer of colic, and a remover of abdominal tumors (gulma).
The tip of a bamboo stalk is called *karīra*, as is the sprout of a bamboo; likewise, the sprout of a barley fruit.
Its knot is called *paru*, its joint *parva*, and also the internode-joint (*kāṇḍasandhi*).
Karīra is pungent, bitter, sour, astringent, light, and cooling;
it destroys bile, blood disorders, burning sensations, and dysuria, stimulates the appetite, and its joints are devoid of nodes.
Vetra is also called vetasa, yogidaṇḍa, and sudaṇḍa; it has soft joints.
Vetra is of five kinds; it is cooling, astringent, and removes disorders of *bhūta* and *pitta*. Mākandī, Bahumūlā, Mādanī, Gandhamūlikā, Viśadamūlī, and another called Śyāmalā—these are the others.

Mākandī is pungent, bitter, and sweet; it is a supreme digestive stimulant, appetizing, and slightly increases vāta. It is wholesome, yet it is not particularly beneficial during the rainy season. Śolī is wild turmeric, and śolikā is also known as vanāriṣṭā.
Śolikā is pungent and sweet, appetizing, bitter, and digestive. Śṛṅgāṭaka— also known as śṛṅgaruha, jalavallī, jalāśraya,
śṛṅgakanda, śṛṅgamūla, and viṣāṇī— is thus named by seven names.
Śṛṅgāṭaka removes blood and bile, is light, laxative, and especially highly aphrodisiac;
it alleviates the three doṣas, fever, fatigue, and swelling, provides relish, and is a cause for strengthening the urinary tract.
Bhṛṅgāhvā, bhramaracchallī, bhramarā, and bhṛṅgamūlikā are synonyms for the plant known as bhṛṅga.
Bhṛṅgacchallī is pungent and hot; it is bitter and stimulates digestion and the appetite. (Rajni 7.47) Peūr is called vanārdrakā, and it is also known as vanajā and araṇyajārdrakā.
Peūr is pungent and sour; it improves the taste, provides strength, and stimulates digestion. (Rajni 7.48)

Rasona, laśuna, ariṣṭa, mlecchakanda, mahauṣadha, bhūtaghna, ugragandha, and śītamardaka are synonyms for garlic (laśuna). Rasona, also known as amlarasona, is heavy and hot; it subdues phlegm and wind.
It destroys loss of appetite, worms, heart disease, and swelling, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
Garlic (rasona) is hot, pungent, slimy, unctuous, heavy, and sweet in taste;
it is extremely strengthening, aphrodisiac, and beneficial for the intellect, voice, complexion, and eyesight; it fortifies the bones and joints, is very sharp, and is highly beneficial.
Another variety of garlic is the *gṛñjana*, which has long leaves, broad leaves, and a thick bulb;
it is favored by the Yavanas and is beneficial for strength.
Regarding the *gṛñjana*, they teach that its bulb is sweet and pungent, while its stalk is astringent.

The wise declare that the leaf-cluster is bitter, and they say the seed-pod is salty. The great garlic (mahārasona) destroys heart disease, chronic fever, colic in the belly, constipation, abdominal tumors, loss of appetite, urinary distress, swellings, hemorrhoids, leprosy, disorders of wind, exhaustion, parasites, and diseases of phlegm.
Onion (*palāṇḍu*) has sharp bulbs; it is called *ullī* and is a defiler of the mouth.
It is dear to Śūdras, destroys worms, stimulates digestion, and imparts a scent to the mouth.
It has many leaves, possesses a pervasive fragrance, is appetizing, and is known by the name of Rudra.
The onion is of two kinds: one with white bulbs and the other with yellow ones.
It is pungent, strengthening, heavy, and it removes phlegm and bile;
it is aphrodisiac, appetizing, unctuous, emetic, and destroys the [three] humors.
Another is *rājapalāṇḍu*, known as *yavaneṣṭa* and *nṛpāhvaya*;
it is also called *rājapriya*, *mahākanda*, *dīrghapattra*, and *rocaka*.
It is further named *nṛpeṣṭa*, *nṛpakanda*, *mahākanda*, and *nṛpapriya*.
Raktakanda and Rājeṣṭa—these are the thirteen names here. Palāṇḍu is preceded by the word "nṛpa" (king); it is cooling, destroys bile, removes phlegm, is digestive, and likewise induces much sleep.
The characteristics of the *nṛpapalāṇḍu* shall be described: it is alkaline, pungent, and sweet;
it bestows relish, alleviates dryness of the throat, is highly digestive, pacifies phlegm and bile, and is extremely nourishing.
It is known as *kaṇḍūla*, *śūraṇa*, *kanda*, *sukanda*, and *sthūlakandaka*.
Durnāmāri, Suvṛtta, Vātāri, Kanda, Śūraṇa, Arśoghnā, Tīvrakanda, Kandārha, Kandavardhana,
Bahukanda, Rucyakanda, and Śūrakanda is the sixteenth.
*Śūraṇa* is pungent, appetizing, and digestive; it cures worms, phlegm, and wind.
It removes asthma, cough, vomiting, and hemorrhoids; it pacifies colic and abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and it increases the blood.
(Rajni 7.64) *Sita-śūraṇa*, however, is wild; it is called *vanakaṇḍa*, *araṇya-śūraṇa*, and *vanaja*.

That forest tuber known as *śvetaśūraṇa* and the one called *kaṇḍūla* are sevenfold. The white *śūraṇa* is appetizing, pungent and hot, a destroyer of worms, a remover of disorders such as abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and colic, and it cures loss of appetite.
Mukhāluka, maṇḍapāroha, dīrghakanda, sukandaka,
sthūlakanda, mahākanda, and svādukanda— these are the seven types. Mukhāluka is sweet, cooling, and destroys pitta.

It is appetizing, increases wind (vāta), and removes burning sensations, emaciation, and thirst. Piṇḍālu is known as granthila, piṇḍakanda, kandagranthi, romaśa, romakanda, romāhva, tāmbūlapattra, lālākanda, and piṇḍaka; it has these ten names.
Piṇḍālu is sweet, cooling, cures dysuria and disease,
destroys burning sensations, emaciation, and urinary disorders (prameha), is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and heavy. Another variety is raktapiṇḍālu, also known as raktālū or raktapiṇḍaka.
Lohita, raktakanda, and lohitālu have six names.
Raktapiṇḍāluka is cooling, sweet and sour, and removes fatigue;
it alleviates bile and burning sensations, is aphrodisiac, promotes strength and nourishment, and is heavy.
It is sevenfold: kāsālu, kāsakanda, kandālu, āluka, ālu, viśālapattra, and pattrālu. Kāsālu removes severe itching and diseases caused by vāta and śleṣman.
It cures loss of appetite, is delicious, wholesome, and stimulates the digestive fire.
The *phoṇḍālu*, the *lohitālu*, the *raktapattra*, and the *mṛducchada*—
the *phoṇḍālu* destroys phlegm and wind, and it is pungent, hot, and a stimulant of digestion.
*Pāṇiyālu* is the same as *jalālu*; *anupālu* is *avāluka*.
*Pāṇiyālu* destroys the three *doṣas* and is supreme for providing nourishment.
*Nīlālu* is *asitālu*, *kṛṣṇālu*, and *śyāmalāluka*.

The *nīlālu* is sweet and cooling; it removes bile, burning sensations, and fatigue. The *śubhrālu*, *mahiṣīkanda*, *lulāyakanda*, *śuklakanda*, *sarpākhya*, *vanavāsī*, *viṣakanda*, and another called *nīlakanda* [are also varieties].
The rhizome of *mahiṣī* is pungent and hot; it removes diseases caused by *kapha* and *vāta*.
The white variety is pleasing to the taste, removes numbness of the mouth, and brings about great success.
*Hastikanda*, *hastipattra*, *sthūlakanda*, and *atikandaka* [are synonyms].
Bṛhatpattra, atipattra, hastikarṇa, sukarnaka, tvagdosari,
kusthahanta, girivasi, nagasraya,
gajakanda, and nagakanda— these are known as the fourteen names [of the plant]. (Rajni 7.80–81)

Hastikanda is pungent and hot; it removes diseases caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, cures skin disorders and fatigue, and destroys leprosy, poisons, and erysipelas (*visarpa*). Kolakanda is an anthelmintic; it is also called *pañjala* and *vastrapañjala*.
Puṭālu, Supuṭa, and Puṭakanda are of seven kinds. Kolakanda is pungent and hot; it destroys worms and defects, alleviates vomiting and dysentery, and wards off the effects of poison.
*Vārāhī*, *śūkarī*, *kroḍakanyā*, *gṛṣṭi*, *viṣvaksenakāntā*, and *varāhī* are synonyms for the sow.
*Kaumārī*, *brahmaputrī*, *trinetrā*, *krauḍī*, *kanyā*, *gṛṣṭikā*, and *mādhaveṣṭā* are synonyms for the wild boar.
*Śūkarakanda*, *kroḍa*, *vanavāsī*, *kuṣṭhanāśana*, and *vanya* refer to the wild boar.
Amṛta, Mahāvīrya, Mahauṣadhi, Śabarakanda,
Varāhakanda, Vīra, Brāhmakanda, Sukandaka, Vṛddhida, and Vyādhihantā— these are the names consisting of eighteen [syllables]. (Rajñī 7.86–87)
Vārāhī is bitter and pungent; it removes poison, bile, and phlegm.
It cures skin diseases, urinary disorders, and worms; it is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and a rejuvenative elixir.
Viṣṇukanda is also known as Viṣṇugupta, Supuṣṭa, and Bahusampuṭa.
Jalavāsa, bṛhatkanda, dīrghavṛnta, and haripriya;
Viṣṇukanda is sweet, cooling, and destroys bile (pitta);
it removes burning sensations and swelling, is appetizing, and is an excellent nourisher.
Dhāriṇī, dhāraṇīyā, vīrapattrī, sukandaka, kandālu, vanakanda, kandādya, and daṇḍakandaka— these are the varieties. Madhuro dhāriṇīkanda removes disorders of phlegm and bile.

It pacifies defects of the mouth and destroys leprosy and itching. *Nākulī*, *sarpagandhā*, *sugandhā*, *raktapattrikā*, *īśvarī*, *nāgagandhā*, *ahibhuk*, and likewise *svarasā*— [Note: The provided text contains a fragment of verse 7.92 followed by a list of synonyms for *nākulī*. The translation reflects the structure of the source.]

*Sarpādanī*, *vyālagandhā*, and *jñeyā*—these are known as the ten names [of this plant]. Furthermore, there is another called *mahāsugandhā*, *suvahā*, *gandhanākulī*, *sarpākṣī*, *phaṇihantrī*, *nakulāḍhyā*, and *ahibhuk*. (RājN 7.93–94)
Viṣamardanikā, ahimardinī, viṣamardinī, mahāhigandhā, and ahi-latā—this [plant] is known by these twelve names. The pair of nākulī plants is bitter, pungent, and hot; it conquers the three doṣas.
A certain second [variety] is the most excellent, destroying many kinds of poison.
Now, there are the *mālākanda*, the *ālikanda*, and the *paṅktikanda*;
with its three-pointed leaves, knotted leaves, and stalks, it is celebrated as being of six types.
*Mālākanda* is very sharp (*sutīkṣṇa*), a destroyer of *gaṇḍamālā*, an appetizer (*dīpana*), a remover of abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and a reducer of wind and phlegm (*vāta-śleṣman*).
*Vidārikā* has sweet tubers; it is known as *sitā*, *śuklā*, and *śṛgālikā*.
Vidārī is known as vṛṣyakandā and viḍālī, and vṛṣyavallikā;
bhūkuṣmāṇḍī, svādulatā, gajeṣṭā, and vārivallabhā should be known as kandaphalā; it is considered to have names numbering seven (the number of Manu).
Vidārī is sweet, cooling, heavy, unctuous, and a conqueror of blood-bile (asrapitta);
it should be known as a producer of phlegm (kapha), nourishing, strengthening, and an increaser of virility.
Another variety is Kṣīravidārī, also known as Ikṣugandhā and Ikṣuvallarī.
Iksuvalli, kṣīrakanda, kṣīravallī, payasvinī,
kṣīraśuklā, kṣīralatā, payaḥkandā, payolatā, and payovidārikā— these should be known as the twelve names [of this plant]. (Rajni 7.102–103)
Kṣīravidārī is known to be sweet, sour, astringent, and bitter;
it destroys bile and colic, and removes diseases such as urinary disorders (mūtrameha).
Kṣīrakanda is said to be of two kinds: that without a stalk and that with a stalk.
Without its stalk, it is a remover of disease; with its stalk, it is an arrestor of the aging process.
Śālmalīkandaka, vijula, vanavāsaka, vanavāsī, malaghna, and malahantā are its six names. (Rājani 7.105–106)
The sweet *śālmalīkanda* overcomes the accumulation of impurities and obstructions;
it is cooling and destroys the pain of bile, burning sensations, emaciation, and fever.
It is said that *caṇḍālakanda* may also be called *ekapattra* or *dvipattraka*.

It is distinguished by having three, four, or five petals. The Caṇḍālakaṇḍa is sweet; it conquers the humors of phlegm, bile, and blood, destroys the defects caused by poisons and spirits, and is to be known as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
Now, the *tailakanda* is said to have leaves marked with sesame seeds; it is known as *drāvakakanda*, *karavīrakanda*, and *tilacitrapattraka*. It is described by the *bāṇa* verses [as follows]:
"The *tailakanda* melts metals; it is pungent and hot, removes wind-disorders (*vāta*) and epilepsy (*apasmāra*), and is an antidote to poison."

It destroys swelling, acts as a styptic for the vital essence (*rasa*), and swiftly brings about the perfection of the body. (Rājñī 7.111) Resembling the leaf of the *aśvāri* plant, marked with sesame-like spots, situated in very moist soil below the surface, and extensively spread out, is the *tilakanda*. (Rājñī 7.112)
Triparṇikā has large leaves and is also known as Chinnagranthinikā;
it is called Kandāla and Kandabahalā, and as Amlavallī, it removes poison. Triparṇī is sweet and cooling, and it destroys asthma and cough.
It pacifies the provocation of *pitta* and is supreme in healing wounds caused by poison. *Musalī*, *tālamūlī*, *suvahā*, *tālamūlikā*,
*godhāpadī*, *hemapuṣpī*, *bhūtālī*, and *dīrghakandikā*.
Musalī is sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, and bestows nourishment and strength;
it is slimy, increases phlegm, and is supreme for removing bile, burning sensations, and fatigue.
(Rajni 7.116) Musalī is said to be of two kinds: the white variety and that known by another name.

The *śvetā* possesses very few qualities, while another variety is an elixir (*rasāyanī*). (7.117) The tubers known as *gucchāhva*, *tavakāhva*, *gulucchakanda*, and *vighaṇṭikā*—of these, the *gulucchakanda* is sweet, very cooling, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and a destroyer of burning sensations. (7.118)
Lakṣmaṇā, putrakandā, putradā, nāginī, nāgāhvā, nāgapattrī, tulinī, majjikā, asrabinducchadā, and sukandā— these are its ten names. (Rajñī 7.119)
Lakṣmaṇā is sweet, cooling, and destroys female infertility;
it acts as an elixir (rasāyana), is strengthening, and is supreme in pacifying the three doṣas.
The term *joḍi* is recorded by the best of physicians as a synonym for *hasta*.
Known as *karajoḍi*, it effects the binding of mercury (*rasabandha*) and acts as a subduing agent (*vaśyakṛt*). Vāstuka, vāstu, vāstūka, vastuka,
and *hilamocikā* are celebrated as the king of potherbs (*śākarāja*), the royal potherb (*rājaśāka*), and the universal sovereign (*cakravartin*).

Vāstuka is sweet, very cooling, slightly alkaline, and mildly sour; it conquers the three doṣas, is appetizing, removes fever, destroys hemorrhoids, and purifies the feces and urine. Cukra, cukravāstūka, likuca, and amlavāstuka [are similar].

Dalāmla is known as amlaśāka; it belongs to the group beginning with amlā and is also called hilamocikā. Cukra is amlapattra; it is light and hot, cures wind-disorders (vātagulma), stimulates the appetite, is digestive, wholesome, and is excellent for slightly increasing bile (pitta). (RājN 7.124–125)
Palāśalohitā, cillī, vāstukā, and cillikā are synonyms;
mṛdupattrī and kṣāradalā are also names for it. Vāstukī, however, is called kṣārapattrī.
Cillī is similar to vāstuka; being alkaline, it subdues phlegm and bile.
It cures urinary disorders (*prameha*) and dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), and is wholesome and appetizing.
(7.127) *Śvetacillī*, *vāstūkī*, *supathyā*, *śvetacillikā*, *sitacilly*, and *upacillī*—these names refer to the small *vāstuka* plant, which destroys fever. (7.128)
White *cillī* is very sweet, alkaline, and cooling;
it pacifies the three *doṣas*, is wholesome, and destroys the disorders of fever. Another variety is *śunakacillī*, also known as *sucillī* or *śvānacillikā*.
Śvacillī is pungent and sharp; it removes itching and heals wounds.
(Rajni 7.130) The leaf-vegetable derived from the *śigru* tree is appetizing and dispels wind and phlegm (*vāta-kapha*).
It is pungent and hot, a digestive stimulant (*dīpana*), wholesome, an anthelmintic, and an excellent promoter of digestion (*pācana*). (Rajni 7.131)
Pālakyam is the name for palakyā; madhurā, kṣurapattrikā, supattrā, snigdhapattrā, grāmīṇā, and grāmyavallabhā are synonyms for it. Pālakyam is slightly pungent, sweet, wholesome, and cooling.

It should be known as a cure for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), constipating, and supremely nourishing. Whether preceded by the name "Rājā" or otherwise called "Nagā," it is known as Rājādri, Rājagiri, or Rājaśākinī.
Rājaśākinī is appetizing, pacifies pitta, and is cooling;
that same plant, when very cooling and appetizing, is to be known as Sthūlaśākinī.
Upodakī and Kalambī are slimy and have slimy leaves.
Mohinī, madaśāka, viśālā, and indeed upodakī—upodakī is astringent and hot, pungent and sweet;
it induces sleep and lassitude, is appetizing, and causes constipation and phlegm. (Rajñī 7.136–137)

The *upodakī* is another [variety], small and with delicate leaves, while the *maṇḍapī* is similar to the former in its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect (*rasa-vīrya-vipāka*). The third is the *upodakī* born in the wild, known by the name *vanajā*.
The wild *upodakī* is bitter, pungent, hot, and it promotes the appetite.
*Mūlapotī*, *kṣudravallī*, *potikā*, *kṣudrapotikā*,
the creeper known by the name *kṣupopodaka*, and *śākaṭapotikā*— [these are its synonyms].
The root tuber (mūlapotī) destroys the three doṣas, is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and light;
it promotes strength and nourishment, is appetizing, and stimulates the digestive fire. Kuṇañjara destroys the three doṣas, is sweet, appetizing, and a stimulant of digestion.
Slightly astringent, constipating, it increases pitta and kapha, and is light.

(Rajni 7.142) The *kausumbha* vegetable is sweet, pungent, and hot; it removes disorders of feces and urine, destroys intoxication, especially clarifies the vision, provides relish, and stimulates the digestive fire. (Rajni 7.143)
The leaf of *śatapuṣpā* is warm, sweet, and conquers abdominal tumors and colic;
it subdues wind, stimulates digestion, is wholesome, removes bile, and bestows appetite.
(Rajni 7.144) The leaf of *taṇḍulīyaka* is cooling and destroys hemorrhoids, bile, blood disorders, poison, and cough.
It is astringent and sweet, pacifying burning sensations and dryness in digestion, and providing appetite.
(Rajni 7.145) The leaf of *rājikā* is pungent and hot; it removes worms, wind, and phlegm, cures diseases of the throat, is sweet, and acts as a stimulant for the digestive fire. (Rajni 7.146)
The mustard leaf is very hot; it pacifies the provocation of *rakta-pitta*, is burning, pungent, sweet, aphrodisiac, and provides appetite.
(Rajni 7.147) The *cāṅgerī* vegetable is very hot, pungent, appetizing, and digestive.
It stimulates digestion and overcomes phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, dysentery, and diarrhea.
Gholā, gholikā, gholī, kalandu, and kavalālukam are synonyms for kṣetraja salt; it is appetizing, sour, and removes wind and phlegm.
The *ārāmagholikā* is sour, dry, appetizing, and dispels wind;
another variety is pungent, generates bile and phlegm, is subtle, and cures chronic fever.
The *jīvanta*, with its red stalks, copper-colored leaves, and stalks, [is likewise beneficial].
Śākavīra is sweet, as are jīvaśāka and meṣaka. Jīvaśāka is very sweet, nourishing, a cleanser of the bladder, digestive, appetizing, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and a remover of bile.
Gaurasuvarṇa, suvarṇa, sugandhika, bhūmija, and vārija;
likewise hrasva, gandhaśāka, kaṭuśṛṅgāṭa, and varṇaśāka—these are the varieties of *śāka*.
Gaurasuvarṇa is cooling and removes phlegm, bile, and fever.
It is highly beneficial for removing burning sensations, loss of appetite, vertigo, blood disorders, and fatigue.
*Varṣābhū* and *vasuka* remove phlegm, weak digestion, and wind;
they are very dry in their post-digestive effect and cure abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, and colic.
Phañjikā, jīvanī, padmā, tarkārī, and cucuka are distinct [from the previous group].
They remove disorders of wind (vāta), are astringent, stimulate digestion, and provide relish.
Phañjī and the other four—bheṇḍā, kuṇañja, and likewise tripuṭa—[are also included].
Thus, these leaf-vegetables of the forest, when prepared together, are digestive stimulants,
carminatives, appetizers, and bestowers of strength and complexion;
they pacify the three humors, are wholesome, constipating, aphrodisiac, and bringers of comfort.
*Karkoṭikā*, *kuṣmāṇḍī*, *kumbhāṇḍī*, *bṛhatphalā*, *suphalā*, *kumbhaphalā*, and *nāgapuṣpaphalā* are synonyms for the *muni*.
It removes urinary obstruction, pacifies *prameha*, cuts through painful gravel and stones, dries up feces and urine, alleviates the pain of thirst, and provides nourishment for the emaciated body.

Physicians declare that the pumpkin (*kuṣmāṇḍa*) is the most excellent among vine-fruits; it is aphrodisiac, exceedingly sweet, an antidote to loss of appetite, strengthening, and a remover of bile. (RājN 7.161) The *gorakṣatumbī* is sevenfold: *gorakṣī*, *navālāmbu*, *ghaṭābhidhā*, *kumbhālāmbu*, *ghaṭālāmbu*, and *kumbhatumbī*. (RājN 7.162)

The *kumbhatumbī* is very sweet, cooling, and removes bile; it is heavy, nourishing, appetizing, and bestows vigor, nourishment, and strength. (Rajñī 7.163) The *kṣīratumbī*, *dugdhātumbī*, and those called *dīrghavṛttaphalā* [are similar].
Ikṣvāku is the best of the Kṣatriyas, possessing long roots and great fruit;
it is milky, has seeds like milk, and has seeds like teeth;
it is succulent, a great creeper, and indeed the "alāmbu" plant; it destroys fatigue and covers the ground with its shoots.
The *tumbī* is very sweet, unctuous, a destroyer of *pitta*, and promotes the nourishment of the fetus;
it is aphrodisiac, increases wind (*vāta*), and enhances strength and corpulence.
The *bhūtumbī*, *nāgatumbī*, and that which arises from the rainbow (*śakracāpa*) [are also such]. 7.166–167.
The goddess born from an anthill is the divine *tumbī*, known by six names:
*bhūtumbī*, *kaṭukā*, *uṣṇā*, and it removes the disorder of the three humors (*saṃnipāta*).
*Dantārgala* and *dantarodha* remove defects such as *dhanurvāta*. (Rajñī 7.167–168)
The *kaliṅga* fruit is of nine types: *māṃsalaphala*, *citraphala*, *citravallika*, *citra*, *madhuraphala*, *vṛttaphala*, *ghṛṇāphala*, and *māṃsala*.
The *kaliṅga* is sweet and cooling; it removes bile, burning sensations, and fatigue.
It is aphrodisiac, nourishing, strengthening, and increases virility and nourishment.
Kośātakī has sweet fruit and beautiful flowers; it may also be called karkoṭakī or pītapuṣpā.
Dhārāphalā, dīrghaphalā, and sukośā are names for dhāmārgava, which is known by these nine designations.
*dhārākośātakī* is unctuous, sweet, and alleviates *kapha* and *pitta*;
it slightly increases *vāta*, is wholesome, promotes relish, and bestows strength and vitality.
*Hastikośātakī* is another variety, as is *bṛhatkośātakī*.
The *mahākośātakī* is round; the village *kośātakī* is known as *śara*.
The *hastikośātakī* is unctuous, sweet, and causes flatulence and wind;
it is aphrodisiac, vermifuge, and a healer of wounds.
It is known as *svādupaṭolī*, *paṭolī*, and *maṇḍalī*.
*Paṭolī* is sweet and so forth; it is called *dīrghapaṭolikā*.
*Paṭolikā* is also known by synonyms such as *snigdhaparṇī* and those beginning with "sweet. (Rajni 7.175)
Paṭolī is sweet, subdues pitta, improves the appetite, and destroys fever;
it is known to be wholesome, providing strength and nourishment, and acting as a digestive stimulant and carminative.
(Rajni 7.176) The leaf of paṭola destroys pitta, while its stalk removes kapha.
Its fruit pacifies the three *doṣas*, and its root is a purgative.
It is known as *mṛgākṣī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *mṛgervāru*, *mṛgādanī*,
*citravallī*, *bahuphalā*, *kapilākṣī*, and *mṛgekṣaṇā*.
Citrā, citraphalā, pathyā, vicitrā, mṛgacirbhiṭā, marujā, kumbhasī, devī, kaṭphalā, laghucirbhiṭā,
sendinī, and mahādevī— these are considered by the wise to be the twenty [varieties]. (Rājñī 7.179)
Mṛgākṣī is pungent and bitter, sour in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and destroys wind (vāta).
It generates bile (pitta), cures chronic catarrh (pīnasa), stimulates the digestive fire, and is supreme for creating appetite.
Dadhipuṣpī, Khaṭvāṅgī, Khaṭvā, Paryaṅkapādikā, and Kūpā [are synonyms].
The *khaṭvāpādī*, *vaṃśyā*, *kākolī*, and *kolapālikā* are ninefold.
*Dadhipuṣpī* is pungent and sweet, cooling, and it destroys the afflictions of heat and bile;
however, it causes disorders of wind (*vāta*), is heavy, and likewise cures loss of appetite.
Asiśimbī, Khaḍgaśimbī, Śimbī, Nistriṃśaśimbikā,
Sthūlaśimbī, Mahāśimbī, Bṛhacchimbī, and Suśimbikā;
Asiśimbī is sweet, astringent, and it conquers phlegm and bile.
It removes the impurities of wounds, is cooling, and stimulates the appetite. Karakā, kāravallī, cīripattra, karillakā, sūkṣmavallī, kaṇṭaphalā, pītapuṣpā, and ambuvallikā [are synonyms].

Kāravallī is very bitter and hot; it stimulates digestion, conquers *kapha* and *vāta*, cures loss of appetite, and removes blood disorders. Karkoṭakī has sweet fruit; it is pleasing and beneficial for the mind.
Bodhanā, vandhyākarkoṭī, and devīkaṇṭaphalā are synonyms for karkoṭakī. It is pungent and hot, bitter, and destroys poison;
it subdues wind, removes bile, stimulates digestion, and produces relish in food.
Now, *madhurabimbī*, *madhubimbī*, *svādutumbikā*, *tuṇḍī*, *raktaphalā*, *ruciraphalā*, *soṣṇaphalā*, and *pīluparṇī* are synonyms for the *bimbī*.
The *bimbī* is sweet and cooling; it removes bile, asthma, and phlegm.

The beautiful *gṛhabimbikā* removes blood-fever and cures cough. *Niṣpāvī*, *grāmajā*, and others are synonyms; it is also known as *phalīnī*, *nakhapūrvikā*, *maṇḍapī*, *phalikā*, *śimbī*, and *gucchaphalā*.
The *viśālaphalikā*, the *niṣpāvī*, and likewise the *cipiṭā*;
the *anyāṅgulīphalā* and the *nakhaniṣpāvikā* are recorded [as such].
The *vṛttaniṣpāvikā* is common, while the *nakhapucchaphalā* are arrows.

The two types of *niṣpāva* (flat beans) are greenish-white, astringent, and sweet in taste; they cleanse the throat, promote purity of intellect, stimulate digestion, and increase the appetite. They are astringent and possess equal potency, though the second variety is slightly superior. (Rajni 7.193)
Vārttākī, kaṇṭavṛntākī, kaṇṭālu, and kaṇṭapattrikā;
nidrālu, māṃsalaphalā, vṛntākī, and mahoṭikā;
citraphalā, kaṇṭakinī, mahatī, and kaṭphalā—these are synonyms for the eggplant.

The *vārttākī* has mixed-colored fruits, blue fruits, and likewise red fruits; it is the best of leafy vegetables, possesses round fruits, and is known as a fruit dear to kings. It is pungent, appetizing, sweet, and destroys bile (*pitta*).
It increases strength and nourishment, is pleasing to the heart, heavy, and is condemned in cases of wind disorders.
*Ḍaṅgarī*, *ḍāṅgarī*, *dīrghervāru*, *ḍaṅgari*, *ḍaṅgārī*, *nāgaśuṇḍī*, *gajadantaphalā*, and *muni* [are synonyms]. (RājN 7.196–197)
The *ḍāṅgarī* fruit is cooling, appetizing, and a conqueror of the humors of wind, bile, and blood;
it cures consumption, is nourishing, sweet, removes numbness, and relieves urinary obstruction.
(Rājani 7.198) The young fruit of the *ḍāṅgarika* is very sweet, cooling, and a remover of bile; it destroys thirst and burning sensations, promotes appetite, is nourishing, and bestows nourishment.
This fruit awakens vigor, bestows strength, and destroys the fatigue of delusion; when ripe, it is sweet, yet it increases thirst, causes a burning sensation, and is heavy for the blood.

(Rajni 7.199) Now, the *kharbujā* has sweet fruit, six stripes, and is round; the *karkaṭī* is bitter. The *tiktaphalā* has a sweet post-digestive effect (*pāka*). The *vṛttavāru* and the six-faced (*ṣaṇmukhā*) are also varieties; thus there are nine types. (Rajni 7.200)

Bitter when raw, then sweet and slightly sour upon ripening, once fully cooked it is like nectar—satisfying, nourishing, aphrodisiac, a pacifier of burning sensations and fatigue, a purifier of the urine, a remover of bile-induced insanity, a provider of phlegm, and a producer of virility; such is the kharbuja fruit. (Rajni 7.201) Now, as for the karkaṭī: its leaves are pungent, it cures vomiting and other ailments, treats chronic rhinitis, and its fruit is used for urinary disorders.
Trapusī, hastiparṇī, and lomaśakaṇṭā are the nine names for mūtralā (the cucumber).
Karkaṭī is sweet and cooling; its skin is bitter and conquers phlegm and bile.
When ripe, it causes blood disorders but destroys the pain of urinary obstruction.

The fruit of the *karkaṭikā* alleviates urinary retention, promotes copious urination, cures dysuria and calculi, and subdues *pitta*. It removes vomiting and fatigue, wards off excessive burning sensations, is appetizing, dispels *śleṣman*, and is light.
(Rājani 7.204) *Trapusī*, *pītapuṣpī*, *kaṇṭālu*, *trapusa*, and *karkaṭī* [are synonyms].

The *muni* fruit is very fruitful, has a sheathed fruit, and possesses a bulbous fruit. The *trapusī* fruit is appetizing, sweet, cooling, and heavy; it removes dizziness, bile, burning sensations, and pain, induces vomiting, and increases urine.
The *ervāru* is called *karkaṭī*, *vyālapattrā*, and *lomaśā*;
it is also known as *sthūlā*, *toyaphalā*, and *hastidantaphalā*, according to the Sage.
*Ervāruka* removes bile, is very cooling, cures urinary diseases, is sweet, and provides appetite.

When consumed in abundance, it removes heat and fainting, provides great satisfaction, yet provokes the wind (*vāta*). (Rajni 7.208) Now, there is the *vālukī*, the *bahuphalā*, the *snigdhaphalā*, the *kṣetrakarkaṭī*, the *kṣetraruhā*, the autumnal *madhuraphalā*, and the small *ervāru* with yellow flowers. (Rajni 7.209)
Vālukī is sweet, cooling, relieves flatulence, and removes fatigue;
it pacifies pitta and blood disorders, improves the appetite, and causes cough and chronic rhinitis.
All types of vālukā are difficult to digest and heavy.
They make the digestive fire weak and cure vāta-rakta.
(Rājñī 7.211) Vālukī, grown in autumn, causes the defects born of the rainy season; however, that grown in winter is indeed a remover of pitta and is appetizing.
When half-ripe, it quickly causes chronic catarrh (pīnasa), but when fully ripe, it is exceedingly sweet and produces phlegm (kapha). (Rājñī 7.212)
Cīnakarkaṭikā is known as well as bījakarkaṭikā;
it is very long with striped fruit, while kulakakarkaṭī is like arrows.
Cīnakarkaṭikā is appetizing, cooling, and destroys bile (pitta).
It is sweet, satiating, pleasing to the heart, and removes burning sensations and dryness.
(Rājñī 7.214) The *cirbhiṭā* is called *sucitrā*, *citraphalā*, *kṣetracirbhiṭā*, *pāṇḍuphalā*, *pathyā*, *rocanaphalā*, *cirbhiṭikā*, *karkaṭikā*, and *grahasaṃkhyā*. (Rājñī 7.215)
In its raw state, the *cirbhiṭā* is bitter, slightly sour, and sweet; it is digestive and pungent upon digestion.
When dried, it is dry, destroys phlegm, wind, and loss of appetite, cures numbness, and is both appetizing and digestive. *Śaśāṇḍulī*, *bahuphalā*, *taṇḍulī*, and *kṣetrasambhavā* [are synonyms].

The *kṣudrāmlā* has hairy fruit and smoky, round fruit. The *śaśāṇḍulī* is bitter and pungent; when tender it is combined with pungency and sourness, but when mature it removes phlegm (*kapha*). Upon digestion, it is sour and sweet, causes a burning sensation (*vidāha*), and increases phlegm; when dried, it stimulates the appetite and is digestive.
Kuḍuhuñcī, śrīphalikā, and that which has leaves as its fruit;
it is also called śubhravī, kāravī, bahuphalā, kṣudrakāralikā, and should be known as kandalatā. (Rājñī 7.219)
The *kṣudrādikāravallī* is said to have nine names.
It is pungent, hot, bitter, appetizing, and a stimulant of digestion;
it aggravates blood and wind disorders, yet it is also declared wholesome when its fruit is consumed.
The *kāralī* root destroys hemorrhoids, purifies obstructions of the waste,
removes disorders from the female reproductive tract, and cures miscarriages and poisons.
(Rajni 7.222) Thus ends the detailed description of the names, qualities, and the beautiful sequence of its roots, tubers, fruits, and leaves.

Having observed this group, let the wise man understand it as the application of medicine appropriate for disease. (Rajñī 7.223) This is declared to be the "Group of Leafy Vegetables" (*śākavarga*), which serves as the basis for those leafy vegetables who, by their own power, support even those with weak digestion and loss of appetite who subsist on stone. (Rajñī 7.224)
The virtuous constantly praise him, saying: "This is an incarnation of the twin Aśvins, who removed the stain of doubt from the family of physicians by providing them with mutual assistance.
This great section beginning with *malaka* is concluded in the work of that illustrious Nṛhari; it is the seventh [section] in this crest-jewel of the assembly of lexicons, the *Rājanighaṇṭu*.
The group beginning with *śālmali*: *śālmalī*, its resin (*niryāsa*), *rohita*, and *ekavīraka*;
then *pāribhadra* and *khadira*; the three types of *ari* are known as *khādira*. (Rajñī 8.1)
Two types of *śamī*, two types of *barbura*, and *arimeda*;
*pakvāṇḍa*, *iṅgudikā*, and *niṣpattrī* are mentioned; and *snuhī* is of two kinds.
*Kaṇṭhārikā*, the three types of *eraṇḍa*, *ghoṇṭā*, and *vallīkarañjaka*.
Kārikā, madana in three varieties, bilva, antara, and taraṭṭikā;
śrīvallī, kuñjikā, and likewise rāmakāṇḍa; sayāvana and ālau, the two types of śara, muñja, kāśa, and kuśa in two varieties. Rajni 8.3–4.
Valvaja, kutṛṇa, and then the two types of nala, as well as the four kinds of dūrvā;
kundura is known as bhūtṛṇa, and ikṣudarbhaka is called ukhala. Gomūtrī, śilpī, niśreṇī, garmoṭī, and likewise majjarā.
Giribhū, vaṃśapatrī, manthāna, and pallivāhaka;
paṭutṛṇa and śuka are to be known [as synonyms]; likewise tripaṇyāndha and triguṇḍaka; kaseru is said to be caṇikā, as well as guṇḍālā and śūlikā.
The *paripella*, the *hijjula*, the *sevāla*, and the *śarāṅkadha*;
the *śālmali*—which is long-lived (*cirajīvī*), slimy (*picchila*), and has red flowers;
the *kukkuṭī*, the cotton tree (*tūlavṛkṣa*), and the thorny tree known as *mocā*.

The *raktaphala* (red-fruit), *ramyapuṣpa* (beautiful-flowered), *bahuvīrya* (highly potent), and *yamadruma* (Yama-tree) trees; the *dīrghadruma* (long tree), *sthūlaphala* (thick-fruited), and *dīrghāyus* (long-lived) trees, which are measured by the lunar days (*tithi*). The *śālmalī* (silk-cotton tree) is slimy, aphrodisiac, strengthening, sweet, and cooling.
The astringent taste is light, unctuous, and increases semen and phlegm.
Its juice possesses those same qualities; it is astringent, constipating, and destroys phlegm.
The flower is likewise described as such, and its fruit is of the same nature.
Mocarasa, moca, mocasrāva, mocaniryāsa, picchilasāra, surasa, śālmaliveṣṭa, and mocasāra [are synonyms].
Mocarasa is astringent; when used in combination, it removes phlegm and wind and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
It bestows strength, nourishment, complexion, vigor, wisdom, longevity, and bodily perfection,
and it is astringent. *Rohītaka*, *rohitaka*, *rohita*, *kuśālmalī*,
known as *dāḍimapuṣpa*, *sadāprasūna*, *kūṭaśālmalī*, *virocana*, and *śālmalika*— it has these nine names.
Saptāhva, Śvetarohita, Sitapuṣpa, Sitāhvaya, Sitāṅga, Śuklarohita, Lakṣmīvān, and Janavallabha— these are the varieties of Rohitaka.
They are pungent, unctuous, astringent, and very cooling.
It removes worms, defects, ulcers, splenic disorders, blood diseases, and eye ailments.
"Ekavīra," "Mahāvīra," "Sakṛdvīra," "Suvīraka," and "Vīra"—
it has these six names according to its synonyms such as Ekavīra and the rest.

The *ekavīra* is hot and pungent; it removes piercing pain and wind, and cures sciatica, pain in the hips and back, and injuries to the wings [of the body]. Now, there is the *pāribhadra*, the *mandāra*, the *pārijātaka*, and the *nimbataru*.
Raktakusuma, krimighna, bahupuṣpa, raktakesara, and vasava;
the pāribhadra is pungent and hot, it destroys phlegm and wind,
removes loss of appetite, is wholesome, and is proclaimed to be a digestive stimulant.
The *khadira* tree has young leaves, it is edible, leafy, and patient upon the earth;
it possesses excellent thorns, has curved spines, is a limb of the sacrifice, and serves as a tooth-cleansing stick.
It is also known as *gāyatrī*, *jihmaśalya*, *kaṇṭī*, and *sāradruma*.

Kuṣṭhāri, Bahusāra, and Medhya—these are its seventeen names. Khadira is bitter in taste and cooling; it subdues pitta and kapha, acts as a digestive, and cures skin diseases, cough, hemorrhaging, swelling, itching, and ulcers.
*Khadira* is white-pithed; another is *kārmuka*, *kubjakaṇṭaka*, *somasāra*, *nemivṛkṣa*, *somavalka*, and *pathidruma*. White *khadira* is bitter, astringent, pungent, and hot.
It destroys itching, spirits, and leprosy, and removes phlegm, wind, and wounds.
It is called *rakta*, *raktasāra*, *susāra*, *tāmrakaṇṭaka*,
*bahuśalya*, *yājñika*, and *kuṣṭhatodana*.
The sacrificial post tree (yūpadruma), red khadira, and aparuśa are recorded as ten types.
Red khadira is pungent and hot; it is astringent, heavy, and bitter.
It destroys undigested matter, wind, blood disorders, and wind-diseases, and it removes wounds, malevolent spirits, and fever.
Viṭkhadira, kāmbhojī, kālaskandha, goraṭa, maruja, pattratara, bahusāra, saṃsāra, khādīra, graha, mahāsāra,
and viṭkhadira are pungent, hot, and bitter; they remove the disorders arising from blood and wounds.
It destroys itching, poison, erysipelas, fever, leprosy, insanity, and possession by spirits.
*Arī* is known as *saṃdānikā*, *dālā*, and *khadirapattrikā*.
*Arī* is astringent, pungent, and bitter; it cures blood disorders and pitta.
Khādira is that which arises from the *khadira* tree; its essence (*sāra*) is known as Raṅgada.
It should be understood that Khadirasāra and Raṅga likewise have six names.
Khādira-sāra is pungent, bitter, and hot; it removes phlegm and wind.
It destroys wounds and throat diseases, provides relish, and is a supreme digestive stimulant. Śamī, Śāntā, Tuṅgā, Kacaripuphalā, Keśamathanī, Śiveśā, Naur, Lakṣmī, Tapanatanunaṣṭā, and Śubhakarī;
Havirgandhā, Medhyā, Duritaśamanī, Śaṅkuphalikā, Subhadrā, Maṅgalyā, Surabhi, and Pāpaśamanī. (Rājñī 8.32–33)
Bhadrā, Śaṅkarī, Keśahantrī, Śivāphalā, Supattrā, and Sukhadā are considered to be the twenty-five names [of this plant].
Śamī is parching and astringent; it conquers hemorrhaging, bilious fever, and dysentery.

Its fruit is heavy, sweet, bitter, and hot, and it destroys the hair. Śamī, however, is of two kinds: Śāntā, Śubhā, Bhadrā, Aparājitā, Jayā, and Vijayā; these possess the qualities previously mentioned.
Barbura, yugalākṣa, kaṇṭālu, tīkṣṇakaṇṭaka,
gośṛṅga, paṅktibīja, dīrghakaṇṭa, kaphāntaka, dṛḍhabīja, and śvāsabhakṣya— these are known as its ten names. (Rajni 8.37)

Barbura is astringent and hot; it removes phlegm, cough, and disease, cures undigested matter (āmadoṣa), blood disorders, and diarrhea, and destroys the pain of bile and burning sensations. There is another variety, Jālabarburaka, also known as Chattrāka or Sthūlakaṇṭaka.

The *ṣaḍāhvaya* tree has fine branches, thin shade, and thorns at its nodes; it is known as *jāla* and *barburaka*. It is parching and destroys diseases caused by wind (*vāta*), but increases bile (*pitta*). Being astringent and hot, it removes phlegm (*kapha*) yet causes a burning sensation.
Irimeda, arimeda, godhāskandha, arimedaka,
ahimeda, ahimāra, śitameda, and ahimedaka;
arimeda is astringent, hot, bitter, and a destroyer of malevolent spirits.
It destroys swelling, diarrhea, and cough, and it eradicates poison and erysipelas. Pakvaṇḍa increases the five [elements] fivefold and protects the five;
it is recommended for the application of collyrium for vision, is pungent, and removes chronic fever.
Iṅgudī, hiṅgupattra, viṣakaṇṭha, and anilāntaka;
gaura is said to be supattra, śūlāri, and tāpasadruma. Tīkṣṇakaṇṭa, tailaphala, pūtigandha, and vigandhaka.
The *kroṣṭuphala* tree is known by names numbered by fire (three) and moon (one), that is, four;
[its fruit is] pungent, hot, frothy, and light.
It is an elixir (*rasāyana*) that destroys parasites, diseases of wind (*vāta*), phlegm disorders, and wounds. (Rajni 8.45–46)
The *niṣpattraka*, the *karīra*, the *karīragranthila*,
the *kṛkara*, the *gūḍhapattra*, the *karaka*, and the *tīkṣṇakaṇṭaka*—
this *karīra* causes flatulence, is astringent, pungent, and hot; it produces an abundance of phlegm (*kapha*).
It removes the defects of breathlessness, wind-disorders, loss of appetite, all types of colic, vomiting, itching, and wounds. Snuhī, sudhā, mahāvṛkṣa, kṣīrī, nistriṃśapattrikā,
śākhākaṇṭa, guṇḍā, sehuṇḍa, and vajrakaṇṭaka are its names.
Bahuśākha, Vajravṛkṣa, Vātāri, Kṣīrakāṇḍaka, Bhadra, Vyāghranakha, Netrāri, Daṇḍavṛkṣaka, Samantadugdha, Gaṇḍīra, and Snuk— these twenty are to be known [as the medicinal plants]. (Rājñī 8.50)
Snuhī is hot; it destroys pitta, burning sensations, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), vāta, and urinary disorders (prameha).

Its milk is an excellent remedy for vāta, poisons, flatulence, abdominal tumors (gulma), and abdominal enlargements (udara). There is another type of snuhī called tridhārā, so named because it has three streams [of latex].

This plant, possessing the qualities previously mentioned, specifically bestows the accomplishment of the *rasa*. It is known by eight names: *kaṇṭhārī*, *katharī*, *kaṇṭhā*, *durdharṣā*, *tīkṣṇakaṇṭakā*, *tīkṣṇagandhā*, *krūragandhā*, and *duṣpraveśā*. (Rājñī 8.52–53)

*Kanthārī* is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, alleviates swelling, stimulates digestion, improves appetite, and removes the pain of blood-nodules (*raktagranthi*). (Rajni 8.54) *Śvetairaṇḍa*, *sitairaṇḍa*, *citra*, and *gandharvahastaka* are synonyms for white castor-oil plant.
Āmaṇḍa, taruṇa, śukla, vātāri, dīrghadaṇḍaka,
pañcāṅgula, vardhamāna, and ruvuka— these are the twelve names [of one plant].
Another is raktairaṇḍa, also known as vyāghra, hastikarṇa, and ruvu.
Uruvūka, nāgakarṇa, cañcu, uttānapattraka, karaparṇa, yācanaka, snigdha, vyāghradala,
tatkara, citrabīja, and hrasvairaṇḍa— thus the eraṇḍa is of fifteen kinds.
White castor (*śvetairaṇḍa*) is slightly bitter, pungent, and hot; it destroys afflictions caused by *kapha*, removes fever, cures wind-disorders and cough, and is worthy of being used as a juice.
Red castor (*raktairaṇḍa*) promotes the maturation of swellings and is light; it removes vomiting, blood-afflictions, anemia, vertigo, dyspnea, fever, and *kapha*, and destroys loss of appetite.
The thick-stemmed castor (*sthūlairaṇḍa*), the large castor (*mahairaṇḍa*), and others such as the great five-fingered plant (*mahāpañcāṅgula*) are likewise known.
The large castor plant (*sthūlairaṇḍa*) is rich in qualities regarding its taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation.
Ghoṇṭā, badarikā, ghoṭī, golikā, śatrukaṇṭaka,
karkaṭī, turaṅgī, and turagāhvā are known as the eight varieties [of the jujube].
Ghoṭikā is pungent and hot, yet sweet; it destroys wind disorders and removes wounds, itching, leprosy, blood disorders, and swelling. Latākarañja, Duḥsparśa, Vīrāsya, and Vajravīraka [are synonyms].
Dhanadākṣa, kaṇṭaphala, and kuberākṣa are its seven names.
The leaf of latākarañja is pungent and hot; it subdues phlegm and wind.
Its seed is digestive, wholesome, and removes the pain of colic and abdominal tumors.
Kārī, kārikā, kāryā, girijā, and kaṭupattrikā are synonyms;
among them, one is kaṇṭakārī, while the other is ākarṣakārikā.
Kārī is astringent and sweet, and both varieties destroy pitta.
It is illuminating, astringent, palatable, a cleanser of the throat,
and heavy. Madana, śalyaka, kaiḍarya, piṇḍī, dhārāphala, taraṭa, karahāṭa, rāhu, and piṇḍātaka are known as synonyms for it.
Kaṇṭāla, viṣamuṣṭi, chardana, viṣapuṣpaka,
ghaṇṭāla, mādana, harṣa, ghaṇṭākhya, vastirodhana,
granthiphala, golaphala, and madanāhva— these are the twenty names [of the Madana tree]. (RājNī 8.67)

Madana is pungent, bitter, and hot; it removes phlegm, wind, and wounds, cures swelling and disorders, and is highly recommended for emesis. Another variety is the Vārāha, which is black in color, large, and known as Mahāpiṇḍītaka.
There is another, the *snigdhapiṇḍītaka*, as well as the *sthūlavṛkṣaphala*. Two other excellent types of *madana* possess pungent and bitter tastes;
they induce vomiting and cleanse the heart, the diseases of *kapha*, and both the receptacle of undigested food (*āmāśaya*) and the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*).
The *bilvāntara*, *cīravṛkṣa*, *kṣudhākuśalasaṃjñaka*, *dīrghamūla*, *vīravṛkṣa*, and *kṛcchrāri* are the six names [of this plant].
The *bilvāntara* is pungent and hot; it destroys urinary distress (*kṛcchra*) and alleviates pain in the joints.
It kindles the digestive fire, is wholesome, and destroys diseases caused by Vāta. Taraṭī, tāraṭī, tīvrā, kharburā, and raktabījakā—
among these, taraṭī is bitter-sweet, heavy, strengthening, and removes phlegm (kapha).
Śrīvallī, Śivavallī, Kaṇṭavallī, Śītalā, Amlā,
Kaṭuphalā, Aśvatthā, and Durārohā— thus it is eightfold.
Śrīvallī is pungent and sour, and it removes wind, swelling, and phlegm.
Its fruit destroys the application of oil, is extremely sour, and is a supreme promoter of appetite.
(8.75) Another plant called Nikuñjikāmlā—also known as Kuñjikā and Kuñjavallarī—is called Nikuñjikā by the wise; it resembles Śrīvallī in its qualities. (8.76)
The *aparvadaṇḍa*, the long *rāmabāṇa* beloved by kings,
the *rāmakāṇḍa*, the *rāmaśara*, and the arrow of Rāma (*rāmeṣu*)— these are the seven [varieties].
The root of the *rāmakāṇḍaja* is slightly warm and provides relish.
In taste, it is sour and astringent; it generates pitta and removes kapha and vāta.
(Rajni 8.78) Then there is yāvanāla, nadīja, dṛḍhatvak, vārisambhava, yāvanālanibha, and kharapattra—these are its six names. (Rajni 8.79)
The root of the *yāvanāla* and *śara* grasses is slightly sweet and pleasant,
cooling, a destroyer of bile and thirst, and provides strength to animals.
(Rajñī 8.80) *Śara*, *bāṇa*, *iṣu*, *kāṇḍa*, *utkaṭa*, *sāyaka*, and *kṣura* are synonyms for an arrow.
The *ikṣura*, the *kṣurikāpattra*, and the *viśikha*—these are the ten names [of the arrow].
Another is the thick one (*sthūla*), the thick-arrowed (*sthūlaśara*), the great-arrowed (*mahāśara*), and that which is called the thick-pointed shaft (*sthūlasāyakamukha*).
The sages have named the *ikṣuraka*, the *kṣurapattra*, the many-rooted (*bahumūla*), and the long-rooted (*dīrghamūlaka*).
The two types of *śara* grass are sweet, very bitter, and slightly warm; they remove phlegm, dizziness, and intoxication.
When consumed regularly, they always provide strength and virility, though they slightly increase wind (*vāta*).
*Muñja* is known as *mauñjītṛṇa* and is called *tejanā*; it is sacred to Brahmā.
Vānīraja, muñjanaka, śārī, and that which is called darbha;
dūramūla, dṛḍhatṛṇa, dṛḍhamūla, bahupraja, rañjana,
and śatrubhaṅga— these are its fourteen names.
Muñja grass is sweet and cooling; it conquers the disorders born of phlegm and bile.
It is purifying for rites of initiation and protection against planetary spirits, and it destroys malevolent beings.
Kāśa is known as kāṇḍekṣu, ikṣvāri, kākekṣu, and vāyasekṣuka.
Ikṣura, ikṣukāṇḍa, śārada, sitapuṣpaka,
nādeya, darbhapattra, lekhana, kāṇḍa, kāṇḍaka,
and kaṇṭhālaṃkāraka— these are known as the fifteen names.
Kāśa is cooling, sweet, appetizing, and removes bile and burning sensations;
it is nourishing, strength-promoting, aphrodisiac, and cures consumption caused by undigested matter (āma).
Another variety is miśira, also known as gaṇḍā, aśvāla, nīraja, and śara.
Misira is sweet and cooling; it removes bile, burning sensations, and consumption.
Sitadarbha, hrasvakumbha, pūta, yajñiyapattraka, vajra, brahmapavitra, tīkṣṇa, and yajñasya bhūṣaṇa are synonyms for it.
Sūcīmukha, puṇyatṛṇa, vahni, pūtatṛṇa, and dviṣaṭ are synonyms for *darbha* grass.
The root of *darbha* is cooling, appetizing, sweet, and a destroyer of bile;
it cures blood-fever, thirst, dyspnea, jaundice, and disorders of wasting.
Kuśa, anya, śarapattra, haridgarbha, pṛthucchada, śārī,
rūkṣadarbha, dīrghapattra, and pavitraka— these are the types of darbha grass. Two types of darbha are equal in quality, yet the white one is superior.
If, however, white kuśa grass is unavailable, the physician may employ other alternatives:
balvaja, dṛḍhapattrī, tṛṇekṣu, tṛṇabalvaja, mauñjīpattrā, dṛḍhatṛṇā, pānīyāśvā, and dṛḍhakṣurā.
Balvajā is sweet, cooling, and removes bile, burning sensations, and thirst;
it aggravates wind (vāta), is appetizing, and is excellent for cleansing the throat.
(Rajni 8.96) Kutṛṇa, kattṛṇa, bhūti, bhūtika, and rohiṣa are synonyms for tṛṇa grass.
Śyāmaka, dhyāmaka, pūti, mudgala, and davadagdhaka,
along with kutṛṇa and daśanāmāḍhya, remove phlegm (kapha) due to their pungent and bitter qualities;
they destroy the defects caused by weapons and foreign bodies, and eradicate afflictions by malevolent spirits (bālagraha).
Another variety is the long *rohiṣaka*, which has firm stalks and firm leaves;
it is the longest, possesses a long stalk, and has a bitter pith, being considered inferior.
Long *rohiṣaka* is bitter, pungent, and hot; it conquers phlegm and wind.
It destroys spirits, seizing demons, and poisons, and it heals wounds and injuries.
Nāla, Naḍa, Nala, Kukṣirandhra, Kīcaka, Vaṃśāntara, Dhamana, Śūnyamadhyha, and Vibhīṣaṇa— [these are its names].
Chidrānta, mṛdupattra, randhrapattra, mṛducchada, nālavaṃśa, and poṭagala— these are its five names. Nala is cool, astringent, sweet, and appetizing.
It pacifies *raktapitta*, stimulates digestion, and increases virility.
Another is *mahānala*, *vanya*, *devanala*, and the best of *nalas*;
it is also called *sthūlanāla*, *sthūladaṇḍa*, *suranāla*, and *suradruma*.
Devanāla is extremely sweet, aphrodisiac, and slightly astringent;
*nala* is superior in potency and is recommended for the preparation of medicinal juices.
*Nīladūrvā*, *haritā*, *śāmbhavī*, *śyāmā*, *śāntā*, *śataparvikā*, and *amṛtā* [are synonyms].
Pūtā, śatagranthi, anuṣṇavallikā, śivā, śiveṣṭā, maṅgalā, jayā, subhagā, bhūtahantrī, śatamūlā, mahauṣadhī,
amṛtā, vijayā, gaurī, and śāntā— these constitute the twenty-one [names].
Blue dūrvā grass is sweet, bitter, cooling, and appetizing;
it cures hemorrhaging and diarrhea, and removes phlegm, wind, and fever.
(Rajñī 8.108) White dūrvā is known as golomī, sitā, caṇḍā, bhadrā, bhārgavī, and durmarā.
Gaurī, beloved of Vighneśāna, Anantā, Śvetā, Divyā, Śvetakāṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā;
Sahasravīryā, Sahasrakāṇḍā, Sahasraparvā, and Suravallabhā;
Śubhā, Suparvā, Sitacchadā, Svacchā, Kacchāntaruhā, and Abdhihastā. (Rājñī 8.109–110)

White *dūrvā* is extremely cooling, sweet, and overcomes vomiting and *pitta*; it destroys undigested matter (*āma*), diarrhea, and cough; it improves the appetite and removes burning sensations and thirst. (RājN 8.111) *Mālādūrvā*, *vallidūrvā*, *alidūrvā*, *mālāgranthi*, *granthilā*, and *granthidūrvā* [are synonyms].

The root-knot (mūlagranthi), the creeper-knot (vallarīgranthi), the joint-growing (rohatparvā), the joint-creeper (parvavallī), and that called white (sitākhyā)—these are the dūrvā creepers. They are very sweet and bitter, and they are cooling;
they pacify the disorder of bile and remove phlegm, vomiting, and thirst. (Rajñī 8.112)

Gaṇḍālī is gaṇḍadūrvā; atitīvrā is matsyākṣī, also known as vāruṇī and mīnanetrā. Śyāmagranthi is granthilā and granthiparṇī; growing in water, it has needle-like leaves (sūcīpatrā), dark stems (śyāmakāṇḍā), and is called śakulākṣī, kalāyā, and citrā—thus having fifteen names.
Gaṇḍadūrvā is sweet, removes fever caused by vāta and pitta, is cooling, destroys the dual humors (dvaṃdvadoṣa), and alleviates vertigo, thirst, and fatigue.
Dūrvā grasses are astringent, sweet, and cold; they destroy pitta, thirst, loss of appetite, and vomiting.

It always provides relief from fainting, seizures, and possession by spirits, and it bestows satisfaction while destroying phlegm and fatigue. Kunduru, kandura, ruṇḍī, dīrghapattra, kharacchada, rasābha, kṣetrasambhūta, sutṛṣṇa, and mṛgavallabha are its names.
Gaulya and the root of kunduruka are cooling, they cure pitta-type diarrhea,
are recommended for purificatory therapies, and increase strength and nourishment.
Bhūtṛṇa, rohiṇa, bhūti, bhūtika, and kuṭumbaka are synonyms.
Mālātṛṇa, Sumālī, Chattra, and likewise Atichattraka; Guhyabīja, Sugandha, Gulāla, Puṃstvavigraha,
Badhira, Atigandha, Śṛṅgaroha, and Rasenduka.
Bhūtṛṇa is pungent and bitter; it destroys wind and fever, and it kills possession by spirits and demons as well as terrible poisons.
There is another fragrant bhūtṛṇa called surasa and likewise surabhi.
Gandhatṛṇa, sugandha, mukhavāsa, and ṣaḍāhvaya are its six names.
Gandhatṛṇa is fragrant, slightly bitter, and an elixir (rasāyana);
it is unctuous, sweet, and cooling, and it removes phlegm, bile, and fatigue.
Ukhalo, bhūripattra, sutṛṇa, and tṛṇottama;
ukhalo bestows strength, is pleasing to the taste, and is always beneficial for livestock.
Ikṣudarbhā, sudarbhā, pattrālu, and tṛṇapattrikā.
Ikṣudarbha is known to be very sweet, unctuous, slightly astringent,
a destroyer of phlegm and bile, appetizing, light, and nourishing. Gomūtrikā is a red grass that grows in fields and on black soil.
Gomūtrikā is sweet, aphrodisiac, and provides cow’s milk. Śilpikā, śilpinī, kṣetrajā, and mṛducchadā are cooling;
śilpikā is sweet and cooling, and its seeds bestow strength and virility.
Niḥśreṇikā, Śreṇikā, Nīrasā, Vanavallarī,
Niḥśreṇikā, Nīrasoṣṇā, Paśūnām-abalapradā,
Garbhoṭikā, Sunīlā, Jaraḍī, and Jalāśrayā. (Rājñī 8.129–130)
Jaraḍī is sweet, cooling, nourishing, and a remover of burning sensations;
it cures blood disorders, is appetizing, and provides milk for livestock. Majjara is said to be wind-alleviating, while sutṛṇa has glossy leaves.
It has soft joints, is sweet, and yields the milk of a cow.
Abounding in grass and mountain-turf, rich in leaves, and dear to deer,
it provides strength and nourishment, is appetizing, and is always beneficial for livestock.
Vaṃśapattrī, vaṃśadalā, jīrikā, and jīrṇapattrikā are synonyms for vaṃśapattrī.
It is very sweet, cooling, and destroys bile;
it removes blood disorders, is appetizing, and provides milk for animals. (Rajñī 8.134)
Manthānaka is green, has firm roots, and is the lord of grasses;
it is glossy, dear to cows, milky, sweet, and possesses great potency.
Pallivāha is long-grained, has beautiful leaves, and is copper-colored.
The *adṛḍha* grass, *śākapattrādi*, and others provide strength to cattle.
*Lavaṇatṛṇa* (salt-grass), *loṇatṛṇa*, *tṛṇāmla*, *paṭutṛṇaka*, and *amlakāṇḍa*;
as well as *kaṭutṛṇaka*, *kṣārāmla*, and *kaṣāyastanya*—these increase the vigor of horses.
*Paṇyāndha*, *kaṅgunīpattra*, *paṇyāndhā*, and *paṇadhā*—these are its names. *Paṇyāndhā* is equal in potency to [the others]; it is bitter, alkaline, and laxative.
It is supreme for healing wounds caused by weapons at the time of injury.
The *paṇyāndhā* is known to be of three kinds—long, medium, and short—and it bestows qualities that are middling in terms of taste (*rasa*), potency (*vīrya*), and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*).
The *guṇḍa*, however, is the *kāṇḍaguṇḍa*; it has long stalks and is triangular in shape.
The *chattraguñcha*, the *asipattra*, the *nīlapattra*, and the *tridhāraka*;
the *vṛttaguṇḍa*, another *vṛtta*, and the *dīrghanāla* which dwells in water;
there is also another, the *sthūla* and the *laghu*—thus this [lotus] is of twelve names, divided into three types.

Guṇḍa tubers are sweet, cooling, and they remove phlegm, bile, and diarrhea; they alleviate burning sensations and blood disorders, and among them, the thicker variety is superior. Guṇḍakaṇḍa is *kaseru*, which is the same as *kṣudramustā* and *kaserukā*.
Śūkareṣṭa, sugandhi, sukanda, and gandhakandaka;
kaseruka is astringent, slightly sweet, and very hard.
It pacifies raktapitta (blood-bile), is cooling, and removes burning sensations and fatigue.
The Caṇikā yields milk, is sweet, very dark blue, grows in cultivated fields, and is cool;
it is aphrodisiac, strengthening, extremely sweet, beneficial for livestock through its seeds, and nourishing through its grasses.
Guṇḍāsinī, however, is known as guṇḍā, guṇḍālā, gucchamūlakā, and cipiṭā.
Tṛṇapattrī, jalavāsā, pṛthulā, suviṣṭarā, and navāhvā are synonyms for guṇḍāsinī.
It is pungent in taste, removes bile, burning sensations, and fatigue;
it is bitter and hot, destroys swelling, and eradicates the defects of wounds.
Śūlī, however, is also called śūlapattrī, aśākhā, dhūmramūlikā,
jalāśrayā, mṛdulatā, picchilā, and mahiṣīpriyā. Śūlī is slimy, hot, heavy, sweet, and bestows strength.
It removes burning sensations caused by pitta, is appetizing, and promotes the increase of breast milk.
Paripella, plava, dhānya, gopuṭa, kuṭannaṭa, sitapuṣpa, dāsapura, gonarda, and jīrṇabudhnaka are synonyms for this plant.

Paripella is pungent and hot; it destroys phlegm and wind, cures burning sensations in wounds, colic, and fever, and is supreme for removing blood disorders. *Hijjala*, *nadīkānta*, *jalaja*, and *dīrghapatraka* [are synonyms].

The *nicula* growing by rivers is called *rakta* and *kārmuka*. The *hijjala* is pungent and hot; it is purifying, destroys malevolent spirits (*bhūta*), removes diseases of wind (*vāta*), and overcomes the defects caused by the movement of various planetary influences (*graha*).
"Śaivāla is known as jalanīlī and śaivala; it grows in water.
Śaivāla is cooling, unctuous, and destroys fever and wounds. (Rajni 8.155).
Thus, [this section] is rich with an extensive treatment of grasses such as the castor plant (*eraṇḍa*), as explained in the context of various thorny shrubs and trees.

A learned physician, desiring to be known for his proficiency in the field of medicine, should study this section on the qualities of cultivated and wild medicinal plants. This section, esteemed by the virtuous, brings relief to those afflicted by the fear of cruel diseases—those that are difficult to ward off, which break down even those who know how to treat themselves, which are exceedingly hard to bear, and which, though subtle, manifest with violent force; it is indeed a source of peace for those who dwell within the vast wilderness of the great medical scriptures.

He who is the king of the twice-born (*dvija*) triumphs by composing this collection of medicinal plants (*oṣadhigaṇa*), and he is esteemed as one who maintains the state of being a bestower of immortality (*amṛtakara*) for men. This section of his work, composed by Nṛhari, seeks its place within the composition of that crest-jewel of names, the *Rājanighaṇṭu*, beginning with the *śālmali* and others, [numbered] by the eight Vasus.
The group beginning with *prabhadrā* consists of five types: *kāśmarya* preceded by "light" (*laghu*), two kinds of *agnimantha*, two kinds of *śyonāka*, and *ajaśṛṅgikā*. (Rajni 9.1)
Then there are *kāśmarī*, *aśmantaka*, and likewise the two types of *karṇikāra*;
*vṛścikālī*, *kuṭaja*, its seeds, and *śirīṣaka*;
the six kinds of *karañja*, *aṅkola*, *nīla*, *sarja*, and *aśvakarṇaka*.
The *tāla*, the auspicious *tāla*, the *hintāla*, the *māḍa*, the *tūla*, and the *tamālaka*; the fourfold *kadamba*, then the *vānīra*, the *kumbhīvetasa*,
the *dhava*, the *dhanvana*, the *bhūrja*, the *tiniśa*, and then the *arjuna*.
The haridru, dagdha, and śākhoṭa; then the śāka and the triad of śiṃśapās; the three types of asana, the varuṇa, and the piṇḍikā;
the kāraskara, the two types of kaṭabhī, the kṣavaka, and the devasarṣapa.
The ḍahu, the vikaṅkata, and the *svarābdhi*— these are enumerated in sequence.
Now, the prabhadraka, picumanda, pāribhadraka,
nimba, kākaphala, kīreṣṭa, netāriṣṭa, and sarvatobhadra have been declared.
Dhamana, viśīrṇaparṇa, pavaneṣṭa, pītasāraka, śīta, varatikta,
ariṣṭaphala, jyeṣṭhāmālaka, hiṅguniryāsa, chardana,
and agnidhamana— these are known as the twenty names [of this plant].
Prabhadraka is cooling and bitter; it prevails for the pacification of phlegm, wounds, worms, vomiting, and swellings.
It destroys *balāsa*, conquers many poisons and disorders of *pitta*, and especially brings relief from burning sensations in the heart.
Mahānimba is also known as Madodreka, Kārmuka, and Keśamuṣṭika.
Kākāṇḍa, Ramyaka, Akṣīra, Mahātikta, and Himadruma;
Mahānimba is cooling, astringent, pungent, and bitter. It destroys hemorrhaging, burning sensations, and phlegm, and it is a destroyer of intermittent fevers.
