Kaiḍarya, mahānimba, rāmaṇa, ramaṇa,
girinimba, mahāriṣṭa, śuklaśāla, and kaphāhvaya are synonyms.
Kaiḍarya is pungent, bitter, astringent, cooling, and light.

It removes fever, wasting, leprosy, blood disorders, worms, spirits, and poison. Bhūnimba is known as nāryatikta, kairāta, and rāmasenaka; it is also called kairātatiktaka, haima, kāṇḍatikta, and kirātaka.
Bhūnimba is wind-aggravating (vātala), bitter, and it removes phlegm, bile, and fever;
it heals wounds, is wholesome, and destroys skin diseases, itching, and swelling.
Nepālanimba, naipāla, tṛṇanimba, and jvarāntaka [are synonyms].
Nāḍītikta and Ardhatikta are enemies of sleep and destroyers of *saṃnipāta* disorders. Nepālanimba is cooling and heating, a vehicle for various combinations, and light;
it is bitter and removes excessive phlegm, bile, blood disorders, swelling, thirst, and fever.
Kaṇḍūla, Kṛṣṇagarbha, Somavalka, Pracetasī, Bhadrāvatī, Mahākumbhī, Kaiḍarya, Rāmasenaka, Kumuda, Ugragandha, Bhadrā, and likewise Rañjanaka.

Kumbhī, laghukāśmarya, and śrīparṇī are of three and five kinds respectively. Kaṭphala is pungent and hot; it removes cough, dyspnea, and fever, alleviates severe burning sensations, improves the appetite, and brings relief to diseases of the mouth.
Agnimantha, agnimathana, tarkārī,
vaijayantikā, vahnimantha, araṇī, ketu, śrīparṇī, karṇikā, jayā, nādeyī, vijayā, and anantā— these thirteen are synonyms for the plant known as *nadyāmalakī*. (RājNī 9.22)
*Tarkārī* is pungent and hot; it is bitter and removes wind and phlegm.
It destroys swelling, phlegm, weak digestion, hemorrhoids, constipation, and flatulence. *Kṣudrāgnimantha*, *tapanī*, *vijayā*, and *gaṇikārikā*— *The Rājani-guṇa-vidhi*, 9.23–24.1.*
Araṇi, laghumantha, tejovṛkṣa, and tanutvacā—
these two types of agnimantha are equal in their potency, taste, and other qualities;
one should employ them according to the specific application and with one's own discretion.
Śyonāka, śukanāsa, kaṭvaṅga, kaṭaṃbhara,
mayūrajaṅgha, araluka, priyajīva, and kuṭannaṭa; furthermore,
śyonāka, pṛthuśimba, bhallaka, and dīrghavṛntaka.
Potavṛkṣa, ṭeṇṭūka, bhūtasāra, and munidruma;
niḥsāra, phalguvṛntāka, pūtipattra, and vasantaka;
maṇḍūkaparṇa, pītāṅga, jambūka, and pītapādaka.
Vātāri, pītaka, śoṇa, kuṭana, virecana,
bhramareṣṭa, barhijaṅgha, and netranetra— these are its names. The pair of śyonākas is bitter, cooling, and a conqueror of the three doṣas.
It destroys bile and phlegm, cures diarrhea, and removes fevers caused by the combination of all three humors (saṃnipāta).
The *teṇṭu* fruit is pungent and hot, alleviates phlegm and wind, and is light;
it stimulates digestion, promotes the digestion of undigested matter, is beneficial for the heart, improves appetite, and is salty and sour.
Ajaśṛṅgī, meṣaśṛṅgī, vartikā, sarpadaṃṣṭrikā, cakṣuṣyā, tiktadugdhā, putraśreṇī, and viṣāṇikā [are synonyms].
Ajaśṛṅgī is pungent and bitter; it conquers phlegm, hemorrhoids, colic, and swelling.
It is beneficial for the eyes and overcomes diseases of the respiratory system and heart, as well as poison, cough, and severe skin diseases.
(Rajni 9.33) The fruit of *ajaśṛṅgī* is bitter, pungent, and hot; it conquers phlegm and wind.
It stimulates the digestive fire, is beneficial for the heart, and is appetizing, possessing salty and sour qualities. (Rajni 9.34)
Kāśmarya, kāśmarī, kṛṣṇavṛntā, hīrā, bhadrā, and sarvatobhadrikā are synonyms.
Śrīparṇī, sindhuparṇī, subhadrā, kambhārī, kaṭphalā, and bhadraparṇī are also names for it.
Furthermore, kumudā, gopabhadrā, vidāriṇī, kṣīriṇī, and mahābhadrā [are synonyms].
Madhuparṇī, svabhadrā, kṛṣṇā, śvetā, rohiṇī, and gṛṣṭi;
sthūlatvacā, madhumatī, suphalā, medinī, and mahākumudā;
and sudṛḍhatvacā—these are declared to be the twenty-nine names by which she is to be known. (Rājñī 9.36–37)

Kāśmarī is pungent, bitter, heavy, and hot; it destroys phlegm and swelling, and conquers the three doṣas, poison, burning sensations, pain, fever, thirst, and disorders of the blood. Aśmantaka, induka, kuddāla, and amlapattraka [have similar properties].
Ślakṣṇatvak and pīlupattra are known as yamalapattraka. Aśmāntaka, induśapharī, śilānta, and ambuda are known as pāṣāṇāntaka; its name consists of the numbers fire (three) and moon (one).

Aśmantaka is sweet, astringent, and very cooling; it removes *pitta*, conquers urinary disorders (*prameha*), and alleviates burning sensations, thirst, and irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*). It also removes the affliction of poison, vomiting, and subdues malevolent spirits (*bhūta*). (Rajni 9.41) Now, there is the karṇikāra, the rājataru, the pragraha, and the kṛtamāla.
Suphala, parivyādha, vyādhiripu, paṅktibījaka, and vasusaṃjña;
karṇikāra is bitter in taste, pungent and hot, and it removes phlegm and colic.
It destroys abdominal ailments, worms, and urinary disorders, and it prevents wounds and abdominal tumors.
Āragvadha is also called manthāna, rocana, caturaṅgula,
ārevata, dīrghaphala, vyādhighāta, nṛpadruma,
hemapuṣpa, rājataru, kaṇḍūghna, and jvarāntaka.
Aruja, svarṇapuṣpa, svarṇadru, and kuṣṭhasūdana;
it is called karṇābharaṇaka and is known as mahārājadruma;
karṇikāra is said to be mahādi—thus nineteen names have been declared.
Āragvadha is extremely sweet, cooling, and a remover of colic;
it destroys fever, itching, skin diseases, urinary disorders, phlegm, and constipation.
Vṛścikālī and Viṣāṇī are destroyers of poison and cures for eye diseases.
Uṣṭrikā, aliparṇī, and likewise dakṣiṇāvartakī;
kalikā, āgamāvartā, and likewise devalāṅgulikā;
karabhā, bhūridugdhā, karkaśā, and that which is cāmarā. (Rājñī 9.48–49)
Svarṇapuṣpā, Yugmaphalā, Kṣīraviṣāṇikā, Bhāsurapuṣpā, and Vasucandrasamāhvayā are thus described.
Vṛścikālī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it purifies the heart and the mouth.
It cures blood-bile (raktapitta), is strengthening, and removes constipation and loss of appetite. Kuṭaja, kauṭaja, śakra, vatsaka, girimallikā,
kaliṅga, mallikāpuṣpa, prāvṛṣya, and śakrapādapa are synonyms for it.
Varatikta, yavaphala, saṃgrāhī, pāṇḍuradruma, prāvṛṣeṇya, and mahāgandha—these are the fifteen names [of the kuṭaja tree]. Kuṭaja is pungent, bitter, hot, and astringent; it conquers diarrhea.
Among these, *āsita* (black indrayava) destroys blood-bile (*asrapitta*) and cures skin diseases and hemorrhoids.
*Indrayavā*, *śakrāhvā*, *śakrabījāni*, and *vatsaka* are synonyms;
likewise, *vatsakabījāni*, *bhadrajā*, and *kuṭajāphala* refer to the same fruit.
Jñeyā, bhadrayavā, bījāntā, and that which is named kuṭaja, as well as kaliṅgabījāni—these are the ten synonyms.
Indrayavā is pungent, bitter, and cold; it removes phlegm, wind, blood disorders, and bile.
It pacifies burning sensations and diarrhea, and destroys various fevers, humors, and colic. Śirīṣa is known as Śītapuṣpa, Bhaṇḍika, Mṛdupuṣpaka, Śukeṣṭa, Barhipuṣpa, Viṣahantṛ, and Supuṣpaka.
Uddānaka, śukataru, lomaśapuṣpaka, kapītana, kaliṅga, śyāmala, śaṅkhinīphala, madhupuṣpa, and vṛttapuṣpa— these are known as the seventeen names [of the tree]. (Rājñī 9.59)

The śirīṣa is pungent and cooling; it is supreme for removing poison and wind, and it destroys scabies, blood disorders, leprosy, itching, and skin diseases. Karañja, naktamāla, pūtika, and cirabilvaka [are likewise beneficial].

Pūtiparṇa, vṛddhaphala, rocana, and prakīryaka; karañja is pungent, hot, beneficial for the eyes, and a destroyer of wind (vāta). Its oil is extremely unctuous, subdues wind, and bestows stability and a bright luster.

Ghṛtakarañja is another name for Prakīrya and Ghṛtaparṇaka; it is also known as Snigdhapatra, Tapasvin, Viṣārin, and Virocana. (Rājani 9.63) Ghṛtakarañja is pungent and hot; it removes wind and destroys wounds.
The Mahākarañja is known as the pacifier of all skin diseases and the destroyer of the touch of poison. Other [plants] are the Ṣaḍgrantha, the Hasticāriṇī,
the Udakīryā, the Viṣaghnī, the Kākaghnī, and the Madahastinī.
Aṅgāravallī, śārṅgeṣṭā, madhusattā, and avamāyinī;
hastirohaṇaka and hastikarañjaka should be known [as such];
sumanā, kākabhāṇḍī, and madamatta—these are the sixteen.
The mahākarañja is sharp, hot, and pungent;
it destroys poison and cures itching, scabies, leprosy, skin disorders, and wounds.
The prakīrya, rajanīpuṣpa, sumanā, and pūtikarṇika [are also mentioned].
Pūtikarañja, kaiḍarya, and kalimāla are the seven [types].
Another is gucchakarañja; [then] snigdhadala, gucchapucchaka, nandī, gucchī, mātṛnandī, sānanda, and dantadhāvana are the eight Vasus.

Karañja is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys the afflictions caused by poison and wind, and it cures itching, eczema, leprosy, and skin diseases caused by contact. Another variety is Rīṭhākarañjaka, also known as Gucchala and Gucchapuṣpaka.

Rīṭhā, gucchaphala, ariṣṭa, maṅgalya, kumbhabījaka, prakīrya, somavalka, phenila, and rudrasaṃjñaka are synonyms for the soapberry tree (*Sapindus saponaria*). Rīṭhākarañja is bitter, hot, pungent, unctuous, and a conqueror of wind (*vāta*).
It destroys phlegm and cures skin diseases, itching, poisons, and eruptive boils. Aṅkola is also known as koṭhara, recī, gūḍhapatra, nikocaka, guptasneha, pītasāra, madana, and gūḍhamallikā.
The yellow variety is known as *tāmraphala*; it is long-lasting and rich in qualities.
It is also called *kola*, *kolambakarṇa*, *gandhapuṣpa*, *rocana*, *vijñānatailagarbha*, and is recorded by the name *smṛtisaṃkhyā*.

Aṅkola is pungent and unctuous; it removes the defects caused by poison, spiders, and the like, subdues phlegm and wind, purifies mercury, and acts as a purgative. Nīla, however, is the blue tree (nīlavṛkṣa), known as vātāri and nakha; it destroys swellings.
Nakhavṛkṣa, nakhālu, and nakhapriya are names for the elephant-eared plant (diggajendra).
Nīlavṛkṣa, however, is pungent, astringent, hot, and light;
it pacifies wind-related diseases and destroys various types of swelling.
Sarja, sarjarasa, śāla, kālakūṭa, rajodbhava,
vallīvṛkṣa, cīraparṇa, rāla, kārśya,
ajakarṇaka, vastakarṇa, kaṣāyī, lalana, and gandhavṛkṣaka.
Vaṃśa, śālaniryāsa, divyasāra, sureṣṭaka, śūra,
agnivallabha, yakṣadhūpa, and susiddhaka— these are the types of *sarja*.
Sarja is pungent, bitter, hot, cooling, unctuous, and it conquers diarrhea.
It destroys the humors of bile and blood, leprosy, itching, and eruptions, and conquers wind disorders. The Jaraṇadruma, Aśvakarṇa, Tārkṣyaprasava, Śasyasaṃvaraṇa,
Dhanya, Dīrghaparṇa, Kuśikataru, and Kauśika are also [names for this tree].
Aśvakarṇa is pungent, bitter, unctuous, and destroys bile and blood disorders;
it cures fever, eruptive boils, and itching, and eliminates pain caused by diseases of the head.
Tāla, tāladruma, patrī, dīrghaskandha, and dhvajadruma are synonyms for the palmyra tree.
Tṛṇarāja, Madhurasas, Madāḍhya, Dīrghapādapa,
Cirāyus, Tarurāja, Gajabhakṣya, Dṛḍhacchada,
Dīrghapatra, Gucchapatra, and Āsavadru— these are the sixteen.
The *tāla* is sweet and removes cold-pitta, burning sensations, and fatigue;
the *sara* destroys kapha and pitta, causes intoxication, and cures burning sensations and emaciation.
The *śrītāla*, *madhutāla*, *lakṣmītāla*, and *mṛducchada* are likewise.
The *viśālapatra*, the *lekhārha*, the *masīlekhyadala*,
the *śirālapatraka*, and the nine-fold *yāmyodbhūta* are likewise [described]. The *śrītāla* is exceedingly sweet and slightly astringent.
It conquers pitta, produces kapha, and slightly aggravates vāta.
Hintāla, Sthūlatāla, Valkapatra, Bṛhaddala, Garbhasrāvī, Latātāla, Bhīṣaṇa, and Bahukaṇṭaka [are synonyms]. (Rājñī 9.87–88)
Sthirapatra, Dvidhālekhyā, Śirāpatra, Sthirāṅghripa, Amlasāra, and Bṛhattāla—thus it is known by fourteen names.
Hintāla is sweet and sour; it increases phlegm and alleviates bile and burning sensations.
It removes fatigue and thirst, is cooling, and cures disorders of the wind (*vāta*).
The *māḍa* tree—also known as *māḍadruma*, *dīrgha*, *dhvajavṛkṣa*, *vitānaka*, *madyadruma*, *mohakārī*, *madadru*, *ṛju*, and *aṅkadhā*—[is so called]. (RājN 9.90–91)

Māḍa is cooling, pleasing to the taste, and astringent; it generates pitta and burning sensations, removes thirst, increases wind (vāta), relieves fatigue, and produces phlegm (śleṣman). Tūla, tūda, brahmakāṣṭha, brāhmaṇeṣṭa, and yūpaka [are also known by these names].
Brahmadāru, supuṣpa, surūpa, nīlavṛntaka, kramuka, and viprakāṣṭha are soft-wooded trees found on two levels.
Tūla, however, is sweet and sour; it alleviates wind and bile and is laxative.
It allays burning sensations, is aphrodisiac, astringent, and destroys phlegm. Tamāla is known as nīlatāla, kālaskandha, tamālaka, nīladhvaja, tāpiñcha, kālatāla, and mahābala.
The *tamāla* is sweet, strengthening, aphrodisiac, cooling, and heavy;
it is excellent for alleviating phlegm, bile, thirst, burning sensations, fatigue, and dizziness.
The *kadamba*, with its globular flowers, is fragrant and dear to women.
The *kādambarī*, *sindhupuṣpa*, *madāḍhya*, and *karṇapūraka* are synonyms for the *kadamba*.
The *kadamba* is bitter and pungent, astringent, and subdues wind (*vāta*).
It is cooling, destroys afflictions caused by phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*), and increases semen.

The *dhārākadamba* blooms in the rainy season; it is covered in bristling hairs, is dear to bees, and is fond of the arrival of clouds. It is known as the *nīpa*, the *prāvṛṣeṇya*, and the *kadambaka*. The *dhūlīkadamba* is the flower of the *kramuka*, a pollen-flower, and is designated as *balabhadra*.
Vasantapuṣpa, makarandavāsa, bhṛṅgapriya, and reṇukadambaka— these are the eight. Bhūmīkadamba, bhūnimba, bhūmija, bhṛṅgavallabha, laghupuṣpa, vṛttapuṣpa, viṣaghna, and vraṇahāraka.
The *trikaḍamba* trees are described as pungent, cooling, and alleviators of poison and swelling;
they are astringent, increase bile, are bitter, and are supreme for increasing virility.
*Vānīra*, *vṛttapuṣpa*, *śākhāla*, and *jalavetasa* [are also included].
Vyādhighāta, parivyādha, nādeya, and jalasambhava are synonyms for the vānīra tree. It is bitter and cooling, destroys demons, cleanses wounds,
subdues the humors of pitta, blood, and kapha, is astringent, and possesses a decoction-like quality.
Kumbhī is also known as romāluviṭapī, romaśa, and parpaṭadruma.
Kumbhī is pungent, astringent, and hot; it is constipating and removes wind and phlegm.
Vetasa is to be known as nicula and vañjula, and it has long leaves.
The *kalana*, *mañjarīnamra*, *suṣeṇa*, and *gandhapuṣpaka* varieties of cane (*vetasa*) are pungent,
sweet, cooling, and destroyers of malevolent spirits (*bhūta*).
They should be known as provokers of bile (*pitta*), appetizers, and excellent stimulants of digestion.

It destroys diseases arising from blood and bile, as well as the disorder of leprosy (kuṣṭha). Dhava is a very firm tree, pale in color, with astringent and sweet bark; it is known by nine names: śuklavṛkṣa, pāṇḍutaru, dhavala, and pāṇḍura.
The *dhava* tree is astringent, pungent, a destroyer of *kapha*, and a subduer of *vāyu*;
it aggravates *pitta*, is appetizing, and should be known as an excellent digestive stimulant (*dīpana*).
The *dhanvana* tree has red flowers; it is called the bow-tree (*dhanuvṛkṣa*) and possesses great strength.
The *picchalaka* tree removes pain; it is dry and possesses sweet fruit.
The *dhanvana* tree is pungent and hot, astringent, and destroys phlegm (*kapha*);
it causes burning and dehydration, is constipating, and provides relief from diseases of the throat.
Bhūrja is the bark-tree, Bhūrja, Sucarma, Bhūrjapatraka,
Citratvak, Bindupatra, Rakṣāpatra, Vicitraka, Bhūtaghna, and Mṛdupatra; it grows on the lord of mountains, has two layers of bark, and possesses two levels.

The *bhūrja* tree is pungent, astringent, and hot; it is a supreme protector against spirits, pacifies the three *doṣas*, is wholesome, and destroys wicked crookedness. The *tiniśa* is known as *syandana*, *cakrī*, *śatāṅga*, *śakaṭa*, and *ratha*.
Rathika, bhasmagarbha, meṣī, and jaladhara—these are the ten [types of tin].
Tiniśa is astringent and hot; it conquers disorders of phlegm, blood, and dysentery.
It is an astringent, generates a burning sensation, and is excellent for removing diseases caused by wind (vāta).
Arjuna, Śambara, Pārtha, Citrayodhin, Dhanañjaya, Vairāntaka, Kirīṭin, Gāṇḍīvin,
Śivamallaka, Savyasācin, Nadīsarja, Karṇāri, and Kuruvīraka.
Kaunteya, Indrasūnu, Vīradru, Kṛṣṇasārathi, Pṛthāja, Phālguna, Dhanvī, and Kakubha—these are the twenty-one names [of Arjuna].
Arjuna, moreover, is astringent and heating; it destroys phlegm and heals wounds.
It destroys the afflictions of bile, fatigue, and thirst, but provokes diseases of the wind (vāta).
Haridru, pītadāru, pītakāṣṭha,
pītaka, kadambaka, supuṣpa, surāhva, and pītakadruma are synonyms for the yellow wood tree.
Haridru is cooling, bitter, auspicious, and a conqueror of bile and vomiting;
it bestows luster to the limbs, is strengthening, and destroys various skin diseases.
Dagdhā, dagdharuhā, dagdhikā, and sthaleruhā are said to be [synonyms for] the same plant.
*Romashā*, *karkaśadalā*, *bhasmarohā*, and *sudagdhikā*— also known as *dagdhā*—
are pungent, astringent, and hot; they destroy phlegm and wind, aggravate bile,
and stimulate the digestive fire.
Śākhoṭa is known as bhūtavṛkṣa; gavākṣī is yūkāvāsa and bhūrjapatra, and it is yellow.
Kauśikī is ajakṣīranāśa and sūkta; this [group] is bitter and hot, increases pitta, and removes vāta. Śāka has serrated leaves (krakacapatra), and is also called kharapatra and atipatraka.
Mahīsaha is the best of woods, possessing firm pith; it is the tree of the house. Śāka is said to be *sāraka*; it removes bile, burning sensations, and fatigue.
The bark of the Śāka tree is sweet, astringent, appetizing, and destroys phlegm.
The *śiṃśapā* tree is of several types: the *mahāśyāmā*, the *kṛṣṇasārā*, the *dhūmrikā*, the *tīkṣṇasārā*, the *dhīrā*, the *kapilā*, and the *kṛṣṇaśiṃśapā*.
Among these, the *śyāmā* and other varieties of *śiṃśapā* are bitter, pungent, and hot; they alleviate *kapha* and *vāta*.

The *dīpyā* variety removes indigestion caused by loss of digestive fire and cures swelling and diarrhea. Another *śiṃśapā*, known as *śvetapatrā* and *sitāhvā*, along with other white varieties of *śiṃśapā*, is bitter and cooling; it subdues bile and burning sensations.
The *kapilā* and the other, the yellow *kapila-śiṃśapā*,
the *sāriṇī*, the *kapilākṣī*, the *bhasmagarbhā*, and the *kuśiṃśapā*—
the *kapilā-śiṃśapā* is bitter, cold in potency, and removes fatigue.
It destroys fever caused by vāta and pitta, and cures vomiting and hiccups. (Rajni 9.130) The three types of śiṃśapā improve the complexion, alleviate coldness, swelling, and erysipelas;
they pacify pitta and burning sensations, and are highly strengthening and appetizing. (Rajni 9.131)
The *asana* trees are the mahāsarja, saurika, bandhūkapuṣpaka, priyaka, bījavṛkṣa, nīlaka, and priyaśālaka.
The *asana* is pungent, hot, and bitter; it removes the affliction of wind (*vāta*) and subdues the bodily humors (*doṣa*).
*Sāraka* destroys throat disorders and cures erythema (*raktamaṇḍala*). The second is *nīlabīja*, which has blue leaves and is very dark blue;
it is called *nīladruma*, *nīlasāra*, and *nīlaniryāsaka* because of its juices.

The seeds and the trees are pungent and cooling, astringent, and destroy skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*); they are pithy and cure itching and *dadrū*. Of these two, the black variety is the best. Varuṇa, Śvetapuṣpa, Tiktaśāka, and Kumāraka [are also mentioned].

The *śvetadruma* is a virtuous tree, while the *tamāla* wards off the wind. The *varuṇa* is pungent and hot; it is supreme for removing blood disorders (*raktadoṣa*), curing head-wind ailments (*śīrṣavāta*), being unctuous, digestive, and overcoming abscesses and wind disorders.
Putrajīva is pure, a bestower of embryos, and a sustainer of sons;
it is also known as Kuṭajīva, Apatyajīva, Siddhida, and Apatyajīvaka.
Putrajīva is cooling, aphrodisiac, increases phlegm, and sustains the embryo.
Beneficial for the eyes, it pacifies bile (*pitta*) and wards off burning sensations and thirst.
It is called *mahāpiṇḍītaru*, as well as *śvetapiṇḍītaka*.
It is also known as *karahāṭa*, *kṣura*, *śastrakośataru*, and *sara*.

The piṇḍītaka tree has an astringent and hot decoction; it pacifies the three doṣas and removes skin diseases, specifically conquering blood disorders. The kāraskara, however, is the kimpāka, the viṣatindu, and the viṣadruma.
The *garadruma* has pleasant fruit but is poorly digested; it is *kālakūṭaka*. The *kāraskara* is pungent, hot, and bitter, and it destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
It removes disorders of wind (*vāta*), blood disorders, itching, phlegm, hemorrhoids, and wounds.
Kaṭabhī, nābhikā, śauṇḍī, pāṭalī,
kiṇihī, madhureṇu, kṣudraśāmā, kaiḍarya, and śyāmalā— these are the nine [plants].
Śitā-kaṭabhī, śvetā, kiṇihī, and girikarṇikā [are also included].
Śirīṣapatrā, Kālindī, Śatapādī, Viṣaghnikā, Mahāśvetā, Mahāśauṇḍī, and likewise Mahākaṭabhī—
Kaṭabhī is pungent and hot; it destroys disorders of abdominal tumors (gulma), poison, flatulence, colic, and humors.

The white variety (*śvetā*) among them is endowed with qualities that pacify disorders of wind (*vāta*), phlegm (*kapha*), indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), and pain. (9.146) *Kṣavaka*, *kṣuraka*, *tīkṣṇa*, *krūra*, *bhūtāṅkuśa*, *kṣava*, *rājodvejanasaṃjña*, *bhūtadrāvī*, and *grahāhvaya* are synonyms for the plant [used against] spirits. (9.147)

Bhūtāṅkuśa is pungent-smelling, astringent, hot, and likewise bitter; it destroys the afflictions caused by spirits and planetary grahas, and it cuts through phlegm and wind disorders. Devasarṣapaka, akṣa, badara, and raktamūlaka [are also such].
The *surasarṣapa* is known as *aindra* and also as *sūkṣmadala*;
the *sarṣapa* is called *nirjarādi* and has nine names, including *kurarāṅghri*.
That which is named *devasarṣapa* is pungent, hot, and destroys phlegm (*kapha*).
It removes the defects caused by insects, is appetizing, and cleanses diseases of the mouth.
The lakuca, likewise called likuca, śāla, kaṣāyī, dṛḍhavalkala, ḍahu, kārśya, śūra, and sthūlaskandha, has nine names.
The lakuca fruit is bitter in its natural juice, astringent, hot, and light;
it removes the disorder of phlegm, causes a burning sensation, and promotes the accumulation of waste matter. The vikaṅkata is also known as vyāghrapāda, granthila, and svādukaṇṭaka.
The *kaṇṭhapāda*, the *bahuphala*, the *gopaghoṇṭā*, and the *sruvadruma*;
the *mṛduphala*, the *dantakāṣṭha*, the *yajñīya*, and the *brahmapādapa*;
the *piṇḍarohiṇaka*, the *pūta*, and the *kiṅkiṇī*—these are the fifteen kinds [of tooth-sticks].
The *vikaṅkata* is sour-sweet, extremely sweet in its post-digestive state (*pāka*),
light, digestive, a destroyer of jaundice and blood disorders, a promoter of digestion, and a subduer of bile. Thus,
by this primary method of proclaiming the names and qualities of wild trees— rendered brilliant by the vast splendor of its manifold and varied designations— [the work proceeds].

Indeed, let the physician, being a master of knowledge, having fully understood this entire class [of medicinal trees], suddenly and at his own will destroy the multitude of diseases through the expansion of the light of wisdom. Those which cut away the most grievous diseases of men, attacking them with the sword of their potency; those which, even while standing in the forest, provide protection for the afflicted by means of their own inherent quality—of those forest-dwelling trees, this peerless abode known as the "class of trees" has been described by physicians as possessing great and boundless majesty.

This ninth section, beginning with the *prabhadra* group, is established within the *Abhidhāna-śekhara-śikhā-cūḍāmaṇi*, the crown jewel of lexicons, composed by Narahari— who, though a swan in the lotus grove shining with the Kashmiri lineage, is constantly served with affection by those whose minds are fixed on the ever-rejoicing Nīlakaṇṭha (Śiva), and whose fortune remains unbroken. *Rājanighaṇṭu*, Chapter 9, Verse 158.
The group beginning with *karavīra* is fourfold: *karavīra*, the three types of *dhattūra*, *kovidāra*, *abdhi*, *arka*, *nameru*, and likewise *kiṃśuka*. (Rajñī 10.1)
The *punnāga*, the *tilaka*, the *agastya*, and two kinds of *pāṭalī* are recorded;
likewise, the *aśoka*, the *campaka*, the *dhanvī*, and two kinds of *ketakī*;
as well as the *sindūrī*, the *jātī*, the *mudgara*, and the *śatapatrikā*.

The *mallikā* is of four kinds, as are the *vāsantī* and the *navamallikā*. The *atimukta* is of two kinds: the *yūthī*, the *kubjaka*, the *mucakundaka*, the *karuṇī*, the *mādhavī*, the *gaṇikārī*, and the *kundaka*.
Bakaka, vika, bandhūka, trisandhi, and likewise japā;
bhramaramārī is proclaimed, as well as taruṇī and amlānaka;
then kiṅkirāta, that which is called bālā, jhiṇṭikā, and uṣṭrakāṇḍikā.
Tagara, the two types of damana, tulasī, and the two kinds of maruva;
arjaka, caturgaṅgā, patrī, pācī, and bālaka; barbarī, mañcikāpatra, and what is called ārāmaśītalā. (Rājani 10.6–7)
Then there are the *kamala*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *kokanada* lotuses, as well as the *padminī*;
likewise the *padmākṣa*, the *mṛṇāla*, its bulb (*kanda*), and the filaments (*kesara*).
Also the *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *kuvalaya*, and the *utpalinī*—these are known by names such as *aṅka* and *vasu*.
In this section titled "Uttaṃsa," substances are taught here:
karavīra, mahāvīra, hayamāra, aśvamāraka, hayaghna, pratihāsa, śatakunda, and aśvarodhaka. (Rājñī 10.9–10)
Hayāri, Vīraka, Kunda, Śakunda, Śvetapuṣpaka, Aśvāntaka, as well as Aśvaghna, Nakharāhvaya, and Aśvanāśaka; it is called Sthalādikumuda, Divyapuṣpa, and Harapriya. Rajñī 10.11.

Gaurīpuṣpa is celebrated as Siddhapuṣpa and Dvikarāhva. Karavīra is pungent and sharp; it destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and itching, pacifies the pain of wounds, poisons, and eruptions, and bestows swiftness of mind.
The red *karavīra* is another [name for it], as are *raktaprasava*, *gaṇeśakusuma*, *caṇḍīkusuma*,
*krūra*, *bhūtadrāvī*, and *ravipriya*, according to the sages. The red *karavīra* is pungent, sharp, and purifying.
It removes skin diseases, wounds, itching, and leprosy, and it destroys poison. Another variety is the yellow Karavīraka, which has yellow blossoms and fragrant flowers;
the black variety has black flowers, and these four types are equal in their qualities.
Dhattūra is called Kitava, Dhūrta, Unmatta, Kanakāhvaya,
Śaṭha, Mātulaka, Śyāma, Madana, and Śivaśekhara;
it is also known as Kharjūghna, Kāhalāpuṣpa, Khala, and Kaṇṭaphala.
The *mohana* (deluding), *kalabha-unmatta* (intoxicated by the young elephant), and *śaiva* (belonging to Śiva) are names for the thorn-apple (*dhattūra*), which has seventeen synonyms.
It is pungent and hot, bestows luster, and relieves the pain of wounds;
it removes skin diseases, itching, scratching, and fever, yet it induces delusions.
*Kṛṣṇadhattūraka* is known as Siddha, Kanaka, Saciva, Śiva,
Kṛṣṇapuṣpa, Viṣārāti, and Krūradhūrta. Another is *Rājadhattūraka*, also called Rājadhūrta and Mahāśaṭha.
The *nistraiṇipuṣpaka*, *bhrānta*, *rājasvarṇa*, and the six-named [plant] are mentioned. There are *dhattūra* plants with white, blue, black, red, and yellow flowers;
they possess common qualities, yet among them, the one with black blossoms is the most richly endowed with virtues.
Kovidāra, kāñcanāra, kuddāla, kanakāraka, kāntapuṣpa, karaka, kāntāra,
yamalacchada, pītapuṣpa, suvarṇāra, girija, and kāñcanāraka.
The Yugmapatra and Mahāpuṣpa have fourteen varieties.
Kovidāra is astringent, promotes the healing of wounds,
is digestive, subdues phlegm and wind, and cures dysuria.
Arka is called kṣīradala, pucchī, pratāpa, kṣīrakāṇḍaka, vikṣīra,
bhāskara, kṣīrī, kharjūghna, and śivapuṣpaka; it is also known as bhañjana,
kṣīraparṇī, savitā, and vikīraṇa.
Sūryāhva, sadāpuṣpa, ravi, āsphoṭaka, tūlaphala, śukaphala, and viṃśati are its twenty synonyms.
Arka is pungent and hot; it conquers wind and stimulates the digestive fire.

It removes swelling and wounds, and destroys itching, leprosy, and worms. Śuklārka, tapana, śveta, pratāpa, sitārka, supuṣpa, śaṅkarādi, atyarka, and vṛttamallikā are synonyms for the white sun-plant (śvetārka).
The white *arka* is pungent, bitter, and hot;
it acts as a purifier of the impurities [of the body] and destroys urinary distress (*mūtrakṛcchra*), blood disorders, swelling, pain, and defects of wounds.
(Rajni 10.30) *Rājārka*, *vasuka*, *alarka*, *mandāra*, and *gaṇarūpaka* are synonyms for the *rājārka*.
Kāṣṭhīla and Sadāpuṣpa are to be known here as the seventh [in this group].
Rājārka is pungent, bitter, and hot; it removes phlegm, fat, and poison.
It destroys wind-disorders, leprosy, and wounds, and it cures swelling, itching, and erysipelas.
The white mandāraka is another; it is known as pṛthvīkuravaka, dīrghapuṣpa, sitālarka, dīrghātyarka, and rasāhvaya.
The white mandāraka is extremely hot, bitter, and a cleanser of impurities.

It cures dysuria, wounds, and even extremely virulent worms. Nameru, surapunnāga, sureṣṭa, suraparṇikā, and suratuṅga— these five names denote the *punnāga*, which possesses the same qualities as the *punnāga* tree itself.
Palāśa, kiṃśuka, parṇa, vātapotha, yājñika, triparṇa, vakrapuṣpa, pūtadru, brahmavṛkṣaka, brahmopanetā, and kāṣṭhadru— these are recorded as the eleven synonyms [of the Palāśa tree]. (Rajni 10.36)
The *palāśa* is astringent and hot; it destroys worms and disorders.
Its seed cures scabies, itching, ringworm, and skin diseases. Its flower is also hot and destroys itching, leprosy, and pain.

It is distinguished by flowers that are red, yellow, white, or blue. Even when the qualities are equal, the white *kiṃśuka* is traditionally held to bestow wisdom. The *punnāga* is masculine, as is the *tuṅga*; the *pāṭala* is also a male [flower].
This tree, known by nine names, is called raktapuṣpa, raktareṇu, and aruṇa.
The punnāga is sweet, cooling, fragrant, and a destroyer of bile;
it dispels malevolent spirits and propitiates the deities.
The *tilaka*, *viśeṣaka*, *mukhamaṇḍanaka*, *puṇḍraka*, and *puṇḍra* are synonyms for a forehead mark.
The *sthirapuṣpa*, *chinnaruha*, *dagdharuha*, *recaka*, and *mṛtajīvī* are also varieties.
The *taruṇīkaṭākṣakāma*, *vāsanta*, *sundara*, and *abhīṣṭa* are likewise types of marks.
Known as the forehead ornament (bhālavibhūṣaṇa), it should be understood by fifteen names.
The *tilaka* is sweet, unctuous, and removes wind, bile, and phlegm;
it bestows strength and nourishment, is pleasing to the heart, light, and increases fat (*medas*).

The decoction of *tilaka* bark is hot; it destroys virility, removes dental defects, kills worms, cures swellings and ulcers, and eliminates blood disorders. (Rajni 10.45) *Agastya* is the "quick-flowering" plant, while *agasti* is the "sage-tree."
The *agasti* (vraṇāri) has long fruits, crooked flowers, and is beloved by the gods.
There are four varieties of *agasti* according to the distinction of their flowers—white, yellow, blue, and red.
It is sweet and cooling, destroys the three *doṣas*, fatigue, and cough, and is a destroyer of evil spirits (*bhūtaghna*).

Agastya is cooling, sweet, a destroyer of the three *doṣas*, a remover of fatigue, and it destroys phlegm, cough, discoloration, and malevolent spirits while increasing strength. *Pāṭalī*, *tāmrapuṣpī*, *kumbhikā*, and *raktapuṣpikā* [are likewise].
Vasantadūtī, cāmoghā, sthālī, and viṭavallabhā; sthiragandhā, ambuvāsī, kālavṛntī, and indubhūhvayā (pāṭalī)—
pāṭalī is bitter in taste, pungent and hot, and it conquers phlegm and wind.
It pacifies swelling, flatulence, vomiting, and asthma, and it destroys the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta). Sitapāṭalikā is another name for sitakumbhī,
phaleruhā, sitā, moghā, kuberākṣī, sitāhvā, and kāṣṭhapāṭalā.
Pāṭalī is said to be white and is known by the name vasumitā.
Sitapāṭalikā is bitter, heavy, and hot; it conquers disorders of wind (vāta), destroys vomiting, hiccup, and phlegm (kapha), and removes exhaustion and wasting.
Aśoka is the destroyer of grief; viśoka is the vañjula tree. Madhupuṣpa, apaśoka, kaṅkeli, and likewise keli, raktapallavaka, citra, vicitra, and karṇapūraka are synonyms for it.
Subhaga, smarādhivāsa, doṣahārī, prapallava,
rāgī, taru, hemapuṣpa, rāmāvāmaṅghrighātaka,
piṇḍīpuṣpa, naṭa, and pallavadrū— these are the twenty-two names.
The *aśoka* is cooling, pleasing to the heart, and removes the burning sensation caused by *pitta* as well as fatigue;
it destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), colic, abdominal enlargement, and flatulence, and it acts as a vermifuge. The *campaka*, also known as *svarṇapuṣpa* and *cāmpeya*, has cool leaves.
Subhaga, Bhṛṅgamohin, Śītala, and Bhramarātithi;
Surabhi, Dīpapuṣpa, Sthiragandha, Atigandhaka,
Sthirapuṣpa, Hemapuṣpa, and another, Pītapuṣpa.

Hemāhva, sukumāra, vanadīpa, and aṣṭabhūhvaya; its buds are gandhaphalī, bahugandhā, and gandhamodinī—these three types [of campaka]. Campaka is pungent, bitter, cooling, and a destroyer of burning sensations.
The *rājacampaka* is rich in qualities and removes skin diseases, itching, and wounds.
Another variety, beginning with *kṣudracampaka*, is known as *nāgacampaka*;
it is called *phaṇicampaka*, *nāgāhva*, *vanajacampaka*, and *śara*. (Rājaniighaṇṭu 10.60–61)

The wild campaka is pungent and hot; it destroys wind and phlegm, improves the complexion, is beneficial for the eyes, heals wounds, and—by virtue of its medicinal properties—stills the digestive fire. Bakula, however, has the fragrance of *sīdhu* wine, possesses a longing for the honey of women’s mouths, and is a flower that attracts bees.
Surabhi, Bhramarānanda, Sthirakusuma, Kesara, Śāradika,
Karaka (known as Sīdhu), Viśārada, Gūḍhapuṣpaka, Dhanvī, Madana, Madyāmoda, and Cirapuṣpa— these are the seventeen names.
The *bakula* is cooling, pleasing to the heart, and a destroyer of the defects of poison;
it is sweet and astringent, rich in intoxicating power, and bestows delight.
The *bakula* flower is appetizing, rich in milk, fragrant, cooling, and sweet.
The *snigdhakaṣāya* (glossy decoction) when boiled acts as a collector of impurities.
The *ketakī*, the *tīkṣṇapuṣpā*, the *viphalā*, the *dhūlipuṣpikā*,
the *medhyā*, and the *kaṇṭadalā* are disliked by Śiva but are dear to kings.
*Krakacā*, *dīrghapatrā*, *sthiragandhā*,
*pāṃśulā*, *gandhapuṣpā*, *indukalikā*, *dalapuṣpā*— it is of five or three kinds. Another, such as the golden *ketakī* and so forth, should be known as *hemaketakī*.
Kanakaprasavā, Puṣpī, Haimī,
Chinnaruhā, Viṣṭaruhā, Svarṇapuṣpī, and Kāmakhaḍgadalā are synonyms for it.
The Ketakī flower is praised as a destroyer of hair odor.
It is golden-hued, increases passion and intoxication, and bestows happiness.
Her breast is exceedingly cool, pungent, and removes bile and phlegm;
it acts as an elixir, is strengthening, and is supreme for providing firmness to the body.
Sindūrī, vīrapuṣpa, tṛṇapuṣpī, karacchada, sindūrapuṣpī, and śoṇādipuṣpī are known as the six names [of this plant]. Sindūrī is pungent, bitter, and astringent; it conquers phlegm and wind.
It is a reliever of headache, a destroyer of malevolent spirits, and dear to Caṇḍī.
Jātī possesses a fragrant scent; Sumanā is beloved by the gods.
Cetakī is Sukumārā, while Sandhyāpuṣpī is Manoharā.
Rājaputrī, manojñā, mālatī, tailabhāvinī, janeṣṭā, and hṛdyagandhā—these are its fourteen names. Mālatī is cooling and bitter; it destroys phlegm and cures inflammation of the mouth.
*Kudmala* destroys eye diseases and removes wounds, eruptions, and leprosy.
*Mudgara*, *gandhasāra*, *saptapatra*, *kardamī*, *vṛttapuṣpa*, *atigandha*, *gandharāja*, and *viṭapriya* [are synonyms]. *Rājñī* 10.75.
It is fond of songs, beloved by people, desired by deer, and equal to Rudra.
The *mudgara* [wind] is sweet, cool, fragrant, and a bestower of happiness;
it is pleasing to the mind, causes joy through the drinking of honey-wine, and removes the provocation of *pitta*.
Śatapatrī, however, is known as sumanā, suśītā, śivavallabhā, saumyagandhā, śatadalā, suvṛttā, and śatapatrikā.
Śatapatrī is cooling, bitter, and astringent; it destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

The *mallikā*— also known as *bhadravallī*, *gaurī*, *vanacandrikā*, *śītabhīru*, *priyā*, *saumyā*, *nārīṣṭā*, *girijā*, and *sitā*— removes eruptions on the face, is appetizing, fragrant, and alleviates bilious fever and burning sensations. (Rajñī 10.79)
Mallī, damayantī, candrikā, modinī, and manu;
mallikā is pungent and bitter, beneficial for the eyes, and a remover of mouth-sores;
it is supreme in curing leprosy, eruptions, itching, poisons, and wounds.
Vallikā, Modinī, another called Vaṭapatrā, Kumārikā, Sugandhāḍhyā, Vṛttapuṣpā, and Muktābhā— these are the varieties of Vṛttamallikā. Vṛttamallikā destroys eye diseases and is pungent and hot.

The *vraṇaghnī* (wound-healer) is rich in fragrance and destroys diseases arising in the mouth. The *vārṣikā* has nine names: *tripuṭā*, *tryasrā*, *surūpā*, *sulabhā*, *priyā*, *śrīvallī*, *ṣaṭpadānandā*, *muktabandhā*, and *navā*.
The *vārṣikā* is pleasant in the cool season, heart-pleasing, fragrant, and a destroyer of *pitta*.
It destroys *kapha*, *vāta*, poison, eruptions, worms, disorders, and nausea.
Due to the distinction of its long and round flowers, it has various designations.
Another, scented with musk, is to be known as *kastūrīmallikā*.
One *mallikā* blooms in the morning, while another opens at evening;
that might be the *vanamallikā*, but it is the *āsphotā* which possesses qualities equal to both.
Vāsantī, Prahasantī, Vasantajā, Mādhavī, Mahājāti,
Śītasahā, Madhubahalā, Vasantadūtī, and Vasunāmnī;
Vāsantī is cool, heart-pleasing, fragrant, and dispeller of fatigue.

Fragrant as braided hair, bestowing the mild intoxication of passion, exceedingly delightful like the new jasmine, it is the jasmine of summer, born in the heat of summer; it is the seven-flowered, the delicate, the fragrant, and the needle-jasmine.
*Sugandhā*, *śikhariṇī*, and *nevālī* are synonyms for the plant known as *indubhū*. (Rājñī 10.90) *Navamallikā* is exceedingly cooling, fragrant, and removes all diseases.
(Rājñī 10.91) That same [plant] is called *atimuktaka*, and another variety is said to be named *puṇḍraka*.
It is intoxicating, a delight to bees, beloved by Kāma, and known as Pañca. Atimukta is astringent, cooling, and dispels fatigue;
it wards off bile disorders, burning sensations, fever, insanity, hiccups, and vomiting.
Yūthikā, Gaṇikā, Ambaṣṭhā, Māgadhī, Bālapuṣpikā,
Modanī, Bahugandhā, Bhṛṅgānandā, and Gajāhvayā;
another Yūthī is called Suvarṇā, Sugandhā, and Hemayūthikā.
Yuvatīṣṭā, Vyaktagandhā, Śikhaṇḍī, Nāgapuṣpikā,
Hariṇī, Pītayūthī, Potikā, Kanakaprabhā,
Manoharā, and Gandhāḍhyā— these are declared to be the thirteen names [of the plant]. (Rājñī 10.95–96)
The pair of *yūthikā* flowers is sweet, cooling, and relieves the affliction caused by sugar;
it removes bile, burning sensations, and thirst, and destroys various skin disorders.
*Yūthikā* flowers are said to be named white, yellow, blue, and black according to their blossoms. (Rajni 10.97)
They are bitter and cooling, destroyers of diseases caused by *pitta* and *kapha*, fevers, and wounds; they remove all such defects.
Among all varieties of *yūthikā*, however, there is equality in taste, potency, and other qualities;
yet the golden *yūthikā* (*svarṇayūthī*) is especially beautiful and rich in fragrance.
The *kubjaka* is a beautiful young tree with rounded flowers and few filaments;
it is called *mahāsaha*, rich in thorns, short in stature, and crowded with swarms of bees.
The *kubjaka* is fragrant and cooling, and it removes blood-bile (*raktapitta*) and phlegm (*kapha*).
Its flower is cooling, complexion-enhancing, a destroyer of burning sensations, and a conqueror of wind and bile.
The *mucukunda* has many leaves, beautiful petals, is dear to Hari, and possesses fine flowers;
it is worthy of honor, is called *lakṣmaṇaka*, has red blossoms, and is named after the Vasus.

Mucakunda is pungent and bitter; it destroys phlegm and cough, removes disorders of the throat, pacifies skin diseases and swellings, and indeed eradicates wounds and scabies. Karuṇī, grīṣmapuṣpī, raktapuṣpī, and vāruṇī [are synonyms].

Rājapriyā, rājapuṣpī, sūkṣmā, and brahmacāriṇī—these are synonyms for *karuṇī*. It is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys phlegm and wind, and cures flatulence, poison, vomiting, pain in the chest, and upward dyspnea.
Mādhavī, Candravallī, Sugandhā, Bhramarotsavā,
Bhṛṅgapriyā, Bhadralatā, and Bhūmimaṇḍapabhūṣaṇī are synonyms for Mādhavī.
Mādhavī is pungent, bitter, and astringent, and it possesses the scent of intoxication.
It destroys bile, cough, and wounds, and it eliminates burning sensations and wasting.
Gaṇikārī, kāñcanikā, kāñcanapuṣpī, vasantadūtī,
gandhakusumā, atimodā, vāsantī, and madamādinī [are synonyms].

The *gaṇikārī* is exceedingly fragrant, pacifies the three humors (*tridoṣa*), removes burning sensations and wasting, and possesses a spreading restlessness that captivates the senses like the pride of the god of love. *Kunda*, *makaranda*, *mahāmoda*, and *manohara*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion given.]
Muktāpuṣpa, Sadāpuṣpa, Tārapuṣpa, Aṭṭahāsaka, Damana, Vanahāsa, Manojña, and Rudrasammita; Kunda is extremely sweet, cooling, astringent, and promotes the growth of hair.
It pacifies both *kapha* and *pitta*, is laxative, and stimulates digestion and metabolism.
Baka, Pāśupata, Śaiva, Śivapiṇḍa, Suvrata, Vasuka, Śivāṅka, Śiveṣṭa, and Kramapūraka— [these are its names].
Śivamallī, Śivāhlāda, and Śāmbhava are twelve in number.
Baka is extremely cooling, bitter, sweet, and honey-scented;
it removes bile, burning sensations, phlegm, asthma, and fatigue, and it is digestive.
Kevikā, kavikā, kevā, bhṛṅgāri, nṛpavallabhā,
bhṛṅgamārī, mahāgandhā, rājakanyā, and alimohinī— kevikā is sweet and cooling, and it removes burning sensations, bile disorders, and fatigue.
It destroys diseases caused by wind and phlegm and cures bile-related vomiting.
Bandhūka is known as bandhujīva, oṣṭhapuṣpa, arkavallabha,
madhyandina, raktapuṣpa, rāgapuṣpa, and haripriya.
Bandhūka is of four kinds, distinguished by its flowers being black, white, yellow, or red;
it removes fever, pacifies various grahas and piśācas, and brings clarity to the sun. Trisandhi, Sāndhyakusumā, Sandhivallī, and Sadāphalā [are synonyms].
*Trisandhyakusumā* is lovely and delicate, produced at the junctions [of the day]. *Trisandhi* should be known as threefold: red, another which is white, and blackish-white.
It removes phlegm and cough, is appetizing, and the other [variety] pacifies skin diseases.
Known as *japā* and *oḍrakā*, it is also called *raktapuṣpī*, *javā*, *arkapriyā*, *raktapuṣpī*, *prātikā*, and *harivallabhā*.
The *japā* is pungent and hot; it destroys *indraluptaka* (alopecia).
The mother of the *vicchardi* insect, the means for propitiating the Sun;
the enemy of bees, the slayer of *bhṛṅga*, the foe of *bhṛṅga*, the one with fleshy flowers;
the enemy of leprosy, the bee-like one—thus should the sage Yaṣṭilatā be known. (Rajñī 10.122–123)
Tiktā, also known as Bhramaramārī, removes wind (vāta), phlegm (śleṣman), and fever;
it destroys swelling, itching, and leprosy, and cures defects of wounds and disorders of the bones. Taruṇī, Sahā, Kumārī, Gandhāḍhyā, Cārukesarā, and Bhṛṅgeṣṭā [are synonyms]. 10.124–125a.
The *rāmataruṇī* has beautiful petals, many leaves, is dear to bees, and is called *daśāhvā*. It is cooling, unctuous, and removes bile, burning sensations, and fever;
it is sweet, cures mouth ulcers, and wards off thirst and vomiting.
Mahatī, rājataruṇī, mahāsahā, varṇyapuṣpaka,
amlāna, amilātaka, supuṣpa, and suvarṇapuṣpa are known as the seven names of the rājataruṇī plant.
Rājataruṇī is an astringent (kaṣāya) and increases phlegm (kapha).
It is pleasing to the eye, heart-gladdening, delightful to the heart, fragrant, and beloved by the gods.
(Rājñī 10.128) Now, that which is red and does not fade is called *raktasaha* and also *aparimlāna*;
it is also known as *raktāmalāntaka*, *raktaprasava*, and *kuravaka*. (Rājñī 10.129)
The spring festival (*madhūtsava*) is the source of passion, desiring the embrace of Rāma;
may this [festival], which is like the crescent moon of the fortnight, be a source of joy for the bees and auspicious.
The *kuravaka* flower is hot and pungent, destroying wind-disorders, swellings, and fever.

It pacifies flatulence, colic, cough, asthma, and pain, and it improves the complexion. When drunk, that *kiṅkirāta*—known by seven names—is called *pītāmlāna*, *kuraṇṭaka*, *kanaka*, *pītakurava*, *supīta*, and *pītakusuma*. (Rājani 10.131–132)

Kiṅkirāta is astringent, hot, and bitter; it conquers phlegm and wind, stimulates digestion, and destroys swelling, itching, and skin disorders. That [variety] with blue flowers is called dāsī, while nīlāmlāna is the chādana.

Bālā, Ārttagalā, and Nīlapuṣpā are of six varieties. Ārttagalā is pungent and bitter; it removes phlegm, wind, and colic, destroys itching, skin diseases, and ulcers, and eliminates swelling and disorders of the skin.

The *kaṇṭakaraṇṭa* is the *jhiṇṭī*; that which is yellow is its forest companion (*vanyasahacarī*). That which is red is named *kuravaka*, as well as the thorny red *jhiṇṭikā*. Another is the blue *jhiṇṭī*, the blue *kuraṇṭa*, and the blue-flowered one.

Bāṇa, bāṇā, dāsī, and kaṇṭārttagalā—these are the seven names [of the plant]. Jhiṇṭikā is pungent and bitter; it provides relief from dental ailments, destroys colic, and acts as a destroyer of wind, phlegm, swelling, cough, and skin disorders.
Uṣṭrakāṇḍī, raktapuṣpī, karabhakāṇḍikā, raktā, lohitapuṣpī, and varṇapuṣpī are known as the six names [of this plant].
(Rajñī 10.139) Uṣṭrakāṇḍī is bitter and hot; it improves the appetite and cures heart disease.
Its seed is known to be sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, and nourishing.
Tagara is called kuṭila, vakra, vinamra,
kuñcita, nata, śaṭha, nahuṣa, dadruhasta, and barhaṇa.
Piṇḍītagaraka, pārthiva, rājaharṣaṇa,
kālānusāraka, kṣatra, dīna, jihma, and munīndudhā— these are synonyms for *tagara*. Tagara is cooling, bitter, and destroys defects of vision.

It is wholesome for alleviating the affliction of poison and removes the fear of possession and insanity. Now, *damanaka* is also known as *damana*, *dānta*, *gandhotkaṭa*, *muni*, *jaṭila*, *daṇḍin*, *pāṇḍurāga*, *brahmajaṭā*, and *puṇḍarīka*.
*Tāpasapatra*, *patrī*, *pavitraka*, *devaśekhara*, *kulapatra*, *vinīta*, and *tapasvipatra*—these are the seven names of *dhātrī*.
It is a subduer (*damana*), cool, bitter, astringent, and pungent; it removes the defects of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
It pacifies dual and triple humors (doṣas) and removes disorders caused by poison and eruptions. Furthermore, there is another plant called *vanyadamanaka*, also known by the synonym *damanaka*;
it causes the retention of semen, bestows strength, and removes the disorder of *āmadoṣa*.
Tulasī is auspicious, powerful, purifying, and beloved by Viṣṇu;
she is to be known as Surejyā, Surasā, Kāyasthā, and Suradundubhī.
She is also called Surabhi, Bahupatrī, Mañjarī, and Haripriyā.
Apetarākṣasī, Śyāmā, Gaurī, Tridaśamañjarī, Bhūtaghnī, and Pūtapatrī—these nineteen names are to be known [for Tulasī].
Tulasī is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is fragrant and conquers phlegm and wind.

It destroys living organisms, worms, and parasites; it creates relish and pacifies wind disorders. Black Tulasī is indeed Kṛṣṇā, while the white variety is Lakṣmī, known by the name Sitā; it removes cough, wind, worms, vomiting, and afflictions from spirits, and is purifying.
Maruva is known as kharapatra, gandhapatra,
phaṇiñjhaka, bahuvīrya, śītalaka, surāhva, and samīraṇa.
Jambīra is likewise known as prasthakusuma and maruvaka.
Ājanmasurabhipatra and marīca are thirteen [in number].
Maruvaka is said to be of two kinds: white and non-white (black).
The white variety is used for medicinal purposes, while the other is for the worship of Śiva.
Maruva is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys worms and skin diseases (kuṣṭha), cures constipation, flatulence, and colic, and eliminates sluggish digestion and skin disorders.
Arjaka, kṣudratulasī, kṣudraparṇa, and mukhārjaka are synonyms for it.
Ugragandha, jambīra, kuṭhera, and kaṭhiñjara;
sitārjaka, vaikuṇṭha, vaṭapatra, and kuṭheraka;
jambīra, gandhabahula, sumukha, and kaṭupatraka.
*Kṛṣṇārjaka*, *kālamāla*, *mālūka*, and *kṛṣṇamāluka* are synonyms;
it is also called *kṛṣṇamallikā*. *Vanabarbara* is said to be *garaghna*.
(Rājñī 10.158) The three types of *arjaka* are pungent and hot; they remove disorders of phlegm (*kapha*) and wind (*vāta*).
They cure eye diseases, are appetizing, and facilitate easy childbirth.
Another variety is the *vanabarbarikā*, which is fragrant and very clear;
it agitates the humors (*doṣa*), destroys poison, and is called *sumukha* and *sūkṣmapatraka*.
The ten-named [plant] is sleep-inducing, a remover of swelling, and possesses a beautiful face.
Vanabarbarikā is hot, fragrant, and pungent;
it destroys Piśācas, vomiting, and spirits, and is supremely refreshing to the sense of smell.
Gaṅgāpatrī is indeed patrī, sugandhā, and gandhapatrikā.
Gaṅgāpatrī is pungent and hot; it conquers wind (vāta) and heals wounds.
Pācī, marakatapatrī, haritalatā, haritapatrikā, and patrī [are synonyms].
Surabhi, mallāri, ariṣṭā, and gārutmatapatrikā;

pācī is pungent, bitter, and hot, possessing astringency, and it destroys disorders caused by wind (vāta). It provokes disturbances from planets and spirits, pacifies skin diseases, and is beneficial for wounds.
Bālaka, vāriparyāya, hrīveraka, keśya, vajra, udīcya, piṅga, lalanāpriya,
bāla, kuntala, uśīra, kacāmoda, and śaśīndudhā are synonyms for vetiver grass (vānīra).

Bālaka is cooling and bitter; it removes vomiting and thirst caused by pitta, destroys fever, skin diseases, and diarrhea, benefits the hair, and cures vitiligo and wounds. Barbarī, Sumukha, and Kṛṣṇabarbarī are destroyers of poison. *Rājani-ghaṇṭu* 10.166.
Sukandana, Gandhapatra, Pūtagandha, and Surārhaka; Barbaraka is pungent, hot, fragrant, and a destroyer of vomiting. It destroys erysipelas and poison, and likewise pacifies skin diseases.
Suraparṇa, devaparṇa, vīraparṇa, sugandhika,
mañcipatra, sūkṣmapatra, devārha, and gandhapatraka—
suraparṇa is pungent and hot, and it conquers worms, asthma, and phlegm.
It is an illuminant, subdues phlegm and wind, improves the complexion, and is likewise beneficial for children. Ārāmaśītalā, Nandā, Śītalā,
Sunandinī, Rāmā, Mahānandā, Gandhāḍhyā, and Ārāmaśītalā.

The *ārāma* (lotus) is cooling, bitter, and cold; it removes *pitta*, pacifies burning sensations and wasting, and heals eruptions and ulcers. *Pāthoja*, *kamala*, *nabha*, *nalina*, *ambhoja*, *ambujana*, *ambuja*, *śrīpadma*, *amburuha*, *abja*, *padma*, *jalaja*, *ambhoruha*, and *sārasa* are synonyms for the lotus.
Paṅkaja, sarasīruha, kuṭapa, pāthoruha, puṣkara, vārja, tāmarasa, kuśeśaya, kaja, kañja, aravinda, śatapatra, bisakusuma,
sahasrapatra, mahotpala, vāriruha, sarasija, salilaja, paṅkeruha, and rājīva— these are the names for the lotus, numbering thirty-six (vedavahni). 10.173–174.
The *kamala* is cooling, sweet, and removes the affliction of blood-bile (*raktapitta*) and fatigue;
it is fragrant, bestows relief from delusion and fever, and is supremely satiating.
The *puṇḍarīka*, the white-petaled, the white-lotus, and the white water-born [are similar].

The autumnal lotus, beloved of Śambhu, has eyes like a deer; it is a white lotus (puṇḍarīka), cold, bitter, and sweet. It destroys bile (pitta), removes the defects of burning sensations, blood disorders, and fatigue, and cures the ailments of thirst.
*Kokanada*, *aruṇakamala*, *raktāmbhoja*,
*śoṇapadma*, *raktotpala*, *aravinda*, *ravipriya*, *raktavārija*, and *vasava* are synonyms for the red lotus.
The *kokanada* is pungent and bitter, sweet, cooling, and removes blood disorders (*raktadoṣa*).
It pacifies pitta, kapha, and vāta; it is nourishing and aphrodisiac. Utpala, nīlakamala, nīlābja, nīlapaṅkaja, nīlapadma, bāṇāhva, and nīlādika are synonyms for the blue lotus.
The blue lotus is cooling, sweet, fragrant, and a destroyer of *pitta*;
it is appetizing, excellent for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*), beneficial for the hair, and bestows firmness upon the body.
A slightly white lotus is called *padma*, and one that is slightly reddish is called *nalina*. 10.181–182.
The blue lotus (*utpala*) is slightly bluish; this constitutes the threefold *kamala*.
This group, beginning with the *utpala*, clarifies burning sensations and blood-bile (*rakta-pitta*);
it removes thirst, burning, heart disease, vomiting, and fainting. (Rajni 10.182–10.183)
Padminī is said to be Nalinī, Kūṭapinī, and likewise Abjinī;
thus, she should be known by these synonymous names for the lotus according to their application.
Padminī is sweet, bitter, astringent, and supremely cooling.
It pacifies bile, worms, consumption, vomiting, vertigo, and fever.
Padmabīja, padmākṣa, gāloḍya, and kandalī are synonyms.
Bheḍā, krauñcādanī, and krauñcā are synonyms for śyāmā, which is the same as padmakarkaṭī.

The lotus seed (padmabīja) is pungent and sweet; it is an excellent remedy for bile and vomiting, pacifies burning sensations and blood disorders, acts as a digestive, and stimulates the appetite. (Rajni 10.187) Mṛṇāla, padmanāla, mṛṇālī, and mṛṇālinī [are synonyms for the lotus stalk].
Bisa (the lotus root), padmatantu (the lotus fiber), bisinī (the lotus stalk), and nalinīruha (the lotus plant)—these are known as mṛṇāla.
They are cooling and bitter, slightly astringent, and conquer pitta, burning sensations, and urinary distress.
They are excellent for curing disorders of dysuria and vomiting of blood.
Padmakanda, śālūka, padmamūla, kaṭāhvaya, śālīna, and jalālūka— thus it has six names. Śālūka is pungent, causes constipation, is dry, appetizing, and subdues phlegm.

Kaṣāya destroys cough and bile, and wards off thirst and burning sensations. Kiñjalka, makaranda, kesara, padmakesara, kiñja, pīta, parāga, tuṅga, and cāmpeyaka are the nine [names for the filaments of the lotus].

The filaments (kiñjalka) are sweet, dry, and pungent; they heal wounds of the mouth, destroy pitta, are cooling, improve the appetite, and alleviate thirst and burning sensations. The blue lotus (utpala), the night-blooming water lily (rātripuṣpa), and the water lily (jalāhvaya) are likewise not hot [in potency]. *Rajni* 10.193.

The Himalayan lotus, the cold-water lotus, and the night-blooming lotus are of seven kinds. The *utpala* is cooling and sweet; it removes the afflictions of bile and blood, and is supreme for alleviating burning sensations, fatigue, vomiting, vertigo, worms, and fever.

The white water-lily (dhavalotpala), the night-lotus (kumuda), the kahlāra, the kairava, the śītalaka, the śaśikānta, the indukamala, the candrābja, and the candrikāmbuja— these are the nine [varieties]. Kumuda is cooling, sweet, bitter in digestion, and it removes phlegm (kapha).

It removes blood disorders and pacifies burning sensations, fatigue, and bile. The blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), the *utpalaka*, the *kuvalaya*, the *indīvara*, the *kandottha*, the *saugandhika*, the *sugandha*, the *kuḍmalaka*, and the black lotus (*asitotpala*)— these are the nine kinds.
The blue lotus is extremely sweet, cooling, fragrant, and brings comfort;
however, it is intensely bitter in its post-digestive transformation (pāka) and removes blood-bile (raktapitta).
The utpalinī, kairaviṇī, kumudvatī, and kumudinī are beloved by the Moon.

Kuvalayinī, indīvariṇī, and nīlotpalinī are to be known [as synonyms]. Utpalinī is cold and bitter; it removes blood disorders, destroys pitta, and is known to pacify heat, phlegm, cough, thirst, fatigue, and vomiting. (Rajni 10.200–201)
Puṣpadrava, puṣpasāra, puṣpasveda, puṣpaja, puṣpaniryāsaka, and puṣpāmbuja are the six names [of this substance].
Puṣpadrava is fragrant, cold, astringent, and sweet; it destroys burning sensations, fatigue, excessive vomiting, delusion, and diseases of the mouth.
It removes the afflictions of thirst, bile, and phlegm; it is laxative, nourishing, and for a long time dispels loss of appetite.
(Rājñī 10.203) The *jātī* flower shines with a soft, charming, and sweet fragrance for two *muhūrta*s; the *mallikā* is twice as intoxicating and possesses superior scent;

the *yūthikā* lasts one day; the *navamālikā* is intoxicating for three days; the *campaka* has an intense fragrance for eight days; and the *ketakī* is endowed with fragrance for a period of ten days. (Rājñī 10.204)

Having recited this group [of verses], which is skilled in proclaiming his virtues through its proficiency in describing the names, forms, and positions of various celebrated flowers such as the *sumana*,

*patra*, and *padma*, and which possesses the stable fragrance of eloquent speech, let the physician quickly perfume the lotus of his face with its eternal scents. (Rajñī 10.205) Even the minds of self-controlled ascetics, though they had gradually attained a stability comparable to mountain rocks through meditation on Him, became susceptible to being pierced by the arrows of the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva).

This collection of flowers, consisting of leaves and blossoms that adorn the heads of the gods and others, is considered the "Section of Flowers" (*sumanasām vargaḥ*), known by the name *Uttamṣavarga* (the Section of Ear-ornaments). In this work, the crest-jewel of the collection of titles, this tenth section—consisting of the *karavīra* and other flowers—has found its place; it is the tenth section of the work of the Lord Nṛsiṃha, the moon among scholars, whose pure fame, spreading through contact with the worlds, immediately perfumes them and adorns the quarters like full-blown flowers.
In the *Rājanighaṇṭu*,
in the section on the Mango and other trees (*Āmrādivarga*), it is stated that there are five kinds of mangoes and four kinds of rose-apples (*jambū*).
The jackfruit, the plantain, the coconut, and likewise two types of areca nut;
the date palm is fivefold, as well as the *cāra*, the *bhallātaka*, and the *rāyaṇī*;
the pomegranate, the two kinds of *tinduka*, and then the *akṣoṭa* and the two types of *pīluka*.
Pārevata, madhūka, and bhavyāruka are each of two kinds respectively;
drākṣā is of three kinds; then karmāra, paruṣa, pippala, and vaṭa;
vaṭī and aśvatthikā; likewise plakṣa and udumbara is of three kinds.
Tattva, badara, abdhi, and bījapūra are considered to be of three kinds;
likewise, there are two types of āmalakī, as well as ciñcā and the juice of ciñcā;
then āmrātaka, nāraṅga, nimbū, and the two types of jambīraka.
The *kapittha*, *tumbara*, *rudrākṣa*, *bilva*, *śallakī*,
*kataka*, *karkaṭa*, and likewise the two kinds of *śleṣmātaka*;
the *muṣkaka*, *karamarda*, and similarly the *tejaḥphala*.
Vikaṇṭaka, śivā, and saptā are remembered as sevenfold; akṣa and pūga are remembered as eightfold.
Nāgavallī is sevenfold, and cūrṇa is remembered as eightfold.
Thus the groups beginning with āmra have been stated according to the numbers zero, one, and two.
The mango is known as *kāmaśara*, *cūta*, *rasāla*, *kāmavallabha*,
*kāmāṅga*, *sahakāra*, *kīreṣṭa*, and *mādhavadruma*. It is also called *bhṛṅgābhīṣṭa*, *sīdhurasas*, *madhūlī*, and *kokilotsava*.
The spring messenger, the sour-fruit, the one rich in intoxication, the abode of Love;
the dwelling of honey, the highly amorous, the passion of the cuckoo, the favorite of kings;
the beloved of water, the home of the kokila—this is called by the name Trika.
The young mango fruit has an astringent-sour taste, is fragrant, cures throat ailments, and stimulates the digestive fire;

however, it provokes pitta and causes disorders of vāta and blood, while providing sharpness and a relish for food. The immature fruit increases pitta, vāta, and kapha; likewise, when its seeds are removed, the ripe fruit pacifies all three doṣas, being sweet, nourishing, and heavy.

The fruit produced from the mango tree is known to cause an abundance of bodily elements (*dhātu*), provide nourishment, and bestow luster; it serves to pacify thirst and fatigue. (RājN 11.13) The *kośāmra*, the thick-stemmed (*ghanaskandha*), the forest mango (*vanāmra*), the *jantupādapa*, the small mango (*kṣudrāmra*), the red mango (*raktāmra*), the lac-tree (*lākṣāvṛkṣa*), and the very red one (*suraktaka*) [are varieties thereof]. (RājN 11.14)
The *kośāmra* fruit is sour, dispels wind (*anila*), increases phlegm (*kapha*) and pitta, is heavy, and causes burning sensations, swelling, and inflammation.
When ripe, it becomes sweet and slightly sour; it is pungent and other qualities that stimulate the appetite, promote digestion, nourish, and provide strength.
The *rājāmra*, also known as *rājaphala*, *smarāmra*, and *kokilotsava*, is another variety.
The *madhura*, the *kokilānanda*, the *kāmeṣṭa*, and the *nṛpavallabha*;
the other, the *mahārājacūta*, as well as the *mahārājāmraka*, the *sthūlāmra*,
the *manmathāvāsa*, the *kaṅka*, and the *nīlakapitthaka*.
The prince, the son of the king, is the weapon of desire, the fruit of desire,
the great king as fruit, and the great mango tree— these are thirteen. Furthermore, another mango tree, the *rasāla*, was previously planted by him as the most excellent.
Jñeya, Cakralatāmra, Madhvāmra, Sitajāmra, Vanajya,
Manmathānanda, Madanecchāphala, and Muni— these are the Rājāmras. They are all tender, pungent and sour, and they cause bile and burning sensations.
Well-ripened, sweet and delicious, they bestow nourishment, virility, and strength.
Regarding the three royal mangoes (*rājāmra*), it is said that while their flavor is equal, their qualities should be understood as superior in each successive variety. (Rājñī 11.20–21)

The unripe mango fruit increases phlegm, blood, wind, and the affliction of asthma, and produces pitta; the middling fruit is of the same nature but with an abundance of the [other] doshas, being further astringent and sour.
If ripe, it is sweet, pacifies the three doshas, and relieves thirst, burning sensations, fatigue, asthma, and loss of appetite; it is heavy, cooling, aphrodisiac, and is called the "excellent mango.
The mango bark is astringent, and the root is fragrant and of the same nature.
The flower is pleasing, astringent, cooling, and stimulates the appetite.
The *jambū* tree has fragrant leaves, blue fruit, and is dark-hued with a massive trunk;
it is worthy of kings, bears royal fruit, is dear to parrots, gladdens the clouds, and is called by nine names.

The *jambu* fruit is astringent and sweet; it pacifies fatigue, bile, burning sensations, throat afflictions, and dryness; it destroys worms and disorders, and it eliminates asthma, diarrhea, phlegm, and cough. It causes constipation, yet it is both appetizing and digestive. The *mahājambū*, *rājajambū*, *svarṇamātā*, and *mahāphalā* [are varieties thereof].

The *mahājambū*—known as *śukapriyā*, *kokileṣṭā*, *mahānīlā*, and *bṛhatphalā*—is hot, sweet and astringent, and removes fatigue. When held in the mouth, it instantly dispels numbness and improves the voice. It produces constipation, pacifies dryness, and alleviates exhaustion, diarrhea, pain, labored breathing, phlegm, and cough. (Rajñī 11.26–27)
The *kākajambū* is also known as *kākaphalā*, *nādeyī*, *kākavallabhā*,
*bhṛṅgeṣṭā*, *kākanīlā*, *dhvāṅkṣajambū*, and *dhanapriyā*.
The *kākajambū* is astringent and sour, but it is sweet upon digestion and heavy.
It cures burning sensations, fatigue, and diarrhea, and bestows vigor, nourishment, and strength.
Furthermore, there is another, the *bhūmijambū*, which has small fruits and is dear to bees;
it is called *hrasvā*, *bhūjambū*, *bhramareṣṭā*, *pikabhakṣā*, and *kāṣṭhajambū*.

The *bhūmijambu* is astringent and sweet; it subdues *śleṣman* and *pitta*, is pleasing to the heart, constipating, and removes disorders of the heart and throat; it bestows vigor and nourishment. (Rajni 11.31) The *panasa* is also known as *mahāsarja*, *phalina*, and *phalavṛkṣaka*.
The *sthūla*, the *kaṇṭaphala*, the one known as *mūlaphalada*,

the *apuṣpaphalada*, the *pūtaphala*, and likewise the *aṅkamita* [are types of jackfruit]. The *panasa* (jackfruit) is sweet, very mucilaginous, heavy, beneficial for the heart, and increases strength and virility.

It destroys fatigue, burning sensations, and dehydration; it improves the appetite, is astringent, and is extremely difficult to digest. Its seed is slightly astringent and sweet, increases wind (vāta), and is heavy; the fruit of that [tree] cures disorders, improves the appetite, and destroys skin diseases.

The unripe jackfruit is said to be tasteless yet pleasing to the heart; when half-ripe, it is digestive and, when seasoned with salt and other spices, it is known to stimulate the appetite. The plantain is a fine fruit, called *rambhā*; it is delicate and bears fruit only once.
Mocā, gucchaphalā, hastiviṣāṇī, gucchadantikā, kāṣṭhīrasā, niḥsārā, rājeṣṭā, bālakapriyā,
ūrustambhā, bhānuphalā, and vanalakṣmī— these are the sixteen [names]. (Rājñī 11.36–37)
The young fruit of the plantain (*kadalī*) is sweet, slightly astringent, removes *pitta*, and is cool and refreshing, yet it is not sufficient [in quantity].
Its flower is likewise beneficial and destroys worms; its bulb and leaf alleviate colic.
The ripe fruit of the plantain is astringent-sweet, strengthening, cooling, and likewise subdues *pitta* and blood disorders; it is heavy and wholesome, though not for those with weak digestion.

It provides an immediate increase in semen, removes fatigue, allays thirst, bestows luster, gives comfort to those with a stimulated digestive fire, increases *kapha*, is nourishing, yet is difficult to digest.
(Rajni 11.39) *Kāṣṭhakadalī*, *sukāṣṭhā*, *vanakadalī*, *kāṣṭhikā*, *śilārambhā*, *dārukadalī*, *phalāḍhyā*, *vanamocā*, and *aśmakadalī* are synonyms for the plantain tree. (Rajni 11.40)
The *kāṣṭhakadalī* is palatable, cures hemorrhagic disorders (*raktapitta*), and is cooling; it is heavy, generates weak digestion, is difficult to digest, and is exceedingly sweet.
The *girikadalī*, *girirambhā*, *parvatamocā*, and *araṇyakadalī* are also [known by these names].

The *vanarambhā* (wild plantain) is called *bahubījā*, *girijā*, and *gajavallabhā*. The *girikadalī* is sweet and cooling; it bestows an increase in strength and virility, is appetizing, and alleviates thirst, bile-fever, burning sensations, and emaciation; yet it is difficult to digest and heavy.
There were other golden plantains: the Suvarṇakadalī, the Suvarṇarambhā, and the Kanakarambhā;
the yellow Suvarṇamocā, the Campakarambhā, the Surambhikā, and the Subhagā;
as well as the Hemaphalā, the Svarṇaphalā, the Kanakastambhā, and the Pītarambhā.

The *gaurā*, *gaurarambhā*, *kāñcanakadalī*, *surapriyā*, *ṣaḍbhū*, *suvarṇamocā*, *madhurā*, and *himā* are light in digestion; they stimulate the digestive fire when eaten in small quantities, remove thirst, alleviate burning sensations, increase phlegm, act as aphrodisiacs, and are heavy. (Rājani 11.45–46)

The coconut tree is known as *rasaphala*, *sutuṅga*, *kūrcaśekhara*, *dṛḍhanīla*, *nīlataru*, and likewise *maṅgalyoccataru*. It is also called *tṛṇarāja*, *skandhataru*, *dākṣiṇātya*, and *durāruha*. (Rājñī 11.47)
The lāṅgalī, tryambakaphala, and likewise the dṛḍhaphalasthiti;
the coconut is heavy, unctuous, cold, and a destroyer of pitta.
When half-ripe, it alleviates thirst and emaciation, though it is extremely difficult to digest.

The water of the coconut is light, strengthening, cooling, and sweet; it is heavy in digestion, pacifies bile, catarrh, thirst, fatigue, and burning sensations, alleviates wasting, and bestows comfort.
Even when ripe, it is said here to slightly increase bile, yet it is appetizing, sweet, digestive, strength-promoting, heavy, aphrodisiac, and increases virility—so they say.
The pulp (*khubara*) of the coconut is unctuous, heavy, and difficult to digest.
It relieves burning sensations and constipation, is appetizing, and increases strength and virility.
*Madhunārikelaka*, *mādhvīkaphala*, *madhuphala*, *asitajaphala*, *mākṣikaphala*, *mṛduphala*, *bahukūrca*, and *hrasvaphala*—these are the eight varieties [of coconut]. (Rājñī 11.51–52)
Sweet coconut juice is said to be cooling, a remover of burning sensations, thirst, distress, and pitta;
it bestows strength and nourishment, produces supreme luster, increases virility, and is appetizing.

(Rājñī 11.53) Madhvīka liquor and coconut fruit are exceedingly sweet, difficult to digest, and cause the formation of worms; they are unctuous, pacify wind, diarrhea, and fatigue, yet they destroy the intensity of the digestive fire.

It generates an increase in phlegm and mucus, produces a beautiful luster and strength, maintains the stability of the body, increases the arts of intense passion, and destroys bile (pitta). The *kharjūrī* tree has a rough trunk, is difficult to assail, and hard to climb;
it serves as a ladder, is astringent, is favored by the Yavanas, and is dear to Hari.
The *kharjūrī* fruit is astringent; when ripe, it is sweet and astringent.
It subdues *pitta*, increases *kapha*, generates worms, and is aphrodisiac and nourishing.
(Rajni 11.56) Furthermore, there is another variety, the *madhukharjūrī*, also known as *madhukarkaṭikā* and *kolakarkaṭikā*.
Kaṇṭakinī, madhuphalikā, mādhvī, madhurā, and madhurakharjūrī;
madhukharjūrī is sweet, aphrodisiac, and brings relief from fever and bile. It is cooling, beneficial for living beings, and promotes the increase of great virility.
Bhūkharjūrī, bhuktā, vasudhākharjūrikā, and bhūmikharjūrī are synonyms for the earth-date palm.
Bhūkharjūrī is sweet, cooling, and removes burning sensations and bile.
Dīpyā, piṇḍakharjūrī, sthalapiṇḍā, and madhusravā are synonyms for the date palm.
Phalapuṣpā, Svādupiṇḍā, Hayabhakṣyā, and Svarābhidhā; likewise, there is another called Rājakharjūrī, Rājapiṇḍā, and Nṛpapriyā;
then Munikharjūrikā, Vanyā, Rājeṣṭā, and Ripusammitā. (Rajñī 11.60–61)
The pair of *piṇḍakharjūra* dates is sweet in taste, cooling, and heavy;
it destroys bile, burning sensations, pain, and asthma; it removes fatigue, increases virility, and is nourishing and restorative.

(Rajni 11.62) [The date] is a destroyer of burning sensations, sweet, a pacifier of blood-bile (*raktapitta*), a remover of thirst, afflictions, and disorders; it is cooling, a remover of the onset of asthma, phlegm, and fatigue, and it provides nourishment and promotes growth.

The date known as *piṇḍākhyakharjūrikā* is said to alleviate the dullness of the digestive fire (*vahni*), counteract poison, be pleasing to the heart, bestow strength, be unctuous, and increase virility.
*Cāra*, *khadru*, *kharaskandha*, *lalana*, *cāraka*, *bahuvalka*, *priyāla*, *navadru*, and *tāpasapriya* are synonyms for the *khadira* tree.
The upavaṭa has oily seeds, while the kareṇu has edible seeds. The ripe fruit of the cāra is aphrodisiac, sweet-sour, and heavy;
its seeds are sweet, aphrodisiac, and destroy the pain of bile and burning sensations.
Bhallātaka is fire, the burner, the heater, the scorcher, and the flame;
it is the destroyer of worms, the seed of oil, the enemy of wind, and the seed of pustules.
It is the tree of distinct seeds, the tree of bow-seeds, the bhallāta, and the tree of seeds.

Vahni and Varataru are to be known as its sixteen names. Bhallātaka is pungent, bitter, astringent, and hot; it conquers worms and destroys phlegm, wind, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, urinary disorders, and hemorrhoids.
The fruit of the *bhallātaka* is astringent-sweet, slightly warm, and destroys phlegm-related ailments, fatigue, dyspnea, abdominal distension, constipation, colic, stomach bloating, and worms.

Its marrow alleviates dehydration and burning sensations, removes *pitta*, is nourishing, cures wind-disorders and loss of appetite, and quickly generates digestive fire and removes *pitta*. *Rājādana*, *rājaphala*, *kṣīravṛkṣa*, and *nṛpadruma* are synonyms for the *bhallātaka* tree.
The nimba tree has seven names: *nimbabīja*, *madhuphala*, *kapīṣṭa*, *mādhavodbhava*, *kṣīrī*, *gucchaphala*, and *śukeṣṭa*. The *rājavallabha* (the king’s favorite) has five names:
*śrīphala*, *dṛḍhaskandha*, *kṣīraśukla*, *tri*, and *pañcadhā*. (Rājñī 11.70–71)

The *rājādanī* is sweet, removes bile, is heavy, satiating, aphrodisiac, causes corpulence, is pleasing to the heart, very unctuous, and destroys urinary disorders. (Rajni 11.72) The *dāḍima*, the essence of the pomegranate (*dāḍimīsāra*), *kuṭṭima*, and *phalaṣāḍava* [are also mentioned].
Kāraka, raktabīja, suphala, dantabījaka,
madhubīja, kucaphala, rocana, śukavallabha, maṇibīja, as well as valkaphala and vṛttaphala.
Sunīla and Nīlapatra are to be known as the seventeen names [of this fruit].
The pomegranate (dāḍima) is sweet, sour, and astringent; it destroys cough, wind, phlegm, and bile.
It is constipating, stimulates the digestive fire, is light and hot, yet cooling, removes fatigue, and provides relish for food.
The wise have declared that the pomegranate is of two kinds: one is sour and the other is sweet.
Of these, the sour variety dispels wind and phlegm, while the sweet variety removes heat, is light, and is wholesome.
Tinduka, nīlasāra, kālaskandha, and atimuktaka [are synonyms].
Sphūrjaka, rāmaṇa, sphūrjana, and that which is called syandana;
the tinduka is astringent, constipating, and highly provocative of wind (vāta).
When ripe, however, it is sweet, unctuous, difficult to digest, increases phlegm (śleṣman), and is heavy.
Tinduka is also known as kākapīlu, kākāṇḍa, kākatinduka,
kākasphūrja, kākendu, kākāhva, and kākabījaka.
Kākatindu is astringent and sour, heavy, and causes disorders of wind (vāta).
When ripe, it is slightly sweet, increases *kapha*, and removes *pitta* and vomiting. The mountain acorn (*akṣoṭa*) has fruit-oil, contains jaggery, is beloved by parrots,
is called *kandarāla*, has honey-like marrow, and possesses large leaves.
The walnut (akṣoṭa) is sweet, strengthening, unctuous, and hot;
it conquers wind and bile, pacifies blood disorders, is cooling, and aggravates phlegm.
The pītu, the sahasrāṃśī, the dhānī, and likewise the guḍaphala are also cooling.
The *virecanaphala* tree is dark-colored and beloved by young camels (*karabha*).

Known as *aṅka*, it is pungent (*kaṭuka*), a *pīlu* tree that is astringent (*kaṣāya*), sweet-sour (*madhurāmlaka*), laxative (*sara*), and delicious; it pacifies abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and is an excellent digestive stimulant (*dīpana*).

Furthermore, there is the *bṛhatpīlu*, the *mahāpīlu* which has large fruit, the *rājapīlu*, the great tree, and the *madhupīlu*; these are its six names. The *mahāpīlu* is sweet, aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of poison.
It pacifies bile, improves the appetite, destroys undigested matter (*āmadoṣa*), and stimulates the digestive fire. Pārevata, raivata, ārevataka, and also raivataka;
it has sweet fruit, is called amṛtaphala, and pārevataka is known by seven names.
The *pārevata* fruit is sweet, it removes worms and wind, is aphrodisiac, and alleviates thirst, fever, and burning sensations;
it is pleasing to the heart, destroys fainting, vertigo, fatigue, and emaciation, and is described as unctuous, appetizing, and bestowing great potency.
There is also another, the *mahāpārevata*, as well as the *svarṇapārevata*.

That which is produced in Sāmrāṇija, Khārika, and Raktaraivataka is called Bṛhatpārevata; that which is born on an island is Dvīpakharjūrī. Mahāpārevata and Gaulya increase strength and promote nourishment.
It is aphrodisiac, cures fainting and fever, and is superior in its qualities to what was previously mentioned.
Madhūka is known as madhuvṛkṣa, madhuṣṭhīla, and madhusrava;
it is also called guḍapuṣpa, lodhrapuṣpa, vānaprastha, and mādhava.
Madhuka is sweet, cooling, and removes bile, burning sensations, and fatigue;
it increases wind (vāta), destroys parasites and disorders, and promotes virility and nourishment.
Another variety is Jalamadhūka, also known as Maṅgalya, Dīrghapatraka, and Madhupuṣpa.
The *kṣaudrapriya*, *pataṅga*, *kīreṣṭa*, and *gairikākṣa* should be known as varieties of *jalamadhūka*. It is sweet, destroys wounds, is aphrodisiac,
removes vomiting, is cooling, promotes strength, and is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
Madhūka flower is sweet, aphrodisiac, pleasing to the heart, cooling, and removes pitta and burning sensations;
its fruit destroys diseases of wind and pitta—thus both types of Madhūka should be known. Bhavya, bhava, bhaviṣya, and bhāvana cleanse the mouth.
Likewise, the *picchalabīja* is considered to be the same as *lomaphala*.
The unripe fruit is wholesome, sour, pungent, and hot; it removes wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*).
When ripe, however, it is sweet and sour, stimulates the appetite, and cures colic associated with undigested matter (*sāma-śūla*).
One should know that there are four varieties of *āruka*— namely *vīrasena*, *vīra*, and *vīrāruka*— distinguished by their leaves, flowers, and so forth. All types of *āruka* are sweet and cooling.
And they destroy hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, and blood-related diseases. Drākṣā is known as āruphalā, kṛṣṇā, priyālā, tāpasapriyā, gucchaphalā, rasālā, and amṛtaphalā.
Grapes (*drākṣā*) are extremely sweet and sour, cooling, and they conquer the pain of *pitta* and burning sensations;

they remove disorders of the urine, are appetizing, aphrodisiac, and supremely nourishing. (Rajñī 11.101) Another variety is the brown grape (*kapiladrākṣā*), known as *mṛdvīkā*, *gostanī*, and *kapilaphalā*.
Amṛtarasā, dīrghaphalā, madhuvallī, madhuphalā, and madhūlī;
haritā, hārahūrā, suphalā, mṛdvī, and himottarāpathikā; haimavatī, śatavīryā, kāśmīrī, and gajarājamahī—these are the varieties counted [by experts]. (Rājñī 11.102–103)
The *gostanī* grape is sweet, cooling, pleasant to the heart, and exhilarating;
it destroys burning sensations, fainting, fever, asthma, thirst, and nausea.
Another variety is the *kākalī-drākṣā*, and the *jambukā* is the best of fruits.

The small, seedless, and well-rounded grape is appetizing, cooling, and beloved by people; it destroys asthma and nausea. (Rājñī 11.105) The young fruit of the grape is pungent, hot, and clear; it produces the disorders of pitta and blood. When it reaches the middle stage, its taste becomes sour; it is appetizing and provides excessive digestive fire once it has reached the final stage of ripeness.

If ripe, it is sweet and combined with acidity; it removes thirst and blood-bile (rakta-pitta). When ripe and very dry, it pacifies the pain of fatigue, provides nourishment, and bestows strength. Cold, sweet, and oily in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), it subdues the defects of bile and blood. It is highly palatable, beneficial for the eyes, and pacifies asthma, cough, fatigue, and vomiting. It destroys swelling, thirst, and fever. Being extremely nourishing when ripe and dried, it dispels burning sensations, flatulence, vertigo, and other ailments. Even those whose virility is utterly wasted, it renders capable of the playful arts of love.
Karmāra, karmaraka, pītaphala, karmara,
mudgaraka, mudgaraphala, dhārāphalaka, and karmāraka—
karmāraka is sour and hot; it subdues wind (vāta) and generates bile (pitta).
When ripe, it is sweet and sour, and bestows strength, nourishment, and relish.
The *parūṣaka*, *tīlaparṇa*, *giripīlu*, *parāvaram*, *nīlamaṇḍala*, *alpāsthi*, *paruṣa*, and likewise *paru*—these are its names. (Rājñī 11.109–110)
Its fruit is harsh, sour, and pungent; it conquers afflictions caused by *kapha*, removes *vāta*, and increases *pitta*.
When ripe, it is warm, sweet, appetizing, removes *pitta*, and when drunk, it alleviates swelling.
The *aśvattha* tree is the abode of Acyuta, possesses trembling leaves, and is purifying.
The auspicious Bodhi tree, the Sacrificial one, and the Elephant-eater;
