the illustrious Milk-tree, the Brahmin, the Auspicious, and that Dark one;
the Pippala, the Secret-flowered, the One to be Served, the Truthful, and the Pure Tree.

The *caityadruma* (sacred tree) and the *dharmavṛkṣa* (tree of dharma) are to be known by twenty names. The *pippala* (fig tree) is very sweet, astringent, and cooling; it destroys phlegm and bile, pacifies blood and burning sensations, and indeed, when ripe, it is said to instantly remove disorders of the female reproductive tract.
The fruits of the aśvattha tree, when ripe, are exceedingly pleasing to the heart and cooling;
they destroy the disorders of bile, blood, poison, pain, burning sensations, vomiting, emaciation, and loss of appetite.
Furthermore, it may be called vaṭa, jaṭāla, nyagrodha, rohiṇa, and avarohī.
The tree with spreading branches, red fruit, growing from a trunk, circular in form, and providing great shade;
the horned tree, the abode of yakṣas, the yakṣa-tree, the one that climbs from the base, the blue one;
the milky one, the one growing from a root-stalk, the many-footed one—these are called *vanaspati*, born of the ninefold [classification].
The banyan tree (vaṭa) is astringent, sweet, cooling, and conquers phlegm and bile;
it removes fever, burning sensations, thirst, delusion, wounds, and swellings.
It is also known as nadīvaṭa, yajñavṛkṣa, siddhārtha, vaṭaka, and vaṭī.
Amarā, Saṅginī, and Kṣīrakāṣṭhā are thus proclaimed.
Vaṭī is astringent and sweet, cooling, and removes bile;
it is supreme for alleviating burning sensations, thirst, fatigue, dyspnea, and vomiting.
Aśvatthī should be known as Laghupatrī, Pavitrā, Hrasvapatrikā,
Pippalikā, Vanasthā, Kṣudrā, and Aśvatthasaṃnibhā. Aśvatthikā is sweet, astringent, and subdues blood-bile (asrapitta).
It pacifies the burning sensation caused by poison and is beneficial for pregnant women.
Plakṣa, kapītana, kṣīrī, supārśva, kamaṇḍalu, śṛṅgī,
varohaśākhī, gardabhāṇḍa, and kapītaka.
Dṛḍhapraroha, Plavaka, and the very powerful Plavaṅga; furthermore, Plakṣa, Hrasva, Suśīta, Śītavīryaka,
Puṇḍra, Mahāvaroha, and Hrasvaparṇa, who is indeed Pimpari.

The *plakṣa* tree, which is fragile and possesses an auspicious luster, should be known as having twenty-two names. It is pungent and astringent, cooling, and it conquers blood disorders (*raktadoṣa*).
It destroys fainting, dizziness, and delirium; the small *plakṣa* (*hrasvaplakṣa*) is particularly effective in this regard.
The Udumbara is a milky tree with golden latex, always bearing fruit;
it is known as Kālaskandha, fit for sacrifice, sacrificial, well-established,
Śītavalka, Jantuphala, flowerless, and Purifying (Pavitraka).
It is declared that the one named *manu* is mild and has cooling fruit. The *udumbara* is astringent when unripe, but sweet and cold when ripe;
it generates worms, destroys bile and blood disorders, and removes fainting, burning sensations, and thirst.
The fruit of the *audumbara* tree is exceedingly cooling, sweet when well-ripe, and removes bile; it alleviates fatigue and swelling.
When unripe, it is astringent, highly digestive, and appetizing; it promotes the growth of flesh and cures disorders of the discharges.
There is also another variety, the river-*udumbara*, which has small leaves and fruits. *Rājñī 11.129*
The *laghuhemadugdhā* is said to be the small variety of *sadāphalā*.
The one called *laghvādyumbarā* is also proclaimed as *bāṇāhvā*,
and it is slightly inferior to the former in its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect.
Kṛṣṇodumbarikā, another [variety], kharapatrī, and rājikā;
the hard udumbarī, which destroys leprosy, and phalguvāṭikā;
ajākṣī, phalgunī, malapū, and citrabheṣaja.
And *kākodumbarikā*, also known by the name *dhvāṅkṣa*, is the thirteenth [fruit].
*Kākodumbarikā* is cooling; when ripe, it is sweet and sour, pungent, and it destroys skin diseases, bile, and blood disorders. Its bark likewise stops excessive diarrhea.

The bark of the *udumbara* is cooling, astringent, and a destroyer of wounds; it is beneficial for protecting the fetus of a pregnant woman and promotes the flow of breast milk. *Badara*, *badarī*, *kolī*, *karkandhū*, *kola*, and *phenila* [are synonyms].
Sauvīraka, guḍaphala, bāleṣṭa,
phalaśaiśira, dṛḍhabīja, vṛttaphala, kaṇṭakī, vakrakaṇṭaka, subīja, suphala, svaccha, surasa, and smṛtisammita. (Rājñī 11.136–137)
The jujube fruit (badara) is sweet, astringent, sour, and when fully ripe, it is sweet-sour and hot.
It increases phlegm, yet it destroys fever, diarrhea, blood disorders, exhaustion, emaciation, and pain; it is also appetizing.
An application of jujube leaves acts as a destroyer of fever and burning sensations.

The bark pacifies eruptions, and the seed removes eye diseases. The *rājabadara* is beloved by kings; it is also called *nṛpabadara*, *rājavallabha*, *pṛthukola*, *tanubīja*, *madhuraphala*, and *rājakola*. (Rājani 11.139–140)
The *rājabadara* is very sweet, cooling, and removes the pain of burning sensations, as well as *pitta* and *vāta*. It is aphrodisiac, increases virility, and alleviates consumption and fatigue.
*Bhūbadarī*, *kṣitibadarī*, *vallībadarī*, and *badarivallī* [are synonyms].

The *bahuphalikā*, the small jujube (*laghubadarī*), the jujube-fruiting (*badaraphalī*), and the fine-jujube (*sūkṣmabadarī*)— the earth-born jujube (*bhūbadarī*) is sweet and sour, it removes disorders of phlegm and wind, is wholesome,
acts as a digestive stimulant and promoter of digestion, slightly increases bile and blood, and is appetizing. (RājN 11.142–143)
The *sūkṣmaphala* (small-fruit) is a small jujube with many thorns and fine leaves; it is difficult to touch, sweet, a food for the *śambara* deer, and is specified as being dear to peacocks.
The small jujube is sweet and sour when ripe; it destroys phlegm and wind, and is appetizing.
The *bījapūra* is unctuous, it produces worms, and slightly cures the affliction of bile, burning sensations, and emaciation. It is called *bījapūrṇa*, *pūrṇabīja*, *sukesara*, *bījaka*,
*keśarāmla*, *mātuluṅga*, and *supūraka*.

The *rucaka*, *bījaphalaka*, *jantughna*, *danturatvaca*, *pūraka*, and *rocanaphala* are measured by two deities and one sage (*muni*). The fruit of the citron (*bījapūra*) is sour, pungent, and hot; it alleviates asthma and cough, and acts as a digestive.
The immature (*bāla*) mātuluṅga is supreme for cleansing the throat; it is light, pleasing to the heart, digestive-stimulant, appetizing, and promotes digestion.
It produces *pitta*, wind, phlegm, and blood. The middling variety is of a similar nature. When ripe, it improves the complexion, is pleasing to the heart, and nourishes nourishment and strength.
This mātuluṅga always conquers colic, indigestion, constipation, wind, phlegm, dyspnea, pain from weak digestion, cough, anorexia, and swelling; it brings about their pacification. (Rajni 11.148–149)

The rind of the *bījapūra* is bitter and difficult to digest; it destroys worms, phlegm, and wind. The pulp is unctuous, hot, and moderate; it pacifies colic, pain, and *pitta*, and cures all types of anorexia. The sweet variety (*gaulya*) destroys wind-related ailments and is pungent-hot; it removes abdominal diseases and stimulates the appetite. The filaments (*kesara*) are sour and stimulate digestion. The seeds are bitter and beneficial for curing phlegm, hemorrhoids, and swelling.
The wild *bījapūra* is another variety known as *vanabījapūraka*, *vanaja*, *vanapūraka*, and *vanabīja*.
Atyamlā, Gandhāḍhyā, Vanodbhavā, and Devadūtī;
Pītā, Devadāsī, Deveṣṭā, and Mātuluṅgikā;
Pavanī and Mahāphalā—this is known as the Vedabhūmimitā. (Rājñī 11.151–152)
The wild *bījapūra* is sour, pungent, and hot;
it provides relish, destroys wind (*vāta*), cures the defects of acidity, destroys worms, removes phlegm (*kapha*), and alleviates asthma.
The sweet *bījapūra*, known as *madhuparṇī*, *madhurakarkaṭī*, and *madhuvallī*, [is likewise beneficial].

The *madhukarkaṭī* has sweet fruit, large fruit, and is called *vardhamānā*. (RājN 11.154) The *madhukarkaṭī* is sweet, cooling, and destroys burning sensations; it pacifies the three *doṣas*, is appetizing, aphrodisiac, heavy, and difficult to digest. (RājN 11.155)
Āmalakī, vayaḥsthā, śrīphalā, dhātrikā,
amṛtā, śivā, śāntā, and likewise śītāmṛtaphalā;
jātīphalā, dhātreyī, and dhātrīphalā are likewise to be known [as synonyms].
The *vṛttaphalā* (round-fruit) is aphrodisiac, while the one called *śarabhū* (growing on thorny shrubs) is appetizing. The *āmalaka* is astringent-acidic, sweet, cooling, and light;
it destroys burning sensations, bile, urinary disorders, and swelling, and acts as a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).

The fruit of the *āmalakī* is pungent, sweet, and astringent, slightly sour, subdues *kapha*, stimulates the appetite, and is extremely cooling; it destroys bile, blood disorders, and heat, while pacifying fatigue, vomiting, constipation, flatulence, and the afflictions of indigestion; it is like nectar.
Furthermore, it is called both *āmalaka* and *kāṣṭhadhātrīphala*.
That which is called *kṣudrāmalaka* is the small *jātīphala*. The fruit of the *kāṣṭhadhātrī* is astringent in taste as well as pungent;
it is cooling, destroys the defects of *pitta* and blood, and possesses qualities superior to those previously mentioned.
Ciñcā, cukrikā, cukrā, sāmlikā, śākacukrikā,
amlī, sutintiḍī, amlā, and cukrikā are the nine names for the tamarind tree.
The ciñcā is extremely sour when unripe, but when ripe it is sweet and sour.
It subdues wind (vāta) but aggravates the defects of bile (pitta), burning sensations, blood, and phlegm (kapha).
The unripe fruit of the tamarind (*amlikā*) is extremely sour, light, and increases bile;
when ripe, however, it is sweet and sour, is purgative, and overcomes constipation and wind.
The juice of the ripe tamarind fruit is sweet and sour, it stimulates the appetite,
causes inflammation to suppurate when applied as a paste, and destroys the defects of wounds. The leaf of the tamarind tree likewise cures swelling and removes the pain caused by blood disorders.
The alkaline extract from its dry bark destroys colic and weak digestion.
Sour essence (amlasāra), sour vegetable juice (śākāmla), sour sorrel (cukrāmla), sour dock (amlacukrikā),
sour tamarind (ciñcāmla), sour citron (amlacūḍa), and tamarind juice (ciñcārasa) constitute the sevenfold [sour category].
The essence of the *amlasāra* fruit is extremely sour; it subdues wind (*vāta*) but produces phlegm (*kapha*) and burning sensations (*dāha*).
When mixed with sugar in equal proportions, it removes burning sensations, bile (*pitta*), phlegm, and pain.
The *āmrātaka*, *pītanaka*, *kapicūta*, and *amlavāṭaka* are synonyms for the hog-plum tree.

The *śṛṅgī* is rich in monkey-juice (*kapirasa*), has thin latex, and is dear to monkeys. The *āmrātaka* is astringent and sour; it removes undigested matter (*āma*) and refreshes the throat. When ripe, however, it is rich in sweet and sour flavors, unctuous, and pacifies *pitta* and *kapha*.
The orange is known as *nāraṅga*, *nāgaraṅga*, *suraṅga*, *tvaggandha*, *airāvata*,
*vaktravāsa*, *yogīraṅga*, *nāgara*, *yogaraṅga*, *gandhāḍhya*, *gandhapatra*, and *ravīṣṭa*.
The orange is sweet and sour, heavy, hot, and pleasing to the sight.
It destroys wind-disorders, worms, and colic; it removes fatigue and bestows strength and relish for food.
(Rajni 11.172) Nimbūka is known as Amlajambīraka; it is called Vahni, Dīpya, Vahnibīja, Amlasāra, Dantāghāta, Śodhana, Jantumārī, Nimbū, Rocana, and Rudrasaṃjña. (Rajni 11.173)
The lime fruit is well known for its sour taste; it is pungent and hot, removes abdominal tumors, disorders of the stomach, and wind, and increases the digestive fire.
It is beneficial for the eyes, and when fully ripe, it is extremely palatable, removing cough, phlegm, pain in the throat, and vomiting.
(Rajni 11.174) Jambīra, dantaśaṭha, jambha, jambhīra, and jambhala are synonyms.

Rochanaka is a cleanser of the mouth, an enemy of dullness, and a conqueror of parasites; it is ninefold [in its benefits]. (Rajni 11.175) The fruit of the *jambīra* is sour-sweet in taste; it dispels wind (*vāta*), generates bile (*pitta*), and is wholesome. It is digestive, appetizing, strength-promoting, and increases the digestive fire (*agni*).

If ripe, it is sweet, pacifies afflictions of phlegm (*kapha*), removes the disorders of bile and blood (*pittāsra*), improves the complexion, increases virility, creates relish for food, provides nourishment, and is satiating. (Rajni 11.176)
There are six names for it: *madhujambīra*, *madhujambha*, *madhurajambhala*, *śaṅkhadrāvī*, *śarkaraka*, and *pittadrāvī*.
The *madhujambīra* is sweet, cooling, and subdues phlegm and bile.

It cures wasting diseases, is nourishing, aphrodisiac, removes fatigue, and promotes nourishment. The *mālūra* (wood-apple) is also called *kapittha*; it is auspicious, as are the *nīlamallikā*, curd, the *grāhīphala*, the *cirapākī*, the *granthiphala*, the *kucaphala*, and the *dadhiphala*.
Gandhaphala, kapīṣṭa, vṛttaphala,
karabhavallabha, dantaśaṭha, kaṭhinaphala, and karaṇḍaphalaka— these are the seventeen names [of the wood-apple].
The kapittha is sweet and sour, astringent, bitter, and cooling.
It is aphrodisiac, destroys pitta and vāta, is constipating, and heals wounds.
Raw wood-apple is sour and hot, destroys kapha, is constipating, and increases vāta;
when ripe, it removes all three doṣas, has a sweet-sour taste, and is heavy.
The unripe *kapittha* causes throat pain and excessive numbness of the tongue; it increases the three *doṣas*, yet it is an antidote to poison, astringent, and appetizing.
When ripe, it removes asthma, vomiting, fatigue, and is capable of dispelling hiccups; it is entirely astringent and provides relish, and therefore it should always be consumed.
*Tumbaru*, *saurabha*, *saura*, *vanaja*, *sānuja*, and *dvija* [are synonyms].
Tīkṣṇavalka, tīkṣṇaphala, tīkṣṇapatra, mahāmuni, sphuṭaphala, and sugandhi—this [tree] is said to have twelve names.
Tumburu is sweet, bitter, pungent, and hot; it subdues phlegm and wind.
It destroys colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, and worms, and it kindles the digestive fire.
Rudrākṣa, Śivākṣa, Śarvākṣa, Bhūtanāśana, Pāvana, Nīlakaṇṭhākṣa, Harākṣa, and Śivapriya are its names.

Rudrākṣa is sour and hot; it subdues wind, destroys phlegm, alleviates headaches, improves the appetite, and destroys evil spirits and planetary influences. Bilva is also known as śalya, hṛdyagandha, śalāṭu, śāṇḍilya, śrīphala, and karkaṭāhva.
Śailūṣa, śaivapatra, śiveṣṭa, patraśreṣṭha, gandhapatra, and tripattra;
lakṣmīphala, gandhaphala, durāruha, triśākapattra, triśikha, and śivadruma;
sadāphala, satphalada, subhūtika, samīrasāra, and the one known as śikhinetra. (RājNī 11.188–189)
The *bilva* fruit is sweet, pleasing to the heart, astringent, and conquers *pitta*;
it is heavy, destroys *kapha*, fever, and diarrhea, stimulates the appetite, and is a supreme digestive stimulant.
The root of the *bilva* destroys the three *doṣas*, is sweet, light, and subdues *vāta*.
The fruit, when unripe, is tender, oily, heavy, constipating, and digestive.
That same fruit, when ripe, should be known as sweet, succulent, and heavy;
it is pungent, bitter, astringent, and hot, and being constipating, it conquers the three *doṣas*.
Sallaka, sallakī, sallī, sugandhā, surabhisravā, surabhi,
gajabhakṣyā, suvahā,
gajavallabhā, gandhamūlā, mukhāmodā, suśrīkā, and jalavikramā.
The *kuṇṭarikā* is said to be heart-pleasing and to have triangular fruits;
it is known by eighteen names, including *chinnaruhā* and *gandhaphalā*.
The *sallakī* is bitter-sweet and astringent, and is highly astringent in its action.

It destroys the afflictions caused by skin diseases, blood disorders, phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, and wounds. Kataka is known as a purifier of water, and likewise as katu and tiktapala; it is considered appetizing, scarifying, and is traditionally known as gudaphala.
Prokta, kataphala, tiktamarica, and navāhvaya are synonyms for *kataka*.
*Kataka* is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is beneficial for the eyes, destroys worms and disorders, promotes appetite, cures colic, and its seeds clarify water.
Karkaṭa, kārkaṭa, karka, kṣudradhātrī, kṣudrāmalaka, and karkaphala— these six are thus recorded.
The fruit of the kārkaṭa is appetizing, astringent, and highly digestive.
It subdues phlegm and bile, is constipating, beneficial for the eyes, light, and cooling.
Śleṣmātaka is also called bahuvāra, picchila, dvijakutsita,
śelu, śītaphala, śīta, śākaṭa, and karbudāraka.
The *bhūtadruma* is known as the "fragrant-flowered" tree and has eleven names.
The *śleṣmātaka* is pungent, cold, sweet, and astringent; it is palatable and promotes digestion.
It removes worms and colic, alleviates the pain of many wounds, boils, and eruptions caused by the obstruction of impurities from undigested matter (*āmāsradoṣa*), and increases *kapha*.
Another is the *bhūkarbudāraka*, as well as the *kṣudraśleṣmātaka*; the *bhūśelu* and the *laghuśelu*; the *picchala* and the one beginning with *laghu*;
the *laghuśīta*, the *sūkṣmaphala*, and that which is the *laghubhūtadruma*.
Bhūkarbudāra is sweet, destroys the defects caused by worms,
slightly aggravates vāta, is cooling, and is a destroyer of gold. Muṣkaka, mocaka, muṣka, mokṣaka, and likewise muñcaka [are synonyms].
Gaulika, mehana, kṣāravṛkṣa, and pāṭali;
viṣāpaha, jaṭāla, vanavāsī, and sutīkṣṇaka;
white and black—these are the thirteen varieties known by these names.
Muṣkaka is pungent and sour, an excellent appetizer and digestive;
it destroys diseases of the spleen, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen, and exists in two forms possessing equal qualities.
Karamarda, suṣeṇa, karāmla, and karamardaka are synonyms.
The *avigna*, *pāṇimarda*, and *kṛṣṇapākaphala* are known as *muni*. The *karamarda* is slightly bitter and sour; when raw, it stimulates digestion and causes a burning sensation.
When ripe, it pacifies the three *doṣas*, overcomes loss of appetite, and destroys poison.
Tejaḥphala, Bahuphala, and likewise Śālmalīphala; Phala, which is endowed with sharpness and other qualities, and Phalāntastavakādika;
Steyīphala, Gandhaphala, and Kaṇṭavṛkṣa are proclaimed [as names of trees].
Tejaḥphala is pungent, sharp, fragrant, and an excellent digestive stimulant;
it destroys wind, phlegm, and loss of appetite, and is supreme for protecting children.
Vikaṇṭaka has soft fruit, is knotty, and has sweet thorns.
Gokaṇṭaka, Kākanāśa, Vyāghrapāda, Ghanadruma, Garjāphala, Ghanaphala, Meghastanitodbhava,
Mudiraphala, Prāvṛṣya, Hāsyaphala, and Stanitaphala— these are the fifteen names.
Vikaṇṭaka is an astringent; it is pungent, dry, and provides relish.
It stimulates digestion, removes phlegm, and serves as a dye for cloth.
Harītakī is known as Hemavatī, Jayā, Abhayā, Śivā, Avyathā, Cetanikā, and Rohiṇī.
Pathyā, prapathyā, pūtanā, amṛtā, jīvapriyā, jīvanikā, and bhiṣagvarā;
jīvantī, prāṇadā, jīvyā, kāyasthā, and śreyasī; she is also known as devī, divyā, vijayā, and by names numbering three and two (five). Rajñī 11.214–215.
Harītakī possesses five tastes; it is purgative, destroys diseases of the digestive tract, and is devoid of salt.

It is an elixir, removes eye ailments, cures skin diseases, and is indeed "yogavāhinī" (acting according to its application). Its seed and kernel are bitter and sweet, while the inner bark portion is pungent and hot in potency.
When combined with meat, sour, and astringent substances, this *harītakī* is said to possess five tastes.
This *harītakī*, born from the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), is declared to have seven varieties;
I shall now describe its names and colors in due order.
Vijayā, Rohiṇī, Pūtanā, Amṛtābhayā,
Jīvantī, and Cetakī— these are considered the seven types by name. Of these, Vijayā has a navel like that of a gourd, while Rohiṇī is regarded as being well-rounded.

Pūtanā is known to have very thin bark, while Amṛtā is remembered for its thick flesh. Abhayā should be known as five-sided, Jīvantī possesses a golden color, and one should recognize Cetakī as being three-sided; such is the description of their forms.
On the Vindhya mountain grows *vijayā*; that which originates from the Himālayas is *cetakī*; in Sindh it is *pūtanā*, while *rohiṇī* is born in Pratiṣṭhāna.

In Campā, *amṛtā* and *abhayā* are produced, and in the land called Surāṣṭra, *jīvantī* is found; thus the wise declare that there are seven varieties of *harītakī*. For all general applications, *vijayā* and *rohiṇī* are used, but for ointments applied to wounds, *pūtanā* is prescribed.

In purgation, *amṛtā* possesses superior qualities; here, *jīvantikā* is the conqueror of chronic diseases. *Cetakī* is the remover of all ailments, and they say that *abhayā* destroys eye diseases. Thus, when administered according to its requirements, this [medicine] should be known as rich in virtues, and never otherwise.

As long as the *cetakī* held in the hand remains with the embodied being, it is purged by force through its power; of this there is no doubt. Among all seven types of plants, *vijayā* is considered the foremost.
Easy to prepare and easy to administer, it is recommended for all diseases. That [ghee] which sinks when dropped into water should be known as "virtuous" by the best of physicians;
that which sinks further [deeper] than another is richer in qualities.

Because it forcibly removes diseases and the body crosses over [them] once again, it is called *harītakī*; therein, the syllable *hari* denotes radiance. Furthermore, *harītakī* [is used] in cases of thirst, lockjaw, and throat-obstruction.
It is not recommended for those suffering from consumption, acute fever, chronic fever, or for pregnant women.

The *vibhītaka* has oil-bearing fruits; it is the abode of spirits (*bhūtāvāsa*), the tree of the Kali age (*kalidruma*), the destroyer (*saṃvartaka*), the spring-blooming (*vāsanta*), the tree of Kalki (*kalkivṛkṣa*), and the purifier (*vaheḍaka*).
Hārya, karṣaphala, kalki, dharmaghna, akṣa, anilaghnaka, bahuvīrya, and kāsaghna—it is said to have these sixteen names. Vibhītaka is pungent, bitter, astringent, and hot; it removes phlegm.
It is beneficial for the eyes, removes gray hair, sweet in its post-digestive effect, and light.
The *pūga* tree—also known as *pūgavṛkṣa*, *kramuka*, *dīrghapādapa*, *valkataru*, *dṛḍhavalka*, *cikkaṇa*, and considered by sages as *muni*—is so named. (RājN 11.232–233)
The resin of the *pūga* tree is cooling, stupefying, and heavy;

it is hot in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), slightly alkaline and sour, subdues wind (*vāta*), and increases bile (*pitta*). *Pūga* is also called *cikkaṇī*, *cikkā*, *cikkaṇa*, and *ślakṣṇaka*.
Udvega is known as the areca nut (*kramukaphala*), while *pūgaphala* is *vasu*.
Serī is sweet, appetizing, astringent, sour, and likewise pungent;
it is wholesome, destroys phlegm and wind, and the *sārikā* variety removes defects of the mouth.
Tāli fruit is sweet, appetizing, cleansing to the throat, light, pacifies the three *doṣas*, stimulates digestion, is flavorful, promotes digestion, and is balanced.
*Gaulya* (jujube) is a cave-dweller’s food; it is smooth, astringent, pungent, and promotes digestion.

It removes constipation and abdominal distension, acts as a liquefier, and is light. Ghoṇṭā is pungent, astringent, and hot; it is hard, improves the relish for food, pacifies the obstruction of waste products, removes pitta, and stimulates digestion.
The betel nut known as *ceula*, which is famous for its fragrance in the Koṅkaṇa region,
removes phlegm, stimulates the digestive fire, aids digestion, bestows strength, promotes nourishment, and is rich in flavor.
The betel nut produced in villages in Koṅkaṇa, called *valligula*, alleviates the three *doṣas*.

The betel nut originating from Candrapura removes undigested matter (*āmāpaha*), is pleasing to the taste, and promotes digestion (*pācana*); it cures constipation (*viṣṭambha*) and abdominal ailments, stimulates the appetite (*dīpana*), destroys phlegm (*kaphaghna*), and purifies the waste products (*malaśodhana*).
It is pungent, sweet, and astringent, and it is appetizing, digestive, and carminative.
Betel nut originating from the Andhra country is astringent and sweet in taste;
it conquers wind, removes numbness of the mouth, is slightly sour, and alleviates phlegm.
All betel nut causes fainting, is astringent, sweet, and purgative.
It pacifies the three *doṣas*, is appetizing, and removes moisture and impurities from the mouth.

Raw betel nut (*pūga*) is astringent, clears oral impurities, provides purification of the throat, pacifies blood, phlegm, and bile, cures abdominal distension, and is laxative. Dry betel nut is said to destroy diseases of the throat, stimulate the appetite, and act as a digestive and purgative. If combined with its leaf (*parṇa*), it quickly dispels anemia, wind disorders, and consumption.
Now, there is the *nāgavallī*, the *tāmbūlī*, and the *phaṇilatā*, which has seven heads;
it is also called *parṇalatā*, *phaṇivallī*, *bhujagalatā*, and *bhakṣyapatrī*.
The *nāgavallī* is pungent, sharp, and bitter; it conquers catarrh and disorders of wind (*vāta*).

It removes phlegm and cough, stimulates the appetite, causes a burning sensation, and is a supreme digestive stimulant. Though it is a single substance, it becomes diverse in form and quality within the body due to differences in its locations— such as the groves of *śrīvāṭa*, *amlā* trees, and various other villages— as well as the specific nature of the soil of the region.
Śrīvāṭī is sweet and pungent; it removes wind, bile, and phlegm.
It is rich in juice, fragrant, appetizing, and is known to be cooling in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
Amlavāṭī is pungent, sour, and bitter; it is sharp and hot, and causes inflammation of the mouth.
It causes burning, aggravates bile and blood, produces constipation, and subdues wind.
It is cooling, sweet, sharp, pungent, and hot;
it is digestive, removes abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and flatulence, and is an excellent stimulant of appetite and digestion.

In the cave-dwelling, the seven-headed [plant] is well-known; it is exceedingly fragrant, pungent, sweet, and very pleasing to the heart. It is digestive, aphrodisiac, and highly strengthening. (Rājñī 11.251) Another, known by the name Āmlasarā, is very sharp and sweet, appetizing, cooling, and a remedy for burning sensations. It alleviates an excess of bile, is a great stimulant of digestion, strengthening, and perfumes the mouth.

It increases female beauty, is intoxicating, and is always beloved by kings; it is said to cure abdominal tumors, flatulence, and constipation, and it is found in Mālava. In Andhra, there is a decoction called *paṭulikā*, which is hot and pungent;
it removes impurities from the throat, produces bile, and destroys wind.
The *hveṣaṇī* is pungent, sharp, beneficial for the heart, and possesses long leaves;
it subdues *kapha* and *vāta*, is appetizing, pungent, and acts as a digestive stimulant and carminative.

(Rajñī 11.254) If eaten while still freshly plucked, it causes oral diseases, numbness, and derangement of the *doṣas*; it produces a burning sensation, loss of appetite, and blood disorders, and being constipating, it induces vomiting.

If a betel leaf that has been nourished by abundant drinking of water is chewed after a long time, it is excellent, appetizing, improves the complexion, and alleviates the afflictions of the three *doṣas*.
(Rājñī 11.255) A black leaf is bitter, hot, and astringent; it produces a burning sensation, oral diseases, and impurities.
A white leaf destroys disorders of phlegm and wind (*śleṣma-vāta*), is wholesome, appetizing, digestive, and carminative. (Rājñī 11.256)

One whose intellect is impaired shall become impoverished and will not remember Hari at the end [of life]. (Rajni 11.258) If there is an excess of leaves, it causes inflammation and bestows a sense of agitation; if there is an excess of betel nuts, it causes dryness and brings hardship; if there is an excess of heartwood in the *khadira* variety, it causes emaciation; and if there is an excess of powder, it produces bile and a foul odor. (Rajni 11.259)
Powder derived from the *Arjuna* tree removes phlegm and destroys abdominal tumors; that called *arka* destroys swelling; *kuṭaja* and that produced from *karañja* dispel wind and provide relish;

that born of water (*jalaja*) destroys bile and bestows strength, digestive fire, and relish; that called *śaila* produces bile; *sphāṭikya* produces firm rows of teeth; and that produced from mother-of-pearl and the like provides dryness.
Thus [is the essence] of the beautiful fragrance and skillful arrangement of the distinct explanations of the names and qualities of various fruits, trees, and creepers.
The physician of knowledge should indeed bring this group to fruition through the abundance of sacred tradition—a group that is the essence of the playful dance upon the balcony of the lotus-face.
(Rajni 11.261) That which becomes a fruitful tree of worldly existence for those who enjoy it—this collection of such fruits is called the "Group of Fruits" (phalavarga). (Rajni 11.262)

From which there arises a profusion of flowers consisting of a mass of stainless, ever-expanding fame, and which wondrously bears the fruits desired by the wise— the glorious hand is indeed a celestial tree.
(Rājanighaṇṭu,
Candanādivarga)
Śrīkhaṇḍa, śabara, pīta, patrāṅga, raktacandana, barbara,
and harigandha— these are known as the seven types of sandalwood (candana).
Devadāru is said to be of two kinds, as are cīḍā and saptacchada.
Sarala, kuṅkuma, kaṅgu, kastūrī, and likewise rocanā; karpūra, javādi, nandī, jātipatrikā,
jātīphala, kakkola, and lavaṅga are said to constitute the "sweet" (svādu) group.
Agarūya is threefold; there are three types of māṃsī, turuṣka, and guggulu;
rāla, kunduruka, kuṣṭha, and two kinds of sārivā and nakha;
as well as spṛkkā, sthauṇeyaka, murā, śaileya, and coraka.
Padmaka, prapauṇḍarīka, lāmajja, the two kinds of rohiṇī,
śrīveṣṭa, uśīra, nalikā, and those with names consisting of seven or five syllables;
śrīkhaṇḍa is called candana, and that which is highly prized is known as śvetacandana.
Gośīrṣa, tilaparṇa, and the auspicious sandalwood from Malaya;
gandharāja, sugandha, and the cool sarpāvāsa;
gandhāḍhya, gandhasāra, bhadraśrī, and bhogivallabha.

Sandalwood (*malayaja*), known by the names *pāvana*, *aṅkabhū*, and *śrīkhaṇḍa*, possesses cool fragrance. It is characterized by pungent, bitter, and cold qualities; it is astringent in taste. It provides relief from bile disorders, delusions, vomiting, fever, worms, thirst, and burning heat. It is aphrodisiac, removes ailments of the mouth, and spreads luster across the bodies of embodied beings when applied. When smeared, it subdues the onset of the rut and the intense passion of the sleeping elephant of the mind.
That sandalwood which possesses excellent hollows and cup-like cavities, has good knots and great weight, is red when cut, and is likewise pure and yellow when rubbed;
which is bitter and pungent in taste, very fragrant, cool, and possesses few qualities—or is diminished in quality and endowed with only half its virtues—is said to be middling sandalwood.
Sandalwood is declared to be of two kinds, known as *beṭṭa* and *sukvaḍi*.
The *beṭṭa* [sandalwood] has moist joints, while the *svayaṃśuṣka* (naturally dried) is very hard.
The mountains situated near the Malaya range are known by the name *beṭṭa*;
according to some opinions, the sandalwood produced there is called *beṭṭa*.
Beṭṭacandana is exceedingly cooling, pacifies burning sensations and pitta, and removes fever;
it is bitter and alleviates vomiting, delusion, thirst, skin diseases, blurred vision, cough, and hemorrhaging.
Sukvaḍicandana is bitter and cures difficult urination, pitta, blood disorders, and burning sensations.
When moist, it provides coolness and fragrance; when dry, its effect in an ointment is otherwise.
The *kairāta*, *śabara*, and *candana* sandalwoods are fragrant, as are the wild *gandhakāṣṭha*, the beloved *kirātaka*, and the *śailagandha*. (Rājñī 12.13–12.14)
Kairāta is hot and pungent yet cooling; it destroys phlegm and wind, removes fatigue and bile, cures eruptive skin diseases, scabies, and the like, quenches thirst, and dispels fever and delusion.
Pītagandha, however, is Kālīya; it is yellow and dear to Mādhava.
Kālīyaka, pītakāṣṭha, barbara, and pītacandana—
these yellow substances are cooling and bitter; they remove skin diseases (kuṣṭha),
phlegm, and wind, destroy itching, eczema, ringworm, and worms, and bestow supreme luster.
Pattaṅga, patrāṅga, raktakāṣṭha, suraṅgada, patrāḍhya, paṭṭarāga, bhāryāvṛkṣa,
raktaka, lohita, raṅgakāṣṭha, rāgakāṣṭha, and kucandana.
Paṭṭarañjanaka and suraṅga are the fourteenth.
Patrāṅga is pungent, dry, sour, and cold; however, gaulyaka is sweet.
It destroys wind, bile, and fever, and removes eruptions, insanity, and possession by spirits.
This red sandalwood, as well as the red, the blood-red, and the yellow sandalwood, the cooling [variety],
the red-essence, the copper-essence, the small sandalwood, and the arka-sandalwood—
red sandalwood is exceedingly cooling, bitter, and removes eye diseases, hemorrhage, and disorders of the blood.
It overcomes disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as cough, fever, delusions, parasites, vomiting, and thirst. Barbaraka, originating from *barbara*, and likewise *śvetabarbaraka*—
known as *śīta*, *sugandhi*, *pittāri*, and *surabhi*— are of seven types.

Barbara is cooling and bitter; it conquers *kapha*, *vāta*, and *pitta*, destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), itching, and wounds, and especially conquers blood disorders (*raktadoṣa*). *Haricandana* (yellow sandalwood) is worthy of the gods, possessing a divine fragrance; it is known as *indracandana* and is celestial.
There is the celestial great fragrance born of the Nandana grove, known as the "new" red sandalwood.
But divine yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*), which is bitter and cooling, is difficult for humans to obtain here;
like [ordinary] sandalwood, it destroys the swelling of bile and removes fatigue, dehydration, and fever.
Sandalwoods are equal in terms of their taste and potency;
they differ, however, by their fragrance, among which the first is the most excellent.
Devadāru, suradāru, dāruka, snigdhadāru, and amarādidāru—these are the types of pine wood.

Bhadradāru, śivadāru, śāmbhava, bhūtahāri, bhavadāru, and rudravat—these are known as snigdhadāru (oleaginous pine). It is bitter, unctuous, and hot; it conquers phlegm and wind, and destroys disorders of undigested matter (āmadoṣa), constipation, hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, and fever.
Devakāṣṭha, pūtikāṣṭha, bhadrakāṣṭha, sukāṣṭhaka,
asnigdhadāruka, and kāṣṭhadāru— these are the six names [of this wood].
Devakāṣṭha is bitter and hot, dry, and it subdues phlegm and wind.
When applied to the limbs, black *kālika* wood removes the defects of the elements.
Devadāru should be known to be of two kinds: the first is *snigdhadāruka*, and the second is *kāṣṭhadāru*; the names of both are used interchangeably.
Cīḍā, dārugandhā, gandhavadhū, gandhamādanī,
taruṇī, tārā, bhūtamārī, maṅgalyā, kapāṭinī, and grahabhītijit;
cīḍā is pungent and hot, it destroys cough, conquers phlegm, and is an excellent digestive stimulant.
When cultivated constantly, it indeed removes the delusions caused by the disorder of *pitta*.
*Saptaparṇa* is known as *patravarṇa*, *śuktiparṇa*, *suparṇaka*,
*saptacchada*, *gucchapuṣpa*, *ayugmaparṇa*, and *municchada*.

Bṛhattvak, Bahuparṇa, Śālmalipatraka, Madagandha, and Gandhiparṇa are to be known as having five, four, three, two, and one [property] respectively, according to fire and earth. Saptaparṇa, however, is bitter and hot, destroys the three doṣas, and is a digestive stimulant (dīpana).
This Madagandha suppresses wounds, blood disorders, diseases, and worms.
Sarala, Pūtikāṣṭha, Tumbī, Pītadru, Utthita, Dīpataru, Snigdhadāru, Snigdha, Mārīca, and Patraka—these are the nine types [of resin]. 12.36–37.

Saraḷa is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys phlegm and wind, cures skin diseases, swelling, itching, and ulcers, and provides purification of the digestive tract. Kuṅkuma should be known by the names agnisekhara, asṛk, kāśmīraja, pītaka, kāśmīra, rudhira, vara, piśuna, rakta, śaṭha, and śoṇita.

Vāhlīka, ghusṛṇa, vareṇya, aruṇa, kāleyaka, jāguḍa, kānta, vahniśikha, kesaravara, gaura, and karākṣīrita—these are the varieties of saffron. Saffron is fragrant, bitter, pungent, and hot; it cures cough, disorders of wind and phlegm, and ailments of the throat; it destroys headaches and the defects of poison, promotes relish, and bestows beauty upon the body.
Tṛṇakuṅkuma, tṛṇāsra, gandhitṛṇa, śoṇita, tṛṇapuṣpa, gandhādhika, tṛṇottha, tṛṇagaura, lohita, and navasaṃjña—these are the names for tṛṇakuṅkuma.
Tṛṇakuṅkuma is pungent and hot; it destroys phlegm, wind, and swelling.
It is the supreme Bhāskara, which destroys itching, scabies, leprosy, intoxication, and disorders. Priyaṅgu, Phalinī, Śyāmā, Priyavallī, Phalapriyā,
Gaurī, Govandanī, Vṛttā, Kārambhā, Kaṅgu, and Kaṅgunī.

The *priyaṅgu* creeper is fragile, beautiful, leaf-piercing, auspicious, yellow, auspicious, most excellent, and grows on the earth marked by the footprints of the goddess. It is cooling and bitter, and it conquers the disorders of burning sensations, bile, and blood.
It removes vomiting, delusions, and fever, and destroys numbness of the mouth.
*Kastūrī*, *mṛganābhi*, *madanī*, *gandhacelikā*, *vedhamukhyā*, *mārjārī*, *subhagā*, and *bahugandhadā* [are synonyms for musk]. (Rājñī 12.45–46)
Sahasravedhī, Śyāmā, Kāmānandā, Mṛgāṇḍajā, Kuraṅganābhī, Lalitā, Mada, Mṛgamada, Śyāmalī, and Kāmamodī— these should be known as the eighteen names [of musk]. (Rajñī 12.47)
Musk is fragrant, bitter, beneficial for the eyes, and a conqueror of diseases of the mouth;
it removes vitiligo, phlegm, foul odors, wind-disorders, misfortune, and impurities.
Musk is of three kinds—tawny, reddish-brown, and black—respectively.

It is produced in Nepal, as well as in Kashmir and Kāmarūpa. That single *kharikā* is then known as *tilakā*, another as *kulitthā*, and yet another as *piṇḍā*; this other one is called the *nāyikā*. These are the five varieties designated by name. This pure [musk] from the musk deer (*mṛganābhi*), according to its sequence, is fit for kings; the *kastūrikā* produced on the three days beginning with the first day of the lunar fortnight is highly praised.

The *kharikā* is in the form of powder; the *tilakā* resembles sesame seeds; and the *kulitthakā* is like the seed of the *kaulattha* bean. The *piṇḍikā* is thicker than that by some measure, and if it is slightly larger than that, it is called the *nāyikā*. In taste it is bitter, yellowish-brown in color, possesses the fragrance of *ketakī* flowers, and is light when weighed.

That musk which, when placed in water, does not undergo any change of color, is fit for royal use and is highly praised. (Rajñī 12.52) That musk which steals away the fragrance of the *ketakī* flower, surpasses the rut of elephants in scent and color, and is bitter or pungent in taste; which, when weighed, crushed, or rubbed, remains light and smooth;

and which does not burn with a crackling sound (*śimi-śimiti*) even when held in fire for a long time, but instead emits the scent of leather in the flames—that musk produced from the body of the noble deer is excellent, worthy of being enjoyed by kings, and shines with glory. (Rajñī 12.53)

In a child, an old man, a deer, one who is emaciated, or one who is diseased, musk possesses only a faint fragrance; yet in a youth overcome by passion, it becomes intensely fragrant. (Rājñī 12.54) That which is oily and carries the scent of smoke when cast into water, causing the water within to turn entirely yellow; that which, once placed in the fire, is instantly reduced to ashes.

That which, when placed on a scale, gains weight, yet when rubbed, becomes coarse—this, indeed, should be known by those of discerning mind as artificial musk; it must certainly not be used. (Rājñī 12.55) Whether pure or soiled, what does it matter? The musk deer’s secretion possesses an inexhaustible treasure of wonder: its singular quality is fragrance.

It is because of this that it serves as the sole abode of Cupid’s ornaments, finding a place upon the forehead, the cheek, the throat, the base of the arms, and the circle of the breasts of fawn-eyed women. (Rājñī 12.56)
Gorocanā, ruci, śobhā, rucirā, śobhanā,
śubhā, gaurī, rocanā, piṅgā, maṅgalyā, piṅgalā,
śivā, pītā, gautamī, gavyā, vandanīyā, and kāñcanī. (Rajñī 12.57)
Medhyā, Manoramā, Śyāmā, Rāmā, and Bhūmikarāhvā;
Gorocanā is cooling, it destroys the defects of poison, is appetizing, promotes digestion, and cures worms and skin diseases.
It pacifies the influence of spirits and planetary grahas, is wholesome, brings about joy and auspiciousness, and is enchanting to people.

Karpūra, ghanasāraka, sitakara, śīta, śaśāṅka, śilā, śītāṃśu, himavālukā, himakara, śītaprabha, śāmbhava, śubhrāṃśu, sphaṭika, abhrasāra, mihikā, tārābhra, candrābhra, indu, candrāloka, tuṣāra, gaura, and kumuda— these are the eleven names [of camphor], each paired with the next. Furthermore, potāsa, bhīmasena, sitakara, śaṃkarāvāsasaṃjña, prāṃśu, piñja, abdhasāra, himayutā, vālukā, jūṭikā, and so forth.

After that, its frost—cool and accompanied by snow—and then the "matured" variety of camphor; these distinctions are visible through the eyes of a physician by virtue of their brilliance of quality and flavor. (Rajni 12.61) Fresh camphor is bitter, unctuous, hot, and causes bleeding and burning sensations.
When kept for a long time, it destroys the defect of burning; when washed, it is supremely auspicious. (Rajni 12.62)
Camphor is known to be of three kinds: *śiras*, *madhya*, and *tala*.
That which is produced at the top of the stalk is *śiras*; that which is on the leaf-surface is *madhya*; and that which is on the underside of the leaf is *tala*.
Among these, the *śiras*-produced variety is radiant, pure, and possesses fine granules (*pulaka*), while the *madhya* variety is [similarly] characterized by such features.
Ordinary *pulaka* is clear; however, on the surface, it is white powder. That which is situated within the core of a pillar is excellent, while that on the exterior of the pillar is middling.
Clear, slightly turmeric-colored, and bright—this is considered middling. One should say that *pulaka* born on the exterior is very firm, bright, and dry.
If camphor is clear, has leaf-like markings, is very light and bright when weighed, bitter in taste, cool, pleasant, and bestows the fragrance of thick, pervasive perfume;

if it is free of oiliness, possesses firm leaves, and is most auspicious—then it is excellent and fit for a king. Otherwise, it is abundant in food yet causes eruptions and wounds. *Cīnaka* and *cīnakarpūra* are artificial, white, and pungent.
Meghasāra, tuṣāra, and that which is produced from dvīpa and karpūra are thus remembered.
Cīnaka is pungent, bitter, and hot, slightly cold, and it removes phlegm;
it cures disorders of the throat, promotes intelligence, is digestive, and destroys worms.
Javādi, Gandharāja, Kṛtrima, Mṛgacarmaja,
Samūhagandha, Gandhāḍhya, Snigdha, Sāmrāṇikardama,
Sugandha, Tailaniryāsa, and Kuṭāmoda— these are the ten varieties. (Rājñī 12.69)
The *saugandhika* and *javādi* types are unctuous, hot, and bring comfort;
they are beneficial for wind (*vāta*) disorders and serve as causes of enchantment and delight for kings.
The blue *javādi* is unctuous, slightly yellow, and provides fragrance.
It possesses abundant fragrance when exposed to the sun; it is suitable for kings and not otherwise.
Tūṇīka, tūṇika, tūṇī, pītaka, kacchapa, nandī, kuraka, kānta, and nandīvṛkṣa are its nine names.

The *vṛkṣa* tree is pungent, bitter, and cold; it conquers bitter blood, burning sensations, headache, and white leprosy (*śveta-kuṣṭha*). It is fragrant and bestows nourishment and virility. *Jātīpattrī*, *jātikośa*, and *sumanaḥpattrikā* are also names for it.
Mālatīpatrī, Pañcanāmī, and Saumanasāyinī—
Jātīpatrī is pungent, bitter, fragrant, and destroys phlegm;
it produces clarity of the mouth and cuts away the defect of dullness.
Jātīphala, jātiśasya, śālūka, mālatīphala, majjāsāra, jātisāra, puṭa, and sumanaḥphala [are synonyms].
Jātīphala is astringent and hot; it is pungent and overcomes diseases of the throat and pain.

It cures wind-disorders, diarrhea, and urinary disorders; it is light, aphrodisiac, and digestive. Kakkolaka, kṛtaphala, kolaka, and kaṭukaphala are synonyms for vidveṣya, sthūlamarica, karkola, and mādhavocita.

Kaṅkola is said to be the same as kaṭphala; mārīca is equal to rudra. Kakkola is pungent, bitter, and hot; it is supreme for removing numbness of the mouth, stimulates digestion, promotes the digestive fire, improves the appetite, and destroys phlegm and wind.
Lavaṅgakalikā, divya-lavaṅga, śekhara, lava, śrīpuṣpa, devakusuma, rucira, vārisambhava,
tīkṣṇapuṣpa, bhṛṅgāra, and likewise gīrvāṇakusuma.
Puṣpaka, candana, and so forth—these are to be known as the thirteen [names]. (Rajni 12.81) Lavaṅga is cooling, bitter, beneficial for the eyes, and an appetizer;
it destroys wind, bile, and phlegm, is sharp, and cures headaches. (Rajni 12.82)
Lavaṅga is hot, sharp, sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cooling;
it destroys wind, bile, phlegm, and desire, and removes wasting, cough, and disorders of the eyes.
Agaru-sāra is sweet, while Gandhadhūmaja is excellent for incense smoke.
Sweet, pungent, astringent, and hot, it overcomes smoke, fragrance, and wind.
Black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāgaru*) is known as *agaru*, *śṛṅgāra*, *viśvarūpaka*,
*śīrṣa*, *kālāgaru*, *keśya*, *vasuka*, and *kṛṣṇakāṣṭhaka*.

Dhūpārha, vallara, and gandharājaka are the twelve names [of black aloe]. Black aloe (kṛṣṇāguru) is pungent and hot; it is cooling when used as an ointment, slightly removes pitta when drunk, and is declared to destroy the three doṣas.

Other varieties of *agaru* (aloe) are yellow and metallic in color; they clarify the complexion but are ignoble, lacking essence, and infested with insects—such is the wood. Wood-*agaru* is pungent and hot; when used as an ointment, it is dry and removes phlegm (*kapha*).
Dāhāgaru, dahanāgaru, dāhakakāṣṭha, and vahnikāṣṭha;
dhūpāgaru, tailāgaru, pura, and that which is beloved by the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva).
Dāhāgaru is pungent and hot; it promotes the growth of hair and improves the complexion.
It removes defects of the hair and continuously spreads a sweet fragrance.
The *mallikā* is auspicious, its scent being that of auspicious agallochum (*agaru*).
It is auspicious, heavy, cool, rich in fragrance, and acts as a vehicle for other perfumes when blended.
Māṃsī, jaṭilā, peśī, kravyādī, piśitā, miśī,
keśinī, jaṭā, hiṃsrā, jaṭāmāṃsī, māṃsinī, jaṭālā,
naladā, meṣī, tāmasī, and cakravartinī are synonyms for jaṭāmāṃsī.
Mātā, bhūtajaṭā, jananī, jaṭāvatī, and mṛgabhakṣā—these are its twenty-one names.
Surabhi, however, is jaṭāmāṃsī; it is astringent, pungent, and cooling.
It removes phlegm, destroys the burning sensation caused by spirits, subdues bile, and brings delight to the heart.
The second is known as Gandhamāṃsī, Keśī, Bhūtajaṭā, Piśācī, Pūtanā, Bhūtakeśī, and Lomaśā.

Jaṭālā, laghumāṃsī, and that known by the name cāṅgerikā are famous [as synonyms]. Gandhamāṃsī is bitter and cooling; it removes disorders of phlegm and the throat, cures hemorrhaging and bile, improves the complexion, and dispels poisons, spirits, and fever.
Ākāśamāṃsī is another subtle variety, known as Nirālambā and Khasambhavā;
it is also called Sevālī, Sūkṣmapattrī, Gaurī, and Parvatavāsinī.
Abhramāṃsī is cold and removes swelling, wounds, fistula-in-ano, and pain.
It removes spider webs, donkey hair, and the like, and it imparts a beautiful complexion.
Turuṣka, Yāvana, Dhūmra, Dhūmravarṇa, Sugandhika, Sihlaka, Sihlasāra, Pītasāra, and likewise Kapi— these are the varieties.
Piṇyāka, kapija, kalka, piṇḍita, piṇḍatailaka,
karevara, kṛtrimaka, lepana, and munibhūhvaya are synonyms for oil-cake.
Turuṣka is fragrant, bitter, pungent, unctuous, and a conqueror of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
It conquers the afflictions caused by phlegm, bile, urinary stones, urinary obstruction, and fevers born of spirits.
Guggulu is known as Yavanadviṣṭa, Bhavābhīṣṭa, Niśāṭaka, Jaṭāla, Kālaniryāsa, Pūra, Bhūtahara, and Śiva. (Rajni 12.101–102)
Kauśika, Śāmbhava, Durga, Yātughna, Mahiṣākṣaka, Deveṣṭa, Marudeśya, Rakṣohā, Rūkṣagandhaka,
and Divyamahiṣākṣa— these are the twenty names. Rajni 12.103.
Guggulu is pungent, bitter, and hot; it conquers phlegm, wind, and cough.
It destroys worms, wind-related abdominal enlargements, splenic disorders, swellings, and hemorrhoids, and it is a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
Gandharāja, svarṇakaṇa, suvarṇa, and kaṇaguggulu are synonyms for it.

Kanaka, vaṃśapota, surasa, palaṅkaṣa, and kaṇaguggulu are pungent and hot; they are fragrant, destroy wind, and alleviate colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, and phlegm; they are also rejuvenative elixirs.
Guggulu is the third other [type], born of the earth; that born from the flesh of a Daitya; Durgāhlāda, born of Iḍā; that produced from the enemy of Āśādi;
that born of marrow; that born of intoxication; and that produced from the Asura Mahiṣa.

Guggulu, born of the earth, is bitter, pungent, and hot; it conquers phlegm and wind, is dear to Umā, destroys malevolent spirits, promotes intelligence, and always bestows fragrance. Rāla, sarjarasa, śāla, and that which arises from kanakala—these are likewise [beneficial].
Lālana, śālaniryāsa, deveṣṭa, and likewise śītala;
bahurūpa, śālarasa, and likewise sarjaniryāsaka;
surabhi, suradhūpa, yakṣadhūpa, and agnivallabha.
Kāla is said to be born from the *kalala* stage and is marked by the number seventeen. Rāla, however, is cooling, unctuous, astringent, and bitter;
it subdues wind and bile and destroys eruptions, itching, and ulcers.
Kunduruka, saurāṣṭra, śikharī, kunduruka-kunduka, tīkṣṇa, gopuraka, bahugandha, pālinda, and bhīṣaṇa are its ten names.
Kunduru is sweet and bitter; it removes the affliction of phlegm and bile, as well as burning sensations.
Used as a drink or an ointment, it is cooling and brings about the pacification of the disease of *pradara*. Kuṣṭha, rujāgada, vyādhi, āmaya, pāribhadraka,
rāma, vānīraja, vāpya, tvagdoṣa, and utpala are to be known as synonyms for the same substance.
Kutsa, pāṭava, padmaka, and that which is named manu—
kuṣṭha is pungent, hot, and bitter; it conquers phlegm, wind, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha),
and it provides beauty while curing erysipelas, poison, itching, scabies, and ringworm.
*Sārivā*, *śāradā*, *gopā*, *gopavallī*, *pratānikā*,
*gopakanyā*, *latāsphotā*, *navāhvā*, and *kāṣṭhasārivā* are synonyms.
Another *sārivā* is *kṛṣṇamūlī*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *candanasārivā*.
Bhadrā, candanagopā, candanā, and kṛṣṇavallī are synonyms.
The two types of sārivā are sweet and they destroy phlegm, wind, and hemorrhaging;
they remove leprosy, itching, and fever, and they eliminate the foul odor of urine.
Nakha, kararuha, śilpī, śukti, śaṅkha, khura, śapha, bala, kośī, and karaja; likewise hanu and nāgahanu;
pāṇija, badarīpattra, dhūpya, and paṇyavilāsinī.

The *saṃdhināla* and *pāṇiruha* are known by eighteen names. The *nakha* is hot and pungent; when applied, it destroys poison, cures leprosy, itching, and ulcers, and is supreme for driving away malevolent spirits.
Nakha, Anya, Balanakha, Kūṭastha,
Cakranāyaka, Cakrī, Cakranakha, Tryasra, Kāla, Vyāghranakha, Dvīpinakha,
Vyālanakha, Khapuṭa, and Vyālapāṇija.
Vyālāyudha, vyālabala, and vyālakhaḍga are sixteen [in number].
Vyālanakha is bitter and hot, astringent, and it conquers phlegm and wind;
it destroys skin diseases, itching, and wounds, improves the complexion, and is an excellent provider of fragrance.
Spṛkkā, Devī, Piśunā, Vadhū, Koṭi, Manu, Brāhmaṇikā, Sugandhā, Samudrakāntā, Kuṭilā, Mālālikā, Bhūtalikā,
Laghvī, Nirmālyā, Sukumārā, Mālālī, and Devaputrikā.

Pañcagupti is said to be blood, and nakha-puṣpī consists of twenty [parts]. Spṛkkā is pungent, astringent, and bitter; it conquers phlegmatic ailments and cough, destroys phlegmatic urinary disorders, urinary stones, and strangury, and provides fragrance.
Sthauṇeyaka, barhiśikha, śukacchada, mayūracūḍa, śukapucchaka, vikīrṇaroman, kīravarṇaka, vikarṇa, and harita—these are the nine names for this substance.
Sthauṇeya destroys phlegm and wind; it is fragrant and possesses pungent and bitter tastes.
It pacifies the provocation of *pitta* and increases strength and nourishment.
Murā, Gandhavatī, Daityā, Gandhāḍhyā, Gandhamādanī, Surabhi, Bhūrigandhā, Kuṭī, and likewise Gandhakuṭī—[these are its names]. (Rājñī 12.128–129)

Murā is bitter, pungent, cooling, and astringent; it removes phlegm and bile, and cures asthma, blood disorders, poison, burning sensations, pain, vertigo, fainting, and thirst. (Rajni 12.130) Śaileya, śilaja, vṛddha, śilāpuṣpa, and śilodbhava [are synonyms].
*Stavira*, *palita*, *jīrṇa*, and likewise *kālānusāryaka*;
*śilottha*, *śilādadru*, *śailaja*, *giripuṣpaka*, *śilāprasūna*, *subhaga*, and *śailaka*—these are the sixteen names. (Rājñī 12.131–132)
Śaileya is cooling, bitter, fragrant, and it conquers phlegm and bile;
it destroys burning sensations, thirst, vomiting, dyspnea, and the defects of wounds.
Coraka, Śaṅkita, Caṇḍā, Duṣpattra, Kṣemaka, and Ripu [are synonyms].
Capala, Kitava, Dhūrta, Paṭu, Nīca,
Niśācara, Gaṇahāsa, Kopanaka, Coraka, Phalacoraka,
Duṣkula, Granthila, Sugranthi, and Parṇacoraka.
Granthiparṇa, granthidala, and granthipattra are its three names.
Coraka is pungent-smelling, hot, and bitter; it removes wind and phlegm and destroys diseases of the nose and mouth, indigestion, and worms.
Padmaka is yellow, yellowish, from Mālaya, cool, snowy, white, born in a field, red, and resembling the Pāṭalā flower;
it is called by twelve names, being the wood of the Padma tree. (Rajni 12.137)
Padmaka is cooling and bitter; it destroys blood-bile (raktapitta) and brings relief from delusion, burning sensations, fever, dizziness, leprosy, and eruptive boils.
Prapauṇḍarīka, Puṇḍarya, and Puṇḍarīyaka are beneficial for the eyes.
Pauṇḍarya, supuṣpa, and its younger sibling (anuja) are traditionally known as such.
Prapauṇḍarīka is beneficial for the eyes, sweet, bitter, and cooling;
it destroys bile, blood disorders, and wounds, and removes fever, burning sensations, and thirst.
Lāmajjaka is known as sunāla, amṛṇāla, lava, laghu,
iṣṭakāpathaka, śīghra, dīrghamūla, and jalāśraya. Lāmajjaka is cooling, bitter, sweet, and it conquers wind and bile.
It removes thirst, burning sensations, fatigue, fainting, pain, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta),
and fever. Māṃsarohiṇī, atiruhā, vṛttā,
carmakaṣā, vikasā, māṃsarohī, and māṃsaruhā are known as synonyms for this plant, according to the Sage.
Anyā, māṃsī, sadāmāṃsī, māṃsarohā, rasāyanī, sulomā, lomakaraṇī, rohiṇī, and māṃsarohikā are synonyms for *māṃsī*.
It is astringent, pungent, bitter, and likewise hot; it restores the voice and is beneficial for the senses.
Through the application of elixirs (rasāyana), it is considered a remover of all diseases;
it is an astringent, tonic for the complexion, and a purifier of blood-bile (raktapitta).
The pair of Rohiṇīs is cooling, astringent, and a destroyer of worms.
It purifies the throat, is palatable, and destroys disorders of the wind (vāta). Śrīveṣṭa, vṛkṣadhūpa, cīḍāgandha, rasāṅgaka, śrīvāsa,
śrīrasa, veṣṭa, lakṣmīveṣṭa, and veṣṭaka are its names.
Veṣṭasāra, Rasāveṣṭa, Kṣīraśīrṣa, Sudhūpaka, Dhūpāṅga, Tilaparṇa, and Saralāṅga—these are the sixteen [varieties].
Śrīveṣṭa is pungent, bitter, and astringent; it conquers phlegm and bile.
It cures disorders of the female reproductive tract, pain, indigestion, ulcers, and overcomes the affliction of flatulence.
Uśīra is known as amṛṇāla, jalavāsa, and haripriya;
mṛṇāla is called abhaya, vīra, vīraṇa, and samagandhika.
Raṇapriya, vāritara, śiśira, śitimūlaka, veṇīgamūlaka, jalāmoda, sugandhika,
sugandhimūlaka, śubhra, bālaka, and grahabhūhvaya. (Rajñī 12.151)

Uśīra is cooling and bitter; it is supreme for removing burning sensations and fatigue, pacifies the affliction of pitta-fever, and imparts fragrance to water. Nalikā, vidrumalatikā, kapotabāṇā, nalī, and nirmathyā [are also used].
Suṣirā, dhamanī, stutyā, raktadalā, nartakī, naṭī, and rudrā;
nalikā is bitter, pungent, sharp, sweet, and cooling.
It destroys worms, wind, abdominal diseases, hemorrhoids, and colic, and it purifies the waste matter.

Thus, having studied this chapter— a creation radiant and distinguished by the art of explaining the potencies of the multitude of aromatic substances, worthy of delighting the lotus-face [of the teacher]— may that physician shine in the midst of this assembly.
(Rajni 12.155) Those which perfume all the lands upon the earth, and those which bring happiness to those who long for fragrance;

This group, renowned as the "Section on Fragrances" (*gandhavarga*), consisting of these substances such as sandalwood (*malayaja*) and others, attains its fame. May this [work], beginning with the *śrīcandana* and others, find its place within the composition of that skillful Narahari, whose own conduct— having practiced the lofty and coolly fragrant deeds of that truthful-souled one— has swiftly dispelled the misfortune born of association for those people of evil conduct.
The twelfth chapter, the Varṇādivarga, ends with the jewel that adorns the crest of the Naigama merchants.
(Rājanighaṇṭu,
Suvarṇādivarga 12.157)
Gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, the two types of iron (malleable and cast),
bell-metal, steel, vartaka, kāntaloha, slag, muṇḍaloha, and tīkṣṇaloha;
as well as realgar, vermilion, antimony, cinnabar, and the two types of red ochre.
Tuvarī, yellow orpiment, sulphur, and bitumen; beeswax, the two types of kāsīsa, the two kinds of mākṣika, the five types of añjana,
kampilla, tuttha, rasaka, mercury, and abhraka— these four [groups].
Crystal, small conch, large conch, cowrie shell, mother-of-pearl of two kinds,
chalk, milky stone, gem, and that which consists of camphor and the like;
sand, double-sized thumb-joint, and vimalā are considered to be of two kinds.
Likewise, there are the Akhu-prastara and those called Śara-veda-mita.
Now I shall describe the nine types of gems, beginning with the ruby (padmarāga), in their proper order:
ruby (māṇikya), pearl (muktāphala), coral (vidruma), emerald (gārutmata), and topaz (puṣparāga).
Vajra and nīla, followed by nine in sequence including gomedaka and vaiḍūrya;
then sphatika, sūryakānta, vaikrānta, candrakāntaka,
rājāvarta, and perāja— these are the two types of bāṇa according to their number.
Gold, *suvarṇa*, *kanaka*, radiant *kāñcana*, auspicious *hāṭaka*, *hiraṇya*, and the charming;
*gāṅgeya*, *gairika*, great silver (*mahārajata*), fire-potent (*agnivīrya*), *rukma*, *agni-hema*, *tapanīya*, and *bhāskara*;
*jāmbūnada*, *aṣṭāpada*, *jātarūpa*, *piñjana*, *cāmīkara*, and *karbura*.
Gold possesses immense splendor, tawny like refined gold (*kārtasvara*) and white like silk (*bharma*), and is yellowed by glowing fire.
It is known as *māṅgalya*, *saumerava*, *śātakumbha*, *śṛṅgāra*, *candra*, *ajara*, *jāmbava*, and *āgneyaniṣka*—names determined by the ocean of its qualities. (RājN 13.9–10)

Gold is unctuous, astringent, bitter, and sweet; it destroys the three *doṣas*, is cooling, palatable, a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), and promotes relish. It is beneficial for the eyes, bestows longevity, and produces wisdom, heroism, strength, memory, and clarity of voice. It bestows luster upon the body and, through its wearing by men, effects the destruction of sins and brings about prosperity. (RājN 13.11) Furthermore, that which is red when heated and white when cut, and which shines with the luster of saffron on a touchstone— [The remainder of the verse continues: ...that gold is indeed auspicious. That gold which is smooth, possesses weight, and when weighed on a scale is of noble quality, is soft and reddish-yellow.

That gold is of three kinds: that produced by chemical transmutation (*rasavedhaja*), that which is born naturally from the earth (*bhūmija*), and another which arises from the mixture of many metals.
Among these, the first is indeed yellowish-red, the second is red, and the other is *mairāla*; beyond that, this [last] would be the best of each preceding type.
Silver is bright, the best of riches, radiant, and the metal of the moon;
it is also called śvetaka (the white), mahāśubhra (greatly pure), rajata (silver), and taptarūpaka (refined form).
It is known as candrabhūti (moon-essence), sita (white), tāra (transcendent), kaladhauta (purified by water), and indulohaka (moon-metal).
Base metals, washed [silk], as well as silver, moonstone, and *munīnduka* [gems]; silver is unctuous, astringent-sour, sweet in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*),
laxative, removes wind and bile, improves the appetite, and destroys wrinkles and graying hair.

That which is white, glossy, and heavy when subjected to heating, cutting, and rubbing, and which remains rich in color even under intense friction, is declared to be the best. Copper is called *mlecchamukha*, *śulva*, *tapana*, *iṣṭa*, and *udumbara*.

Tryambaka, Aravinda, Raviloha, Ravipriya, Rakta, Nepālaka, and Raktadhātu possess the color of the moon. Well-refined copper is sweet and astringent, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cold in potency.
It subdues phlegm, removes bile, destroys constipation, colic, anemia, abdominal enlargement, and tumors;
it withstands heavy hammering, is unctuous, possesses pure red leaves, is soft,
produced from a pure mine, auspicious, and unmixed with other metals.
Trapu, trapusa, māṇḍūka, vaṅga, kurūpya,
piccaṭa, raṅga, and pūtigandha— these are the ten names for tin.
Trapusa is pungent, bitter, cold, astringent-saline, laxative, and cures urinary disorders.

It pacifies worms, burning sensations, and anemia; it bestows luster and is indeed a rejuvenative elixir (rasāyana). White, light, soft, clear, unctuous, removing heat, and cooling—such tin (trapu), which produces a leaf-like surface and is beautiful, is declared to be the best.
Lead (sīsaka) is dull, lead (sīsa), desired by the Yavanas,
"serpent" (bhujaṃgama), desired by yogins, "city of serpents" (nāgapuraga), "bad limb" (kuvaṅga), and "well-ground" (paripiṣṭaka).
Soft black iron is known as "lotus" (padma) and as that which effects the purification of silver.
Sirāvṛtta and vaṅga (tin) are sixteen parts, as is cīnapiṣṭa.
Lead (sīsa), however, is equal to vaṅga in its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect;
it is hot, destroys phlegm and wind, cures hemorrhoids, is heavy, and is scraping.
In gold, blue, soft, glossy, stainless, and very bright [are the best qualities];
for silver, purification is swift; and lead is excellent for that.
Brass, base gold, Siṃhalaka, Piṅgala, and Pittalaka [are the types of copper alloys].
Lauhītaka, ārakuṭṭa, piṅgalaloha, and pītaka—these are the nine [types].
Rajñī, rājarīti, kākatuṇḍī, rājaputrī, maheśvarī, brāhmaṇī, brahmarīti, kapilā, and piṅgalā as well. (Rajñī 13.28–13.29)

The pair of rītikās (brass and bronze) is bitter, cooling, and salty in taste; it is purifying, destroys anemia and wind disorders, and overcomes worms, splenic pain, and pitta. [Rajni 13.30] Pure, unctuous, soft, cool, possessing a beautiful luster, and capable of being drawn into wires and sheets—[such is the quality of well-refined metal].
The Rīti known as Janya is auspicious, clear, and resembles gold.
Kāṃsya, saurāṣṭrika, ghoṣa, kaṃsīya, vahnilohaka, dīpta, loha, ghorapuṣpa, dīptaka, and sumanāhvaya [are synonyms]. (Rājñī 13.31–32)

Bell-metal (kāṃsya), however, is bitter and hot; it is beneficial for the eyes, destroys disorders of wind and phlegm, is dry, astringent, appetizing, light, a digestive stimulant, a promoter of digestion, and wholesome. (Rajni 13.33) That which is white, radiant, soft, luminous, resonant with sound, unctuous, and pure—
Bell-metal (kāṃsya) is said to be the best, having one thousand parts of ghanāgni as its constituent.
Vartaloha, vartatīkṣṇa, vartaka, lohasaṃkara,
nīlikā, nīlaloha, lohaja, and vaṭṭalohaka [are varieties thereof].
This iron is pungent and hot, yet bitter and cooling;
it removes phlegm, pacifies bile, is sweet, and cures burning sensations and urinary disorders.
Ayaskānta, kāntaloha, kānta, and lohakāntika are synonyms for magnetic iron.

Magnetite (kāntāyasa) is black iron and is of seven kinds, including *bhrāmaka*, followed by those called *cumbaka* and *romaka*, and that which is known as *chedaka*; thus it is fourfold. The qualities of these magnet stones increase in sequence, bestowing strength, beauty of limbs, luster, blackness of hair, and freedom from disease.

There are specific types of magnets, such as the *bhrāmaka* and *cumbaka*, all of which produce elixirs (*rasāyana*) and are supreme for achieving physical perfection. Without mercury (*sūta*), there is no magnet (*kānta*); without the magnet, there is no mercury.

The elixir (rasāyana) is said to result from the final union with *sūtaka*. Iron dross (*lohakiṭṭa*) is indeed *kiṭṭa*; it is iron powder, the impurity of iron, the black powder produced from iron, and likewise the blackness (*kārṣṇya*) of iron impurity.

Iron rust, however, is sweet, pungent, and hot; it destroys worms and wind-disorders, and cures colic of the digestive tract, colic of the wind, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, pain, and swelling. Muṇḍa, muṇḍāyasa, loha, dṛṣatsāra, and śilātmaja are synonyms for iron.
Stone-born, cultivated iron, ore, black iron— these are the nine [types].
Sharp weapon-iron, the weapon, the lump, lump-iron, the deceitful,
tempered iron, the fierce, and the sword-iron born of Muṇḍaja.
Citrāyaḥ is said to be that which originates from China and measures four times the [measure of] the Vedas (fourteen).
Iron is dry, hot, and bitter; it subdues vāta, pitta, and kapha.
It destroys urinary disorders, anemia, and colic; it is sharp and is considered superior to muṇḍaloha.

Gold that is not properly purified causes fatigue, induces perspiration, and is difficult to endure; silver generates dullness and sluggishness of the digestive fire; copper causes vomiting and confusion; lead and tin produce defects in the limbs;

iron gives rise to disorders such as abdominal tumors (gulma); steel causes colic; and magnetite (kāntaloha) is said to cause blackness of the skin, diseases, and eruptions. If the metals muṇḍa and tīkṣṇa are devoid of purification, though they may alleviate hunger, they bestow heaviness and abdominal tumors.
Bell-metal and iron cause moisture and heat; tin and lead cause delusion and dryness. (RājNī 13.47) Realgar is known as *kunaṭī*, *manojñā*, *śilā*, *manohvā*, and *nāgajihvā*.
It is also called *nepālikā*, *manasaguptā*, *kalyāṇikā*, *rogaśilā*, and *daśāhvā*. (RājNī 13.48)
Realgar (manaḥśilā) is pungent, unctuous, scraping, and a destroyer of poison;
it removes possession by spirits, fear, and insanity, and acts as a means of subjugation.
Vermilion (sindūra) is known as nāgareṇu, rakta, and likewise sīmantaka.
Nāgaja, nāgagarbha, śoṇa, and vīrarajas are known [as varieties of red]. Gaṇeśabhūṣaṇa, saṃdhyārāga, and śṛṅgāraka are known [as such];
likewise, saubhāgya and aruṇa are auspicious and equal to the Manu [standard].

Sindūra is pungent, bitter, and hot; it heals wounds and is supreme for pacifying leprosy, blood disorders, poisons, itching, and erysipelas. It is fragrant, fire-resistant, fine, unctuous, clear, heavy, and soft.
Pure gold-dust and vermilion are bestowers of auspiciousness.
Bhūnāga, kṣitināga, bhūjantu, raktajantuka,
kṣitija, kṣitijantu, bhūmija, and raktatuṇḍaka [are synonyms].
The *bhūnāga* is the "vajra-killer," the producer of various consciousnesses;
it is said that in the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury, that essence (*sattva*) is indeed an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Cinnabar (*hiṅgula*) is known as *barbara*, *rakta*, *suraṅga*, and *sugara*.
Rañjana, Darada, Mleccha, Citrāṅga, Cūrṇapārada,
and another called Māraka, as well as Maṇirāga, Rasodbhava, Rañjaka, and Rasagarbha— these are numbered at fifty-five. (Rajni 13.56–57)

Cinnabar (hiṅgula) is sweet and bitter; it alleviates heat, wind, and phlegm. When consumed, it removes fever arising from the three doṣas or from combinations of two doṣas. Gairika is red mineral, mountain-mineral, and gavedhuka.
Dhātu, *suraṅgadhatu*, *girija* (which arises from mountain-clay),
*suvarṇagairika*, another called *svarṇadhatu*, *suraktaka*, *sandhyabhra*, *babhrudhatu*, and *siladhātu*— these are the six names [of this substance]. (Rājñī 13.59–60)

Gairika is sweet, cooling, astringent, and heals wounds; it destroys eruptions, hemorrhoids, and burns from fire. Gold and other such precious metals are excellent and auspicious. Tuvarī, mṛd, saurāṣṭrī, mṛtsnā, saṅgā, and surāṣṭrajā are synonyms for alum.
Bhūghnī, mṛtālaka, kāsī, mṛttikā, suramṛttikā,
stutyā, kāṅkṣī, sujātā, and [the one] to be known— these are the fourteen. Tuvarī is bitter, pungent, astringent, and sour, and it is scraping (lekhanī).

It is beneficial for the eyes and removes disorders of the *grahaṇī*, vomiting, and the burning sensation caused by *pitta*. Haritāla (yellow orpiment) is also known as godanta, pīta, naṭamaṇḍana, gaura, citrāṅga, piñjaraka, āla, tālaka, and tāla.
Kanakarasa, kāñcanaka, biḍālaka, citragandha, piṅga, piṅgasāra, and gaurīlalita— these are the seventeen names.
Haritāla is pungent and hot, unctuous, and it destroys skin diseases.
It pacifies the delusions caused by spirits and overcomes the pain of poison and wind-diseases.
Gandhaka, gandhapāṣāṇa, gandhāśmā, gandhamodana,
pūtigandha, atigandha, vaṭa, and likewise saugandhika— these are its names.
Sugandha, divyagandha, gandha,
rasagandhaka, kuṣṭhāri, krūragandha, kīṭaghna, and śarabhūmita;
gandhaka is pungent, hot, intensely fragrant, and a great stimulator of the digestive fire.
It is an antidote to poison and destroys skin diseases, itching, scabies, and disorders of the skin.
(Rajni 13.69) Sulphur is known to be of four types according to its color—white, red, yellow, and blue—and each distinct variety possesses its own specific set of qualities. (Rajni 13.70)

White [śilājatu] is a remover of leprosy; red is used for the application of iron; yellow is fit for the application of mercury; and blue is suitable for other medicinal preparations. Śilājatu is that which originates from stone; it is called śaila, girija, and aśmaja.
*Aśmalākṣā*, *aśmajatuka*, and *jatvaśmaka* are recorded as synonyms for *śilājatu*. Śilājatu is bitter, pungent, and hot;
it is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) that destroys urinary disorders, insanity, urinary calculi, swelling, leprosy, and epilepsy.
Sikthaka, madhuka, siktha, madhuja, madhusambhava, madanaka, madhūcchiṣṭa, madana, and makṣikāmala; it is also called kṣaudreya, pītarāga, snigdha, and mākṣikaja. (Rajni 13.74)
Kṣaudraja, madhuśeṣa, drāvaka, makṣikāśraya, madhūṣita,
and madhūttha— these nineteen are said [to be varieties of honey].
Sikthaka is tawny, sweet, soft, and it conquers skin diseases and wind disorders.
Pungent and unctuous when applied as a paste, it heals cracked limbs. Kāsīsa, dhātukāsīsa, kesaraka, haṃsalomaśa, śodhana, pāṃśukāsīsa, and śubhra are considered the seven names [of this substance].
Kāsīsa is astringent, cooling, and it conquers poison and leprosy;
it destroys worms and dates, is beneficial for the eyes, and increases luster.
Second is *puṣpakāsīsa*, as well as *vatsaka* and *malīmasa*.

The *hrasva* herb should be applied as an eye medicine, as should clear blue clay (*nīlamṛttikā*). Pushpākāsīsa is bitter and cooling; it removes eye diseases and, when used as an ointment, destroys various skin disorders such as excessive moisture and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). (Rajni 13.79–80)
Mākṣika, mākṣīka, pītaka,
dhātumākṣika, tāpīja, tāpyaka, tāpya, āpīta,
and pītamākṣika; āvarta is honey-ore, and likewise another is honey-mineral (kṣaudradhātu).

Mākṣikadhātu is declared to be vedabhū, and hemamākṣika is [also known as] mākṣika. Mākṣika is sweet, bitter, sour, and pungent; it removes phlegm and cures vertigo, nausea, fainting, pain, asthma, cough, and poison. (Rajni 13.82–83)
Mākṣika is said to be of two kinds: that called *hemāhvam* (golden) and *tāramākṣika* (silver-mākṣika).
Due to the distinction in their colors, their taste, potency, and other qualities are distinct.
Among those beginning with *tāravāda*, *tāramākṣika* is highly praised.

Gold and other such substances are recommended for the body; they remove disease and bestow strength and nourishment. (Rajñī 13.85) Collyrium from the Yamunā river is black, as is that from the Nadeya region; likewise, *srotoja* is dark blue and beneficial for the eyesight. *Sauvīra* is produced in Suvīra and is blue. (Rajñī 13.86)
Likewise, blue antimony (*nīlāñjana*) is beneficial for the eyes and originates from water;
it is also called *kapotaka* and *kāpota*, and is said to measure seven *śara*s in size. Blue antimony is declared to be cold, pungent, bitter, and astringent.

It is beneficial for the eyes, destroys phlegm and wind, is an antidote to poison, and acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). Kulatthā is pleasing to the sight and beneficial for the eyes; likewise, kulatthikā, kulālī, locanahitā, kumbhakārī, and malāpahā [share these qualities].
Kulatthikā is beneficial for the eyes, astringent, pungent, and cooling;
it eradicates the defects of poison, eruptions, itching, and ulcers.
Puṣpāñjana is also known as puṣpaketu, kausumbha, and kusumāñjana.

Rītika, rītikusuma, rītipuṣpa, and pauṣpaka—these are known as puṣpāñjana and hima. It cures bile disorders, hiccups, and burning sensations; it destroys the pain of poison and cough, and removes all eye diseases.
Rasāñjana is known as rasodbhūta, rasagarbha, rasāgraja, kṛtaka,
bālabhaiṣajya, and likewise as that which arises from the decoction of dārvī;
it is also called rasajāta, tārkṣyaśaila, and varyāñjana.
It is known as *rasanābha*, *agnisāra*, and *dvādaśāhva*.
When bell-metal (*rīti*) is being smelted, its dross is *rasāñjana*;
in the absence of that, it should be prepared from the decoction of *dārvī*.
Srotoñjana, vāribhava, and likewise the other, srotodbhava, which arises from the river;
sauvīrasāra, kapotasāra, valmīkaśīrṣa, and that which is named after the Sage (munisaṃmitāhvam).
Srotoñjana is cold and pungent, astringent, and destroys worms.
Rasāñjana is suitable for medicinal preparations and is excellent for increasing breast milk.
That which has the shape of an anthill peak, the luster of crushed blue collyrium,
and the color of red ochre when rubbed— that is the best *srotoñjana*.
Kampillaka, raktāṅga, recana, recaka,
rañjaka, lohitāṅga, kampilla, and raktacūrṇaka [are synonyms].
Kampillaka is purgative, pungent, hot, and a destroyer of wounds.

It removes the affliction of phlegm-induced cough, destroys worms and parasites, and is light. Tuttha is produced from blue stone (nīlāśmaja), is blue, and is also called haritāśma, tutthaka, mayūragrīvaka, tāmragarbha, and amṛtodbhava.
Mayūratuttha is declared to have ten names, beginning with *śikhikaṇṭha*.
Tuttha is pungent, astringent, and hot; it removes leucoderma and eye diseases, is recommended for all types of poison-related disorders, and acts as an emetic.

The second is *kharparītuttha*; likewise, *kharparī*, *rasaka*, *cakṣuṣya*, *amṛtotpanna*, and *tutthakharparikā*—these are the six. *Kharparī* is pungent, bitter, beneficial for the eyes, and a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
It pacifies skin diseases, is appetizing, stimulates digestion, and increases nourishment. Mercury is the king of liquids, the lord of taste, the great elixir, the essence,
the one of great splendor, the metal of liquid form, and the best of essences.

The king of elixirs (sūtarāja), the fickle one (capala), the victorious (jaitra), the seed of Śiva (śivabīja), Śiva himself, the nectar (amṛta), the lord of mercury (rasendra), the lord of the world (lokeśa), the rogue (dhūrtara), the sovereign (prabhu),
the son of Rudra (rudraja), the splendor of Hara (haratejas), the mineral of mercury (rasadhātu), and that which is born from the inconceivable (acintyaja).
He is called Khecara and Amara; he bestows the body and destroys death.
O Queen, Skanda, Skandāṃśaka, Sūta, Deva, Divyarasa, Rasāyanaśreṣṭha, Yaśodada, and Tritridhāhvaya—thus has he been proclaimed. (Rajñī 13.107–108)
Mercury (pārada) is the destroyer of all diseases, possesses the six tastes, and is a universal vehicle for all medicinal formulations.

It is proclaimed to consist of the five elements and bestows the supreme perfection of the body and of iron. When processed by maceration (mūrchita), it removes diseases; when bound (baddha), it grants the power of flight (khecaratva).
Blue and restrained, it bestows all accomplishments and grants the perfection of the body.
Because it brings mortals to the further shore even amidst the perils of various diseases, fears, birth, death, and old age,
it is therefore called *pārada* (the one who carries across).

Abhraka, abhra, bhr̥ṅga, vyoma, ambara, antarikṣa, ākāśa, bahupattra, kha, ananta, gaurīja, and gaurijeya—these are the synonyms for mica (abhraka). White, yellow, red, and blue: mica undergoes these four varieties, each suitable for different medicinal applications.
White in silver, yellow in gold, reddish-yellow in copper, and blue in iron—this is the foremost, most excellent, and quality-rich [diamond].
It may be of four types: the dark-cloud-like, the frog, the Pināka, and the Vajra; their examination is now described in order.
When cast into the fire, the frog (*bheka*) emits its characteristic croak; the serpent (*dardura*) hisses; and the Pināka bow indeed takes on the sound of a bowstring.

Yet the thunderbolt (*vajra*) undergoes no change at all. By using these [herbs] in succession, one becomes respectively afflicted with a swelling, then a wound, then a loathsome disease, and finally becomes free from illness.
When Śiva and Śivā are mutually permeated by the emotions of their minds...
At that time, it is said, Abhra and Pārada were born from the cave.
Sphaṭī is called Sphaṭikī; she is white, bright, and bestowing beauty (raṅgadā).
She is Raṅgadṛḍhā, Dṛḍharaṅgā, and Raṅgāṅgā—these eight names correspond to the eight Vasus.

Sphaṭī is pungent, unctuous, and astringent; it cures uterine prolapse (pradara), and destroys urinary disorders, dysuria, worms, consumption, and the humors, while strengthening the limbs. Kṣullaka is the same as kṣudraśaṅkha; śambūka is the same as nakhaśaṅkhaka.

The *kṣullaka* is pungent, bitter, a remover of colic, and a digestive stimulant. Indeed, the *śaṅkha*, born of the waters, the *kambu*, born of the sea, the *jalaja*, possessing a purifying sound, the curved one,
the one with a great internal resonance, the *kambū*, the pure one, and the *sunādaka* [are synonyms].
Having a beautiful sound, a long resonance, and many notes, it is dear to Hari;
thus the white conch, which bestows auspiciousness, is known to be of sixteen kinds.
The conch has a pungent taste, is cold, and bestows nourishment, virility, and strength.
It cures abdominal tumors and colic, destroys dyspnea, and removes the defects of poison.

Known as *krimiśaṅkha*, *krimijalaja*, *krimivāriruha*, and *jantukambu*, it is described by those of refined intellect as being similar to a conch shell in its taste, potency, and other qualities. (Rajni 13.122–13.123)
*Kapardaka*, *varāṭa*, *kapardi*, and *varāṭikā* are synonyms for the cowrie shell;
it is also called *carācara*, *cara*, *varya*, and *bālakrīḍārana*.
