Regarding its properties: *kaparda* is pungent, bitter, and hot; it cures earache and wounds.
It destroys abdominal tumors, colic, and diseases, and it eliminates defects of the eyes.
*Śukti*, *muktāprasū*, *mahāśukti*, and *śuktikā* are synonyms;
so too are *muktāsphoṭa* and *tautika*, which is the mother of pearls.
The pearl-oyster (mauktika-śukti) is known as the mother of pearls (muktā-mātāṅka-dhā).
Pearl-oyster shell is pungent, unctuous, a remover of asthma and heart disease,
a pacifier of colic, appetizing, sweet, and an excellent digestive stimulant.
Jalaśukti, vāriśukti, krimisū,
kṣudraśuktikā, śambūkā, jalaśukti, puṭikā, and toyaśuktikā are synonyms.
Jalaśukti is pungent, unctuous, digestive, and a remedy for abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic (śūla).

It removes the defects of poison, is appetizing, digestive, and strength-giving. Khaṭinī, khaṭikā, and khaṭī are synonyms for white clay; sitadhātu and śvetadhātu mean white mineral, while pāṇḍumṛt and pāṇḍumṛttikā refer to pale earth.

Khaṭinī is sweet, bitter, and cooling; it removes bile and burning sensations, destroys wounds, disorders, phlegm, and blood, and eradicates eye diseases. Dugdhāśmā, also known as dugdhapāṣāṇa, is milky and resembles gomedaka.
Vajrābha, Dīptika, Saudha, Dugdhī, and Kṣīrayava;
as well as Dugdhapāṣāṇaka—these are palatable, slightly warm, and alleviate fever.
They destroy bile disorders, heart disease, and colic, and they eliminate cough and flatulence.
The word *karpūra* is used at the beginning [of the name] and the word *maṇi*, which denotes a gem, at the end;
thus this substance named *karpūramaṇi* removes disorders such as wind (*vāta*) through its application.
*Sikatā*, *vālukā*, *siktā*, *śītalā*, and *sūkṣmaśarkarā* are synonyms for sand.
The fine powder of water, arising from a flowing stream, is very smooth and subtle;
it is sweet and cool, destroying fever and fatigue.
Through the application of sprinkling, it removes heat from the limbs and wards off wind.
Kaṅkuṣṭha, kālakuṣṭha, viraṅga, raṅgadāyaka, recaka, pulaka, śodhaka, and kālapālaka;
kaṅkuṣṭha is said to be of two kinds: namely, tāra-kaṅkuṣṭha and hema-kaṅkuṣṭha. (Rajni 13.137)
It is pungent, destroys phlegm and wind, acts as a purgative, and removes pain from wounds.
(Rajni 13.138) Vimala, nirmala, svaccha, amala, and svacchadhātuka—these are the names declared for [silver]; it is known to be of two kinds: silver and gold. (Rajni 13.139)
Vimala is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys skin diseases and wounds.
It is equal [to others] in taste, potency, and other qualities, yet it possesses a distinct potency in its chemical action (*vedha*). First is the name of *mūṣaka*, and then the name of *pāṣāṇa*.
"This [object] is called 'mole-stone' (ākhupāṣāṇa), for it causes iron to become mixed [with gold].
Because all people seeking wealth take such great delight in it,
it is therefore designated as a 'jewel' (ratna) by those expert in the science of grammar."
*Dravya*, *lakṣmī-bhogya*, *vasu*, *vastu*, *sampad*,
*vṛddhi*, *śrī*, *vyavahārya*, *draviṇa*, *dhana*, *artha*, *rāḥ*, and *svāpateya* refer to wealth or property.
*Ratna*, *vasu-maṇi*, *upala*, *dṛṣad*, *draviṇa*, *dīpta*, and *vīrya* refer to precious stones or gems.
*Rauhiṇaka*, *abdhisāra*, *khānika*, and *ākaraja* are synonyms.
*Māṇikya*, *śoṇaratna*, *ratnarāja*, *aviratnaka*, *śṛṅgāri*, *raṅgamāṇikya*, *tarala*, and *ratnanāyaka* [are synonyms for ruby].
Rāgadṛk, padmarāga, ratna, śoṇopala, saugandhika, lohitaka, kuruvinda,
śarenduka, māṇikya, madhura, and snigdha— these destroy wind and bile disorders.

It is the supreme elixir for those who possess the wisdom of gem application. Smooth, heavy-bodied, radiant, clear, and beautifully colored—such a *māṇikya* of noble birth and other qualities brings auspiciousness through its wearing. (Rajni 13.147–148)
A wise person should not wear a ruby that has two shadows, is covered by clouds, is rough and gritty, is cracked or smoky, lacks luster, is deformed, or is light in weight.

If it is red, one should know it as a *padmarāga*; if it is yellowish-red, it is of two kinds; that which is reddish-brown among these is a *kuruvindaka*, while the fragrant variety is the *saugandhika*.

If that blue [gem] is known by the wise as "blue-scented" (*nīlagandhika*), it is of four kinds; they say that a *māṇikya* (ruby) which remains unimpaired in its color even when rubbed on a touchstone is of noble birth (*jātya*). *Muktā*, *saumyā*, *mauktika*, *mauktikeya*, *tāra*, *tārā*, *bhautika*, *tārakā*, *ambhaḥsāra*, *śītala*, *nīraja*, *nakṣatra*, *indraratna*, and *valakṣa* are synonyms for pearl.

*Muktāphala*, *binduphala*, *muktikā*, *śaukteyaka*, *śuklamaṇi*, *śaśipriya*, *svaccha*, *hima*, *haimavata*, *sudhāṃśubha*, *sudhāṃśuratna*— these are the names for pearl, numbering nine. (Rājñī 13.152) Furthermore, pearl (*mauktika*) is sweet, very cooling, a pacifier of eye diseases, and a destroyer of poison.
It destroys consumption and diseases of the mouth, and increases strength, vigor, and nourishment for those who are emaciated.

(Rajni 13.153) A pearl that has the luster of a star, is circular, perfectly free [of flaws], glossy, thick, stainless, and without blemishes; which, when placed on a scale, maintains its weight—it is priceless and bestows happiness. (Rajni 13.154)
That pearl which is lusterless, deformed in body, stained by contact with the oyster shell, or possesses a reddish tint;

that which resembles the eye of a fish, is rough, or is unevenly convex and concave—this should not be worn by a wise man, as it bestows defects. (Rājñī 13.155) Furthermore, the pearl gem clearly arises in eight ways: from the belly of the elephant, the serpent, the fish, and the boar; from the head; and from the bamboo, the conch, the water-bearing cloud, and the oyster shell.

Their shadows are generally pale-red, blue, yellow, or white; however, among these seven types, the others are rarely found, while the *śaukteyaka* variety is most prominent. (Rājñī 13.156) That pearl which, when placed in a vessel filled with cow’s urine containing powdered salt and alkali, remains unchanged even after being rubbed with rice husks, is of genuine (*jātya*) origin. (Rājñī 13.157)
*Pravāla*, *aṅgārakamaṇi*, *vidruma*, *ambhodhipallava*, *bhaumaratna*, *raktāṅga*, *raktāṅkura*, and *latāmaṇi* are synonyms for coral.
Coral is sweet and sour; it removes disorders such as phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
Worn by women, it bestows vigor, beauty,
and auspiciousness. One should wear a pure, firm, dense, well-rounded, smooth-bodied, and beautiful coral that is even, heavy, and free of veins.

One should reject coral that is pale-yellow, covered with water-stains, crooked, fine, hollow, rough, black, light, or white; such coral is inauspicious. Coral that arises from the waters of the ocean is like a creeper of coral-red as the rays of the rising sun.
That which does not lose its natural luster even when rubbed on a touchstone is known as *jātya* (of noble birth).
The *gārutmata*, *marakata*, *rauhīṇeya*, *harinmaṇi*, *sauparṇa*,
*garuḍodgīrṇa*, *budharatna*, and *aśmagarbha* [are types of emeralds].

The emerald (garalāri), which is the enemy of poison, belongs to Vāyu; it is associated with Garuḍa and is equal to Rudra. It destroys poison, is cooling, sweet in taste, removes undigested matter and bile, is appetizing, provides nourishment, and destroys malevolent spirits.
One should wear an auspicious emerald that is transparent, heavy, well-colored, glossy, endowed with softness in its body, free from defects, multicolored, and full of erotic charm.
One should not wear one that is gravelly, turbid, rough, dirty, light, lacking luster, or mottled.

Even an immortal would not consume an emerald that is joined with flaws or has deformed limbs. That which possesses the eightfold characteristics—resembling the color of moss, a peacock’s crest, young grass, or glass; resembling the wing of a blue jay, a firefly, the body of a young parrot, or a *śirīṣa* flower; and which, when heated by the sun’s rays, radiates light on all sides—is designated as genuine emerald.
The yellow [stone] is the *puṣparāga* (topaz), as well as yellow crystal (*pītasphaṭika*) and yellow-red [stone].

Yellow stone is the *guru-ratna* (heavy gem) and the yellow jewel (*pītamaṇi*), which is the *puṣparāga*. The *puṣparāga* is sour and cold; it subdues wind (*vāta*) and is an excellent digestive stimulant (*dīpana*).
Through its wearing, it bestows upon men longevity, prosperity, and wisdom.

(13.169) He who possesses a pure topaz that has a fine luster, is yellow, heavy, with beautiful color and purity, glossy, free from flaws, perfectly round, and very cool, nourishes his fame, great valor, happiness, long life, and wealth. (13.170)
A topaz that is marked with black spots, rough, white, dirty, light, lusterless,
or resembles sugar or charcoal is considered defective. When rubbed on a touchstone, it should exhibit its own characteristic color even more intensely.
Indeed, by virtue of its excellence, this is called *puṣparāga* (topaz) by experts.
The diamond (*vajra*) is known as *indrāyudha*, *hīra*, *bhidura*, *kuliśa*, *pavi*, *abhedyam*, *aśira*, *ratna*, *dṛḍha*, and *bhārgavaka*.
It has six corners and many facets, measuring one hundred crores, four oceans, and one earth [in size].
It is a vajra endowed with the six tastes, which removes all diseases,
pacifies all sins, bestows happiness, strengthens the body, and is an elixir (*rasāyana*).

One should discard that vajra which gives rise to defects— namely, one whose surface is like ash, marked with crow-feet, crossed by lines, circular, baseless, dirty, marked by spots of terror, cracked, blue-hued, flattened, or rough. (Rājñī 13.175)
Because it is white, red, yellow, and dark-blue, there are four types of luster; that these signify for this [diamond] the status of a Brahmin and so forth, as the wise declare, is indeed true.

When worn according to one's own [caste], it bestows vast, unsurpassed fame and prosperity; however, for mortals, a diamond worn improperly is nothing other than a calamity. (13.176) That which is not rubbed away by a multitude of abrasives on a stone surface, nor marked with a line when struck by harsh mortars, iron hammers, or heavy mallets;

Whatever else it may shatter by its own mere play, or that which is split by a thunderbolt—experts declare that to be a genuine diamond; it is praiseworthy and of great value. (Rājñī 13.177) Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa diamond is powerful in alchemical elixirs (*rasāyana*) and bestows the eightfold supernatural attainments (*aṣṭāṅgasiddhi*); a Kṣatriya diamond conquers wrinkles and grey hair for men and easily overcomes death;
a Vaiśya diamond grants the power of attracting wealth; and a Śūdra diamond becomes the remover of all diseases. Thus has been described the praiseworthy quality of the diamond. (Rājñī 13.178)
Nīla is the solar gem (sauriratna), as well as nīlāśman, nīlaratnaka,
nīlopala, tṛṇagrāhī, mahānīla, and sunīlaka;
masāra is indranīla, while gallarka is born from the ruby (padmarāga).
Blue, slightly bitter, and warm, it removes phlegm, bile, and wind;
that which bestows strength upon the body shall be auspicious and a giver of well-being.
O Queen, it is not sunken, pure, smooth to the limbs, heavy, and radiant.

One that seizes grass, is soft, blue, and endowed with auspicious marks is difficult to find. A blue horse that is mixed with clay, gravel, and stones; lacks luster; is dirty, light, rough, cracked, or full of holes—such a defective blue horse should be rejected.

These shadows—white, red, yellow, and black—are said to appear in sequence upon the blue [sky] for the sake of attaining the castes of the Brāhmaṇa and so forth; its retention, like that of the *vajra*, is likewise fruitful. It is solid, flowing with moonlight, beautiful, and filled with milk.
That which quickly colors a vessel [with its hue] is called the noble blue (*jātya-nīla*).
Gomedaka is *gomedha*, Rāhuratna is *tamomaṇi*;
this gem has six names, including *svarbhānu* and *piṅgasphaṭika*.
Gomedaka is sour and hot; it conquers disorders caused by the provocation of Vāta.
It is digestive, carminative, and when worn, it destroys evil. That which has the luster of cow's urine, is soft, glossy, charming, possesses a pure radiance, and bears weight—[that is Gomedaka].
This reddish-gold gem is suitable for the illustrious; the wise declare it to be the gem known as *gomeda*.
When placed in a vessel, the water therein becomes bright like cow’s urine;
even when rubbed, its luster does not diminish—the wise know that to be the genuine *gomeda*.
The wise man should avoid a *gomeda* that is colorless, white or black in its parts, marked with lines or spots, lusterless, or as brittle as sugar-candy.
Likewise, he should avoid *vaiḍūrya*, the *keturatna*, and that which is fraudulent or produced from the seed of a child.
Prāvṛṣya, abhraloha, khaśabda, aṅkuraka,
as well as the gem known as vaiḍūrya and that which is born from vidūra—
vaiḍūrya is hot and sour, and it destroys phlegm and wind.
It pacifies ailments such as *gulma*, is adorned, and brings auspiciousness.

(Rajni 13.191) One should recognize a *vaiḍūrya* gem by its threefold luster: that which possesses the delicate brilliance of bamboo leaves, the splendor of a peacock’s neck, and the tawny hue of a cat’s eye.

When it imparts a sense of weight to the body and is exceedingly glossy, the wise declare it to be free from defects; indeed, they say that a *vaiḍūrya* is beautiful when it is pure and transparent. (Rajni 13.192)
One should avoid from afar a lapis lazuli that is lusterless, containing earth or stone, light, rough, cracked, accompanied by fear-inducing flaws, harsh, or black; however,
when rubbed by oneself upon a touchstone, it should be clear and reflect its own shadow.

That which clearly displays this [quality] is said to be genuine *vaiḍūrya*. One should assign ruby (*māṇikya*) to the Sun, the most pure pearl (*mauktika*) to the Moon, coral (*pravāla*) to Mars, incomparable emerald (*marakata*) to Mercury, topaz (*puṣparāga*) to Jupiter, diamond (*kuliśa*) to Venus, sapphire (*nīla*) to Saturn, and *gomedaka* to Rāhu; furthermore, *vidūra* is assigned to Ketu. (Rājñī 13.195)
Thus, for whoever should give or even wear these jewels in their respective order according to their specific designations,
the planets will be gracious toward them; provided that,
in every other case except for a combination [of all], one excludes the diamond (*vajra*) alone.
Lightness and softness should be understood as common defects.
The five great gems are ruby, diamond, pearl, emerald, and sapphire;
lapis lazuli, topaz, coral, hessonite, and others are of inferior quality.
Gomedaka, pravāla, vāyavya, devejya, maṇīndra, taraṇikānta, and others—
rich in various colors and qualities— should be recognized by the wise as varieties of crystal (*sphaṭika*).
Crystal is a white stone, a stainless gem, a pure stone, and is transparent.
The *svacchamaṇi*, the stainless jewel, the pure gem, dear to Śiva, is of nine kinds:
crystal (*sphaṭika*), which is of equal potency and removes the defects of bile, burning sensations, and pain.
A rosary made of it grants ten-millionfold fruit to those who recite mantras.

That which is as pure as a drop of Ganges water, stainless, pleasing to the eye and heart, lustrous, with a clean interior, sweet, exceedingly cool, and a remover of bile, burning sensations, and blood; which, even when rubbed by stones and cracked, never abandons its innate transparency—that wonderful Śaiva-jewel of noble birth, though rarely obtained, brings about auspicious accumulation. (Rājñī 13.202) Now, it is called *sūryakānta*, *tapanamaṇi*, *tapana*, and *ravikānta*.

The *dīptopala*, *agnigarbha*, *jvalanāśman*, and *arkopala* are names for the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*). It is hot, pure, and an elixir (*rasāyana*). It removes wind and phlegm, promotes intellect, and through its worship, it grants satisfaction to the Sun.
Pure, smooth, without blemish, free from husk, and polished within,
that which attains clarity in the sky and emits fire upon contact with the rays of the sun— this is the *sūryakānta* (sun-stone) born of its own nature.
Furthermore, there are *vaikrānta*, *vikrānta*, *nīcavajra*, and *kuvajra*.
Gonāsa is *kṣudrakuliśa* (small thunderbolt) and *cūrṇavajra* (powdered thunderbolt), as is *gonasa*.
In the absence of *vajra*, *vaikrānta* is equal to it in its taste, potency, and other qualities;
it destroys consumption, leprosy, and poisons, bestows nourishment, and is a divine elixir (*rasāyana*).
Because it forcibly seizes all diseases by its very nature as a diamond (*vajra*),
that which possesses such prowess is called *vaikrānta* by the wise.
(Rājñī 13.208) It is also known as *indrakānta*, *candrakānta*, *candrāśman*, and *candrajopala*.

The cool stone (*śītāśman*), that which melts in moonlight (*candrikādrāva*), and the moonstone (*śaśikānta*)—these are the seven types. The moonstone (*candrakānta*) is cooling, glossy, and removes bile and blood disorders; it is pleasing to Śiva, transparent, and destroys planetary misfortunes and inauspiciousness.
That which is glossy, white, or yellow, possesses clarity within its core like that of the sages,
and exudes a flow upon contact with moonbeams— this is the noble gem known as the *candrakānta* (moonstone).
It is also called *rājāvarta*, *nṛpāvarta*, and *rājanyāvartaka*.
The *āvartamaṇi* is called *āvarta*; this is known by the name *śara*. *Rājāvarta* is pungent, unctuous, cooling, and destroys bile (*pitta*);
when employed in ornaments, it brings good fortune to men.

They say that the *rājāvarta* is a noble gem when it is poreless, lustrous, blue, heavy, stainless, highly radiant, resembling the throat of a peacock, and gentle. *Peroja*, *haritāśma*, *bhasmāṅga*, and *harita* are of two kinds.
Pippalī (pepper) may be slightly astringent, yet it is exceedingly sweet and digestive.

Whether poison be of stationary or mobile origin, or even that which arises from a combination [of factors], it quickly destroys all such [poisons] as well as colic caused by the humors of spirits and the like. (RājNī 13.215–216)
The perfected ones have declared that mercury, mica, various minerals, and metals—as well as all gems here—bestow success through proper processing (*saṃskāra*).

For among these, that which is devoid of processing, or that which is processed incorrectly, is mortal and destroys like poison; therefore, the methods of processing must be understood by the wise. These substances, such as mercury and the rest, when processed, bestow auspicious qualities, whereas otherwise they bring about defects.
Those technical terms which indeed exist here have not been elaborated upon, as we fear excessive prolixity.

(Rājñī 13.218) Having mastered this section, with its clear syllables manifesting the names and qualities of metals, minerals, gems, and their varieties, a wise person should become skilled in the expert application of the ancient medical treatises. (Rājñī 13.219)

Those things which, by means of their own quality—the traveler of the essence—render even the aging bodies of men ever-new, for them this group of gold and other substances is established under the name of the "Section on Elixirs" (rasāyana-varga). Those whose qualities are eternally radiant with abundant inner auspiciousness, and who are so skillful at captivating the heart that they transform the three worlds with their abundance; ||| Rajni_13.220 ||| [they are like the elixirs].
Thus, in this *Nāmādicūḍāmaṇi* composed by the one whose form is Nṛsiṃha, the section beginning with "Gold" concludes here, consisting of thirteen divisions. (Rājanighaṇṭu,
Pānīyādivarga 13.221)
Pānīya, jīvana, vana, amṛta, puṣkarāmbhas, pātha, ambu, śambara, payas, salila, udaka, āpas, kavāruṇa, kabandha, jala, nīra, kīlāla, vāri, kamala, viṣa, arṇasī, bhuvana,
dahanārāti, vāsta, toya, sarvatomukha, and kṣīra. (Rājñī 14.1)
And the juices produced from clouds over rivers of thick essence—these are measured by fire (three).

Water is sweet, cooling, appetizing, and removes thirst and parching; it dispels delusion and confusion, brings about the perfect digestion of food consumed, and expels sleepiness and lethargy. It is a destroyer of poison, a great restorative for the exhausted, and generates intelligence, strength, vigor, and contentment in men; it bestows nourishment upon wasted limbs.
Divyodaka (divine water), kharāri, ākāśasalila,
vyomodaka, antarikṣajala, and iṣu are synonyms for celestial water.
Vyomodaka destroys the three doṣas, is sweet, and is supremely wholesome.
It is palatable, stimulates digestion, and removes thirst, fatigue, and urinary disorders.
Rainwater that has fallen recently and remains on the ground is turbid and causes the bodily humors (doṣas) to increase;
however, water that has stood for a long time is light, clear, wholesome, sweet, and brings comfort.
Yādonātha, Samudra, Sindhu, Jalada, Kūpāra, Pāthodhi, Pārāvāra, Payodhi, Sāgara,

Sarinnātha, Vārāṃnidhi, Ambhorāśi, Sarasvat, Ambudhi, Nadīnātha, Abdhinitya, Arṇava, Udanvat, Vāridhi, Vārdhi, Kadhi, Apāṃnātha, and Ratnākara— these are synonyms for the ocean. Ocean water is foul-smelling, salty, causes blood diseases, and is hot.
It causes discoloration and various defects, and especially produces the pain of burning and an excess of *pitta*.
The river— *nadī*, *dhunī*, *nirjhariṇī*, *taraṅgiṇī*, *sarasvatī*,
*śaivalinī*, *samudragā*, *kūlaṃkaṣā*, *kūlavatī*, *nimnagā*, *śaivālinī*, *sindhu*, and also *apagā*.
*Hradinī*, *samudrakāntā*, *sāgaragā*, *hrādinī*, *sarit*, *karṣū*,
*srotasvinī*, *sunīrā*, *rodhovakrā*, *vāhinī*, *taṭinī*,
and *nādeya* refer to water. It is clear, light, and it stimulates digestion and promotes the digestive fire (*pācana*).
It is pleasing, thirst-quenching, wholesome, sweet, and slightly warm. The Gaṅgā, Yamunā (Sūryaputrī), Revā, Candrabhāgā,
Sarasvatī, Madhumatī, Vipāśā, Śoṇa, and likewise the Ghargharaka.
The Vetrāvatī, Kṣaudravatī, Payoṣṇī, Tāpī, Vitastā, Sarayū, and Sindhu;
the Mahāśatadru, then the Gautamī, the Kṛṣṇā, the Tuṅgā, and the daughter of Kaveri—
these and all other such rivers, as well as tanks, ponds, lakes, wells, and the like.
Other varieties of marshy regions should also be inferred by oneself through their respective names.
Water originating from the atmosphere, such as that which falls in streams and so forth,
should be examined and understood by those who know water, just as it has been described.

The Gaṅgā is the foremost river of heaven, flowing through the three paths; she is the Mandākinī, the Jāhnavī, the holy Viṣṇupadī, the one blessed by the ocean, the Bhāgīrathī, the golden river, the one with three streams, the long pond of the gods, the celestial river, the stream of the Siddhas, the river of heaven, the eldest daughter of Jahnu, the mother of Bhīṣma, the radiant one, and the daughter of the Lord of Mountains. Her waters are cool, sweet, clear, exceedingly pleasing, wholesome, digestive, purifying, and the destroyer of sins.
This water of the Bhāgīrathī destroys thirst and delusion, kindles the digestive fire, and bestows wisdom.
(Rājñī 14.17) The Yamunā—born of the Sun, daughter of Kalinda, sister of Yama, and known as Kālindī—[is described as follows:
It removes bile, burning sensations, vomiting, and fatigue; it is sweet, generates wind, and is a digestive stimulant. (Rājñī 14.18)
This water from the Yamunā kindles the digestive fire, is radiant, and bestows strength.
The Revā, Mekalakanyā, Somasutā, and Narmadā are to be known [as such].
Their cool water is very wholesome, yet it provokes pitta and kapha.

The water arising from the Mekalakanyakā (Narmadā) crushes all diseases, is pleasing to the taste, and is sweet. The exceedingly cool water of the Candrabhāgā pacifies burning sensations and bile, and subdues wind.
The Sarasvatī, originating from the Plakṣa tree, is the bestower of speech; she is the virtuous wife of Brahmā and is Bhāratī herself.
Vedāgraṇī, Payoṣṇijātā, Vāṇī, Viśālā, Kuṭilā, and Daśāhvā are the ten [rivers].
(Rajñī 14.23) The water of the Sarasvatī is sweet, pure, and removes all diseases;
it is appetizing, stimulates digestion, is wholesome, bestows luster upon the body, and is light. (Rajñī 14.24)
The water of the Cāndrabhāgā bestows an equilibrium of qualities; furthermore, the water of the Mādhumatī kindles the digestive fire.

(Rajñī 14.25) The very cool, light, sweet, and pure water of the Śatadrū, Vipāśā, and the union with the Sindhu river destroys all diseases; it is digestive, promotes digestion, and bestows strength, intellect, wisdom, and longevity. (Rajñī 14.26)

In the Śoṇa and Ghargharaka rivers, the water is pleasing to the taste, removes heat and exhaustion, is wholesome, stimulates the digestive fire, bestows strength, and provides nourishment for emaciated limbs.

There, other rivers bear waters that are very sweet, granting luster and nourishment, aphrodisiac, digestive, carminative, and strength-inducing; such is the Vetrāvatī and the Tāpinī. The water of the Payoṣṇī is appetizing, purifying, and a destroyer of sins.
The water of the Vitastā removes all diseases, provides happiness, bestows strength and luster, and is light. It is sweet, pacifies the three *doṣas*, is light,
bestows wisdom and intellect, is wholesome, and is supreme in removing fever and lethargy.
The water of the Sarayū is sweet, bestowing strength and nourishment. The Godāvarī, originating from Gautama and born from the mountain of Brahmā, is also known as the Gautamī;
it removes the afflictions of bile, blood, and wind, is highly wholesome, stimulates the digestive fire, and destroys sins.

The water of the Godāvarī removes the defects of diseases such as leprosy and wards off thirst. The Kṛṣṇā river originates from Kṛṣṇa; it is also known as the Kṛṣṇaveṇā and the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā. Its blackness causes coldness, yet its water is sweet, pure, and aggravates bile and blood.

The water of the Kṛṣṇaveṇā is clear, pleasing, digestive, and promotes digestion. The Bhīmarathī removes impurities; when it reaches the landing-stairs (ghaṭṭa), it becomes equal in quality to the water of the Kṛṣṇā.
Nevertheless, the water from the Malāpahā and the Ghaṭṭa is wholesome, light, more delicious, and bestows great luster.
The water of the Tuṅgabhadrā is unctuous, pure, sweet-tasting, and heavy;
it generally causes itching and increases pitta and blood, yet it is most excellent as a wholesome diet when it accords with one's constitution.
The water of the Kāverī is sweet, dispels fatigue, is light, and stimulates the digestive fire.
It destroys ailments such as ringworm and skin diseases, and bestows intelligence, wisdom, and a relish for food.

(14.37) Thus, the waters of other rivers should be understood by those of refined intellect to be endowed with their respective qualities according to the differences in location, defects, and other factors. (14.38)
Every river flowing eastward is heavy, while that flowing westward is certainly light;
due to the specific qualities of each region, it possesses weightiness or lightness accordingly.
Furthermore, any river from the Vindhya mountains flowing east, south, west, or north becomes heavy, light, light, and heavy respectively.

It brings about the aggravation of wind (vāta), the loss of phlegm and bile, an excess of bile, and the digestion of wholesome food. That river which originates in the Himavat, the Malaya mountain, the Vindhya, and the Sahya mountain is said to produce defects such as headaches and the like; however, that which is born from the Pāriyātra mountain dispels them.

Rivers born in the rainy season cause swelling, phlegm, asthma, distress, and cough; those born in autumn are wholesome and remove wind and phlegm; those born in winter bestow intelligence; those born in the cool season and spring pacify fever and grant well-being; and those born in summer, like excellent virtues, alleviate the afflictions of thirst, burning sensations, vomiting, and exhaustion. Water from marshy regions is sweet, unctuous, pacifies bile, and is heavy.
It causes skin diseases, itching, phlegm, wind-disorders, and fevers.
(Rajni 14.43) The water of the Jāṅgala region is sweet, destroys the three humors, and stimulates the appetite;
it is wholesome and bestows longevity, strength, vigor, nourishment, and supreme luster. (Rajni 14.44)

Water from common (ordinary) sources is pleasing to the taste, stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, is light, removes fatigue and thirst, subdues wind and phlegm, destroys impurities, and bestows nourishment.

However, water produced from copper-colored earth bestows the defects of wind and other humors; depending on the region, it causes dullness, is very difficult to digest, brings about disorders, and is greyish in color.

Water originating from a stone spring (*śilāśira*) is wind-alleviating, pure, wholesome, light, and sweet; it is excellent. Water from black soil (*śyāmamṛd*) pacifies the three *doṣas* and cures all diseases. (Rājñī 14.46) Lake water generates digestive fire, is sweet, removes phlegm and wind, and is wholesome. (Rājñī 14.47) Spring water is clear, light, sweet, appetizing, and stimulates digestion. (Rājñī 14.48)
The water of a pond is sweet, slightly astringent, and increases wind (vāta). The water of a large oblong tank (vāpī) is heating, produces wind and phlegm (śleṣman), and is heavy.
Well-water destroys phlegm, is alkaline, increases bile (pitta), and is light.

Water from springs is known to pacify bile and is light. Water from irrigated fields is sweet in its post-digestive effect but increases the humors and is heavy; that same water, when stagnant, especially increases the humors.
Water that has not been drawn from a river, placed in new earthen jars, heated by the rays of the sun, set out at night under the moonbeams, and stirred by a gentle breeze;

scented with cardamom and other fragrant substances, this "Hamsodaka" (swan-water) is praised as a remover of fatigue and beneficial in cases of bilious fever, heat-stroke, poisoning, fainting, hemorrhaging, and alcoholism.
The wise man who always drinks cool, sweet water at midnight or at dawn, or even drinks it through the nostrils, [attains great merit].

Thus, he immediately vies with the lord of birds in the power of his eyes, mocks the preceptor of heaven with his intellect, and rivals the two Aśvins with his body. One should not drink water that is fouled by excrement, urine, red or blue poison, heated, thick, frothy, graspable by the teeth, out of season, salty, covered with moss, mixed with swarms of living creatures, heavy, turbid with masses of leaves and mud, obscured by the rays of the moon and sun, stagnant, and full of defects.

One should avoid cold water in cases of pain in the flanks, catarrh, disorders of wind (vāta), acute fever, and afflictions such as hiccups and flatulence. [Rājñī 14.57] One should also avoid it in cases of depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu-kṣaya), blood disorders, vomiting, hemorrhage, urinary disorders, and the disturbances caused by poison.

In chronic fever and when the *saṃnipāta* has become weakened, boiled water that has been cooled is recommended. Water heated and then reduced by one-quarter part is declared wholesome for destroying diseases born of *vāta*;
reduced by half a part it destroys *vāta* and *pitta*, while that which is reduced by one-quarter [of its original volume] destroys all three *doṣas*.
In the winter, [the water] is reduced by one-quarter; in the autumn, by one-eighth;
and in the rainy season, spring, the cool season, and summer, it is reduced by half.
In the cool season and spring, one may drink from a well or a spring.
In the summer, one should indeed resort to *cauḍa* water; otherwise, it would give rise to defects.
Water heated during the day becomes cold at night, while that heated at night becomes heavy by day;
therefore, people should take water that has been heated for the time being, whether by day or by night.

In some cases the water is hot, in some cold, in some lukewarm, and in some it is cooled decoction; thus this regimen is prescribed for people according to the requirements of time, condition, and bodily constitution. It removes the disorder of wind (vāta), quickly breaks up phlegm (kapha), and destroys loss of appetite.

It causes food to digest and nourishes the digestive fire; warm water drunk at midnight is praised for pacifying the disorder of indigestion. Water drunk generally at the end of the night is said to destroy all diseases. When drunk after eating, it produces nourishment; when drunk before eating, it provides nourishment; and when drunk between meals, it is wholesome, improves the appetite, and sharpens the power of the stomach fire.
Food is not properly digested from drinking excessive water, and that same fault arises from not drinking water at all.
Therefore, for the sake of increasing the digestive fire, a person should drink water frequently, but not in large quantities.
Wise men say that there are four kinds of water originating from the atmosphere.
Dhāra, kāra, tauṣāra, and haima—these are the types of water.
Water produced by rain is *dhāra*; that produced from hailstones is *kāra*;
dew-water is *tauṣāra*; and that produced from morning frost is *haima*.
Water is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as that of the Gaṅgā and that of the ocean.
Among these, the water of the Gaṅgā is rich in qualities, free from defects, and is an excellent digestive.
When, in the month of Āśvina, the sun is in the constellations Svāti or Viśākhā, [the water is most auspicious].
"Water released by the clouds at that time is called 'Gāṅga' (of the Gaṅgā) by the wise;
whereas water rained down by the clouds on other occasions during the asterisms of Mṛgaśīrṣa and others is designated as 'sāmudra' (oceanic)."

When it rains from a cloud, water from the Ganges placed for a moment in a silver vessel upon a ball of cooked *śāli* rice smeared with curd may remain unchanged; otherwise, it would become different. The water of the Ganges is sweet, very cool, appetizing, and it removes bile and phlegm.
They say that water obtained from the sky is faultless, clear, light, eternal, and superior in its qualities.
Water originating from the moonstone (candrakānta) destroys bile, is pure and light;
it is beneficial in cases of fainting, hemorrhaging, and burning sensations, as well as in cough and alcoholism.
Ocean water is cool, increases phlegm and wind, and is heavy;
however, when it falls during the asterism Citrā in the month of Āśvina, it becomes rich in qualities like the water of the Gaṅgā.
Whatever water, whether from the Gaṅgā or the ocean, has fallen upon the earth, [it shares these qualities].
Each other rasa and so forth would proceed according to the power of their respective substrata.
If blood and salt fall upon an earthy surface, they remain as such;
however, on a watery [surface] it is said to become sweet, and on a fiery [surface] pungent or bitter.
In the wind [element], the taste would be astringent; in the ether, it is said to be unmanifest.
Among these, that which belongs to the ether alone is declared to be the best, being free from defects. Furthermore, in the month of Āśvina, if the cloud does not rain at all—
In that time when the waters of the Gaṅgā have vanished, diseases will prevail there even more intensely.
In some places the water is hot, in some cold, in some boiled and then cooled;
in some places it is mixed with medicinal herbs, while in others not a drop of water is to be found.
Sugarcane is said to be of five kinds, endowed with various colors and qualities:
white, *puṇḍra*, *karaṅka*, black, and red, in that order.
Sugarcane is also classified as *karkaṭaka*, *vaṃśa*, *kāntāra*, and *sukumāraka*.
Asipattra, madhutṛṇa, vṛṣya, and guḍatṛṇa—these are the nine [types of sugarcane].
Śveteṣu is the same as sitekṣu; kāṣṭheṣu is vaṃśapatraka.
Suvaṃśa, pāṇḍureṣu, kāṇḍeṣu, and dhavaleṣuka are also names for types of sugarcane.
The *sitekṣu* (white sugarcane) is hard, palatable, heavy, and increases phlegm and urine;
it is known to stimulate digestion, destroy bile and burning sensations, and is slightly warm in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*).
The *puṇḍraka*, however, is called *rasāla*, *rasekṣu*, and *sukumāraka*.
The *karbura* is of mixed colors, and the *nepālekṣu* is of seven kinds.
The *puṇḍra* is extremely sweet, cooling, increases *kapha*, and destroys *pitta*;
it removes burning sensations and fatigue, is appetizing, and is supreme as a nourishing tonic in its taste.
*Karaṅkaśāli*, *ikṣuvāṭī*, *ikṣuvāṭikā*,
*yāvanī*, *ikṣuyoni*, *rasālī*, and *rasadālikā* are synonyms for sugarcane.
*Karaṅkaśāli* is sweet, cooling, appetizing, and soft.
It removes burning sensations caused by bile, is aphrodisiac, and increases vitality and strength.
Black sugarcane (*kṛṣṇekṣu*) is called *ikṣura*; dark sugarcane (*śyāmekṣu*) is called *kokilākṣaka*.
It is also known as *śyāmavaṃśa*, *śyāmalekṣu*, and *kokilekṣu*.
The black sugarcane (*kṛṣṇekṣu*) is said to be sweet in its digestion, pleasant to the palate, agreeable to the heart, pungent, and rich in flavor;
it removes the three *doṣas*, bestows tranquility and vigor, provides great strength, and grants abundant vitality.
The red sugarcane (*raktikṣu*) has fine leaves; it is crimson, blood-red, and intense.
The red sugarcane is celebrated as being sweet and having short roots.
The red sugarcane is sweet in digestion, cooling, and mild;
it removes bile and burning sensations, is aphrodisiac, and increases vitality and strength.
The root of the sugarcane is *ikṣunetra*, and that is also called *moraṭaka*;
likewise, *vaṃśanetra*, *vaṃśamūla*, *moraṭa*, and *vaṃśapūraka* [refer to the bamboo root].
From the base upwards, they are sweet, and in the middle, they are exceedingly sweet.

These sugarcanes are progressively saltier and less flavorful toward their tips. They alleviate *pitta* when eaten on an empty stomach, aggravate *vāta* when eaten after a meal, and are heaviest when eaten during a meal; such are the three qualities of sugarcane.

The sugarcane stalk—when crushed gently by the teeth—is aphrodisiac, expert at pacifying blood disorders and hemorrhaging caused by heat (rakta-asrapitta), cooling, slightly increases phlegm (kapha), unctuous, pleasing to the heart, appetizing, brings joy, ensures purity of the urine, bestows luster upon the body, produces great strength, provides nourishment, grants satisfaction, is soft, dark-colored, and intoxicating. When squeezed with the teeth, it is comparable to nectar and pacifies the three humors (doṣas); likewise, that which is produced by a household press is similar, while another kind slightly subdues phlegm and wind (vāta).
This sugarcane juice, when stale, is said to remove wind but generate it further, causing dullness and catarrh; it increases phlegm and wind.
The broth from *yāvanāla* and *śara* grass is sweet, salty, alkaline, unctuous, warm, and appetizing; it is aphrodisiac and destroys wind and phlegm. (Rajni 14.97–98)
Boiled sugarcane juice is unctuous, destroys Kapha and Vata, and is very heavy;
when over-boiled, it causes a burning sensation and produces Pitta, blood disorders, and wasting. Guḍa (jaggery) is the essence of sugarcane, sweet, and produced from the cooking of its juice.
White sugar and the like are dear to children; red sugar is known to be produced from molasses.

It subdues *pitta*, overcomes afflictions caused by *vāta*, stimulates the appetite, is pleasing to the heart, and removes the three *doṣas*. Through its specific combination [of qualities], it especially alleviates fever, bestows relief from burning heat, cleanses disorders of feces and urine, kindles the digestive fire, and puts an end to anemia (*pāṇḍu*) and urinary disorders (*prameha*). Old jaggery (*guḍa*) is unctuous, very sweet, light, removes fatigue, is wholesome, and is oily. *Rajñī 14.100–101*
This jaggery (guḍa), produced from the cooking of the juice of *yāvanāla* grass, is alkaline, pungent, and very sweet; it removes phlegm and wind.

When consumed constantly, it produces bile, generates itching and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), yet it relieves blood-borne burning sensations. White granulated sugar (*śarkarā*) is said to be the same as *mīnāṇḍī* and *matsyaṇḍikā*.
Ahicchatrā, however, is sand-like and white, produced from molasses;
it is sugar (śarkarā), sweet, and cooling, removing bile, burning sensations, and fatigue.
It cures blood disorders and destroys confusion and the provocation of worms.

Pounded sugar-cane candy (*puṇḍraka-śarkarā*) is unctuous, beneficial, helpful for emaciation, loss of appetite, and eye disorders; it increases strength and is very sweet. That produced from *vaṃśa* (bamboo) or *ikṣu* (sugarcane) is dry. That produced from dark sugarcane (*śyāma-ikṣu*) is aphrodisiac, provides satiety and strength, and removes fatigue. That produced from *rasālā* (mango-sugar syrup) is cooling, unctuous, and bestows luster. That produced from red sugarcane conquers *pitta*.
Yava-nālī, *himotpannā*, *himānī*, and *hima-śarkarā* (varieties of snow-sugar) are likewise cooling.

Kṣudraśarkarikā, kṣudrā, gudguḍā, jālabindujā, himajā, and śarkarā are varieties of sugar. That which is sweet (gaulyā) is warm, bitter, and very slimy; it destroys wind (vāta), is appetizing, yet causes burning sensations and increases bile and blood. It is known as sārikā. 14.106–14.107

Sitajā, śarkarajā, mādhavī, madhuśarkarā, and mākṣīkaśarkarā are declared to be types of sugar; sitākhaṇḍa is called khaṇḍaka. Sitākhaṇḍa is extremely sweet, beneficial for the eyes, and a destroyer of vomiting.
It cures skin diseases, ulcers, phlegm, asthma, hiccups, and disorders of bile and blood. Rajani 14.109.
Yavāsaśarkarā, Sudhāmodaka, Tavarāja, Khaṇḍasāra, Khaṇḍajā, and Khaṇḍamodaka are other [varieties]. Rajani 14.110.
Tavarāja is extremely sweet, it removes bile, fatigue, and thirst;
it is aphrodisiac, alleviates burning sensations, fainting, pain, and dizziness, and is laxative.
So too are the candied sugar (khaṇḍa) derived from Tavarāja, as well as that produced from Sudhā and Modaka.
Born from pieces, born from liquids, and produced from the essence of the nectar of perfected sweetmeats—this cooled *siddhakhaṇḍa* indeed always possesses a most sweet flavor;
it wards off burning sensations, removes heat, brings about satiety, and destroys delusion and fainting. It checks labored breathing, refreshes the senses, and is truly beneficial. (Rājñī 14.112–113)
Madhu is honey; it is called *kṣaudra*, *mākṣīka*, *mākṣika*, *kusumāsavam*, *puṣpāsava*, *pavitra*, *pitrya*, and *puṣparasāhvaya*.
Furthermore, *mākṣika* is honey from bees, while *kṣaudra*, *pauttika*, and *chāttraka* are likewise types of honey.

Ārghya, auddālaka, and dāla—these are the eight varieties of honey. Forest bees that feed on the juices of various flowers and are tawny in color produce honey; that which is produced by those that are large is called *mākṣika*.
That honey which is produced by bees that resemble smooth balls of collyrium and are devoted to the nectar of flowers is called *bhrāmara* honey. Furthermore,
there are small, reddish-brown flies well known as *kṣudrā*.
That which is produced by them is called *kṣaudra* honey.
The brown flies born from food are known as *puttikās*;
the honey produced by them is designated by the wise as *pauttika*.
When bees that are yellowish-brown produce a honeycomb shaped like an umbrella, the honey produced from it is called *chāttraka*. Furthermore,
there are flies with sharp beaks that resemble bees.
That which arises from it and is worthy of the *arghya* offering is described as *madhu-arghya*.
The *auddālaka* insects are known to be brownish and to burrow into the earth; that which is produced at the end of an anthill is called *auddālakam*. (Rājñī 14.121–122)

"Bees, with bodies as delicate as sapphire petals, gather the honey located within the hollows of trees; this is known as *dāla*. Thus has its production been described in sequence through its eight varieties.
Now I shall describe to you their colors, potencies, and other qualities in due order: *mākṣika* honey has the color of oil; that of bees (*bhrāmara*) is said to be white;
*kṣaudra* has the appearance of tawny-brown; and *pauttika* resembles clarified butter.
The *chāttra* variety is yellowish-green, while the one named *arghya* is tawny (*piṅga*).
The *auddāla* is like gold in color, and the *dāla* is said to be yellowish.
*Mākṣika* is sweet, parching, light, and removes disorders such as asthma.
Bhrāmara honey is slimy, dry, sweet, and overcomes numbness of the mouth.
Kṣaudra honey is cooling, beneficial for the eyes, slimy, and removes pitta and vāta.
Pauttika honey is dry and hot, and it causes burning sensations such as those of raktapitta.
One should know that *śāttra* is superior in its qualities;
it destroys leucoderma, urinary disorders, and worms, is worthy of honor, sweet, beneficial for the eyes, and removes defects such as phlegm and bile.
*Auddālaka*, however, destroys defects such as leprosy and grants all success.
Dālā is pungent, astringent, sour, and sweet, and it increases pitta.
Fresh honey causes corpulence and is not excessively kapha-producing;
old honey removes corpulence from the body, is constipating, and is scraping (lekhana).

Matured honey destroys the three *doṣas*, dispels various diseases, numbness, and ailments of the tongue, and provides relish, strength, great fortitude, and increases virility. If raw, it destroys undigested matter (*āma*), abdominal tumors, wind-pains, burning sensations from *pitta*, and blood disorders; yet it invariably generates wind (*vāta*) and emaciation, and destroys internal growths. It is used for cleansing wounds, joining fractures, and healing sores.

Honey is beneficial when it is common [to all seasons]; honey-sugar is similar to that. Raw honey, whether taken with hot substances, during the hot season, or even by itself being hot, causes affliction for human beings like poison.

Honey that is infested with insects and the like, honey corrupted by acidity, honey that has stood overnight, honey that is naturally dark, honey found inside thorns or hollows, and honey produced in the home— all these are harmful. However, honey of such a kind that has been struck down with sticks, from which the parts containing insects have been discarded, is fit for use as an elixir (*rasāyana*).

It removes ailments such as hiccups, hemorrhoids, swellings, phlegm, and wounds; otherwise, it causes disorders. Honey, white sugar produced from honey, sugar born of honey, and *mākṣika* sugar—this [last] is sugar produced from *kṣaudra* (bee-honey), known as *kṣaudra-śarkarā*.
Whatever qualities are attributed to each type of honey, those same qualities belong to its respective sugar.
In particular, it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and refreshing for those whose bodies are emaciated.
(Rajñī 14.138) Wine may be *surā*, *prasannā*, *madirā*, or *vāruṇī*; the latter is considered the best.
*Mattā*, *kādambarī*, *śītā*, *capalā*, and *kāminī-priyā*;
*madagandhā*, *mādhvīka*, *madhu*, *saṃdhāna*, and *āsava*;
*parisrut*, *amṛtā*, *vīrā*, *medhāvī*, and *madanī*—these are synonyms for wine. (Rajni 14.139–140)
Supratibhā, Manojñā, Vipānā, Modinī, Hālāhalaguṇā, Ariṣṭa, Saraka, Madhūlikā, Madotkaṭā, and Mahānandā— these are the thirty-two names in sequence. (Rajñī 14.141)

Wine that is very sweet and sour destroys phlegm and wind; it bestows strength and digestive fire, is pleasing to the heart, laxative, and intoxicating. Gauḍī wine is made from jaggery and the juice of the dhātakī flower; mādhvī wine consists of the essence of honey, such as the juice of flowers.
Furthermore, that which is made from various preparations of grain is known as *paiṣṭī*; among these, each preceding type is said to be more intoxicating than the one following it.
They call liquor distilled from the sap and exudations of the *tāla* palm and other trees *saindhī*, while *surā* is also referred to as *hālā*.
A beverage produced from a combination of various ingredients is traditionally called *kādambara*.

Saindhī and Kādambarī are the two types characterized as liquor. Gauḍī is sharp, hot, and sweet; it removes wind, produces bile, bestows strength, stimulates digestion, is wholesome, promotes luster, and is supremely satiating.
Honey-wine (*mādhvī*), however, is sweet, pleasant to the heart, not excessively hot, and removes *pitta* and *vāta*;
it is supreme in pacifying anemia, jaundice, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and urinary disorders.
(Rajni 14.146) Wine made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) is pungent, hot, sharp, sweet, and a supreme stimulant to digestion. (Rajni 14.147)

Saindhī wine is cold, astringent, and slightly sour; it removes pitta but increases vāta. Gauḍī wine should be drunk in the cool season (śiśira), while paiṣṭī wine is to be drunk during the early winter (hemanta) and the rainy season (varṣa).
Mādhvī wine should be consumed during autumn, summer, and spring, and not otherwise.
Wine made from *kādambarī*, sugar, and similar ingredients is very cooling, aphrodisiac, and highly intoxicating;
it is equal to honey-wine (*mādhvī*). Wine produced from grasses and trees is very cooling, heavy, and satiating.
The exudation (*niryāsa*) of all grasses and trees is cooling and heavy.
Sugarcane liquor is intoxicating, strength-promoting, beneficial for the heart, and a destroyer of thirst and fever.
However, liquor made from sugarcane juice is cooling yet intensely intoxicating;
liquor made from barley grain is heavy and causes constipation.
Sugar-cane liquor (śārkara) is prepared from sugar, dhātakī flowers, and water; when cooled, it is enchanting.
It is said to be aphrodisiac, digestive, and intoxicating.
Wise men say there are twelve other varieties of liquor.
Since they are included within those already mentioned, they have not been described separately by others.
Fresh liquor is the cause of all disorders, and indeed bestows all the humors such as wind (vāta) and the rest;
however, when aged, it destroys all diseases, provides strength, acts as an aphrodisiac, and stimulates the digestive fire.
They employ intoxicants among Śūdras and others who are in great distress;
however, these three twice-born castes must not accept them, even if they should revive one who is dead.
Thus, there are various classifications of intoxicants—such as sugarcane juice, molasses, honey, and so forth—which originate from the shores of oceans, rivers, streams, lakes, ponds, and canals.

Before administering this [treatment], the physician—having awakened from [the state of ignorance] regarding names and qualities, having determined the appropriateness of the application, and having resolved his mind according to the true nature of things—should perform the medical action. (14.157) For these tastes, when tasted by men, expel even those humors that are difficult to remove, each according to its own nature; therefore, this collection of tastes is indeed well-known by the name "The Group of Tastes" (*rasavarga*). (14.158)
It does not desire the outflow from the ocean of milk, nor the nectar of all medicinal herbs, nor the milking of the sun, nor medical treatment, nor even the essence of the moon;
yet, having found friendship with the wise folk in this world, the group beginning with water attains renown in this [Rājanighaṇṭu], whose crest-jewel is the *Manu*. (Rājanighaṇṭu 14.159)
The Section on Milk and Related Substances:
Milk is called *kṣīra*, *pīyūṣa*, *ūdhasya*, *dugdha*, *stanya*, *payaḥ*, and *amṛta*. (Rajni 15.1) Curd is produced from milk; its thin portion is *mastu*, and its liquid is *tajjala*. (Rajni 15.2)
Butter produced from curds is *navanīta*; its essence is *haiyaṅgavīna*.
Ghee is called *ājya*, *havis*, *sarpiḥ*, *pavitra*, and that which is born of butter (*navanītajam*);
it is also known as *amṛta*, *abhighāra*, *homya*, *āyus*, and *taijasa*.
Anointing (*mrakṣaṇa*), lubricating (*snehana*), oil (*sneha*), glossiness (*snigdhatā*), and ointment (*mrakṣa*) itself;
as well as massage (*abhyaṅga*), unguent (*abhyañjana*), and *upaḍa* consisting of ghee and other substances;
buttermilk (*takra*) produced from cow's milk, *ghola*, and *kālaśeya* which is stirred curd.

*Ariṣṭa* is sour when struck by a stick; *udaśvit* is the liquid from churned curds. Wise men have stated that *takra* (buttermilk) consists of water mixed with one-third part of curd, while *mastu* consists of water mixed with double the amount of curd.
If the curd and water are equal, they call it *udaśvit*; however, sages say that *mathita* is simply the liquid alone.
Cow’s urine, cow-water, cow-dung, cow-exudate, and cow-drava;
likewise, cow-mash, cow-manure, cow-droppings, and cow-ordure.
[Also] the females of the cow, buffalo, goat, sheep, elephant, horse, donkey, camel, and human.
I shall describe the qualities and defects of milk and other substances in their proper order as appropriate.

Cow’s milk is wholesome, extremely palatable, sweet, and unctuous; it destroys diseases of bile and wind, bestows luster, wisdom, intellect, mental acuity, and nourishment for the limbs, and clearly brings about an increase in virility. (Rajni 15.9–10)
Buffalo milk is pungent (gaulya), cooling in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and heavy;
it bestows strength and nourishment, is aphrodisiac, and destroys pitta, burning sensations, and hemorrhages.
(Rajni 15.11) Because goats have small bodies and consume various kinds of substances...
Milk removes all diseases when one does not drink excessive water and engages in physical exercise.

(Rājñī 15.12) The milk of a small goat (*sūkṣmājadugdha*) is worthy of comparison with cow's milk, yet it is superior in its potency (*vīrya*) and qualities; it is declared wholesome for those whose bodies are greatly emaciated. The milk of a large goat (*sthūlājadugdha*), however, is said to be slightly inferior. (Rājñī 15.13)
Sheep's milk is unctuous, excellent for removing phlegm and bile,
beneficial for curing obesity and urinary disorders, hairy, heavy, and promotes growth.
(Rajni 15.14) The milk of a female elephant is sweet, aphrodisiac, heavy, and astringent.
The milk of the female horse is unctuous, stabilizing, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength.
However, the milk of the male horse is parching, sour, salty, digestive, and light;
it provides stability to the body, is strengthening, and is supreme in producing heaviness and luster.
Donkey’s milk is a strength-builder and is supreme for removing vāta and dyspnea;
it is known to be sweet and sour in taste, parching, digestive, and wholesome.
(Rajni 15.17) Camel’s milk removes skin diseases and swelling, destroys pitta and hemorrhoids, and removes the distension caused by kapha.

When drunk, it quickly destroys abdominal tumors, gulma, dropsy, and those known as *ākhya*, as well as labored breathing and its aggravation. (Rajni 15.18) Human milk is sweet, astringent, cooling, and light;
it is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, is wholesome, promotes digestion, and improves the appetite. (Rajni 15.19)

Milk causes the aggravation of cough and dyspnea; generally, all milk that is heavy and unboiled (āmam) gives rise to the humors (doṣas). However, if it is heated and churned, it is said to be wholesome; furthermore, even raw milk from a woman (nārīkṣīram) destroys disease.
It has been stated that cow’s milk and other such milks, when warm as they flow (dhāroṣṇam), are like nectar.

It removes all diseases, is wholesome, and remains effective for a long time, yet it may aggravate the bodily humors (*doṣa*). Some say that sheep's milk is most wholesome when boiled and heated; however, they say goat's milk is best when boiled and then cooled. Buffalo's milk is best when cooled after milking, while cow's milk is praised when warm as it flows from the udder.
Milk drunk in the forenoon is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and increases the digestive fire; drunk at midday, it bestows strength, removes phlegm, and cures dysuria.
It stimulates the fire in childhood, thereafter provides strength, and bestows virility in old age. Milk pacifies many disorders when consumed at night; therefore, it should be used at all times.
Milk that has stood for three *muhūrtas* becomes spoiled if not heated. (Rājñī 15.23)
If it is hot, it produces a disorder; if it remains for ten nights, it becomes like poison.
(Rājñī 15.24) In a chronic fever, when the phlegm has been depleted, milk is like nectar;
that very same milk, if drunk during an acute fever, kills a person like poison. (Rājñī 15.25)
That which is churned with care after placing water equal to one-fourth [of the milk] is the best;
this highly praised milk destroys all diseases, promotes strength and nourishment, and bestows virility.
Cow’s milk should be used in the forenoon, while buffalo’s milk should be used in the afternoon.

Milk with sugar is wholesome, or whatever is always suitable to one's constitution. Milk that is boiled and then cooled destroys *pitta*; when cooked and warm, it removes *kapha*. That which is not heated at all is cold and causes the disorder of constipation (*viṣṭambha*). However, milk fresh from the udder (*dhāroṣṇa*) is like nectar; it removes fatigue, induces sleep, bestows luster, is aphrodisiac, nourishing, increases the digestive fire, is exceedingly sweet, and pacifies the three *doṣas*.
One should never consume milk that has not been heated, nor should it be taken with salt, nor with flour-based foods,
fermented grains, black gram, green gram, *kośātakī*, tubers, fruits, and the like.
Milk consumed together with fish, meat, molasses, green gram, and radish brings about leprosy.
When consumed with the juices of *śāka* and *jambava*, it quickly kills the ignorant man like a serpent.
One should never consume milk that is oily, cold, or heavy at all times;
it makes a strong digestive fire weak and causes a weak fire to be extinguished entirely.
Buffalo’s milk, when well-cooked and consumed regularly with a strong digestive fire, nourishes all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) and increases strength and nourishment.
The milk of cows, goats, and others is sweet; that of those who have recently calved is alkaline. (Rājñī 15.32)
The dry milk causes burning from bile and produces blood disorders.
The sweet milk of cows that have calved recently pacifies the three humors (doṣas).
The salty-sweet milk of those that have long since calved generates a burning sensation.
The milk of women who have given birth for the first time is devoid of qualities and lacks essence;
that of those in their middle age is said to be a rejuvenative elixir, while that of the elderly is weak.
Furthermore, the milk of those pregnant women, as well as of those [who have recently given birth], after three months has passed, [is likewise ineffective].
When heated, that salt makes milk bitter and produces the disorder of bile (*pitta*).
O Queen, the qualities of milk and other products differ according to the species of the cow and other animals;
some say there is further distinction based on the difference of region.
In various regions and in those various places, according to the defects present in the grass and water,
it is held that the qualities of the milk and so forth produced by cows and other animals are of a corresponding nature through the mere consumption of those [substances].
Cold, unctuous, heavy, sweet, aphrodisiac, and supreme in removing bile (pitta).
Its name is also known as *kīlāṭa* and *payaśchada*.
Cow’s curd (*dadhi*) is extremely pure; it is cooling, unctuous, digestive, and strength-giving.
It is sweet, removes loss of appetite, is constipating, and destroys diseases caused by wind (*vāta*).
Buffalo curd is sweet, unctuous, increases phlegm, conquers blood-bile (raktapitta),
increases strength and semen, is aphrodisiac, removes fatigue, and is purifying.
Goat’s curd destroys phlegm and wind, is light, hot in potency, and cures eye diseases.
It cures dyspnea, cough, and diseases of foul odor; it is appetizing and stimulates digestion and metabolism. (15.42) Sheep's curd is very unctuous, increases phlegm and bile, and is heavy;
it is wholesome in cases of Vāta and blood-related Vāta disorders, and removes swelling and ulcers. (15.43)

The curd from a female elephant is astringent, light, and hot; it pacifies colic of digestion, stimulates the appetite, indeed kindles the digestive fire, destroys diseases caused by phlegm (*balāsa*), increases virility, and bestows strength. (Rājñī 15.44) The curd from a mare is sweet and astringent; it removes the affliction of phlegm and the disease of fainting, and is parching.
It is said on earth that this [curd] is slightly wind-increasing, digestive-stimulating, and a remover of eye disorders.
(Rajñī 15.45) The curd of the female donkey is dry, hot, light, digestive-stimulating, and carminative;
it has a sweet-sour taste, is appetizing, and destroys disorders of the wind (*vāta*). (Rajñī 15.46)

Curd that is pungent, sweet, and slightly sour destroys piles, skin diseases, worms, colic, and abdominal ailments. It is sweet in its post-digestive effect, strengthening, sour, satiating, and heavy.
Curd produced from breast milk is beneficial for the eyes and destroys the afflictions caused by planetary influences.
Sour curd is heavy, pacifies disorders of Vāta, is constipating, promotes urination, is strengthening, causes swelling, improves appetite, and provides relief to the digestive fire.
It is beneficial in cases of cough, asthma, chronic catarrh, and irregular fever with chills; it increases the flow of blood and constantly brings about a great increase in semen.

Curd that is sweet, slightly sour, or sweet-and-sour is beneficial, provided it is not too hot; it is said that the more sweet it is, the more it removes the bodily humors (*doṣa*). Those who are constantly deprived of salt, black pepper, ghee, sugar, mung beans, and the juice of *dhātrī* flowers do not eat this.

One should not eat curd in autumn, in spring, nor during the hot season, nor at night; nor should one eat it when there is a disorder of phlegm (*kapha*) or even when there is a derangement of bile (*pitta*).

(Rājñī 15.51) This [curd], when combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) and mixed with powdered black mustard (*rājikā*), removes phlegm, subdues wind (*anila*), and kindles the digestive fire. Consumed during the cold and winter seasons, it is highly beneficial and brings about firmness of the body and radiance for men. (Rājñī 15.52)

Whey (*mastu*) is praised for being light; it is hot and sour, providing relish and promoting digestion, removing fatigue, strengthening, astringent, laxative, and curbing excessive eating. It destroys thirst, abdominal diseases, splenic disorders, and hemorrhoids; it cleanses the channels, subdues *kapha* and *vāyu*, removes flatulence and colic, and pacifies anemia, respiratory disorders, and abdominal tumors. It is said that *mathita* (churned buttermilk) removes *kapha* and *vāyu*, while *udaśvit* (buttermilk with undissolved solids) is said to remove *kapha* and *pitta* and stimulate the appetite. *Takra* (plain buttermilk), when prepared in greater quantity, removes all three *doṣas*.

The wise declare that the three types of *takra* are excellent and most wholesome for those with weak digestion, loss of appetite, burning sensations, irregular fever, dyspnea, cough, and similar ailments; indeed, they are supreme. *Takra* pacifies the three *doṣas*, stimulates the digestive fire, improves taste, cures vomiting and diarrhea, and removes exhaustion. *Udaśvit* (the watery part of *takra*) provides strength, destroys wind (*vāta*), and is recommended for phlegm, fatigue, and vomiting caused by wind. *Ghola* (curdled milk) is likewise praised. (Rajni 15.54–55)
Sourness instantly destroys wind (vāta), sweetness destroys bile (pitta), and astringency destroys phlegm (kapha).
Just as nectar is for the benefit of the gods, so they say that buttermilk (takra) is for the benefit of men in this world.
It is likewise used in cases of diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra), choleraic disorders (viṣūcikā), fever due to wind, anemia (pāṇḍu), and jaundice (kāmalā).
One should drink buttermilk daily for urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and pain from Vāta; it is also used for loss of appetite.
Buttermilk is recommended during the cold season, in cases of weak digestion, phlegm disorders, anemia, obstructions of the channels, and diseases such as skin ailments (kuṣṭha). (Rajni 15.57–58)
One suffering from *vātodara* (wind-type abdominal enlargement) should drink buttermilk mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*) and salt;

one suffering from *pittodara* (bile-type abdominal enlargement) should drink sweet buttermilk combined with sugar and black pepper (*marica*). For *kaphodara* (phlegm-type abdominal enlargement), [buttermilk] should be combined with *yavānī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), cumin (*ajājī*), and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
In cases of abdominal disorders caused by the combination of humors (*saṃnipāta*), one should administer buttermilk mixed with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), alkali, and rock salt.
One should not give buttermilk to those with chest wounds, nor during the hot season, nor in states of debility, nor when afflicted by thirst or fainting.
It should not be given at all in cases of vertigo, nor in disorders of blood and bile (*pittāsra*), and especially not to a woman who has recently given birth.
Buttermilk mixed with fats causes heaviness of the stomach, induces sleep, and brings about dullness; it is heavy.

When half-remaining, it is ordinary; when completely drained, it is light, wholesome, cooling, bestows complexion and strength, is very sweet, aphrodisiac, astringent, subdues wind, removes phlegm, improves the appetite, and alleviates pain throughout the entire body. (Rajni 15.62)

Freshly extracted butter from a cow cures cough, destroys fatigue, bestows happiness, grants luster, provides nourishment, is beneficial for the eyes, and removes all bodily humors (doṣas). Both fresh butter derived from cow's milk and that from buffalo's milk is praised for children and the elderly; it bestows strength and increases nourishment.
Buffalo butter is astringent and sweet in taste;
it is cooling, aphrodisiac, constipating, a destroyer of pitta, and a provider of strength.
Goat's butter is light, sweet, and astringent, and it alleviates the three doṣas.
Butter is always beneficial; it is pleasing to the eyes, digestive, and strengthening. (RājNī 15.66) Fresh butter derived from goat's milk conquers consumption and cough;
it is strengthening, cures eye diseases, subdues phlegm, and is an excellent digestive stimulant. (RājNī 15.67)
Sheep's butter, however, is cooling and light in its post-digestive effect;
it is always beneficial for womb-pain, phlegm, wind, and hemorrhoids.
Goat's butter is astringent, cooling, and light.
Elephant butter (navanīta) is beneficial for intelligence, the heart, and nourishment; it promotes corpulence and stimulates a sluggish digestive fire.
It is astringent, cooling, light, bitter, causes constipation, destroys living organisms, and cures pitta, kapha, and worms.
The fresh butter from a mare is astringent, it conquers phlegm and wind,
is beneficial for the eyes, pungent, hot, and slightly dispels wind.
Fresh butter from a she-ass, however, is astringent and removes phlegm and wind.
Camel butter is strengthening, stimulates digestion, is light in its post-digestive effect, hot, and removes disorders of the urine.
(Rajni 15.72) Camel butter is light in its post-digestive effect and cooling;
it destroys wounds, worms, phlegm, and blood-borne diseases, subdues wind, and neutralizes poison. (Rajni 15.73)
Fresh butter is considered pleasing to women, light in digestion, beneficial for the eyes, a destroyer of all diseases, digestive, and a neutralizer of poisons.
Freshly extracted butter is cooling, appetizing, very sweet, aphrodisiac, and a subduer of wind; it cures cough, destroys worms, increases phlegm, is constipating, and relieves colic.

Clarified butter produced from curds (*dadhi*) is strengthening, nourishing, a pacifier of thirst and distress, a dispeller of heat, beneficial for the eyes, a remover of fatigue, satiating, and a conqueror of *pitta*. It is said that when it has stood for one day or more, it bestows an increasingly superior fragrance; however, that clarified butter derived from curds which is unpalatable and full of all kinds of impurities is considered inferior.

Cow’s ghee—bestowed by fortune—is the giver of intellect, beauty, and memory; it bestows strength, wisdom, and nourishment; it removes wind and phlegm, pacifies fatigue, and subdues bile; it is pleasing to the heart, increases the digestive fire, is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), is aphrodisiac, grants stability to the body, and possesses manifold qualities worthy of enjoyment. (Rajñī 15.77) Buffalo’s ghee is excellent; it provides fortitude, bestows happiness, and creates luster; it destroys wind and phlegm, bestows strength, and is capable of enhancing the complexion.

It pacifies disorders of the *durnāma* (hemorrhoids) and *grahaṇī*, stimulates a weak digestive fire, is beneficial for the eyes, and among the products of the "nine cows," this [ghee] is most pleasing to the heart and captivating.

(Rajni 15.78) Ghee from a goat (*āja-ājya*), however, is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, increases strength, destroys cough, asthma, and phlegm, and is recommended for cases of *rājayakṣman* (tuberculosis). (Rajni 15.79)
Fresh sheep's ghee is light when digested but aggravates pitta;
it is beneficial in disorders of the female reproductive tract, kapha, vāta, swelling, and tremors.
Goat's ghee, however, should be avoided by those of delicate constitution due to its extreme heaviness.
When consumed, it sharpens the intellect, bestows strength, and improves the bodies of men. Elephant-butter (hastinī-sarpis) destroys phlegm, bile, poisons, and worms;
it is astringent, light, causes constipation, is bitter, and is an excellent stimulant for the digestive fire.
The clarified butter from a mare is pungent, sweet, and astringent;
it slightly stimulates digestion, removes fainting, slightly increases wind (vāta), and is heavy. Donkey's clarified butter is strengthening, digestive, and cures disorders of the urine.
It is light in digestion, hot in potency, astringent, and destroys phlegm.
Goat's ghee is sweet in taste, pungent and cold in its post-digestive effect;
it removes skin diseases and worms, and cures wind, phlegm, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen.

Nārīsarpis is beneficial for the eyes, wholesome, and a remover of all diseases; it stimulates a sluggish digestive fire, improves the appetite, is light in digestion, and destroys poison. It cures intoxication, epilepsy, fainting, and pains arising from the head, ears, and eyes. (Rajñī 15.86)
Ancient clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) conquers [diseases] and cleanses and heals wounds.
It bestows longevity, firmness of body, delicacy, luster, intelligence, memory, and strength;

it destroys cold and is wholesome in childhood, youth, and old age, providing great vitality. There is nothing else in the world that possesses such beneficial qualities or is as wholesome as clarified butter.

Kāñjika, kāñjikā, vīra, kulmāṣābhibhava, avantisoma, dhānyāmla, āranāla, and amlasāraka are synonyms for fermented rice-gruel. Kāñjika destroys wind-swelling (vāta-śopha), subdues pitta, and cures fever.
It destroys burning sensations, fainting, and fatigue, and removes colic, flatulence, and constipation.
(Rajni 15.90) Kāñjika and kāñjika-taila cause premature graying and aggravate Vāta;
they produce a burning sensation and bodily laxity through massage, but not through ingestion. (Rajni 15.91)
Cukra, sahasravedha, rasāmla, cukravedhaka,
śākhāmlabhedana, amlasāra, and cukrikā are synonyms for sorrel.
Cukra is bitter and sour, yet sweet, and it destroys phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta).

It is the supreme remedy for foul odors from the nose and throat, as well as diseases of the head. Sauvīraka is known as the sour gruel made from wheat; that produced from barley is called yavāmlaja or yavottha, while that produced from husks is called tuṣodaka.
Sauvīraka, which has a sour taste, is beneficial for the hair, overcomes disorders of the head,
removes the flaccidity of old age, and is supremely nourishing to strength.
Rice-water (taṇḍulāmbu), derived from rice, is astringent, sweet, and light.

Rice-water (tuṣāmbu) is astringent, destroys poison, vomiting, thirst, burning sensations, and wounds; it stimulates digestion, is beneficial for the heart, and cures heart disease, anemia, and worm infestations. The essence of rice-water (*annodaja-śivarasa*) is auspicious when the liquid has stood for three days.
Sour and sweet [substances] are digestive stimulants, they alleviate burning sensations, and are light and nourishing.
Cow’s urine is pungent, bitter, and hot; it removes phlegm and wind, is light, increases bile, stimulates digestion, improves the intellect, cures skin diseases, and bestows wisdom.
Buffalo urine removes constipation, swelling, abdominal tumors, and disorders of the eyes;
it is pungent and hot, and cures skin diseases, itching, colic, and abdominal pain.
Goat’s urine is pungent, hot, and dry, and it conquers the afflictions of channel-poisoning (*nāḍī-viṣa*).
It removes splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, phlegm, dyspnea, abdominal tumors, and edema, and is light [to digest].
(Rajni 15.100) The urine of a sheep is bitter and pungent, hot, and overcomes skin diseases;
it destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal enlargements, colic, blood disorders, edema, urinary diseases, and poisons. (Rajni 15.101)
Elephant urine is bitter and hot, salty, and it subdues disorders caused by Vāta;
it is bitter and astringent, cures colic, and is supreme for removing hiccup and asthma.
(Rajni 15.102) Horse urine, however, is bitter and hot, sharp, and it conquers the defects of poison.
It pacifies the provocation of wind (vāta), stimulates bile (pitta), and acts as a digestive stimulant.
Donkey urine is pungent, hot, alkaline, sharp, and removes phlegm (kapha);
it is supreme for curing great disorders of wind, as well as possession by spirits, tremors, and insanity.

Camel urine is pungent, bitter, hot, and salty; it aggravates bile, is strengthening, cures abdominal diseases, and destroys disorders of wind (vāta). Human urine destroys undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and removes worms, wounds, and the pain of poisons.
Bitter, hot, salty, and dry, it overcomes disorders of the skin and humors caused by spirits, as well as Vāta.

(Rajni 15.106) In cases of colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, Vāta-related vomiting, and other conditions to be treated with the administration of urine, the wise physician should prescribe cow’s urine. (Rajni 15.107)

All oils—those produced from sesame, mustard, safflower, linseed, and grain; those from castor, *karañja*, and *iṅgudī* fruits; those from the seeds of neem, *akṣa*, and *śigru*; those derived from *jyotiṣmatī* and *abhayā*; those arising from *madhurikā*, *kośāmra*, and *ciñcā*; and those originating from camphor, zinc, and so forth—are described in sequence for the sake of accomplishment. Sesame oil beautifies the hair; it is sweet, bitter, astringent, hot, and sharp.
Mustard oil, produced by strength, removes phlegm, wind, parasites, itching, wounds, and itching; it bestows luster.
Mustard oil is bitter, pungent, and hot;
it destroys disorders of wind and phlegm, produces the defects of bile and blood, destroys worms and skin diseases, and like sesame oil, is beneficial for the eyes.
Safflower oil destroys worms, brings about luster and strength, and removes consumption and impurities;
yet it aggravates the three *doṣas*, causes the loss of nourishment and strength, and produces itching of the eyes.
Linseed oil, however, is sweet, slimy, and subdues wind (*vāta*).
And a decoction of *madagandhi* removes phlegm and cough.

(Rajni 15.112) Oil produced from all grains such as wheat (*godhūma*), barley (*yava*), rice (*vrīhi*), and so forth, pacifies wind (*vāta*), phlegm (*kapha*), and bile (*pitta*); it cures itching, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and other ailments, and is beneficial for the eyes. (Rajni 15.113)
Castor oil destroys the defects caused by worms, cures diseases of the wind (vāta), removes pain from all parts of the body, and alleviates skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

It is sweet, the best of rejuvenatives (rasāyana), increases bile (pitta), and acts as a powerful digestive stimulant. Karañja oil destroys eye ailments, eradicates diseases of the wind, and is hot and sharp in potency.
It removes leprosy, itching, and scabies when applied as an ointment, and it cures various skin disorders. Ingudi oil is unctuous, sweet, and a destroyer of bile;
it is cooling, bestows luster, is strengthening, increases phlegm, and promotes the growth of hair.
Nimba oil is not excessively hot; it destroys worms, skin diseases, and phlegm.
Black sesamum oil is sweet, cooling, beneficial for the hair, heavy, and subdues pitta and vāta.
Śigru oil is pungent and hot; it conquers vāta and destroys kapha.

It is slimy and removes skin diseases, wounds, itching, and swelling. Jyotiṣmatī oil is pungent, bitter, and hot; it destroys wind (vāta), increases the heat of bile (pitta), and enhances intelligence, wisdom, and intellect.
Harītakī oil is cooling, astringent, sweet, and pungent;
it is wholesome, removes all diseases, and destroys various skin disorders.
On the other hand, mustard oil should be known as sharp and a remover of wind (vāta) and other humors.
The oil produced from the *kośāmra* (mango) is cooling, pungent, virilific, beneficial for the hair, and a destroyer of skin diseases;
it is laxative, bitter, sour, and sweet, strengthening, wholesome, appetizing, and digestive. (Rajni 15.122–123)
And the oil produced from *ciñcī* is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*),
scraping (*vilekhana*), it removes phlegm and wind, is appetizing, astringent, and not excessively cold.
[The oils known as] *karpūra-taila*, *himatila-taila*, *sitāṃśu-taila*, *śītābhra-taila*, *tuhināṃśu-taila*, and *sudhāṃśu-taila* [are likewise described].

Camphor oil removes excessive heat, pungency, and phlegm; it cures diseases of the wind (vāta), strengthens the teeth, and pacifies pitta. And that oil which is produced from the seeds of cucumber, gourd, bottle-gourd, pumpkin, and so forth, is sweet, heavy, cooling, beneficial for the hair, destroys phlegm and pitta, and bestows beauty.
A wise person should not use oil of any kind whatsoever;

because its qualities are equal to those of poison, one should not employ it in a medicinal formulation. There is no difference between poison and oil, and no difference between one who is dead and one who is merely asleep.

"There is no difference between grass and a slave; there is no difference between a fool and a log. (Rājñī 15.128) Having understood this section—which begins with the elaboration on the milk of cows and other animals and describes the various oils produced from sesame and so forth, composed of a series of naturally charming and brilliant words—the master physician may treat his patients with confidence. (Rājñī 15.129)
Those who, it is said, go to drink from their own source out of a desire to repay its kindness—
the wise have described their very abode as the "Section on Drinks" (Peṭhavagga).
