Having drunk again and again from the sweet, pure, and cool stream of his fame, virtuous men abandon the wretchedness of association with the wicked.
In the crest-jewel of that Nṛhari, whose name is composed of the very syllables of his own name, the section beginning with *kṣīraka*— numbered according to the lunar days— reaches its conclusion.
(Rājanighaṇṭu, Śālyādivarga 15.131)

Grain is that which is fit for enjoyment, consisting of food and the like, and serving as the means of livelihood; it should be known to be of three kinds, namely called *śūka*, *śimbi*, and *tṛṇa*. Rajni_16.1 That which is here possessed of awns (*śūka*), such as rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth, is *śūkadhānya*; then there are *mudga*, *makuṣṭaka*, and the like.

That which is enclosed within a pod is called *śimbīdhānya* (pod-grain); other grain that grows from grass is called *tṛṇadhānya* (grass-grain). Spiked grain (*śūkadhānya*) pacifies the humors such as wind (*vāta*), is light, and bestows an abundance of luster, strength, and virility.
Grain produced from pods (*śimbībhava*) is heavy, cold, causes constipation, and increases wind; they say that grass-grain (*tṛṇadhānya*) is cooling.
In every region, it is impossible even for the gods to know the number of awned grains;
therefore, we shall explain how many among them are suitable for consumption. *Śāli*, *kalama*, and *vrīhi*—the best of grains, delicious and dear to kings.

Furthermore, the finest grains are to be known as the *kaidāra* and *sukumāraka* varieties. There are ten types of *śāli* rice on earth, known by the names: *rājānna*, *ṣaṣṭika*, *sitatara*, *rakta*, *muṇḍa*, *sthūla*, *aṇu*, *gandha*, *nirapādika*, and *vrīhi*. I shall now describe their qualities and names in order.

*Rājānna* (king's rice), *dīrghaśūka* (long-awned), that which is produced in the autumn season (*kharipu-divasaja*), *ṣaṣṭika* (sixty-day ripener), and *niḥśūka* (awnless)—these two are distinguished by their color; *muṇḍaśāli* (beardless rice) is made clear by its own qualities; three others are known by their own names; and that which ripens in three months is *nirapa*; likewise, that which is produced from rainwater is called *vrīhi*. Thus, these ten types of *śāli* are well-known.
*Śāli* is *nṛpānna* (food of men), *rājānna* (king's food), and is worthy of kings; it is the *dīrghaśūka* variety.
The best of grains, the royal grain, beloved by kings, and long-ripening; it is the food of kings, which destroys the three *doṣas*, is very unctuous, sweet, light, digestive,
strength-giving, wholesome, bestowing luster, and increasing virility.

The food of kings is to be known as threefold according to the distinction of its awns: white, red, and black; and this [food] becomes increasingly superior in taste in that successive order. Furthermore, the rice grains here are generally green, white, and red; yet by their qualities, they are each progressively superior to the preceding ones. *Ṣaṣṭika* is the sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭi-śāli*), born in sixty days, with glossy grains.

This [grain] produced in sixty days is to be known as arising from two months. This *ṣaṣṭika* is of two kinds: white (*gaura*) and blue (*nīla*). The former is pleasing, cooling, a remover of the *doṣas*, strengthening, wholesome, digestive, and provides an increase in virility; the second is slightly inferior to this.

Kṛṣṇaśāli, Kālaśāli, Śyāmaśāli, and Sitetara (are varieties of rice). Kṛṣṇaśāli destroys the three doṣas, is sweet, increases nourishment, imparts complexion and luster, is strengthening, overcomes burning sensations, and increases virility.
Raktaśāli, Tāmraśāli, Śoṇaśāli, and Lohita are synonyms for red rice.
Raktaśāli is very sweet, light, unctuous, and strength-promoting; it improves the appetite, stimulates digestion, is wholesome, and removes numbness of the mouth.
It removes all diseases, is appetizing, and conquers pitta, burning sensations, vāta, and blood disorders.
(16) Muṇḍaśāli, also known as muṇḍanaka, niḥśūka, and yavaśūkaja;
muṇḍaśāli destroys the three doṣas and provides strength, being sweet and sour. (17–18)
Sthūlaśāli, Mahāśāli, Sthūlāṅga, and Sthūlataṇḍula—thus the names of the fragrant and rich Śāli varieties should be inferred by the wise.
Mahāśāli is delicious, sweet, and cooling; it pacifies bile (pitta) and quickly alleviates chronic fever, burning sensations, and abdominal pain.

Beneficial for children, the young, or even the elderly, it should always be consumed by all; it produces digestive fire, strength, and vigor. Sūkṣmaśāli, sūciśāli, potaśāli, and sūcaka—sūkṣmaśāli is very sweet, light, and removes bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations.
It is digestive, promotes digestion, and slightly overcomes disorders of wind (vāta). Gandhaśāli is also called kalmāṣa, gandhālu, kalamottama, sugandhi,
gandhabahula, surabhi, and gandhataṇḍula.
Fragrant rice (*sugandhaśāli*) is sweet, highly aphrodisiac, and pacifies bile, fatigue, hemorrhaging, loss of appetite, and burning sensations.
It promotes breast milk, stabilizes the fetus, slightly increases wind (*vāta*), provides nourishment, slightly increases phlegm (*kapha*), and bestows strength.
Waterless rice is sweet, unctuous, cooling, and conquers burning sensations and bile.

It pacifies the three *doṣas*, is appetizing, wholesome, and removes all diseases. (Rajñī 16.25) The white *vrīhi* rice is sweet and cooling, removes *pitta*, is astringent, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and destroys worms and *kapha*; it alleviates fever and blood disorders. It bestows nourishment, relieves fatigue, promotes virility, is highly appetizing, generates joy, and—unlike the other—is slightly *vāta*-producing. (Rajñī 16.26)
Maṇḍaka, sthūlaśāli, and likewise bimbaśālika;
nijāti, śāṇa, hulya, bimbī, and likewise kausenduka;
prasādhikā, the one called jīraka, along with śyāmā—these are considered sweet.
For kings, there may be *maulikya* rice as well as *urvarī*.
There are also *sūkṣmaśāli*, *kuditikā*, *suśāli*, *guruśāli*, *vanaśāli*,
*guṇḍurūkī*, *kṣīrikā*, and various types of *paṅkti*.
These are the well-known and renowned names of *śāli* rice:
*aśocā*, *pāṭalā*, *vrīhi*, *vrīhika*, *vrīhidhānyaka*, *vrīhisaṃdhānya*, and *ardhadhānya* is also called *vrīhika*. (Rājñī 16.29–30)
*Garbha*, *pākaṇika*, *ṣaṣṭika*, *ṣaṣṭiko*, *balasambhava*, *sudhānya*, *pathyakārī*, *mupavi*, and *prajñavipriya*; *śāli*, *kalamādi*, *kalamo*, and *nākalāyaka*.

The *kadamba* rice has the fragrance of the *kadamba* flower; it is produced in the *kala* [season] and originates from the *kala*. It increases bile and phlegm, is aphrodisiac, and the *kala* rice is likewise sweet. The red variety is *raktaśāli*, as are the *kāṣṭhalohita* and *śāli* varieties.
Ruṇālī, ruṇaśāli, raktaśāli, and suśālyaka;
[these] destroy thirst and cure dysuria, while others are heart-pleasing and bestow intelligence. Mahāśāli is fragrant, and sugandhā is produced from fragrance.
Gandhāḍhyā, Gandhamālyā, Gandhānī, and Gandhamālinī;
Sugandhā, Madhurā, Hṛdyā, and Kaphapittajvarāsrajit;
Jalodbhavā, Jalaruhā, Jalajātā, and Sujātakā.

Red-fingered (*raktāṅgulī*) and *sukārā* are of the same color as saffron (*kuṅkuma*). Saffron is sweet and cooling; it conquers hemorrhaging, bilious fever, and dysentery. That which is born from sesame seeds is called *nīlā*, *dīrghā*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *supūjakā*.
Sweet and fragrant, it is called *tilavāsī*.
*Rājādanī*, *rājapriyā*, *rājabhāvā*, *munipriyā*, *tilanī*, *tilaparṇī*, *āmagandhā*, and *pravāsinī* [are its names]. (Rajñī 16.40–41)
They alleviate phlegm and bile, are unctuous, and are supreme in curing cough and dyspnea;
they cause quick digestion, are pleasing to the heart, light, and increase semen. Produced from a soft diet, they possess great qualities for those who dwell in sesame oil.
It is praised for treating anemia, colic, and āmavāta.
Vaktaka is a type of vakta-śāli rice; it is long-grained and quickly agitates [the humors].
Rājapriyā is wholesome and originates from the Middle Country.
They are said to be light and likewise cause inflammation of the mouth.
Kalāṭaka is Kavila; Garuḍa is known as Gurusa.
Guruvaka is Guraḍaka, Sukhabhojī, and Subhojaka.

Kavila, Gandhakārī, and Laghupākakara remove phlegm and bile; they are sweet and alleviate colic and asthma. Vikala destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), and skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and is auspicious when consumed in food.
The *kuṣmāṇḍikā* (pumpkin gourd) is reddish, very sweet, heavy, fragrant,
difficult to digest, yellow when ripe, and soft with large grains.
The *kumbhikā* is sweet, unctuous, and subdues wind and bile.

*Saurabha*, *śuṇḍika*, and *śuṇḍī* are varieties of rice; *kausumbhī* is hard and without grain. *Kausumbhī* is light to digest and subdues wind and bile. *Umpāsa*, *umpikā-śāli*, and *madhura-taṇḍula* are heavy grains.
The *umpikā* is very fibrous, rich in fragrance, and beloved by young people.
It is sweet, unctuous, fragrant, and astringent;
it pacifies *pitta* and *śleṣman*, is parching, and destroys *vāta*.
He is the one belonging to the winged ones, possessing the beauty of a bird, the king of birds, and the beloved of the sages;
he is produced from thick grains of rice, possesses a pervasive fragrance, and creates an abundant scent.
When the earth was scorched, the *śāli* rice grew there, ripening quickly.
Slightly bitter and sweet, they are digestive and strength-promoting.
Kedāra rice is sweet, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and increases bile;
it is slightly astringent, produces little waste, is heavy, and destroys phlegm.
Those *śāli* rice varieties that grow from cuttings and are dry cause constipation.
Those that are repeatedly transplanted are light, ripen quickly, and possess superior qualities;
they cause a burning sensation, remove the *doṣas*, are strengthening, and increase urine.
Yāvanāla is also called yavanāla, śikharī, vṛttataṇḍula, dīrghanāla,
dīrghaśara, kṣetrekṣu, and ikṣupattraka.
White yāvanāla, however, is known as pāṇḍura and tārataṇḍula.
The *nakṣatrākṛtivistāra* is circular and resembles a pearl or a grain of rice.
*Jūrṇāhvaya*, *devadhānya*, *jūrṇala*, and *bījapuṣpaka* are synonyms for the *jūrṇa*.
Furthermore, *jūnala*, *puṣpagandha*, *sugandha*, and *segurundaka* are also names for it.
White *yāvanāla* is sweet, strengthening, a conqueror of the three *doṣas*, aphrodisiac, appetizing,
a destroyer of hemorrhoids, wholesome, and a remover of abdominal tumors and ulcers. Now, as for *tuvarayāvanāla*, it is astringent and a decoction-like *yāvanāla*.
That red *yāvanāla* is reddish-brown and consists of coarse grain.
(Rājñī 16.63) *Yāvanāla* is astringent, hot, and causes swelling;
it is constipating, pacifies wind, is burning, and causes emaciation. (Rājñī 16.64)
The autumnal *yāvanāla* (millet) increases phlegm, is slimy, and heavy;
it is cooling, sweet, aphrodisiac, pacifies the *doṣas*, and bestows strength and nourishment.
Wheat (*godhūma*) is rich in milk; *apūpa* (cake) is the food of the Mlecchas.
Yavana is dehusked, milky, succulent, and pleasant. Wheat is unctuous and sweet, it subdues wind (vāta) but produces bile (pitta) and burning sensations;
it is heavy, increases phlegm (śleṣman), is strengthening, appetizing, and increases virility.
Another type of wheat is unctuous, light, aphrodisiac, and alleviates *kapha*;
it produces *āmadoṣa*, is strengthening, sweet, and bestows vigor and nourishment.
Barley, known as *sitaśūka*, is sacred, divine, indestructible, and the king of sheathed grains.

Barley (*yava*) has sharp awns, is dear to horses, and is considered a pure grain; it is a favorite among steeds. Barley is astringent, sweet, very cooling, a conqueror of urinary disorders (*prameha*), and a remover of bitter phlegm (*kapha*).
However, awnless barley (*aśūka-muṇḍa-yava*) bestows strength upon men, is aphrodisiac, and provides abundant virility and nourishment.
Veṇuja, veṇubīja, vaṃśaja, vaṃśataṇḍula, vaṃśadhānya, vaṃśāhva, and veṇuvaṃśadvidhāyu are synonyms for bamboo grain.
It is cooling, astringent, sweet, and parching; it destroys urinary disorders, worms, phlegm, and poisons.
The bamboo grain (veṇuyava) is praised for removing bile; it bestows nourishment, vigor, and strength.
(16.72) But the mung bean (mudga) is the best of soups; it is worthy of a fine complexion and possesses the finest flavor.
It provides satiety, delights horses, strengthens the earth, and is the ideal food for steeds. (16.73)
The black mung bean (*kṛṣṇamudga*) is a spring crop, as is the *mādhava* grown in Surāṣṭra.
The black mung bean destroys the three *doṣas*, is sweet, and subdues wind (*vāta*).
It is light, stimulates digestion, is wholesome, and bestows strength, virility, and nourishment to the limbs.
The *śārada* (autumnal) variety is like a green mung bean (*harinmudga*), while another autumnal variety is greyish.
The green mung-bean-like variety is astringent, sweet, and removes phlegm and bile;
it cures diseases of blood and urine, is cooling, light, and stimulates digestion.
And likewise, the grey mung bean (*mudga*) is recorded as being similar in its taste, potency, and other qualities;
it is astringent-sweet, appetizing, and causes an obstruction of *pitta* and *vāta*.
Mung bean soup is light, pacifies the affliction of *pitta*-fever, removes burning heat, and destroys loss of appetite.
This blood-purifier, when combined with rock salt, then becomes a remover of all diseases. Māṣa is also known as kuruvinda, dhānyavīra, vṛṣākara, māṃsala, balāḍhya, pitrya, and pitṛjottama.

The *māṣa* bean is unctuous, produces much waste, is drying, increases phlegm (*śleṣman*), and is hot in potency; it quickly provokes blood-bile (*raktapitta*). When eaten, it destroys wind (*vāta*), provides heavy strength, and is appetizing. Being sweet, it should always be consumed by men who are weary and desire comfort. (Rajni 16.81) It is called *rājamāṣa*, *nīlamāṣa*, and *nṛpamāṣa*, and is fit for kings. (Rajni 16.82)
It removes phlegm and bile, stimulates the appetite, generates wind, and bestows strength. *Caṇa* is also known as *harimantha*, *sugandha*, *kṛṣṇakañcuka*,
*bālabhojya*, *vājibhakṣa*, *caṇaka*, and *kañcukī*.

Chickpea flour (caṇaka) is sweet, parching, and cures urinary disorders; it increases wind and bile, stimulates digestion, improves the complexion, is strengthening, appetizing, and causes flatulence.
Raw chickpea flour is cooling, promotes appetite, is nourishing, and removes burning sensations and thirst.
The decoction of *gaulya* destroys urinary calculi and wasting; it is slightly pungent and promotes virility.

(Rajni 16.86) Black chickpea (*caṇaka*), however, is cold and sweet; it removes cough and bile, cures bile-based diarrhea and cough, is strengthening, and acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). (Rajni 16.87)
Chickpea (*caṇaka*) is white, sweet, strength-promoting, and highly appetizing;
it generates wind (*vāta*), is pleasing to the taste, destroys bile (*pitta*), is cooling, and heavy.
Well-fried chickpea is appetizing, destroys wind, and causes blood disorders (*raktadoṣa*).
Through its potency, it is heating and light, and it removes the coldness of phlegm.
(Rajñī 16.89) The soup of chickpeas (*caṇa*) is sweet and astringent; it subdues phlegm yet acts as a cause for wind disorders.
It brings about the destruction of asthma, upward-coughing, exhaustion, and chronic catarrh, and possesses the quality of strengthening and stimulating the digestive fire. (Rajñī 16.90)
Water boiled and cooled like moonbeams, drunk at dawn, removes the affliction of bile;
it bestows nourishment, possesses its own natural qualities, is satiating when digested, and is endowed with lovely sweetness.
(Rajni 16.91) Makuṣṭaka, mayuṣṭa, vanamudga, and kṛmīlaka—

Amṛta, araṇyamudga, and vallīmudga are thus proclaimed. Makuṣṭaka is astringent, sweet, and a conqueror of blood-bile (raktapitta); it removes fever and burning sensations, is wholesome, stimulates the appetite, and eliminates all the bodily humors (doṣas).
Masūra is known as rāgadālī, maṅgalya, pṛthubījaka, śūra,
kalyāṇabīja, gurubīja, and masūraka. Masūra is sweet, cooling, constipating, and it conquers phlegm and bile.
It causes wind-related disorders, relieves dysuria, and is light. Kalāya, muṇḍacaṇaka, hareṇu, satīnaka, trāsana, nālaka, kaṇṭhī, satīna, and hareṇuka [are synonyms].

Kalāya generates wind (vāta), removes pitta, burning sensations, and kapha; it bestows relish and nourishment, is cooling, astringent, and does not cause the disorders of ama. Laṅkā, karālā, tripuṭā, and kāṇḍikā are drying by nature.
Lanka is pleasing, cooling, sweet, a subduer of pitta, a generator of vāta, and heavy.
Āḍhakī, also known as tuvarī, karavīrabhujā, vṛttabījā, and pītapuṣpā, is excellent; it is of three types: white, red, and black. (Rājani 16.99–16.100)
Āḍhakī is astringent and sweet, it conquers phlegm and bile;
it slightly increases wind, is appetizing, and as a split pulse (vidalā), it is heavy and constipating.
That white variety causes the humors (doṣas) to increase, whereas the red variety is appetizing, strengthening, and a destroyer of bile-fever and other ailments.

If that *śyāmā* is used, it is digestive and destroys bile and burning sensations; and the soup of *āḍhakī* is said to be strengthening. *Kulattha* has copper-colored seeds and white seeds as well as those of other colors.
*Kulattha* is astringent, hot, dry, and removes wind and phlegm.

Kṣava is that which generates hunger, is light, has long pods, is tender, possesses round seeds, and is sweet; it is also called kṣavaka. Kṣava is astringent-sweet, cooling, and removes phlegm and bile.
It is aphrodisiac, removes fatigue, is palatable, and causes wind and flatulence.
(Rājñī 16.106) White niṣpāva is sweet; so too are mādhvīkā, honey-sugar, palaṅkaṣā, thick-podded peas, round peas, honey-white sugar, and white sugar. (Rājñī 16.107)

Madhuśarkarā is very palatable, sweet, slightly astringent, cooling, wind-increasing, strengthening, and it provides nourishment while alleviating flatulence and heaviness. (Rajni 16.108) Another variety is the pungent niṣpāva, as well as the kharvura and that which grows in riverbeds. (Rajni 16.109)
Nadīniṣpāvaka is bitter, pungent,
increases the blood, heavy, increases wind (vāta), increases phlegm (kapha), is dry, astringent, and removes the defects of poison.
Sesame (tila) is a grain for burnt offerings (homa), purifying, and used for the libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
It destroys sin and is pure grain; it grows wild in the forest and has matted roots.

It is unctuous, increases complexion, strength, and digestive fire, alleviates breast-milk and wind, and is heavy. It is hot, generates bile, produces little urine, promotes hair growth, and is highly beneficial for wounds. It is astringent, sweet, combined with astringent and bitter tastes, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). Black sesame is most wholesome; white sesame provides fewer qualities, and other types of sesame are likewise diminished in merit.
*Palala* refers to sesame paste (*tilakalka*), sesame flour (*tilacūrṇa*), and ground meal (*piṣṭaka*).

(RājN 16.113) *Palala* is sweet, appetizing, and provides strength and nourishment for the blood and *pitta*. (RājN 16.114) *Sesame dregs* (*tilakiṭṭa*) are called *piṇyāka*; it is the oil-cake produced from sesame paste, known as *khala*. (RājN 16.115)

Linseed oil-cake is pungent and sweet; it destroys phlegm, wind, and urinary disorders (prameha). Atasī is called picchalā, devī, madagandhā, madotkaṭā, umā, kṣumā, haimavatī, sunīlā, and nīlapuṣpikā.

Atasī is known as madagandhā; it is sweet, provides strength, slightly increases kapha and vāta, removes pitta, and cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and wind disorders. Āsurī, rājikā, rājī, raktikā, and raktasarṣapa are synonyms for black mustard.
Tīkṣṇagandhā, madhurikā, kṣavaka, kṣuvaka, and kṣava are synonyms for āsurī. It is pungent, bitter, and hot; it cures pain and colic caused by wind (vāta) and splenic disorders.
It produces a burning sensation and increases bile (pitta), but it destroys phlegm (kapha), abdominal tumors (gulma), worms, and ulcers.
Rājakṣavaka is black, with sharp fruits; it is known as rājarājikā and rājñī.
It should be understood as being called kṛṣṇasarṣapa and also rājasarṣapa.
Rājasarṣapaka is bitter, pungent, and hot; it alleviates wind-pain (vāta-śūla).

It alleviates burning from bile (*pitta*), and removes abdominal tumors (*gulma*), itching, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and wounds. The white mustard is sharp, difficult to overcome, a destroyer of demons, and a healer of skin diseases; it is perfected in its application and perfected in its efficacy.

Siddhārtha (mustard) is pungent, bitter, and hot; it removes wind-disorders, blood disorders, and seizures; it pacifies skin diseases, improves the appetite, and destroys poisons, spirits, and wounds. Among grains, *kañcukī*, *śimbī*, *bījagupti*, and *śāmbhavī* [are also included].
And those grains that are protected [from the sun] are called *śimbīdhānya*. *Śyāmāka*, *śyāmaka*, and *śyāma* are synonyms; it is also known as *tribīja* and *avipriya*.
It is *sukumārī*, *rājadhānya*, and the best of grass-grains (*tṛṇabījottama*).
Śyāmāka is sweet, unctuous, astringent, light, and cooling;
it increases Vāta, destroys Kapha and Pitta, is constipating, and removes the effects of poison.
Kodrava, Koradūṣa, Kuddāla, and Madanāgraja are likewise [described].
And that [grain] is proclaimed to have various distinctions according to its specific region.
Kodrava is sweet, bitter, beneficial for those with wounds,
it removes phlegm and bile, is parching, causes delusion, increases wind, and is heavy.
Varaka, sthūlakaṅgu, rūkṣa, and sthūlapriyaṅguka are [synonyms].
Varaka is sweet, dry, astringent, and increases wind and bile. Kaṅguṇī is called kaṅgunī; cīnaka is pītataṇḍula.
It is windy (vātala), delicate (sukumāra), and known by various names.
Priyaṅgu is sweet, appetizing, astringent, delicious, and cooling;
it increases wind (vāta), destroys bile (pitta) and burning sensations, is dry (rūkṣa), and binds broken bones.
*Nīvāra* is wild grain; it is the grain of sages, produced from grass. (16.134) *Nīvāra* is sweet, unctuous, purifying, wholesome, and light.
(16.135) *Rāgī*, however, is *lāñchana*; it has many grains on its stalks and clusters of grains. (16.136)
Bitter, sweet, and astringent, it is cooling, destroys bile and blood disorders, and bestows strength. (Rajni 16.137) Kurī, however, is a type of grass-grain; it is sweet and provides strength.
Whether green, old, or ripe, it bestows nourishment upon horses. (Rajni 16.138)
Whatever rice grains are roasted are known as *lāja*.
Barley and other grains that are roasted are proclaimed to be *dhānā*.
Both *lāja* and barley-*dhānā* are satiating and destroy bile (*pitta*).
Those produced from wheat sprouts and young barley, when slightly warm, are digestive stimulants.
Those known as *ākulā* are made from parched, uncooked wheat;
they are heavy, aphrodisiac, sweet, and strength-giving.
Rice grains that are half-cooked and heated are known as *pṛthuka* (flattened rice).
*Pṛthuka* is delicious, unctuous, pleasing to the heart, and increases passion.
*Pūpalā* (cakes) are said to be sweet; they are considered aphrodisiac and strength-giving.
They pacify pitta, are refreshing, pleasant to the heart, unctuous, and increase strength.

Other varieties such as those made from *yāvanāla* and flattened rice (*cipiṭa*), as well as parched grains (*taptataṇḍula*), are nourishing; specifically, flattened rice made from *śāli* or *yāvanāla* increases corpulence.

Those rice grains that have not been parched are proclaimed to be "milk-seeds" (*dugdhabīja*). Milk-seeds are very sweet, difficult to digest, and provide strength and nourishment. However, parched mung beans and chickpeas—such as *sumana* and *laṅkā*—when eaten, immediately cause thirst, loss of appetite, and an increase in bile.

Those grains that produce little wind are indeed pleasant, though they are weak, dry, and yet agreeable to the heart for the young, the elderly, and children. Mung beans, wheat, chickpeas, barley, and so forth are traditionally known [to be beneficial]; however, grain that is half-ripe causes the defects of constipation and flatulence.
The flour of dry wheat is declared to be *karṇikā*.
The husks of chickpeas and other such grains are celebrated as *dāl*.
Grain that is ripe and harvested while still green possesses all beneficial qualities.

That which is dried up, cut, pithless, and parched destroys the vital essence (*sattva*). New grain stored for a year is strengthening and sweet. Fresh grain causes secretions (*abhiṣyandi*), whereas that stored for a year is light.
Grain that has been stored for two years is light and wholesome, but after three years it becomes weak.
Fresh chickpeas, barley, wheat, sesame, and mung beans are beneficial;
however, those that are old, tasteless, and parched are unwholesome, difficult to digest, and strength-depleting.

Grain that has been sown in the best [soil] is known to be of the highest quality; that which is sown in soil where growth is interrupted is to be known as middling; and whatever is sown in soil that is barren and prone to defects is inferior. Even if rice is carefully sown in a forest on burnt ground, or if it grows from what has been cut down, it indeed causes the retention of feces and urine. Grain produced in alkaline water cures diseases of phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Grain produced from very moist soil brings vigor and strength;
grain produced from sandy soil destroys strength, nourishment, and vitality.
The best grain is *ṣaṣṭika*, fit for royal consumption; likewise are the meats of goats, partridges, and quails.

Water originating from black clay is [recommended]; for milk, clarified butter, and so forth, that of cows or goats is praised. (RājN 16.162) Thus, by means of this unbridled play of speech describing the qualities, names, and potencies of well-known grains, may the physician quickly attain this section on traditional lore—a knowledge blessed by granting life to despondent people. (RājN 16.163)
Those grains which are always eaten and those which people who eat consume—
of these grains, this collection is indeed called the "Section on Edibles" (Bhojyavarga).
By that conduct, charming and sweet in its splendor, worthy of great honor and appropriate for an abundance of various grains, the community is constantly sustained.

Thus, in this *Nāmokticūḍāmaṇi* composed by the illustrious Nṛharīśvara, this sixteenth chapter, titled "Grains" (*dhānya*), which contains new compositions, is concluded. (Rājanighaṇṭu, Māṃsādivarga 16.165)
Māṃsa, piśita, kravya, pala, rasam,
asraja, palala, jāṅgala, kīra, and āmiṣa are said to be synonyms for meat.
The flesh of a young animal such as a deer, slaughtered immediately after death, is considered the best.

It should be known that what is fragrant and wholesome is most beneficial for one living in a *jāṅgala* region. (RājNī 17.2) The meat of wild animals and the like found in water—whether from a young animal, an old one, a lean one, a sick one, one burnt by poison or fire, or even a dead one—must be rejected; likewise, meat that is foul-smelling, dried, or has been kept for a long time [is to be avoided]. (RājNī 17.3)

All meat destroys wind (vāta), is aphrodisiac, strengthening, appetizing, and nourishing; yet that meat, according to its region, habitat, individual constitution, and inherent nature, certainly assumes many different forms. Among these, the meat of marshy animals such as the gayal, the ruru deer, the boar, and the rhinoceros is unctuous, wholesome, strengthening, and light; whereas the meat of wild animals originating from the rabbit, the partridge, and so forth, is [light].
The meat of the *ruhu*, deer, boar, and *sāraṅga* antelope provides nourishment and luster; it is appetizing, light, palatable, harmonizing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and pleasing to the taste.
(Rajni 17.5) The meat of the *sārasa*, swan, *rātrivirahin*, *krauñca*, and other such birds is cooling, unctuous, heavy, and removes wind and phlegm; it is sweet and pacifies the three *doṣas*.

The meat produced by the *lāvaka*, partridge (*tittiri*), and others is wholesome, aphrodisiac, and light; however, that originating from the *cakora*, *krauñca*, peacock, and partridge is of this same nature across the three regions. (Rajni 17.6)
There are three modes of movement: the swift, the slow, and the leaping;
and there are also three according to their posture: those that dwell in holes, on land, and in water.
Furthermore, they are classified as rangers by force, peckers, and scatterers.
By nature, three types of beasts and birds have been declared in sequence.
Now, I shall describe their characteristics and qualities according to their groups and in order;
thus, those very beasts and birds are said to be of nine kinds.
Goats, rabbits, deer, and the like, which move swiftly of their own accord, are known as the "swift" (*druta*) group;

the meat produced by them is wholesome, strengthening, provides vigor and exhilaration, and is light. Elephants, rhinoceroses, and other such great beasts are known to be "slow" (*vilambita*) due to their very mode of movement.

The meat of the *balākṛt* (crane) is slimy, heavy, and causes phlegm, cough, wind-disorders, and sluggishness. (RājN 17.11) The *sārasa*, swan (*haṃsa*), crane (*balākā*), ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), curlew (*krauñca*), and others that float upon the water are called "floaters" (*plava*). Their meat is heavy, hot, and bestows strength. (RājN 17.12)
The snake, mongoose, porcupine, monitor lizard, and rat are said to be the primary hole-dwellers;
their meat removes asthma, wind-disorders, and cough, but it increases bile and causes burning sensations.
As for the boar, the ruru deer, the kuraṅga deer, and various other such wild animals—
All those that dwell on land have meat that brings about all [the bodily] qualities. Rajñī 17.14.
Those that dwell in water, headed by fish, crocodiles, crabs, and tortoises, are thus described.
Their meat is watery, aphrodisiac, heavy, cooling, and increases strength and wind (vāta). Rajñī 17.15.

Those headed by tigers, lions, śarabhas, bears, and hyenas, as well as others who kill and overpower [their prey] by force, are called *prasahana* (forcible seizers); their flesh removes hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, abdominal diseases, and lethargy. (Rājñī 17.16) That which extracts the meat after [the prey] has been killed is called *pratuda* (pecker), such as the vulture, hawk, crow, and so forth.

Its meat is delicious, satiating, unctuous, strengthening, and it produces *pitta*, burning sensations, and blood. (RājN 17.17) Furthermore, those such as the domestic fowl (*kukkuṭa*), the grey partridge (*kapotaka*), and the francolin (*tittiri*) scratch the earth with their claws and live upon it; these are indeed called "scattered-feeders" (*viṣkira*). Their flesh is aphrodisiac, astringent-sweet, cooling, and appetizing. (RājN 17.18)
This very quality of birds should be understood according to their sequence;
by the distinction of all their locations, their number and their movement are described.
Wherever these foremost of beasts and birds were stationed, or from whatever place they had come to another region—*Rājñī* 17.19.
By returning each to its own appropriate place, their qualities and transformations would also exist within the flesh.
(Rājñī 17.20) The meat of the rhinoceros (*khaḍga*) bestows strength, is nourishing, and is heavy.
(Rājñī 17.21) The flesh of the gayal (*gavaya*) is strengthening, appetizing, aphrodisiac, and nourishing. (Rājñī 17.22)
The flesh of the Ruru deer is heavy, unctuous, and provides mild digestive fire, strength, and nourishment.
(17.23) The impure flesh of the cow is heavy and increases wind and phlegm.
(17.24) The meat of the wild buffalo is slightly light, stimulates digestion, and bestows strength. (17.25)

The meat of a village buffalo is unctuous, induces sleep, and pacifies *pitta*. (Rajñī 17.26) Elephant flesh is heavy, unctuous, increases *vāta*, and produces *śleṣman*; it provides great nourishment, is difficult to digest, and diminishes the digestive fire. (Rajñī 17.27)
Horse meat is hot, subdues wind (vāta), provides strength, and is light;
however, from excessive consumption of it, it produces bile and a burning sensation in men.
Camel meat, on the other hand, is cooling, pacifies the three doṣas, and is light.
The meat originating from the donkey bestows strength and nourishment, is appetizing, sweet, and increases virility. However, that born of wild animals is somewhat heavy,
yet it is appetizing, cooling, and provides great virility and strength.

The meat of the ena deer is light, cooling, aphrodisiac, alleviates the three doṣas, possesses all six tastes, and is appetizing. The meat of the kuraṅga is likewise sweet, dispels phlegm, and destroys muscle-wasting and bile.
The meat of the sāranga, a forest-dweller, is unctuous, sweet, light, and aphrodisiac.
The meat of the Śikharin deer is light, pleasing to the heart, and bestows strength.
(17.34) The meat of the wild boar is heavy, dispels wind, is aphrodisiac, and produces strength and perspiration.
(17.35) Therefore, the meat of the village boar is even heavier; it increases fat and promotes the growth of strength and virility. (17.36)
The meat of the deer (śaraśṛṅga) is heavy, unctuous, and increases phlegm;
it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and is considered the best for slightly increasing wind.
Goat meat is light, unctuous, not excessively cold, and provides relish. *Rājñī* 17.37.

The meat of a young goat is faultless, subdues wind and bile, is sweet, and bestows strength and nourishment. It is light, cooling, and conquers urinary disorders; that very same meat from one that grazes on grass is slightly lighter and provides strength.
Mutton is sweet, cooling, heavy, constipating, and nourishing. (17.40) The meat of sheep is sweet, somewhat heavy, and bestows strength.
(17.41) The meat of the porcupine is heavy, unctuous, digestive, and a conqueror of asthma and cough. (17.42)
The slippery meat of the mongoose (*nākula*) subdues wind (*vāta*) but increases phlegm (*śleṣman*) and bile (*pitta*).
(17.43) The meat of the monitor lizard (*godhā*), however, subdues wind and removes asthma and cough.
(17.44) The meat of the rabbit (*śaśa*) destroys the three humors (*tridoṣa*), stimulates digestion, and conquers asthma and cough. (17.45)

The meat of other hole-dwelling creatures, such as the *kokaḍa* and the rat, is censured; it causes dullness of the senses, heaviness, and is difficult to digest. (Rajni 17.46) The flesh of the wild cock is pleasing to the heart, removes phlegm, and is light. (Rajni 17.47)
The flesh of the domestic cock is unctuous, subdues wind, stimulates digestion, and is heavy.
(17.48) The flesh of the harita bird is sweet and overcomes the defects of phlegm, bile, and blood. (17.49) Likewise, the flesh of the pigeon increases virility and strength. (17.50)
The meat of the pigeon is unctuous, sweet, heavy, and cooling;
it subdues bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations, promotes strength, and likewise increases virility.
The meat of the partridge is unctuous, light, and bestows vigor and strength.
It is astringent, sweet, and cooling, and is the supreme pacifier of the three *doṣas*. Likewise, the meat of the common quail (*lāvaka*) is considered wholesome, constipating, and light.
Similarly, the meat of the grey partridge (*vartaka*) is free from defects and bestows vigor and nourishment.
The flesh of the sparrow is cooling, light, aphrodisiac, and bestows strength.
Likewise, the meat of the wild sparrow is light and wholesome. The flesh of the grey partridge is cooler than that of the sparrow, and it is appetizing and aphrodisiac.
Likewise, the flesh of the cakora is aphrodisiac and bestows strength and nourishment.
The flesh of the cakravāka, however, is light, unctuous, and provides strength;
it stimulates the digestive fire, cures all types of colic, is heating, and removes disorders of wind (vāta).
The flesh of the crane (sārasa), however, is sweet, sour, and astringent;
it cures severe diarrhea and pitta, and removes the pain of malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids. The flesh of aquatic birds is unctuous, cold, heavy, aphrodisiac, and subdues vāta.
Among those as well, the flesh of the swan is most aphrodisiac and removes cataracts.
Other birds such as the crane and the balākā are heavy due to their consumption of meat;
however, the flesh of deer and other such animals, though not specifically mentioned, should be accepted for its beneficial qualities and so forth.
Fish are unctuous, hot, and heavy; they subdue wind but provoke blood and bile.
Among them, we shall describe some according to their specific characteristics:
the *rohita*, the *gargara*, the *bhīru*, the *bālaka*, and likewise the *barbara*.
The chāgala, raktamatsya, mahiṣa, and likewise the āvila;
the vātūka and the alomaśā—these, beginning with the karṇa and vaśā, should be known.
I shall describe their characteristics, qualities, potencies, and so forth, in due order.
The black fish is scaled, while the white-bellied one is the *matsya*; that which is best is the *rohita*, which has a rounded mouth.
The meat of the *rohita* is slightly warm, strengthening, and it destroys wind (*vāta*); it is unctuous and increases virility.
That which is yellowish in color, with slimy limbs and many lines on its back, is likewise scaled.

The *gargara* is harsh, coarse, dull, and cold; it produces *kapha* and *vāta*. If it has two fins on its back, a tail on its throat, resembles a snake, hisses, and has a rounded snout, it is known as the *śalkī* fish; it is said to be timid, unctuous, aphrodisiac, difficult to digest, and a producer of *vāta*.
One who is not too stout, with a round face, possessing teeth and a beard, and having a tall body, is praised;
such a young elephant, excellent at dawn or at the end of the night, is said to be wholesome, strengthening, and highly aphrodisiac.
That which has thorny protrusions on its back and belly, a long snout, and resembles a serpent, is known as the *barbara*.
It causes flatulence, yet it is dull, strengthening, unctuous, difficult to digest, and aphrodisiac.
They call the white, well-bodied, symmetrical, long, and round fish "chāgalaka," which is devoid of scales;
on its back there is indeed a double-thorned spine, and it is very wholesome, appetizing, and strength-giving. (Rājñī 17.71–72)

That which has red limbs, is neither too long nor too small, nor too thick, is called the *raktamatsya* (red fish). It is cooling, appetizing, nourishing, and digestive; furthermore, it brings about the destruction of the three *doṣas*. That which is black, long-bodied, with thick scales, and possesses great strength—
The fish named Mahiṣa is digestive and bestows strength and virility. That which has white limbs and copper-colored wings is called Svalpāṅga;
it is known as Āvila, is highly pleasing, sweet, strengthening, rich in qualities, and provides nourishment for virility.
That which has a thick body and the form of a buffalo, and which bears a lotus-like luster on the surface of its palate, is the *vātūka*;
it possesses large scales and bestows vigor, stimulates the digestive fire, and provides virility. One that is a span in length, white-bodied, and has fine scales is a great stimulant of digestion.
The fish called *alomaśa* provides strength, virility, and nourishment to the limbs. That which is round, thick-skinned, black-bodied, scaled, and known as *karṇavaśā* is digestive,
carminative, wholesome, aphrodisiac, and bestows strength and nourishment.
Scaleless fish are condemned; all fish possessing scales are beneficial.
They provide firmness to the body and increase vigor, strength, and nourishment.
This applies to those fish found in the waters of lakes, streams, oceans, waterfalls, ponds, and reservoirs.
But those from rivers are dull; however, as one goes further upriver, they become lighter. Fish from saltwater oceans and the like are heavy, cause hemorrhaging and burning, and produce constipation;
for those who eat them, even fish living in sweet water should be known to be dull in the same way when cooked. (Rajni 17.81–82)
"Whatever multitudes of living beings there may be—whether moving on mountains, in forests, in cities, or in water—there are indeed seven categories.
It has been stated here that their flesh is not false; however, due to the fear of excessive length and because it is not currently useful, it has not been detailed.
Cooked meat is beneficial in all cases, increasing strength and virility. (Rājñī 17.83)
Fried meat is burning to the system and causes disorders such as hemorrhoids and wind-diseases.
(Rājñī 17.84) The forepart of a male animal is heavy, while the hind part belongs to a female; indeed, a pregnant woman is heavy, and likewise, a woman who is not pregnant is light.

If it is a bird, the male is light; listen: the flesh located on the head, shoulders, thighs, and back is heavy in sequence, and all that situated in the waist is heavy in every respect. (Rājñī 17.85)
Each subsequent constituent element—chyle, blood, and so forth—is heavier than the preceding one; likewise, the penis, kidneys, liver, flesh, and testicles become increasingly heavy in excess.

(Rajni 17.86) Having thus examined this section, which is complete with the determination of the qualities of meat from various regions, aquatic animals, birds, and sky-dwellers, as well as the specific parts of their bodies, a mortal who consumes food prescribed by a physician after such consideration does not fall into a state of disorder. (Rajni 17.87)

Of that illustrious Lord Nṛsiṃha, whose friend is human valor, this seventeenth section rests within the work titled *Nāmādicūḍāmaṇi*— he, from whose assembly the streams of tears from the eyes of his enemies flowed like a young woman’s thirst for the abundant meat situated within the great frontal globes of the lordly elephants of war. (Rājanighaṇṭu 17.88)
The Section on Humans and Others:
Humans, men, mortals, progeny, offspring, and persons;
bipeds, sentient beings, those dwelling on earth, those born from the earth, those who touch the ground, and the people (viśaḥ). (Rajñī 18.1)
Puruṣa, pūruṣa, nā, nara, pañcajana, and pumān refer to a man;
he is one who relies on wealth, is entitled [to rights], is fit for action, and is a person possessing purpose.
(Rajni 18.2) Strī, yoṣit, vanitā, balā, sunayanā, nārī, sīmantinī, rāmā, vāmadṛś, aṅganā, lalanā, kāntā, puraṃdhrī, and vadhū refer to a woman.

She is fair-browed, of excellent complexion, with beautiful limbs; she is slender, delicate, passionate, and possessed of a slender frame. She is lovely, gazelle-eyed, timid, beloved, and spirited. A woman is called *yoṣit*, *mahelā*, *mahilā*, *vilāsinī*, *nitambinī*, and *mattakāśinī*. She is also *janī*, *sunetrā*, *pramadā*, *sundarī*, *añcitabhrū*, *lalitā*, and *vilāsinī*.

She was proud, possessed of beautiful hips, with limbs bent and a slender waist; she was dark-complexioned, desirable, lovely, and beautiful to behold. (Rajñī 18.5) A husband, a lord, a choice one, a beloved, a suitor, a dear one, and a householder. (Rajñī 18.6)
*Bhāryā*, *patnī*, *priyā*, *jāyā*, *dārāḥ*, and *gṛhiṇī* are synonyms for a wife.
(Rajñī 18.7) *Klība* is a neuter term, as is *tṛtīyā-prakṛti*.
A eunuch is called *ṣaṇḍha* or *paṇḍa*; a woman possessing the characteristics of both male and female is called *poṭā*. (Rajñī 18.8)
Now, the queen (*rājñī*) is the crowned consort (*paṭṭārhā*), the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), and the king’s favorite;
other women who enjoy his pleasures and are playful are those whom the king enjoys.
Those who are the king’s principal concubines are known as *bhaṭṭinīs*.

A courtesan is called a *veśyā*, a *gaṇikā*, a *bhogyā*, a *vārastrī*, or a *smaradīpikā*. (18.12) A Brahmin is called a *brahmā*, a *brāhmaṇa*, a *vipra*, a *ṣaṭkarmā*, or a *dvijottama*. (18.13) A king is called a *sārvabhauma*, a *pārthiva*, a *kṣatriya*, or a *nṛpa*. (18.14)

The Vaiśya is a trader, a farmer, or a merchant; the Śūdra is the fourth, a servant of the twice-born and an attendant. These four—the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—are the social orders (varṇas); among them, the first three are the twice-born (dvijas).
From the inverse and direct order of these very same castes, other castes are born through intermixture (saṃkara).
A child is considered a *bāla*, *pāka*, *arbhaka*, *garbha*, *potaka*,
*pṛthuka*, *śiśu*, *śāva*, *arbha*, *bāliśa*, *ḍimbha*, *vaṭu*, or *māṇavaka*.
A child born for ten days is called an *arbha*; after a month, he is a *pāka*; after three months, he is named a *potaka*;
after six months, a *pṛthuka*; after a year, a *śiśu*; after three years, a *vaṭu*; and after seven years, a *māṇavaka*.
A *bāla* is known to be so for fifteen years, and a *kumāra* for thirty.
A youth becomes old at fifty years, or even beyond that. Childhood lasts until the end of the fifth year; boyhood until the tenth; adolescence until the fifteenth; and youth thereafter.
A youth is one established in his prime; a young man is a *taruṇa*. An old man is a *sthavira*, a *jaran*, a *pravayas*, a *yātayāman*, a *jīna*, a *jīrṇa*, and a *jarjara*.
A child lying on its back is a *bālottānaśaya*; an infant is a *ḍimbha*, a *stanapa*, and a *stanaṃdhayī*.

A maiden who has not yet reached puberty is called *kanyā*, *kumārī*, or *gaurī*; one who has not yet experienced menstruation is called *nagnikā*. She is of middle age when she is established in youth, possesses fine breasts, is a *ciraṇṭī*, of mature years, a *śyāmā*, fully developed, and has seen her menses.
A woman who is pregnant is called *gurviṇī*, *āpannasattvā*, *antarvatnī*, or *garbhiṇī*.
An old woman is *niṣphalā*, *jaratī*, *vṛddhā*, *sthavirā*, or *gatārtavā*.
A menstruating woman is *puṣpitā*, *malinā*, *mlānā*, *pāṃśulā*, or *rajasvalā*.
Barren, hairless, empty, bearing fruitless flowers, and having futile seasons.
(18.29) Tanu, tanū, saṃhanana, śarīra, kalevara, kṣetra, vapu, purāṇi, gātra, mūrti, ghana, kāya, deha, aṣṭāṅgapīḍā, and vigraha are synonyms for the body. (18.30)
Aṅga, māṃsa, pratīka, apaghana, and avayava are also [synonyms for limb]. Śiras, śīrṣaka, muṇḍa, mūrdhan, mauli, and mastaka;
varāṅga and uttamāṅga; and kapāla, which is known as that which bears hair, [are synonyms for head].

Keśa, śirasija, bāla, kuntala, mūrdhaja, kaca, cikura, and karuha are synonyms for hair. Furthermore, those [styles] that encircle it, such as the *kavarī* (braided hair), are its varieties. Dṛg, dṛṣṭi, locana, netra, cakṣus, nayana, and ambaka are synonyms for the eye.

Īkṣaṇa, grahaṇa, akṣi, darśana, and vilocana all mean the eye. Apāṅga refers to the outer corner of the eye, as does nayanopānta. Situated between those two is the tārā, also called bimbinī and kanīnikā, which is the pupil.
They say *bhāla*, *lalāṭa*, and *alikam* refer to the forehead; *godhi*, *bhrū*, and *cillikā* refer to the eyebrow, which is the line of hair above the eye.
That which is between the two [eyebrows] is the *kūrca*; furthermore, *śruti*, *śrotra*, *śrava*, *śravaṇa*, *karṇa*, *vacas*, and *agraha* refer to the ear.
*Oṣṭha*, *adhara*, *dantavāsa*, *dantavastra*, and *radacchada* refer to the lip.
The two regions on either side of those [lips] are the *prāntau*, and the corners of the mouth are the *sṛkkaṇī*. The nose is called *ghrāṇa*, *gandhavaha*, *ghoṇā*, *siṅghiṇī*, and *nāsikā*.
The area near the ear is the *śaṅkha*, and the impurity of the nose is *śiṅghāṇa*.
Tuṇḍa, āsya, mukha, vaktra, vadana, lapana, and ānana denote the mouth.

Oṣṭha and adhara denote the lips; cibuka is the chin; gaṇḍa, galla, and kapolaka denote the cheek. Above that is the jaw (hanu); daśana, danta, dvija, rada, and radana are likewise said to denote the teeth.

The tongue is called the *rasajñā* (taste-knower) and the *rasanā*; it is also termed the *kākuda*, the *tālu*, and the *tāluka*. Above that is the subtle tongue, which is the *ghaṇṭikā* and the *lambikā*.
Another is the downward-rooted tongue, known as the *pratijihvā* or *upajihvikā*.
The joint behind the head is the *avaṭu*, as well as the *ghāṭā* and *kṛkāṭikā*. The neck is called *grīvā*, *kaṃdharā*, *kaṃdhi*, *śirodhi*, and *śirodharā*.
The throat is *kaṇṭha*, *gala*, and *nigāla*; furthermore, the *ghaṇṭikā* is the *galaśuṇṭhikā*.
The *dhamanī* is the vessel; the *śiras* is the shoulder, and likewise the lower peak (*adhaḥśikhara*). Its joint is the *jatru*, while the armpit is known as the root of the arm (*dormūla*).
Below that is the side (*pārśva*), and what is behind the body is called the back (*pṛṣṭha*).

*doḥ*, *doṣā*, *praveṣṭaḥ*, *bāhuḥ*, *bāhā*, *bhujaḥ*, and *bhujā*; *pāṇiḥ*, however, is the five-fingered [hand], as are *karaḥ*, *hastaḥ*, and *śayaḥ*. At the base of the hand is *maṇibandhaḥ*; in the middle of the arm are *kūrparaḥ* and *kaphoṇiḥ*.
Below that is the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*), and the space between the elbow and the shoulder is the upper arm (*pragaṇḍaka*).
The fingers are the branches of the hand; the forefinger is called the index finger (*tarjanī*).
A joint is a finger-joint (*paru*), and it is also described as a knuckle-joint (*parva*).

Now, the five fingers are traditionally known in order as the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger. The nails are called *kāmāṅkuśa*, *kararuha*, *karaja*, *nakha*, and *nakhā*.
The fingers and toes are produced from the palms, and they renew themselves again and again.
Below the hand is the *prapāṇi*, and above it is known as the palm (*karatala*).
In the science of physiognomy (*sāmudrika*), the lines are to be understood as indicators of both auspicious and inauspicious matters.
*Stana*, *urasija*, *vakṣoja*, *payodhara*, and *kuca* likewise denote the breast.
*Stanāgra*, *cūcuka*, *vṛtta*, *śikhā*, and *stanamukha* refer to the nipple.
*Vakṣas*, *vatsa*, *uraḥ*, *kroḍa*, *hṛdaya*, *hṛt*, and *bhujāntara* denote the chest.
*Kukṣi*, *piciṇḍa*, *jaṭhara*, *tunda*, and *udara* are synonyms for the belly.
The vital point (*marman*) where the life-force resides is the *trika*, which is known to be at the edge of the hips.
The *nābhi* is the umbilical whorl; that which is below it is called the *vasti*.
The bladder is the head of the wind (*vātaśīrṣa*), and it is the site of the womb for a woman.
It is known as the *garbhāśaya*, the *jarāyu*, and the receptacle of the embryo (*garbhādhāra*). The space between the navel and the breasts in a living being is known as the stomach (*āmāśaya*).
The receptacle for digested food is indeed below the navel; the bladder is known as the receptacle for urine.
The waist is the *kakudmatī*; the hips are the *nitamba* and the *kaṭīraka*.
The pelvic region is the *āroha*, the *śroṇiphalaka*, the *kalatra*, and the site of the girdle (*rasanā*).
The *nitamba* is the hind part of the hips; for women, the *jaghana* is the front part.

The *kakundara* (the hollows of the loins) exist in all [genders] as the depressions of the buttocks. The *kaṭiprotha* are the fleshy parts of the buttocks (*sphica*). The *pāyu* is the anus (*guda*), which is the seat of the *apāna* wind.
The region between the two testicles is known as the *bhaga*.
The testicle (*muṣka*) is also called the *aṇḍa*, *maṇḍaka-koṣa*, *vṛṣaṇa*, and *bīja-peśikā*.
The penis (*śiśna*) is also called the *śepha*, *liṅga*, *meḍhra*, and *sādhana* (or *mehana*).
The vulva is called *bhaga*, *varāṅga*, *upastha*, or *smaramandira*.
The thighs are *sakthinī*; the joint between the hips and the thighs is the *vaṅkṣaṇa*.
The joint in the middle of the shank and thigh is the *jānu* (knee), also known as *aṣṭhīvat* or *cakrikā*.

The lower leg (*jaṅghā*) is to be known as extended; likewise, the ankle-bone (*piṇḍikā*) is situated in its middle. (RājNī 18.77) The joints at the connection between the lower leg and the foot are called the *ghuṭikā* and also the *gulpha*. (RājNī 18.78) Below the *gulpha* is the heel (*pārṣṇi*); the tip of the foot is considered the *prapada*. (RājNī 18.79)

Vikrama, caraṇa, pāda, pādāṅghri, pada, and krama are synonyms for the foot. Kroḍa, aṅka, and utsaṅga are known as the front part of the body (the chest). A hand with the fingers joined and extended is called kara; it is also termed tala, capeṭa, pratala, and prahastaka.

When the fingers are drawn together and clenched, it is called a *muṣṭi* (fist); when the tips are bent and extended, it is proclaimed as *prasṛta*. When the index, middle, ring, and little fingers are joined with the thumb, these are respectively designated here as *prādeśa*, *tāla*, *gostava*, and *vitasti*. 18.82–83.

A *hasta* is the span of an outstretched hand from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger; when the fist is clenched, it is a *saratni*; an *aratni* is the span from the wrist to the tip of the little finger. A *vyāma* is the distance between the tips of the two outstretched arms.
They know the span of the outstretched arms upwards to be the human measure, the *pauruṣa*.

(Rājñī 18.86) The vital point (*marman*) is the seat of the life-force; it is called the "abode of the life-force. (Rājñī 18.87) And that vital point is said to be manifold, located in various places such as between the eyebrows. (Rājñī 18.88)

Physicians declare that in mortals there are thirty-two vital points (*marmasthāna*)—measured by arrows and eyes [i.e., 32]—located at the middle of the brows, the nape, the throat, the temples, the shoulders, the back, the neck, the rectum, the penis, and the pair of hands and feet; injury to these causes the destruction of the limbs.
Saliva becomes a flow from the mouth; it is called *sṛṇikā* when it trickles down.
Sweat (*sveda*) is perspiration (*gharma*), and *gharmāmbhas* is the water of perspiration; *dūṣikā* is the impurity of the eyes.
*Mala* is excrement (*viṣṭhā*), also called *purīṣa*, *viṭ*, *kiṭṭa*, and *pūtika*.
*Mūtra* is the secret discharge, also known as *prasrāva*, *sravaṇa*, and *srava*.

A wrinkle is a wave of the skin (*carmataraṅga*); it is also called a ripple of the skin (*tvagūrmi*) or a wave of the skin (*tvaktaraṅgaka*). Grayness (*palita*) is a mark of old age (*jarā*), and it consists of the whiteness of the hair.
The [seven bodily constituents] are chyle (*rasa*), blood (*asṛj*), flesh (*māṃsa*), fat (*medas*), bone (*asthi*), marrow (*majjā*), together with semen (*śukra*).
The seven bodily constituents (dhātus) that provide stability to the body should be correctly understood:
rasa is called rasikā, the mother of sweat, and the flow of the body;
carmāmbhas and carmasāra; and rakta-sū is the mother of blood.
*raktāsram*, *rudhiram*, *tvagjam*, *kīlālam*, *kṣatajam*,
*śoṇitam*, *lohitam*, *asṛk*, *śoṇam*, *loham*, and *carmajam* are synonyms for blood.
*Māṃsam*, *piśitam*, *kravyam*, *palam*, and *rasyam* refer to flesh produced from blood.

Palala, jāṅgala, kīra, and āmiṣa are said to be [synonyms for] flesh. Fat (medas), however, is the essence of flesh; it is the oiliness of the flesh, known as vasā or vapā. The bone-element (asthidhātu) is born from fat; it is called kulya and kīkasaka.

The marrow is the essence of the bones; it is the vital heat (*tejas*), the seed born of the bone, the life-giver, the essence of the body, and is known as the unctuousness of the bone. Semen is called virility, *retaḥ*, seed, potency, and manliness.
The transformation of food is the sense-faculty; it is the essence of marrow, providing exhilaration and strength.
From the essence comes blood, from that flesh, from flesh fat, and bone arises from that;
from bone comes marrow, and from that semen—such is the sequence of their production.

The *tilaka*, the *kloma*, and the brain; the fat (*sneha*) is that which arises from the head. The intestines (*antra*) are declared to be the *purītat*, while the spleen (*plīhā*) is known as the *gulma*. Fat (*vasā*), the *vasnasā*, and the sinew (*snāyu*) are called *vatsa*; it is the bark of the body.

That skin [... (10 characters) // Rajni_18.106 The head-born, the neck-tendon, the vessel, the supporter, the earth-bearer, the thread-like, the life-knower, and the channel are proclaimed as Siṃhī. // Rajni_18.107

A *kaṇḍarā* is a large tendon (*mahāsnāyu*) and is also known as a great channel (*mahānāḍī*). The bones of the body are called the skeleton (*kaṅkāla*), while the cage of bones is the *karaṅka*. The channels, apertures, and cavities are the orifices; the *kālakhaṇḍa* is considered to be the liver (*yakṛt*).
The bone of the head is the *karoṭi*; a helmet for the head is called *śīrṣaka*.
They say its fragment is a *kharpara*, and it is also termed a *kapāla*.
The bone of the back is the *kaseru*, while the bone of the limbs is known as the *nalaka*.
The rib-bone is called *parśukā*; such is the determination of the limbs of the body.

(Rajni 18.112) The Self (*ātman*), the embodied one (*śarīrin*), the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the person (*pudgala*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the Lord (*īśvara*), the living being (*jīva*), the all-pervading one (*vibhu*), the male (*pumān*), the Sovereign (*īśa*), the omniscient one (*sarvajña*), Śambhu, and the Imperishable (*avyaya*). (Rajni 18.113)
Pradhāna, Prakṛti, Māyā, Śakti, and Caitanya are synonyms.
Ahaṃkāra is abhimāna; likewise, it is ahaṃtā and ahaṃmati. Mānasa, hṛdaya, svānta, citta, cetas, manas, and hṛd are synonyms for the mind.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas) of the person.
The ear, skin, tongue, eye, and nose constitute the five sense organs (akṣa).
Akṣa, hṛṣīka, karaṇa, varhaṇa, viṣayin, and indriya are synonyms for the sense organ.
Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—these are the objects;
they are the domains of the senses and indeed the qualities of the five elements. Space, wind, water, fire, and earth—these too [are the elements].

The five elements have been proclaimed in sequence by the wise. (Rajni 18.121) Thus, this chapter—filled with the examination of human age, superior complexions, limbs, bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—has been composed by physicians; it is a compendium of the names of many bodily defects, established through the determination of the enumeration of their causes (*nidāna*). (Rajni 18.122)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Jewel Crown of the Collection of Names," composed by Narahari, whose sole boundary of bliss is the joy arising at every moment from the meditative absorption of serving the lotus feet of Paśupati. *Rājanighaṇṭu*, 18.123.
The section on lions and other animals:

The lion has five faces [in its mane], possesses claws, is the king of beasts, is proud, is called *hari*, *kesarī*, *kravyāda*, *nakharāyudha*, *mṛgaripu*, *śūra*, and *kaṇṭhīrava*. It is valorous, the destroyer of elephants, possesses great strength, is radiant, powerful, and courageous. It is known as *haryakṣa*, *dīptapiṅgala*, and it is the lord of beasts (*mṛgendra*). (Rajni 19.1)
The great-horned śarabha, with shoulders like clouds, high-minded, eight-legged, a great lion, wise, and dwelling in the mountains;
the tiger, the five-clawed beast, the serpent-like predator, the śārdūla, and the cave-dweller.

Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra, Puṇḍarīka, Dvīpī, Bhīru, and Nakhāyudha; Citraka and Citrakāya are synonyms for the leopard, as is Upavyāghra and Mṛgāntaka. Furthermore, Śūra, Kṣudraśārdūla, and Citravyāghra are recorded as names for the tiger.
The *ṛkṣa*, *bhallūka*, *bhalla*, *saśalya*, and *durghoṣa* are synonyms; the *bhallaka* is known as the "back-seeing" (*pṛṣṭhadṛṣṭi*).

That which is longest (*drāghiṣṭha*) has long hair and is long-lived; he is to be known as the *duścara* and the *dīrghadarśin*. Furthermore, that which is the *mṛgada* is to be understood as the *tarakṣu*, of terrible appearance.
The jackal is called *śivā*, *bhūrimāya*, *gomāyu*,
*mṛgadhūrtaka*, *śṛgāla*, *vañcaka*, *kroṣṭṛ*, *pherava*, *pheru*,
*jambuka*, *śālāvṛka*, *śivālu*, *pheraṇḍa*, and *vyāghrasevaka*.
The *īhāmṛga* is the *koka*; the wolf is the *vatsādana* and the *avibhuk*.
The *govatsāri*, *chāgalāri*, and *chāgalānta* are those that dwell near water.
The dog is the *kukkura*, *sārameya*, *bhaṣaka*, *śvānaka*, and *śvana*.
The dog is known as *bhūstara*, *vakralāṅgūla*, *vṛkārī*, and *rātrijāgara*.
It is also called *kauleyaka*, *grāmamṛga*, *mṛgāri*, and *mṛgadaṃśaka*.
Furthermore, it is termed *śūra*, *śuni*, *śayālu*, *bhaṣa*, and *śaradikāmuka*.

The cat is the enemy of mice; it is called *vṛṣadaṃśa*, *biḍālaka*, *śālāvṛka*, *mārjāra*, *māyāvī*, and *dīptalocana*. Another variety is the hairy cat (*lomaśamārjāra*), known as *pūtika* and *mārajātaka*.
He was a musk-deer, exuding a fragrant urine. Dvira-da, gaja,
mataṅga-ja, ibha, kumbhin, dvirada, nava-raṇa, hastin, padmin, nāga, kari,
karaṭi, viṣāṇin, kuñjara— these are elephants, as well as those beasts who are intoxicated by the pride of their tusks, rut-fluid, and strength.
Bhadra, stamberama, dantī, drumāri, ṣaṣṭihāyana, mātaṅga, puṣkarī, dantāvala, anekapa, and ibha are synonyms for an elephant.
Elephants are to be known as being of three types: bhadra, manda, and mṛga.
Characterized by his roaming in the forest, his physical resemblance [to an elephant], and his distinct nature, that young one should be known as a colt; he is called a wild beast difficult to tame.
He is one who has burst forth, trumpeted, wandered about, is intoxicated, and is full of rut.

*ibhī* should be known as *kariṇī*, *hastinī*, *dhenukā*, and *vaśā*; likewise, *kareṇu*, *padminī*, *mātaṃgī*, and *vāsitā* refer to the same. *Khaḍga* is the rhinoceros (*khaḍgamṛga*), the wrathful one with horns on its face and strength in its mouth.
Gaṇḍaka, Vajracarman, Khaḍgī, and he who is like a rhinoceros;
Uṣṭra, Dīrghagati, Bala, Karabha, Dāseraka, Dhūsara, Lamboṣṭha, Lavaṇa, Kramelaka, Mahājaṅgha, and Bījāṅghrika;
Dīrgha, Śṛṅkhalaka, Mahān, Mahāgrīva, Mahāṅga, Mahānāda, Mahādhvaga, Mahāpṛṣṭha, and he who is Baliṣṭha.
The buffalo is called *mahiṣa*, *kāsara*, *krodhī*, *kaluṣa*, and *sairibha*;
it is also known as *lulāpa*, *mattaraktākṣa*, *viṣāṇin*, *kavalī*, and *balī*.
The female buffalo is *mahiṣī*, characterized by slow gait, abundant milk, and being full of milk.
A female buffalo is called *lulāpikā*, *kāntā*, *kaluṣā*, or *turaṅgadveṣiṇī*.
A noble bull is a *bhadra*; a young ox is a *balīvarda*; one that is trained is *damya* or *dānta*; and one that is steady and strong is an *ukṣā*.
A draft ox is an *anaḍvān*; it may also be called *kakudmān*, *ṛṣabha*, *vṛṣabha*, or *vṛṣa*.
Dhurya, dhurīṇa, and dhaureya denote a beast of burden; śāṅkara and haravāhana refer to the vehicle of Śiva; rohiṇīramaṇa, voḍhṛ, gonātha, and saurabheyaka are names for a bull.
Furthermore, vṛṣabha and vṛṣa are said to mean a bull, while mahokṣa, puṅgava, and balin denote a powerful, full-grown ox.

He is the lord of cattle, the bull, the steer, the one dear to cattle, and the master of cattle. Here, cattle are to be understood as distinguished by various color variations, such as white, dappled, copper-colored, brindled, and smoky-grey.

A trained, educated, and tamed bull that bears the yoke is called a *dhurya* or a *dhaurika*. A young calf is called a *vatsatara*, while one that is difficult to tame is termed a *gaḍi*. A cow is known as *go*, *mātā*, *usrā*, *śṛṅgiṇī*, *saurabheyī*, *māheyī*, *rohiṇī*, *dhenu*, or *aghnyā*.

The milch-cow is called *bhadrā* and *bhūrimatī*; the ox is *anaḍuh*. The auspicious cow that purifies is both *kalyāṇī* and *arjunī*. (19.28) The wild ox is declared to be the *gavaya*, while the *balabhadra* is the *mahāgava*.
(19.29) The female *gavaya* is the *vanadhenu*, and she is also considered the *bhillagavī*. (19.30)
The yak is known as *camara*, *vyajana*, *vanya*, *dhenuga*, and *bāladhipriya*.
Its female is called *camarī*, *dīrghabālā*, and *giripriyā*.
The boar is *varāha*, *stabdharoman*, *romaśa*, *śūkara*, and *kiri*.
Vakradaṃṣṭra, Kiṭi, Daṃṣṭrin, Kroḍa, Dantāyudha, and the powerful Balin;
Pṛthuskandha, Bhūdāra, Potrī, Ghoṇāntabhedana, Kola, Potrāyudha, Śūra, Bahvapatya, and Radāyudha.
The village pig is called *viḍvarāha*,
*grāmīṇa*, *grāmaśūkara*, *grāmyakroḍa*, *grāmyakola*, *viṣṭhāśī*, and *dāraka*.
The horse is called *aśva*, *ghoṭa*, *turaṅga*, *arvan*, *turaga*, and *turaṅgama*.
Vāha, Vājī, Mudgabhojī, Vīti, Sapti, and Saindhava;
Haris, Haya, Dhārāṭa, Javana, Jīvana, and Javī;
Gandharva, the best of steeds, the brother of Śrī and the uterine sibling of Amṛta.

There are various horses from Āraṭṭa, Sindh, Javana, Ayuja, Pārasīka, Kāmboja, Bāhlika, and other regions; they may also come from places such as Sāmnāna and Śephaka. Furthermore, they differ in many ways according to their color: the white horse is called *karka*, while the red is *śoṇa*; the golden-colored is *haima*, the black is *kṛṣṇa*, and the dark blue is *nīla*.

"With bright eyes, he is designated as *mallikākṣa*; with black eyes, he is called *indrāyudha*. Thus, this horse is to be identified by wise men according to the distinctions of various colors as established in worldly tradition. We have not provided an exhaustive elaboration here; therefore, even a horse of noble lineage (*ājāneya*) is included among those of high birth (*kulīna*)."
A well-bred horse is called *sukula*, and a young horse is a *kiśora* or *turagārbhaka*. A mare is a *vājinī*, a *vaḍabā*, a *prasū*, an *aśvā*, or an *aśvinī*.
A donkey is a *gardabha*, a *śaṅkukarṇa*, a *bāleya*, a *rāsabha*, or a *khara*.
The mule (*bhāravāha*) is a long-distance traveler, a beast of burden, known by the name *dhūsara*.
The *vesara*, however, is born from a horse and a donkey; it carries a single pregnancy, is capable of long journeys, is patient, and is said to be contented.
Being born from a mixture of species, it is called by the mixed term *miśraja* and can bear excessive loads.

The goat (*aja*) is pure (*medhya*), as is the *bukka*; he is also the long-eared animal (*lambakarṇa*). The *chāgala*, *barkara*, and *chāga* are synonyms; that [goat] which possesses milk is called *basta*. (Rājñī 19.44) A milking female goat is called *payasvinī*; a timid one is a *chāgī*; and one with a dewlap and udders is *medhyā*. (Rājñī 19.45)
Meṣa, bheḍa, huḍa, meṇḍhra, ūrṇāyu, uraṇa, eḍaka,
śṛṅgin, avi, urabhra, romaśa, and balī—
these various kinds of sheep exist according to the distinctions of different regions. (Rajni 19.46–47)

*Mṛga*, *kuraṅga*, *vātāyu*, *kṛṣṇasāra*, and *sulocana* denote the deer; *hariṇa* and *ajinayoni* refer to the same; and *eṇa* as well as *pṛṣata* also denote the spotted deer. Furthermore, *kakudvāg*, *sāraṅga*, *śākhiśṛṅga*, and *cittala* [are synonyms for the deer].

The *bhāraśṛṅga* is another [species], as is the *mahāśṛṅga* and the *vanapriya*. The *ruru*, *rauhiṣa*, and *rohī* are synonyms; so too are the *nyaṅku* and the *śambara*. The *nīlaka*, the *pṛṣata*, the *raṅku*, and the *śabalapṛṣṭhaka* are also [types of deer].
Śikhari, upakuraṅga, śrīkārī, and mahājava;
javanī, vegī, hariṇī, jaṅghāla, and the one called jāṅghika.
Vānara, markaṭa, kīśa, kapi, śākhāmṛga, and hari.
Plavaṅgama, vanaukā, plavaṅga, plavaga, and plava are synonyms for monkey.
The golāṅgūla is called gaura (the white one), for its face is dark;
it is to be known as the black monkey, also named mandurābhūṣaṇa.

The *śalyaka* is the porcupine; it is also called *śalyamṛga*, *vajraśukti*, and *bileśaya*. Another species of *śalya* is called *śvāvit*; it is also known as *śalī* and *śalalī*. Regarding its quills, they are to be understood as *śalalī*, *śalala*, and *śala*.
The *kokaḍa* is said to be swift; the *kokovāca* dwells in holes.
The *camarapuccha* should be known as hairy and smoke-colored.
The *nakula* has needle-like teeth, is an enemy of snakes, and has a red face.
The serpent has a tongue-like snout, possesses two tongues, dwells in the netherworld, and is powerful;
he is a descendant of Kadrū, moves crookedly, and is a venomous biter.
He has eyes on his ears, bears poison, has hidden feet, wears earrings, and has a hooded neck.
He is the pannaga, the one who feeds on air, the enjoyer, and the one who moves crookedly;
he is the serpent, the fanged one, the arm-crawler, the snake, the crawler-on-arms, and the reptile;
he is the one with a slough, the long-tailed one, the twice-tongued, and the uraga.
Those hooded beings with white bodies are celebrated as *nāgas*;

others, rich in colors such as red and so forth, are to be understood by names such as *sarpa* (serpent) and the like. The *gonasa* is called *maṇḍalī*, while the one with variegated limbs is the *vyantara*.
Kulika is to be known as green; they know Rājila as the *ḍuṇḍubha*.
Ananta, Vāsuki, Padma, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, Karkoṭa, Kulika, and Śaṅkha—these are the leaders of the Nāgas.
His kinsmen were Kumuda, Kambala, Aśvatara, and others;
Āpahṛt, Dvimukhī, Dhāmiṇī, and yet others;
as well as Mūṣika, Mūṣaka, Piṅga, Ākhu, Unduruka, and Nakhī.
The khanaka, the bilakārī, and the dhānyāri which has many offspring;
another is the mahāmūṣaka, while the mūṣī is the vehicle of Vighneśa.
The mahāṅga, the sasyamārī, the bhūphala, and the bhittipātana.
The *chuchundarī* is called the princess (*rājaputrī*), while another is the *pratimūṣikā*.
The *sugandhimūṣikā* is known as *gandhā*, *śuṇḍinī*, and *śuṇḍamūṣikā*. The *godhā*, however, should be known as *godhikā* and also by the name *dārumatsī*.

The *kharacarmā* is a five-clawed creature with bristling hair and a long tail. The offspring of a lizard is called a *gaudheya*, a *gaudhāra*, or the son of a *godhikā*. The *barbarī*, *ghorikā*, and *ghorā* are long-bodied and terrifying.

The *sthūlacañcu* is the long-legged snake-eater (*guṇārikā*). The *brāhmaṇī* is the house-lizard (*gṛhagodhā*), also known as the *supadī* or *raktapucchikā*. The *saraṭa* is the chameleon (*kṛkalāsa*), while the *pratisūrya* is the *śayānaka*.
One who stays in a dwelling, one who dwells in a thicket of thorns, and one who takes refuge in trees difficult to climb;

the *jāhaka*, the one who contracts his limbs, the *maṇḍalī*, the one of many forms, the one who assumes forms at will, the deformed one, and the cave-dweller— these are proclaimed [as types of ascetics].

The *pallī* is said to be the *musalī*; the house-lizard is the *gṛhālikā*, the *jyeṣṭhā*, the *kuḍyamatsyā*, the *pallikā*, and the *gṛhagodhikā*. The weaver is the *tūrṇanābha*, the spider is the *lūtā*, and the *markaṭaka* is a worm.

Hālāhalā, añjalikā, girikā, and bālamūṣikā; vṛścika and śūkakīṭa are synonyms, and alidroṇa is also used for a scorpion (vṛścika). Furthermore, karṇajalūkā, citrāṅgī, and śatapadī refer to the centipede.

*Pipīlaka* and *pipīla* are masculine terms, while *pipīlikā* is the feminine designation. *Udaṅghā*, *kapijaṅghikā*, and *tailapipīlikā* are to be known as [names for] the same. Furthermore, there is another black variety called *pipīlī*, which is thick and grows upon trees.
A bedbug is a blood-drinker, red-limbed, and a dweller upon a couch.
A "yādas" is an aquatic creature, a water-being that rests in the water;
among those, one whose actions are exceedingly cruel is called a "jalavyāla" (a water-monster).
*Matsya*, *vaisāriṇa*, *mīna*, *pṛthuromā*, *jhaṣa*, and *aṇḍaja* are synonyms for fish.
*Visāra*, *śakulī*, *śalkī*, *pāṭhīna*, *animiṣa*, and *timi* are also types of fish.
Furthermore, *rājīva*, *śakula*, *śṛṅgī*, *vāgusa*, *śalya*, and *pallava* are likewise varieties of fish.
The *pāṭhīna*, the *śakula*, the *nadyāvarta*, and the *rohita*—
as well as the *madgura*, the *timira*, and others— should be known as varieties belonging to that [category of] species.
Another variety of it is called the *makara*, and another is the *mātaṃgamakara*.
The cilicima, the stimi, as well as the other, the timiṅgila,
and the timiṅgilagila— these are considered to be the great fish. The śiśuka is the śiśumāra, and that is also the grāha and the varāhaka.
May he become a crocodile, a *kumbhīra*, or a mighty *galagrāha*;
a tortoise, a *kamaṭha*, a *kūrma*, one with hidden limbs, a supporter of the earth,
one who frequents marshy banks, a dweller in ponds, one who is round, and one with a hard shell.
*Karkaṭa*, *karkaṭaka*, *kulīra*, and *kulīraka* are synonyms for crab;
it is also called *saṃdaṃśaka*, *paṅkavāsa*, *tiryaggāmī*, and *ūrdhvadṛk*.
*Maṇḍūka*, *dardura*, *maṇḍa*, *hari*, *bheka*, and *lūlaka* are synonyms for frog.
The śālūra, the varṣābhū, the plava, the kaṭurava,
the samīḍan, the muṇḍī, the plavaṅga, and the plavaṅgama;
another yellow one is the rājamaṇḍūka, also known as the mahāmaṇḍūka.
Pītāṅga, pītamaṇḍūka, varṣāghoṣa, and mahārava [are names for a type of frog]. Jalūkā, jalaukā, raktapā, raktapāyinī,
raktasaṃdohikā, tīkṣṇā, carmaṭī, and jalajīvinī [are synonyms for the leech].
The *dātyūha* is the water-crow, and it is also known as the *kālakaṇṭhaka*. The *jalapārāvata* is called the *kopī*, and the *jalakapotaka*.
Whatever creatures exist on land, such as elephants, horses, and so forth—
In the water as well, they should be known to be as many, preceded by the word "jala-".
Birds, vihagas, vihaṅgamas, vihaṅga; those wishing to fly, pattrins, patatris, patravāhas;
śakunis, śakunas, viṣkiras, aṇḍajas; viḥ, pataga, patan, nabhasaṅgama; and nagaukas.
He is the swift one, the winged vehicle, the bird, the twice-born, the one born from the nest,
the follower, the śakunta, the pataga, the piccha, the pataṅga, and the vikira. He is the vulture, the son of Tārkṣya, the son of Vinatā, the lord of birds, and the destroyer of serpents.
Vakratuṇḍa, Dākṣāyya, Garutmān, Dūradarśana, Śyena, Śaśāda, Kravyāda, Krūra, Vegin,
Khagāntaka, Kāmāndha, Tīvrasaṃpāta, Tarasvin, and Tārkṣyanāyaka.

The *kāṣṭhakuṭṭa* is called *kāṣṭhabhaṅgī* and *kāṣṭhakūṭa*. The *karaka* has blue tail-feathers (*nīlapiccha*), long ears, and is fond of battle; it is the *raṇapakṣī*, the *picchabāṇa*, the thick-blue (*sthūlanīla*), and the terrifying (*bhayaṃkara*).

The *kaṅka* has a back like iron and a mouth like a pair of tongs; it is harsh, cruel, an ornament of battle, and fond of raw flesh. The crow is called *kāka*, *vāyasa*, and *dhvāṅkṣa*; it is one-eyed, ill-omened, and lays its eggs but once.
Balibhuj, Balipuṣṭa, Dhūlijaṅgha, Nimittakṛt, Kauśikāri,
Cirāyus, Karaṭa, Mukhara, Khara, Ātmaghoṣa, Mahālola, Cirajīvī, and Calācala. (Rājñī 19.108–109)
The *droṇa* is the *droṇakāka*; the *kākola* is the forest crow (*araṇyavāyasa*).
It dwells in the woods, possesses great strength, has a harsh cry, and is fond of fruit.
The *ulūka* is the *tāmasa*, the *ghūka*; it is blind by day, a *kauśika*, and a *kuvi*.
The *naktaṃcara*, the *niśāṭa*, the *kākāri*, and the *krūraghoṣaka*;
the *valgulī*—whose excrement is her mouth—and the *divāndhā*, who wanders at night;
the *svairiṇī*, who sleeps during the day, and the *mātṛvāhinī*, who desires flesh. (Rājñī 19.111–112)
Carmakī, Carmapakṣī, Carmāṅgī, Carmagandhikā,
Kṛtyāśūkāriṇī, Carmī, Carmapattrī, Melikā, Dināndhā, Naktabhojī, Bhrāmaṇī, and the one called Karṇikā. (Rājñī 19.113)
Mayūra, candrakī, barhī, nīlakaṇṭha, śikhī, dhvajī,
meghānandī, kalāpī, śikhaṇḍī, citrapicchaka,
barhiṇa, pracalākī, śuklāpāṅga, and śikhāvala.
The peacock is a consumer of serpents and a singer along with the sound of the clouds.
A mass of feathers is called *kalāpa*; the eye-like spots on the feathers are *candrakās*.
The crest is known as *pracalāka* or *śikhā*, and its cry is said to be *kekā*.

The *kurara* is of harsh cry; the *krauñca* is a crane that moves in a row and is harsh. The blue *krauñca*, however, has a dark body, a long neck, and is very wakeful. The *baka* (heron), the *kaṅka* (bittern), and the *bakoṭa* are those who frequent sacred fords and act like ascetics.
A fisherman, one who meditates falsely, one with motionless feet, and a hypocrite;
Śakunī, Potakī, Śyāmā, Pāṇḍavī, and Śvetapakṣiṇī;
Durgā and Bhagavatī—she is indeed called Satyapāṇḍavī.
The *balākā* is the "poison-throated" crane, with a withered body and a long neck.
The *gharmāntakāmukī* is white, dwelling near water and sounding like a cloud.
The *cakra*, *koka*, *cakravāka*, and *rathāṅga* are the ruddy sheldrake; it is full of passion, moving about in pairs, and is a companion.
He is beloved, full of desire, approaching at night’s end, resembling the breasts of beautiful women, and a lover.
The crane is a connoisseur of rasa, full of desire, blue-bodied, and crying out when addressed;
the peacock has red eyes, a voice like a crow, and is dear to lovers.
The *ṭiṭṭibhī*, the *pītapāda*, the *sadālūtā*, the *nṛjāgara*, the *niśācarī*, the *citrapakṣī*, the *jalaśāyī*, and the *sucetanā*;
and another, the *jalakukkuṭaka*, which dwells in the water and remains in the water. (Rajñī 19.126–127)
The *ṭhika* bird, the *pāśagaḍa*, the *ṭhikka*, the *jalasārya*, and the *tilāśaya*; the *jalapakṣī*, the *mahāpakṣī*, the *jalasāghativāsaka*,
the *jalaśāyī*, the *maṇḍalīna*, the *mandaga*, the *śleṣmala*, and the *aviṣī*.
Sarājī, Rājimant, Jalasarpa,
Dundubhi, Dvivida, Goḍa, Nīla, Citrī, Śalpi, and Gomukha—
these and all the other monkeys were but small cranes.
White, variegated, smoky-colored, and so forth, they follow various colors and names.
(19.132) A swan (*haṃsa*) is a white-winged bird; it is marked with circles and dwells in Lake Mānasa.
(19.133) A *kalahaṃsa*, however, is a *kādamba*; it is a sweet-voiced *marālaka*. (19.134)
Among these, when the beaks and feet are reddish, it is the *rājahaṃsa*; when they are very grey, it is the *mallikākṣa*.
At those times, the *dhārtarāṣṭra* is indeed white; yet even this one, though its body is grey, may be considered unfortunate (*abhavya*).
A female swan (*haṃsī*) should be known as a *varaṭā*, a *varalā*, or a *vāralā*.
The female swan has a graceful gait, bears the mark of a wheel on her feet, and moves with soft steps.
The cock is known as *tāmracūḍa*, the "copper-crested," and is a knower of time (*kālajña*).
He is a fighter (*niyoddhā*), a *kṛkavāku*, a bird that scrapes its food (*viṣkira*), and has claws as his weapons (*nakharāyudha*).
The pigeon (kapota) may be Kokadeva, Dhūsara, Dhūmralocana, Dahana, Agnisahāya, Bhīṣaṇa, and Gṛhanāśana.
The turtledove (pārāvata) is Kalarava, Aruṇalocana, Pārāpata, Madanakākurava, and Kāmī.

This one with blood-red eyes, who delights in the playful speech of Madana-mohana, is called the Kaṇṭhīrava or the domestic pigeon (gṛhakapotaka). The Pārāvata from another region is the Kāmuka, which has a "ghullu" sound. The Jalapārāvata is known as the Kāmī, and it also makes a sound from its throat.
The cuckoo is known as *kokila*, *parapuṣṭa*, *kāla*, *parabhṛta*, and *pika*;
it is also called the messenger of spring (*vasantadūta*), the copper-eyed one (*tāmrākṣa*), the Gandharva, the singer of honey (*madhugāyana*), the spring-bird (*vāsanta*),
the sweet-voiced one (*kalakaṇṭha*), the one blinded by passion (*kāmāndha*), and the one with a warbling cry (*kākalīrava*).
The *kuhūrava* is the cuckoo (*anyapuṣṭa*), intoxicated and reciting its passion;
the *kokilā* is the cuckoo (*anyapuṣṭā*), and she is also called *mattā* and *parabhṛtā*.
She is the *sukaṇṭhī*, sweet-voiced, the *kalakaṇṭhī*, and the one who appears with the onset of spring.
The female cuckoo was Vasantadūtī, with copper-colored eyes and a *kuhū* cry;
she was the springtime messenger, moving at will, a celestial nymph who adorned the forest.
The male parrot was Śuka, red-beaked, intelligent, and a sweet-voiced reciter.
Another was a wise royal parrot named Śatapattra, who was dear to the king;
there was also a sweet-voiced sārikā bird, a messenger, and she was very intelligent.
There were also a kavarī with unattractive limbs and a śārikā with mottled limbs.
