For the *sārikā* has yellow feet, bright eyes, and a red beak;
she is skilled in recitation and discourse, intelligent, and a ground-dwelling *sārikā*. The *gorāṇṭikā*, *gokirāṭī*, and *gorikā* are fond of quarreling.
That *cakora* bird, though it drinks moonlight and lives upon the *kaumudī* moonbeams;
that *cātaka*, *tokaka*, and *sāraṅga* bird, though they live upon the clouds;
that *hārītaka*, though it is a *hārīta*; and that *tejala* and *kapiñjala*. (Rājñī 19.151–152)
Dhūsarī, Piṅgalā, Sūcī, Bhairavī, Yoginī, Jayā, Kumārī, Suvicitrā, and the Mother Koṭaravāsinī; Tailapā, Paroṣṇī, Jatukā, Ajinapattrikā, and [the others]. Rajni 19.153–154.
The *bhṛṅga*, *kuliṅga*, *dhūmyāṭa*, *dārvāghāta*, and *śatacchada* are names for the woodpecker.
The *vyāghrāṭa*, *bharadvāja*, *khañjana*, and *khañjarīṭaka* are names for the wagtail.
The *samantabhadra*, *kṛṣṇa*, *svalpakṛṣṇa*, and *subhadraka* are names for the small black bird.
The island-dwelling sage, who demonstrates the four-month fast,
is called the blue-bodied, auspicious-to-behold Cāṣa and Kikīdivi. The Vartaka, Vartika, Varti, and Gāñjika are also mentioned.

The *kalaviṅka* is the sparrow (*caṭaka*), the lover (*kāmuka*), and the blue-throated one (*nīlakaṇṭhaka*). The female sparrow is the *kalaviṅkī*, and their offspring is the *cāṭakaira*. The *dhūsara* is the wild sparrow (*araṇyacaṭaka*); it is also called the *kuja* and the *bhūmiśaya*.

The *bhārīṭa* is the dark sparrow (*śyāmacaṭaka*), which is seasonal (*śaiśira*) and feeds on grains. Another, the *dhūsara*, is very small; this sparrow feeds on grain, is capable of domestic tasks, is timid, dislikes agriculture, and is fond of grains.
Lāva is said to be Lāvaka, and that Lāva is remembered as Lava. Tittiri is Tittira, and Taittiri is the mountain of the Yajurveda.
Another Tittiri is Kṛṣṇa Śūra, who is Subhūti the Protector.
He is a hater of his own kin, possesses many followers, lives for a hundred years, and brings about success.
He is a small owl, born of birds, tawny-colored, and striped;
he dwells in trees, runs swiftly, has tawny eyes, and is terrifying.
Śyāmā, Varāhī, Śakunī, Kumārī, Durgā, Devī, Caṭakā, Kṛṣṇā,
Potakī, Pāṇḍavikā, Vāmā, Kālikā, and Sitabimbinī are synonyms for the female jackal.
Prabhākīṭa, Khadyota, Khajyotis, and Upasūryaka refer to the firefly.

*Tailinī* is a synonym for *tailakīṭa* (an oil-insect); *ṣaḍbimbā* is that which destroys ringworm (*dadru*). *Śakragopa*, *varṣābhū*, and *raktavarṇendragopaka* refer to the red-colored Indragopa insect.
*Bhramara*, *ṣaṭpada*, *bhṛṅga*, *kalālāpa*, and *śilīmukha* are synonyms for the bee.
The bee is called *puṣpandhaya*, *dvirepha*, *ali*, *madhukṛt*, *madhupa*, and *dvibha*;
it is also known as *bhasara*, *cañcarīka*, *jhaṅkārī*, *madhulolupa*, *indindira*,
*madhuliṭ*, *matta*, and *ghumughumārava*.
The *varvaṇā* is a blue fly; the *saraghā* is the honeybee. The *gandholī*, *varaṭā*, and *kṣudrā* are small, cruel insects that have minute coloration.
The *raṃrika* and *chatrakārī* possess sharp fangs and are highly venomous.
Yellow-colored, with long legs, stingy, and possessing cruel fangs is the *daṃśa* (stinging insect); it has a wicked face and is cruel. The *kṣudrikā* is the forest fly (*vanamakṣikā*).
The fly (*makṣikā*), however, was born from nectar; she is vomit-spitting and fickle.
The Maśaka, the Vajratuṇḍa, the Sūcyāsya, the Sūkṣmamakṣikā,
the Rātrijāgarada, the Dhūmra, and the Nīlābhra are other species.
There is also the Aṣṭāṅghri, the Aṣṭapāda, the Gṛhavāsī, and the Kṛṣṇaka.
The *kālika* is said to be the cuckoo; the *kāluñca* has black fangs.
The *kasārikā* is characterized by long fainting spells, dwells in houses, and lives in holes. The louse (*yūkā*) is a hair-insect, born from sweat, and is considered a six-legged creature.

The *pakṣmajā* is a winged louse (*pakṣmayūkā*); it is minute and possesses six legs. A nit (*likṣā*) arises from the limbs of a white louse on a cloth; it resides upon the cloth worn by the louse. Among those beings thus described, there are even smaller creatures such as scorpions and the like.
In each such case, the wise should know that all of them are designated as "insects" (kīṭa).
The female insect (kīṭikā) is said to be the sparrow (caṭikā), possessing adamantine fangs and many offspring;
she is lean-limbed, characterized by darkness (tāmasī), courageous, bearing the weight of a cricket (kīri), and possessed of great strength.
The *maṅkora*, the *maṅkaṭa*, the black *tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra*, the *viśāluka*,
the six-legged *ṣaṭpādaka*— which is envious— and the *mākoṭa*, whose private parts point upward;
the *ṣaḍbindu*, the *bindukīṭa*, and the long worm (*dīrghakīṭa*) that moves on its feet.
The Prasahas, Vilambitas, Drutaśayas, and Pratudas, as well as the Viṣkiras and Kīṭas—
these are declared to be the ninefold animals here. Having thus understood this class, which is filled with explanations of the various manifold categories of animals, [one attains mastery].
Having thoroughly determined [the requirements] with his intellect, the wise physician should apply the group of meats.

(RājN 19.188) By him through whom the Lord of the Moon-crested [Śiva]—who is worshipped as the five-faced lion, whose elephant is his mount, who wears the deer-moon on his crest, whose garment is tiger-skin, whose ornaments are serpents, and whose gait is like that of a noble bull—is honored;
by that illustrious Lord Nṛhari, this great section on lions and other animals has indeed reached its conclusion in the nineteenth chapter of the *Abhidhānacūḍāmaṇi*. (RājN 19.189)
Rājanighaṇṭu, Rogādivarga: *gada*, *rujā*, *vyādhi*, *apāṭava*, *āmaya*, *roga*, *ātaṅka*, *bhaya*, and *upaghāta* [are synonyms for disease].

Consumption (rājayakṣmā) is the destroyer of digestive power, vitality, health, darkness [of vision], transformation, vigor, decay, uprightness, and life; it is the servant of death. It is called kṣaya (wasting), yakṣmā, the king of diseases, the foremost of ailments, uṣmā (heat), śoṣa (emaciation), atiroga (excessive disease), the lord of diseases, and the malady of kings.
Pāṇḍuroga is called pāṇḍu; visarpa is the disease known as sacivāmaya; śopha is śotha and śvayathu; kāsa is said to be kṣavathu. Kṣuta is also kṣavathu, as is kṣut; and pratiśyāya is pīnasa.

Eye disease is *netrāmaya*, and mouth disease is *mukhāmaya*. Bad skin is *duścarmā*, as are *maṇḍala*, *koṭha*, skin defects, and *carmadūṣikā*. *Puṇḍarīka* is leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), while *śvitra* is *carmacitraka*.
Kilāsa, sidhma, śikhī, śvāsa, pāmā, vicarcikā,
kaṇḍū, kaṇḍūti, kaṇḍūyā, kharjū, and kaṇḍūyana;
saṃcārī, śuṇḍikā, sphoṭa, pāma, and pāma-vicarcikā.
Yellow pustules are *pāmā*, while small pustules are *kañcikā*.
A *piṭakā* is called a *piṭikā*; *masūrikā* resembles lentils (*masūra*).
*Visphoṭa*, *sphoṭaka*, and *sphoṭa* refer to boils; *keśaghna* and *indraluptaka* refer to hair loss.
*Galaśuṇḍī* is *śuṇḍā*; *galagaṇḍa* is *galastana*.
*Dantārbuda* is *dantamūla*, *dantaśotha*, and *dvijavraṇa*.
*Gulma* is a knot in the stomach; *gaḍu* refers to a knot on the back.

Paktiśūla is a type of colic born of digestion, arising from the transformation of food (pariṇāmaja). Lūtā is a skin ulcer; vṛkka refers to the kidneys; nāḍī is a sinus tract, and nāḍīvraṇa is a sinus ulcer.
Ślīpada is elephantiasis; pādavalmīka is a wart-like growth on the foot; pādasphoṭa is cracking of the feet; and vipādikā is a fissure or crack in the soles of the feet.
Viṣṭambha is constipation (vibandha), while ānāha is the obstruction of waste matter.
Arśāṃsi are hemorrhoids (gudakīla), also known as durnāmāni or gudāṅkura. Atīsāra is the excessive discharge of stool (malavega), while pravāhikā is a disease of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-ruk).
Vomiting, spitting up, belching, chardi, vicchardikā, and vami are synonyms.
Heart-disease is called hṛdroga, hṛgada, and hṛdruj; utprāṇa is said to be asthma (śvāsa).
Fever, however, is known as jvara, jvarātaṅka, the foremost of diseases, and mahāgada.
The irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*) such as those caused by cold and other factors arise from the dualities (*dvaṃdvaja*) and originate from the defects of those dualities;
these are distinct from the exogenous (*āgantu*) types, which occur every two days, one day, three days, and so forth.
Blood-bile (*raktapitta*), bile-blood (*pittarakta*), blood-bile (*pittāsra*), and bile-blood (*pittaśoṇita*) [are synonyms].

In this manner, one should describe the dual disorders of blood, wind, and so forth. (Rajni 20.16) Thirst, parching of the mouth, craving, intoxication from grass, the affliction of intoxication, excess drinking, the disease of intoxication, and *mada*—which is an agitated state of mind. (Rajni 20.17)
Fainting (mūrchā), however, is delusion (moha) and stupor (mūḍhi); loss of voice (svarasāda) is the weakening of the voice (svarakṣaya).
Lack of faith (aśraddhā) is lack of desire; likewise, distaste (aruci) is anorexia (arocaka). Urinary disorder (mūtradoṣa) should be known as diabetes (prameha) and also as polyuria (meha).

*Kṛcchra* refers to difficulty in urination (*mūtrakṛcchra*), as well as urinary obstruction and urinary calculi (*aśmarī*). *Vātavyādhi*, *calātaṅka*, *vātaroga*, and *anilāmaya* denote diseases of wind (*vāta*).
Furthermore, *kampa*, *vepana*, *vepa*, *kampana*, and *vepathu* all signify trembling.
*Jṛmbhā*, *jṛmbhikā*, *jambhā*, *jṛmbhaṇaṃ*, and *jambhikā* are synonyms for yawning.
*Ālasyaṃ*, *mandatā*, *māndyaṃ*, and also *kāryapradveṣaḥ* denote laziness.
*Tundaḥ* is said to mean "very corpulent," while *jalodaraḥ* refers to dropsy or abdominal enlargement.
From the imbalance of undigested matter (*āma*) and impurity (*mala*), there arises *raktārti*, a disease of the blood;
it is called *jālagardabhaka*,
the disease of the "donkey-web," and should be known as *jālakharagada* as well as *gardabhagada*.
Vidradhi is a piercing pain; it is also known as hr̥dgranthi and hr̥dvraṇa.
A wound in the region of the vulva is called bhagaṃdara. Headaches and other such ailments should be understood by the names of their respective body parts.
In this manner, physicians should understand other diseases as well arising from the body. *Rajñī* 20.25.
Fever is called *saṃtāpa*, *saṃjvara*, *tāpa*, *śoṣa*, and *uṣmā*; furthermore, that which is a fever of the internal viscera (*koṣṭha*) is known as *antardāha*. *Rajñī* 20.26.

That burning sensation in the mouth, palate, and lips, as well as the distress in the eyes and other organs, and [the heat] in the hands, feet, and roots of the shoulders—that is called *śākhā-pitta*.
*Tandrā* is the lack of cognition regarding sense objects; it is also known as *pramīlā* and *tandrikā*.

Dissolution (*pralaya*) is the sleep of the senses, the cessation of activity, and a state of being dissolved. Madness (*unmāda*) is the derangement of the intellect; it is also called *unmanāyita*. Possession (*āveśa*) is the entry of spirits (*bhūta-saṃcāra*), the overtaking by spirits (*bhūta-krānti*), and the arrival of seizing demons (*graha-āgama*).
Epilepsy, distortion of the limbs, trembling of the body,
possession by spirits, numbness, dullness, sluggishness, coldness, and lack of vigor;
[these are] the wind-born disease arising from *vāta*, and that which arises from *pitta* born of *pitta*.

A *ślaiṣmika* is one produced from phlegm; a *sāṃnipātika* is a collection [of humors]. A sick person is called *vyādhita*, *vikṛta*, *glāsnus*, *glāna*, *manda*, or *ātura*; he is also called *abhyānta*, *abhyamita*, *rugna*, *āmayāvin*, and *apaṭu*.

Its specific varieties are to be understood through the application of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*), such as: one afflicted by fever, one who itches, one with wind-disorders (*vātaka*), one suffering from consumption (*kṣaya*), and one with ringworm (*dadruṇa*). One who is faithful, upright, a believer, of good conduct, generous, compassionate, pure, and free from deceit—even if he were subject to transformation—would be released even from death.
(Rājñī 20.34) Upacāra, upacaryā, cikitsā, ruk-pratikriyā, nigraha, vedanā-niṣṭhā, kriyā, and upakrama are synonyms for medical treatment. (Rājñī 20.35)
Bhaiṣajya, bheṣaja, jaitra, agada, jāyu, auṣadha, āyuryoga, gadārāti, and amṛta— these are the terms by which it is called.
And that is said to be of five kinds, according to the specific application of each.
There are also decoction (rasa), powder (cūrṇa), decoction-liquid (kaṣāya), electuary (avaleha), and paste (kalka).
Decoction (rasa) is that which has been crushed on a stone and combined with divine substances;
powder (cūrṇa) is made from substances ground together; and decoction-liquid (kaṣāya) is made from those same substances boiled down.
From those [medicinal substances] when cooked, there should be an *avaleha* (linctus); from their paste (*kalka*) ground with honey and other ingredients, there are seven types known as:
digestive (*pācana*), purifying (*śodhanīya*), moistening (*kledana*), pacifying (*śama*), appetizing (*dīpana*), nourishing (*tarpaṇa*), and drying (*śoṣa*). (Rajni 20.39–40)

The digestive (pācana) is with half remaining; the purificatory (śodhana) consists of twelve parts; the moistening (kledana) consists of four parts, while the pacifying (śamana) is considered to consist of eight parts. The inflaming (dīpana) consists of six parts, and the satiating (tarpaṇa) consists of five parts.
Drying (*śoṣaṇa*) and the sixteenth part (*ṣoḍaśāṃśa*); these are declared to be the varieties of decoction.
Following the description of the tastes (*rasa*) and so forth, the learned indeed state that the after-drink (*anupāna*) should be known;
they have described this as "slow penetration" (*vilambikrāmaṇa*), and further, they have called this "digestion at night" (*rātripācana*).
That which is beneficial for oneself would be wholesome, life-prolonging, and salutary.
Indeed, *pāṭava*, *ārogya*, *agada*, and *anāmaya* signify freedom from disease;
while *kalpa*, *paṭu*, *ullāgha*, *nirātaṅka*, and *nirāmaya* likewise denote health.

One who is free from disease is called *agada*, healthy (*niruja*), and without affliction (*anātanka*). A physician is known as the best of healers (*agadakāra*), the remover of disease (*rogahārī*), one who follows the medical method (*bhiṣagvidhi*), a knower of diseases (*rogajña*), one who restores life (*jīvana*), the learned (*vidvān*), an expert in Āyurveda (*āyurvedin*), and a practitioner of healing (*cikitsaka*).

A physician who is a Brahmin, a master of medical science, pure, learned in the Vedas, of noble birth, skillful, steadfast, knowledgeable in the divisions of time, possessing a mind of faith, dexterous, wise, and righteous;
who is of good conduct, impartial, compassionate, free from malice, perfected in the sequence of mantras, peaceful, free from lust and greed, and of established fame—such a physician truly shines.
One who is undisciplined, harsh, greedy, diseased, or deficient in training [does not].
Even five physicians equal to Dhanvantari himself would not suffice [without this].
Indeed, the four aims of human life are made truly auspicious solely through the happiness of the senses; that [happiness] is subject only to the constant application of medicine.
And even that [medicine] yields its fruit only when dependent on the compassion of the physician. Therefore, in this world, there is no greater benefactor than such a person.

Just as kings, desiring victory, assemble in the arena of battle and display the valor initiated by their own arms through the rise of their might, so too are medicinal herbs gathered together in this [place] where they achieve success with superior potency; that Brahmin is called a physician himself, as confirmed even by the Śruti. Having properly uprooted [the herbs] grown in a pure location by a twice-born man who knows the principles of time and other factors, [he should prepare them].
Just as medicinal herbs, each according to its nature, draw back even those who have come within the domain of Yama by their superior qualities;
so too, by that [power] with which Brahmā digs for you, with which Bhṛgu digs for you,
with which Indra, Varuṇa, and Keśava dig for you—
"Therefore, I shall dig you up; grant me success, O great herb!
(Rajñī 20.53) Reciting this mantra with a disciplined mind, the brahmin, having dug up the great herb with a stake of *khadira* wood, should employ it according to the prescribed rite. (Rajñī 20.54)
Having manifested their power, the medicinal herbs, as well as the Earth herself, traveling from heaven to earth, spoke thus to one another:
"He whom we, by our own greatness, praise—even though he be a living being on the verge of death—shall never indeed perish.
(Rajni 20.55) Reassured and gladdened by the joyful King Soma, the medicinal herbs spoke these words together.

"O King, the Veda itself declares directly: 'Whosoever a twice-born man bestows medicine upon, we shall protect him immediately. "The king is indeed the lord of these twice-born ones, as recorded and recited in scripture; he exists for their success, even over those who desire a faultless brahmin as their own refuge.
Yet another, who is low in birth and conduct, being empty [of virtue], spreads through them out of pride; these [powers] become enraged and cast him down from the world."

Śambhu has here declared the eightfold science of Ayurveda, which consists of two and four branches: the determination of substances and their names, the treatment of diseases, the maintenance of bodily health, and the medical treatment for those afflicted by arrows, spirits, poisons, seizures, and children; as well as the knowledge of alchemy and the supreme elixirs that cause the body to become firm, along with the means to prolong life. Specifically, these are the eight branches: surgery (śalya), the treatment of diseases above the clavicle (śālākya), internal medicine (kāya), the treatment of diseases caused by spirits (bhūta), the treatment of poisons (viṣa), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), the treatment of aphrodisiacs (rasāyana), and the treatment of rejuvenation (vājīkaraṇa).
Some have declared that this [practice] is an elixir and an aphrodisiac for the ignorant.

Indeed, a skilled physician who knows the eight branches [of medicine], if he is deficient in even one limb [of knowledge], should be known as being limb-deficient; he is not to be praised in the royal court. (Rajni 20.59–60)
He was wise, discerning, learned, far-sighted, steadfast, intelligent, skilled, and of attained renown;
he was a knower of faults, one who sees afar, sagacious, endowed with wisdom, a knower, a master, a man of refined understanding, and profoundly insightful.
He was an expert in the sciences, well-trained, possessed of calculation, possessed of intellect, and accomplished.
One with an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass; a cultivator; one who is skillful, prudent, and wise;
proficient, trained, dexterous, well-initiated, of accomplished mind, and of refined intellect;
one who is thoroughly conversant, clever, learned, one who has performed his duties, and discerning.
Vidagdha, catura, prauḍha, boddhā, viśārada, sumedhāḥ, sumati, tīkṣṇa, prekṣāvān, vibudha,
and vidan; manīṣā, dhiṣaṇā, prajñā, dhāraṇā, śemuṣī, and mati.
Dhī is intellect, understanding, discernment, realization, and volition;
it is consciousness, cognition, perception, thought, intelligence, reflection, and the mind;
it is manifestation, awakening, the writing upon the heart, calculation, and intuition.
Grasping is the cause of disease; its manifestation is the symptom of disease.
Treatment is its remedy, and health is the cessation of illness. Maṇḍa, peyā, vilepī, and yavāgū are the various types of wholesome food.

*Drava* (liquid) is without rice; *maṇḍa* (scum) is mixed with rice; *peyā* (gruel) is accompanied by rice; *vilepī* (thick gruel) contains much rice; and *yavāgū* (thin gruel) has very little liquid. Cooked split pulses such as black gram (*māṣa*) and green gram (*mudga*) are designated as *sūpa* (soup).
Physicians say that a quarter-meal is wholesome; one should know that a half-meal is termed "eating.
A meal less than a quarter is for enjoyment, while any remainder should be known as leading to the production of wind-disorders (*vātadoṣa*).
Food is life, and eating consists of boiled rice, meat, and porridge.
Andha, bhissādana, bhojya, annādya, and likewise aśana;
bhojya, peya, as well as coṣya, lehya, khādya, and carvaṇa; and niṣpeya—these are known as the eight kinds of food that constitute *bhakṣya*. (Rajñī 20.71–72)
Vyañjana refers to soup, vegetables, and the like; miṣṭānna is known as a sweet dish, while temana is considered a seasoned condiment.
Upadaṃśa and vidaṃśa denote the same thing; it is also called saṃdhāna and rocaka.
Jemana, abhyavahāra, pratyavasāna, bhojana, and jagdhi all signify eating.
*Balbhanam*, *aśanam*, *svadanam*, *nighasa*, and *āhāra* denote eating; *nigaraṇam* and *nyādaḥ* denote swallowing.
*Jakṣaṇam*, *bhakṣaṇam*, *lehaḥ*, *svādanam*, *rasanam*, and *svadau* denote tasting.
*Carvaṇam*, *pānam*, *pītī*, *dhayanam*, and *cūṣaṇam* are various forms [of consuming].
Sweet, salty, bitter, astringent, sour, and pungent—
these six are called tastes because they are objects of the sense of taste in food and other substances. They say that sweetness is a state of longing, and it is observed in things such as sugarcane.
Lavaṇa is declared to be pungent (paṭu), and it is seen in rock salt and similar substances. Bitterness (tikta) is clearly tasted in the neem tree and similar things.
Astringency (kaṣāya) is called "dry" (tuvara), and it is found in betel nuts and other such items.
Sourness (*amla*) is found in the fruits of the *ciñcā*, *jambīra*, *mātuluṅga*, and so forth. Pungency (*kaṭu*), which is known as sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), is observed in *marīca* and similar substances.
Furthermore, the sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*) promotes the growth of hair and bestows stability, strength, vitality, and virility upon the body.

Through excessive consumption, salt produces the defects of coldness in urinary disorders (*prameha*), numbness, and dullness. Salted taste creates relish, kindles the digestive fire, promotes digestion, imparts sweetness, and provides strength;
yet through excessive consumption, it brings about old age, increases *pitta*, causes whiteness of the teeth, and produces skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
Bitter (tikta) destroys parasites, leprosy, the distress of fever, cough, and burning sensations; it stimulates digestion and improves the appetite.
However, if consumed excessively and daily by mortals, it bestows severe consumption (rājayakṣmā).
That which is called astringent (kaṣāya) suppresses swelling, improves the complexion of the body, stimulates digestion, and acts as a digestive.
When consumed excessively, it destroys vitality, causes the skin to become flaccid, and makes the body pale.
That which is called sour (amla) produces pleasure and provides relish; it digests the fire and bestows sharpness.
However, when over-consumed, it causes vertigo, leprosy, phlegm-induced pallor, blackness of the skin, and cough.

Pungent (kaṭu) [taste] destroys phlegm (kapha), throat disorders, swelling, weak digestion, and diseases such as leprosy; yet, if consumed excessively, it brings about consumption (kṣaya) and the loss of vitality and strength. Pungent and astringent (kaṣāya) tastes remove phlegm, while sweet (mādhurya) and bitter (tikta) tastes destroy bile (pitta).
The tastes known as pungent and sour, along with wind (vāyu), carry away [diseases]; thus, these taken in pairs remove all ailments.
Sweet and sour, salty and sour, pungent and bitter, pungent and salty, and bitter and salty—these are the combinations of mixed tastes.
Salt and sweet are opposed, as are pungent and sweet, and bitter and sweet;
yet the astringent is common to all, maintaining its equality everywhere.
The sweet assumes acidity, salt maintains its proper state, the one called pungent likewise assumes bitterness, and that named astringent assumes sweetness.

Sourness produces a relish for bitterness, and pungency ultimately turns into bitterness; thus has the condition of these six tastes been described according to their own post-digestive transformations (*vipāka*). Sweet, sour, pungent, bitter, salty, and astringent—these six tastes undergo various combinations through mutual intermingling in successive order.
If the first of the [six] primary tastes, such as sweet and the rest, is joined with each subsequent one individually,
there are fifteen varieties of combinations of two. Likewise, through five permutations,
when the first taste is followed by its immediate neighbor as heard previously, [there are further combinations].
By all four methods, ten divisions are declared for the first;
likewise, six divisions are recorded for the second, three for the third, and one for the fourth—
these twenty are the divisions of the triads.
The first two [notes] are [placed] three times with no interval between them, through their conjunction with each of the six following notes one by one.
When the second [note] is omitted, there are four [notes], joined each with its own following note one by one.
But when the first [note] is omitted, there would be five [notes], joined each with its own following note one by one.
These fifteen varieties of the fourfold division have been taught in sequence.

Then, the six varieties of the fivefold division are recorded as resulting from the omission of each one [of the five] in turn. One is formed by the combination of all; thus, there are seven in the detailed enumeration.
Thus, sixty-three varieties of tastes have been briefly described;
if Śaṅkara himself knows their countless gradations.
That which is nourishing, providing growth, being nourished, excellent, and bestowing corpulence—[is such a taste].
It increases vigor, is aphrodisiac, and acts as a seed for virility (vājīkaraṇa). It is nourishing, satiating, pleasing, and gratifying.
It causes secretions, is expectorant, induces lacrimation from the eyes, and is laxative.
Thus, having described this entire section on the treatment of various diseases and ailments— including the application of diet and wholesome regimens not explicitly mentioned by the physician here—
let that learned man further declare those causal factors of disease which,
though [this work] is like the sun for dispelling the mass of darkness consisting of hundreds of illnesses, have alas been caused to reappear by the enemy. (Rājñī 20.103)
This twentieth chapter, beginning with the word *gada*, concerning the Lord Śrī Nṛsiṃha, has been completed by him as an ornament for the jewel that is the crown of names. (Rājanighaṇṭu,
Sattvādivarga 20.104)

Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are said to be the three qualities (guṇas) of men; within them, respectively, reside these humors (doṣas): phlegm, bile, and wind. Sattva is phlegm, rajas is bile, and tamas is indeed wind.
The measure of a substance follows after each individual person.
*Sattva* is the expansion of the mind; likewise, stability is dependent upon *sattva*.
*Rajas* is staining, excess, turbidity, and the delusion of the intellect.
Darkness, the dimness of gloom, blindness, mental derangement, delusion,
the covering of the heart, obscurity, deep darkness,
and infatuation; the wind, the bearer of fragrance, the air, the purifier, the one of great power.
The wind that touches, the bearer of fragrance, the breeze, the swift-moving Marut;
the breather, Mātariśvan, the sky-dweller, Māruta, Anila;
the agitator, the life-breath of the world, Samīra, and the ever-moving one.
Javana, Pṛṣadaśva, Tarasvī, Prabhañjana,
Pradhāvana, Anavasthāna, Dhūnana, Moṭana, and Khaga—
these and other winds circulate within the body through the network of channels (nāḍīcakra).
Fearing excessive prolixity, I have not explained them at length.
(Rājñī 21.9) For one whose self is under the sway of the three defects permeated by qualities such as *sattva*, both the internal and external nature is fully described. (Rājñī 21.10)

One with a predominance of *sattva* is wealthy, pure, a believer, firm-minded, well-proportioned in limb, righteous, handsome, and possesses many offspring; he is fond of very sweet foods such as milk, a donor who respects the qualities of the recipient, extremely eloquent, compassionate, even-tempered, and fair-complexioned; his dreams involve thick clouds or snow, and he is characterized by phlegm (*śleṣman*).

One with a predominance of *rajas* mostly eats salty, sour, bitter, pungent, and hot food; he is clever, mature, neither too thin nor too stout, yet develops premature gray hair; he is possessed of frequent outbursts of anger.

The person of a *drāghīyas* (long) constitution has a large female disposition; he is generous when asked for something with a motive, possesses a fair complexion, is radiant with the luster of gold and other metals, and is dreamy, having a bilious (*pittātmaka*) temperament.

He is prone to sleep, talkative, very crooked, cruel-minded, and generally atheistic. He is chiefly devoted to stale, very cold, and tasteless food, and is lazy. He has excessive pride in his undertakings, gives at improper times as he pleases, and becomes emaciated. In dreams, he travels through the sky with a dark body, is subject to wind disorders (*vātūlaka*), and is of a tamasic nature. (Rajni 21.12–13)
When the qualities of *sattva* and the others are present there in great measure, mingled together, this should be known by the wise as being of a mixed nature (*miśraprakṛtika*).
When *sattva* and the others are mixed with *rajas*, it is the best; when *sattva* and the others are mixed with *tamas*, [it is middling].

The middle [state] is mixed with *rajas*, while the lowest involves a mixture of all the qualities (*guṇa*). *Sattva* quickly spreads the expansion of the mind and bestows supreme awakening; *rajas*, however, creates turbidity in the mind and initiates indetermination (*avyākṛti*).
Alas! *Tamas* grants blindness to the heart, conceals the intellect from its own true nature, continuously binds it to dullness, and brings about constant drowsiness.
Vāta is spontaneous, light, cold, and dry; it perceives subtle touches and causes pricking sensations.
Due to its sweetness, it becomes provoked by food during the time of clouds (the rainy season), in the afternoon, at dawn, and when food has been digested.
Pitta is bitter and sour in taste, substantial, hot, liquid, and sharp; this [pitta] is abundant in the month of Madhu (spring).
At the end of the rainy season, at midnight, at midday, and during the digestion of food, phlegm (śleṣman) becomes aggravated.
It is heavy, smooth, soft, stable, as well as unctuous, sharp, cold, sluggish, and sweet.
It is greatly provoked in the cold season and spring, at the onset of night, in the forenoon, and after eating.
I shall now correctly explain, in brief, those various divisions of the three *doṣas* that arise from their increase and decrease. Among them,
when each one increases individually, there are three divisions consisting of the three types of increase and decrease.
In that regard, for each single object there are six [qualities], and thus they become twelve.
Through the increase and mutual permutation of these, there are six; and by the triple increase, there is a seventh.
These are: increased, mutually increased, more increased, and most increased.
Through degrees of intensity, these [five] become sixfold; thus, there are twenty-five.
Likewise, in the case of decrease (*kṣaya*), there are as many; therefore, fifty are taught.
Furthermore, there are another six: one that is increasing, one that is mutually equal, and one that is decreasing.
Through two increases and one decrease, and again through the reversal of what was stated, there are six more;
all these twelve multiplied by ten result in sixty-two as they have been declared.
The sixty-third is the final division, which is the state of the three in their primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Having thus understood these specific variations of the three types of *doṣas* according to their true nature, the physician should then administer the treatments appropriate for each particular state. Time (*kāla*), however, is also called *velā*, *samaya*, *anehā*, *diṣṭa*, *cala*, *avasara*, and *asthira*.
This very [time] is indeed spoken of in three ways: as past, as present, and likewise as future.
(Rājñī 21.27) In the past, there is that which has occurred (*vṛtta*), the remote past (*atīta*), yesterday’s (*hyastana*), the departed (*nisṛta*), and the gone (*gata*).
In the present, there is that which is occurring (*bhavat*), today’s (*adyatana*), and the current moment (*adhunātana*). (Rājñī 21.28)
*Anāgata* means "will be" in the future; *śvastana* and *pragetana* mean "of tomorrow" and "of the early morning.
*Vartsyat* and *vartiṣyamāṇa* mean "about to happen," while *āgāmi* and *bhāvi* mean "coming" and "to be.
However, *sādhāraṇa* and *sāmānya* are common [terms] that apply everywhere.
The qualifier and the qualified both reside simultaneously in a single location.
The fourth part, the fourth portion, is likewise described as being "slightly" or "to some extent.

[He is the one] whose crown is revealed by its union with the celestial Gaṅgā—the waters of which flow with a profuse, spontaneous, and unrestrained abundance, clear and bright like the nectar-like rays of the moon that serves as his ornament.
I bow to Śambhu, whose limbs are concealed by Gaurī, who is resplendent with the Meru, Kailāsa, his playful embrace, and the beauty of his waters, and who is swift in his praise.

When the utterance of a word is heavy with all its components and measures sixty syllables, that is the standard for time called a *pala*. Ten of those make a *kṣaṇa*, and six of those make a *nāḍī*; seven and a half of those make a *prahara*, and eight of those are declared by the wise to be one day and night (*ahorātra*).
A fortnight consists of fifteen days and nights; both of these [fortnights] constitute a month.
A year is said to consist of twelve months.
Furthermore, the six seasons are to be understood by means of two months each, beginning with Caitra.
By these three [groups] taken three at a time, respectively, the equinoxes and solstices occur.
A *pala* is said to be a *vighaṭikā*, and twenty-three of those constitute a *nāḍī*.
A *nāḍī* is called a *ghaṭikā*, and two of those make a *muhūrta*.

A *yāma* is called a *prahara*; it is a portion of the day, a division of the day. *Ahorātra*, *divārātri*, *ahardiva*, *aharniśa*, *ghasra*, *dina*, *divasa*, *vāsara*, *bhāsvara*, and *divā* all refer to the day.
Forenoon, afternoon, midday, and evening are its divisions.
Dawn is the beginning of the day, the end of the night;
it is also called *pratyuṣas*, *uṣas*, *vyuṣṭa*, *aharmukha*, *kalya*, *prage*, *prāhṇa*, and *prabhātaka*.
Ātapa is the light of day, the sun’s radiance, the splendor of day,
the illumination of the sun, the shining forth, that which destroys darkness, and the heat of the sun.
Rocis, dīpti, dyuti, śocis, tviṣ, ojas, bhās, ruci, and prabhā are synonyms for light.
Vibhā, lokaprakāśa, tejas, ojāyitam, and ruk;
sāyaṃsandhyā, dinānta, niśādi, and divasātyaya; sāyaṃ, pitṛprasū, and pradoṣa, which is the beginning of night (niśāmukha). (Rajñī 21.43–44)

Chāyā follows the sun, is dark, fears light, and is without heat; she is known as fearlessness, the absence of heat, and that which is merged with existence. Śarvarī, kṣaṇadā, rātri, niśā, śyāmā, and tamasvinī are synonyms for night.
Tamī, triyāmā, śayanī, kṣapā, yāmavatī, and tamā;
naktaṃ, niśīthinī, doṣā, tārābhūṣā, and vibhāvarī;
jyotiṣmatī, tārakiṇī, kālī, and she is also called kalāpinī.
That [night] endowed with moonlight is called *jyautsnī*, while that possessed of darkness is *tamisrā*. Midnight is *ardharātra*, and it is also known as *madhyarātra*.
Moonlight is *jyotsnā*, *candrikā*, *cāndrī*, *kaumudī*, and *kāmavallabhā*.
The moonlight, the moonstone, and the cool wave of nectar; beauty, supreme splendor, radiance, luster, shadow,
auspicious glow, fortune, Lakṣmī, the beloved of Dakṣa, renown, light, brilliance, Umā, and Ramā.
*Tamas*, *tamisra*, *timira*, *dhvānta*, *saṃtamasa*, *tamaḥ*, *andhakāra*, *bhūchāya*, and that which is dense (*ghana*) is called *āndhatamasa*.
*Ātapa* is pungent and dry; *chāyā* is sweet and cool.

Moonlight is the pacifier of the three humors (*tridoṣa*), while darkness is the cause of all diseases. The beginning of the lunar fortnight is called *prathamā*, *pakṣati*, and *pratipad*. The end of the fortnight is the separation of the sun and moon; it is the *parvan* and the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*).

The second parvan, however, is the extreme conjunction of the moon and the sun. Beginning from the first day (pratipad), these fifteen lunar days (tithis), starting with the second and so on, are to be known in sequence within a fortnight; and a fortnight is of two kinds: bright (sita) and dark (asita).
The waxing fortnight is called *sitā*, while the bright, pure, and auspicious fortnight is known as *śuklā* or *śudi*.
The dark, impure, and black fortnight is remembered as *asitā*, *kṛṣṇā*, or *bahulā*, and also as *vadi*.
In either case, it consists of days numbering eighty-four.
The circle of physicians is intended for the application of medical treatment.
The full moon night is known as *pūrṇimā*, *paurṇamāsī*, *jyautsnī*, *indumatī*, and *sitā*;
it should be understood as the former *anumati*, while the latter is *rākā*.
The *darśa* occurs on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), which is the conjunction of the sun and the moon.
That [first day] is considered *sinīvālī*, while the second is regarded as *kuhū*.
A fortnight (*pakṣa*) consists of half a month and comprises fifteen nights.
Two fortnights constitute a month, and those months are twelve, beginning with Caitra.
Caitra, Caitrika, and Caitrī are its names; it is also known as Madhu and Kālādika.
Vaiśākha, Mādhava, and Rādha are synonyms for Jyeṣṭha, which is also called Śukra and Tapa.

Āṣāḍha is called Śuci; Śrāvaṇika, Śrāvaṇa, and Nabhā are also [names for the month]. Bhādra, Bhādrapada, and Prauṣṭhapada are synonyms for Nabhas and Nabhasya. Īṣa and Āśvayuja are names for Āśvina, which is also known as Śārada.
Kārttika is also called Bāhula, Ūrja, and Kārttikika.
Mārga is Sahā, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Āgrahāyaṇika. Pauṣa is Pauṣika, Taiṣa, Sahasya, and also Haimana.

Māgha is Tapas, while Phālguna, the end of the year, is Tapasya. Two months each, beginning with Caitra, constitute the six seasons in sequence by name: Vasanta (spring) consists of Madhu and Mādhava; likewise, Śukra and Śuci are the summer (nidāgha).
Nabhas and Nabhasya are the months when the arrival of clouds occurs; from Īṣa and Urja, they say autumn (śarad) begins.
Hemanta consists of Sahas and Sahasya; Tapas and Tapasya follow in sequence as Śiśira.
These six seasons, beginning with Vasanta, are each said by the wise to consist of two months.
The king of seasons is Vasanta (Spring); it is also known as Surabhi, Mādhava, Madhu, Puṣpamāsa, Pikānanda, Kānta, and Kāmarasa.
Nidāgha, Ūṣmaka, Gharmas, Grīṣma, Ūṣmāgama, and Tapas are synonyms for the summer season.
The hot season is the time of scorching heat; it is known as *uṣṇa* and the arrival of heat. The rainy season is the monsoon period, the end of summer, and the arrival of the clouds;
it is the delight of the peacock and the joy of the *cātaka* bird. (Rājñī 21.77–78)
The end of the rainy season is *śarad*; the conclusion of the monsoon is *meghānta* and *prāvṛḍatyaya*. Hemanta dispels the heat; it is the end of autumn and the arrival of snow.
Śiśira is characterized by trembling, cold, heaps of frost, and biting chill.

Thus, the six seasons have been declared by name in their proper order: Surabhi, Nidāgha, Meghakāla, Śarad, Hima, and Śiśira, which constitute the year (hāyana) in succession. Each season occurs daily starting from the time of sunrise, lasting for ten *nāḍikās*. (Rajñī 21.81–82)
Beginning from the sun's entry into Capricorn (makara), there shall be the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
After the sun's movement into Cancer (karkaṭaka), it is called the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
When the sun's transit occurs sequentially into Libra and Aries, [the two solstices follow].
Then there are the two equinoxes; these two are also known as the *viṣuva*s. Those who know the times have declared sixty years beginning with Prabhava.
Autumn (*śarat*), *saṃvatsara*, *abda*, *hāyana*, *vatsara*, and *samā* are synonyms for a year.
In spring, the wind blows from the south; in the rainy season, from the west;
in the autumnal season, from the north; and in the winter and early winter (hemanta-śaiśira), from the east. Furthermore, the eastern wind is sweet, unctuous, and endowed with pungent flavor.

Guruka pacifies burning sensations, increases vāta, and destroys pitta. Dakṣiṇa possesses six tastes, is beneficial for the eyes, increases strength, pacifies raktapitta, and bestows comfort, luster, and vigor.
The western wind is sharp, it dries up phlegm and fat;
when vitiated, it immediately takes away the life-force of embodied beings and causes emaciation.
The northern wind is unctuous, mild, and sweet.
It has an astringent taste, is cold, and provokes the bodily humors (*doṣas*).
Having established a single limit, that by which the regions to the east and west are thus designated is known as *diś* (direction).
The directions are known as *dig*, *āśā*, *harit*, *kāṣṭhā*, and *kakub*; they are also called *nideśinī*.
According to the division of space, they are conceived as being tenfold.
The luminaries, such as the sun and others, follow the sequence of the rotation of the circle of light (*jyotiścakra*).
Because [the sun] always rises from it, that direction is called "East" (pūrva). East, South, West, and North—
these four are the great directions in the order of circumambulation.
The eastern direction is called *pūrvā*, *prācī*, *purā*, *maghonī*, *aindrī*, and *māghavatī*.
The southern direction is *dakṣiṇā*, *avācī*, *yāmī*, and *vaivasvatī*.
The western direction is *paścimā*, *pratīcī*, *vāruṇī*, and *pratyak*.

The northern direction belongs to Kubera; it is divine and is also called *udīcī*. The intermediate space between each pair of directions, known as a corner (*koṇa*), is called one of the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*) as well as a sub-direction (*upadiś*).
The Āgneyī direction lies between the east and the south; that called Nairṛtyā lies between the south and the west.
The Vāyavyā lies between the north and the west; the Aiśānī lies between the east and the north.
Above is the upward direction, and below is known as the downward direction.
The word *antaḥ* is said to mean "internal," while *antaraṃ* refers to that which is "intermediate" or "in-between.
(RājNī 21.100) A space measured by eight *yavas* should be known as clearly defined by the name "finger" (*aṅgula*).
Twenty-four of those [fingers] constitute a *hasta*, and four *hastas* make one [dhanu]. (RājNī 21.101)
Two thousand *daṇḍas* make one *krośa*, and four of those make one *yojana*;
this is indeed the stated method for measuring distance in the land.
Thus, by way of introduction and because of its utility for a physician, I have [spoken].
Thus, the pair known as *parimāṇa* and *unmāna* is described.
Among these, that which consists of four handfuls of grain for a man is called a *niṣṭikā*;
twice that is to be known as an *āṣṭikā*, and twice that again is a *kuḍava*.
Four of those [prasthas] make one *āḍhakī*, and four of those make one *droṇa*;
twenty of those [droṇas] make one *khārī*.

A quantity measured by two *godhūmas* is said to be one *guñjā*; with that [guñjā] plus a half, there is one *valla*; four *vallas* are considered by physicians to be one *māṣa*, and four of those [make one *karṣa*].
A *niṣka* is said to be one and a half *yugas*; four of those make a *karṣa*, and likewise four of those make a *pala*. A hundred of those make a *tulā*, and twenty *tulās* make a *bhāra*.

Thus, by reciting this section—which elucidates the appropriate calculation of time and place following the sequence of the three qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and which describes the three defects introduced therein—a wise person, having attained renown, proceeds to the assemblies of heaven; for this work brings about the wondrous destruction of the disease of the path of rebirth through the power of the most excellent and radiant physicians.

In the thick darkness of battle, where the dust of the earth is raised by the divine banners fluttering on horses galloping in the embrace of combat, and where the courage of enemies is brought to rest,
even this twenty-first section of the work composed by the virtuous Narahari— this certain group beginning with "Sattva"— finds its peace within the crest-jewel of the Nāmanirmāṇa.
In this chapter on Miscellaneous and Other Groups (Miśrakādivarga),

we shall proclaim the great and noble section known as the Mixed Group (Vimiśraka), for the purpose of describing the nature of those medicinal substances which have been combined with one another and designated by various names by the authors of medical formulations. Rajni 22.1.
Long pepper, black pepper, and ginger— these three mixed together are called *trikaṭu*,
*tryūṣaṇa*, *tryūṣa*, *kaṭutraya*, and *kaṭutrika*.
Harītakī, āmalaka, and vibhītaka— these three [are known as triphalā].
*Triphalā* and *triphalī*, as well as *phalatraya* and *phalatrika*, refer to the three myrobalans. When the fruits of the grape (*drākṣā*), *kāśmarya*, and the date palm (*kharjūrī*) are combined,
they are known as *madhuratriphalā*, the triad of sweet fruits.
Jātīphala, pūgaphala, and the bud of lavaṅga—
these are called the fragrant triphalā, and it is also known as the surabhitriphalā.
Sandalwood, saffron, and water— this triad is the most excellent half [of the set].
That which is combined with one-third part of saffron is called *adyapuṣpaka*.
Saindhava, viḍa, and rucaka—
these mixed together are declared to be the "three salts" (*lavaṇatraya*) and likewise known as *trilavaṇa*.

Sarjikṣāra, yavakṣāra, and ṭaṅkakṣāra are declared to be the "three alkalis" (kṣāratraya) and are also celebrated as "trikṣāra. Harītakī, nāgara, and jaggery— these three in equal parts [constitute another formulation].

It is said that there are three equalities and a triple equality. When sugar, honey, and clarified butter are combined, they are called the "triple sweet" (*madhuratraya*); this is also known as *trimadhu* or *madhutraya*.

Mixed with molasses-born, snow-born, and honey-born [sugars], it is "three sugars" (triśarkarā) and "three sweets" (trisitā); in the case of the three whites, it is "three whites" (sitātraya). When combined with black collyrium (kālāñjana), it is flower-collyrium (puṣpāñjana) and juice-collyrium (rasāñjana).
They call the three ointments *tryañjana* and the three ointments *añjanatraya*.
Wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*)— these three combined together constitute the "three humors" (*doṣatraya*),
which may also be called *tridoṣa* or *doṣatritaya*.
That place where wind, bile, and phlegm always attain a state of equilibrium is called "balanced by the three humors" (*tridoṣasama*),
as well as "having the three humors in balance" (*samadoṣatraya*).
Furthermore, the triad consisting of *bṛhatī*, *agnidamanī*, and *duḥsparśā* [is also so designated].
The three types of *kaṇṭakārī* are called *trikaṇṭa* and *kaṇṭakatraya*.
*Nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, and *mustā*—these three, each weighing one *karṣa*, are known as the *trikārṣika*.
When combined with *guḍūcī*, that group is called *cāturbhadraka*.

Equal parts of cinnamon (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), and clove (*pattraka*) constitute the *trisugandhi*; when combined with *nāgakeśara*, it is called *trijātaka*. When these same ingredients—cinnamon, cardamom, and clove—are joined with black pepper (*marica*), it is known as *cāturjātaka*.
This, along with other pungent substances, is called *cāturjātaka*.
When equal parts of *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *aguru*, *karpūra*, and *kāśmīra* are combined,
this divine unguent (*devakardama*) is fit for one who wears the moon as a crown.
Yakṣadhūpa consists of camphor, agallochum, musk, and kakkola;
all these combined together are desired as yakṣakardama.
[It is] composed of equal parts of saffron, agallochum, musk, camphor, and sandalwood.

They declare this *yakṣakardama* to be the exclusive domain for those solely intent on the worship of the Three-Eyed One (Śiva). When camphor, *kakkola*, clove, jasmine flower, and *guvāka* nutmeg— these five ingredients combined in equal proportions— are joined together, it becomes the enchanting *pañcasugandhika*.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara—
when all these are combined together, it is called pañcakolaka.
[Rajni 22.24] Nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, and vetasa— [their] barks...
When all these are combined together, it is called *pañcavetasa*.
*Śāliparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārikā*,
and likewise *gokṣuraka*— this is the minor *pañcamūla*.

Bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarya, and likewise pāṭalā— when all these are combined, it constitutes the mahāpañcamūla (great five roots). When these two sets of five roots are combined together, [it forms the daśamūla].
Then the physicians declared that the ten-roots (daśamūla) compound is rich in qualities;
when combined with balā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, and the two types of sūpyaparṇī,
this constitutes the middle five-roots (pañcamūla) compound.
Guḍūcī, gokṣura, mūṣalī, muṇḍikā, and śatāvarī—
this combination of five is known as Pañcāmṛta.
Cow’s clarified butter, curd, milk, honey, and sugar combined [form the other five].

The supreme divine five nectars (pañcāmṛta) should be known as combined together in one place. Cow urine, cow dung, milk, clarified butter from a cow, and curd— these, when joined according to their proper application, are declared to be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

The leaves, bark, flowers, fruits, and roots of the *nimb* tree, when combined, are known as "the five *nimb*s" (*pañcanimba*); that group of five bitter *nimb*s is called the "five-fold bitter *nimb*" (*tiktanimbapañcaka*). *Kola*, pomegranate, *vṛkṣāmla*, *cullakī*, and *amlavetasa*— The above is the translation of the provided Sanskrit verses.
