The fruit is designated as *pañcāmla*; it is known as the "five-sour fruits. By mixing equal portions of *jambīra*, *nāraṅga*, sour *vetasa*, *tintiḍīka*, and *bījapūraka*, this second variety, the "five-sour fruits," is declared.
Cāṅgerī, likuca, and amlavetasa combined with jambīraka, pūraka, and nāraṅga constitute *phalaṣāḍava*;
furthermore, *piṇḍāmla* and *bījāmlaka* are mentioned twice along with ambaṣṭhā—these two groups together, when joined with *karamarda* and *nimbu*, are known as the category called *amlavarga*.
Tailakanda, sudhākanda, kroḍakanda, and rudantikā;
These five, known as the "Efficacious Medicines," are endowed with the eyes of serpents. The flower, root, fruit, leaf, and bark of the *śirīṣa* tree—
this formulation is called "the enemy of insects" (*kīṭāri*) and is designated as the "Five-Śirīṣa" (*pañcaśairīṣaka*).

If the bark, leaf, flower, root, and fruit of a single tree are combined together in one place, that is designated as "the five-fold part" (*pañcāṅga*). Vidārigandhā, Bṛhatī, Pṛśniparṇī, Nidigdhikā, [Śālaparṇī, and Prapuṇḍarīka constitute the group known as] Vidārigandhādi.

And *śvadaṃṣṭrā*— this is declared to be the group known as the "five-fold" (*pañcagaṇa*). With *atyamlaparṇī*, *kāṇḍīra*, *mālākanda*, and two types of *śūraṇa*, this group is called the "five *śūraṇas*" (*pañcaśūraṇa*).
Śṛṅgika, kālakūṭa, mustaka, vatsanābhaka,
and saktuka— this is the combination known as the Great Five Poisons (mahāpañcaviṣa).
Snuhī, arka, karavīra, lāṅgalī, and viṣamuṣṭikā.
Those possessed of wisdom say that these five are the "poisonless poisons":
the urine of cows, goats, ewes, buffaloes, and donkeys, when mixed together,
constitutes what is known as the "five urines" (mūtrapañcaka).
Gold, silver, and copper—these three together are called the "three metals" (*triloha*). When combined with tin and lead, they call that the "five metals" (*pañcaloha*).
Gold, silver, copper, tin, and black iron in equal proportions [constitute this].
It should be understood that the second [component] of the planetary limb is the "five metals" (pañcalohaka).
The group known as the "five alkalis" (pañcakṣāra) is said to consist of the alkalis of barley, muṣkaka, sarja, palāśa, and sesame. (Rājñī 22.47–48)

With equal parts of kāca, saindhava, sāmudra, viḍa, and sauvarcala salts, there is what is called *pañcalavaṇa* (the five-salt mixture); when combined with clay, it is known by six names. [One should also use] the roots of dhava, apāmārga, kuṭaja, lāṅgalī, sesame, and muṣka.

These alkalis, when combined, are declared to be the "sixfold alkali" (kṣāra-ṣaṭka). This group consists of the seven bodily constituents (dhātu) known as plasma, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen, which provide stability to the body.
Cinnabar, mercury, sasyaka,
vaikrānta, kānta, abhraka, mākṣika, and vimala— these eight are the great minerals (mahārasas).
Khecarāñjana, kaṅguṣṭha, gandhāla, gairika, and kṣiti— [these are the minor minerals].

The wise declare that the secondary minerals (*uparasa*) are those mixed with *śaileya* and *añjana*. They say there are eight common minerals (*sāmānyarasa*), including *kampilla*, *gaurī*, *capalā*, *kaparda*, *śailasindūraka*, *vahnijāra*, *pāṣāṇabhedaka*, and *vodaraśṛṅgī*. 22.54–55.
The group known as the eight metals (*aṣṭaloha*) is described by the wise as being composed of the five metals together with *kānta*, *muṇḍaka*, and *tīkṣṇaka*.
[The decoction is made] from *śigru*, root of *mūlaka*, *palāśa*, *cukrikā*, *citraka*, fresh ginger (*ārdraka*), and *nimba*.
The first ten [alkalis] are proclaimed as being derived from sugarcane, *śaikharika*, and *mocaka*.

(RājN 22.57) The urines of the elephant, buffalo, camel, cow, horse, ram, donkey, man, and woman—where these ten have been diligently collected together, they appear in the scriptures under the designation "the group of ten urines. (RājN 22.58)

This great formulation known as "Jīvakādi" (beginning with Jīvaka), consisting of Jīvaka, Karṣabhaka, the two types of Medā, the two types of Kākolī, the two types of Sūpyaparṇī, and Madhūka, shines forth here as a sweet-toned remedy for longevity. Jīvaka, Karṣabhaka, the two Medās, the two Kākolīs, Vṛddhi, and Vṛddhikā— these are the components.
In one place, this group of eight is proclaimed as the *militaireta*.
With *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, and *haridrā*, along with *vacā*, *śaileya*, *candana*, *murā*, *karcūra*, and *mustā*,
it is declared as the "all-herbs" (*sarvauṣadha*) mixture.
Cumin, black pepper, ginger, cardamom,
coriander, turmeric, long pepper, and black pepper— this is considered the group known as *veśavāra*.
Dried *āmalaka* rinds combined with all these medicinal herbs [are also used].
When this preparation is made, it is known as *sugandhāmalaka*.
Rice flour mixed with grapes, pomegranate, dates, plantains, and sugar,
along with parched grain flour, honey, and ghee, is declared to be a nourishing tonic (*saṃtarpaṇa*).
A mixture made of roasted barley flour (*saktu*) smeared with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), thoroughly saturated with cold water, and neither too clear nor too thick, is called *mantha*.
Pomegranate, *kiṃśuka*, lac, *bandhūka*, and that which is called *niśā* (turmeric)—these [are used for coloring]. 22.65–66.
Safflower and madder— these constitute the red group (raktavarga).
Conch-shell, pearl-oyster, cowrie-shells, combined with *khaṭinī* and white [substances],
as well as roasted stone-grit— this is declared to be the white group (śuklavarga).
Bhārgī, śaṭī, puṣkara, vatsabīja, durālabhā, śṛṅgī, paṭola,
tiktā, kirāta, viśva, indrakaṇā, indrabīja, dhānya, and tikta suradāru—
this formulation known as the eighteen-ingredient (aṣṭādaśāṅga) yoga should be combined with daśamūla.
This one [type] should be known as beginning with *bhāryā* and so forth; the second, however, begins with *kirātaka* and so forth.

(Rajni 22.69) If one takes curd weighing thirty-two *palas*, eight *palas* of sugar-candy, and half a *pala* of black pepper, combined with cinnamon and cardamom of equal weight, and mixed with honey and clarified butter each weighing half that amount—all these being purified and joined together in a vessel and cooled with ice—it becomes *śikhariṇī*, which is fit for the enjoyment of Śrīkaṇṭha due to its excellent qualities. (Rajni 22.70)

Having understood this section as named "The Mixed" (*miśraka*) because it describes various mixed formulations, the wise physician should employ a compound known by the names found therein together with its "relatives. Lakṣmī herself delights in the absence of fear; Umā is eternally united with Śiva; Vāṇī is the beloved of the Four-faced One (Brahmā); and Śrī is equal to him—she who has taken refuge in this [remedy].

Thus, in this work, the twenty-second section, known as the *Miśraka* (Miscellaneous) division, has reached its conclusion within the crest-jewel of nomenclature for the Lord Nṛsiṃha, composed by the wise.
In the section on synonymous terms (*ekārthavarga*):
*śrī* and *lakṣmī* are known to mean "fruit"; *asana* is the *bījavṛkṣaka* tree;
*śālūka* refers to the lotus-root (*padmakanda*); and *sadāpuṣpa* refers to the *ravidruma* tree. (Rajni 23.1)

*Kubera* is in *nandivṛkṣa*, and likewise *gokaṇṭa* is in *gokṣura*; *dantaphala* is in *pippalī*, and *kaseru* is in *bhadramustaka*. *Nāgarotthā* and *kaccharuhā* are in *aṅkola* and *dīrghakīlaka* respectively.
*Vallakī* refers to the *sallakī* tree; *pūraka*, however, is the *mātuluṅga*. *Brahmaghnī* is the *kumārī*; *gūḍhamallikā* is the *aṅkola*.
*Ativiṣā*, *śvetavacā*, and *upakuñcī* are synonyms for *sthūlajīraka*.
Kavaca is the name for parpaṭaka; lavaṇa refers to that born from the ocean (sea salt).
Bṛhattvak is found in saptaparṇa, as are kāmbhojī and vākucī. Kīṭapādī is the name for haṃsapādī, while kunaṭī is manaḥśilā.
They call Vaikuṇṭha *arjaka*, while *tamālinī* is found in *bhūdhātrī*. *Śatakunda* occurs in *śarīra*, and likewise *agnikāṣṭha* in *aguru*.
*Sūkṣmapattrī* is in *śatāvarī*, and [the term] *kṣīraparṇī* is in *arka*.
*Śauṇḍī* is known as *pippalī*; likewise, *madanī* refers to musk (*kastūrī*).
*Brahmaparṇī* is recorded as being *pṛśniparṇī*, and it is also called *citraparṇī*. *Chattraparṇa* refers to *saptaparṇa*, while *pīluparṇī* is *tuṇḍikā*.
The best of leafy vegetables is the eggplant (*vṛntāka*); *śaṅgara* is said to be *śami*. *Goraṭa* refers to the *viṭkhadira*; *tuṇḍī* is the wild *bimbikā*.
*Viṣṇugupta* is the root of *cāṇakya*; *anantā* is *yavāsaka*.
*Kapikacchu* is *ātmaguptā*; *vātapotha* is found in the *kiṃśuka*.
*Rajanī* should be known as yellow (*pītā*); the *bodhivṛkṣa* is the *pippala*.
*Uśīra* is *samagandhi*; in *hiṅgula* there is *cūrṇapārada*.
Asafoetida (hiṅgu) is that which has an unrestrained fragrance; *godanta* refers to things with a cadaverous smell (*visragandhika*).
They call the *śamyā* "Īśāna," while the owl is termed "day-blind" (*divāndha*).
*Payasyā* is [the name for] *kṣīrakākolī*, and *śatavedhī* is for the *amlavetasa*.
*rocanī* is known as *nārikela*, and *cāruhā* is said to be *bhūdhātrī*.
They say *priyā* refers to *priyaṅgu*, while *kharāhvā* is used for *ajamoda*. *Tagara* is *daṇḍahastī*, and *laśuna* is known as *rasona*.
*Tapasvinī* is *jaṭāmāṃsī*; *meghapuṣpa* is *ajaśṛṅgikā*. *Mātulapuṣpa* should be known as *dhustūra*, while *coraka* is *ripu*.
*Śaṣpa* is said to be young grass (*bālatṛṇa*), and *śaileya* is *aśmapuṣpaka*.
*Śrīpuṣpa* refers to *lavaṅga*; *bālapuṣpī* is *yūthikā*.
*Sthūlapuṣpa* is *jheṇḍūka*, while *dāruṇa* is known to be *citraka*. Furthermore, *viṣapuṣpa* is a flower accompanied by dark leaves.
Balabhadra is another name for the kadamba; the śākhoṭa tree is known as bhūtavṛkṣaka.
Rāmā is found in the tamāla leaf, while carmadala is considered to be bhūrja.
Ātmaśalyā refers to śatāvarī, and kalabhavallabhā is used for pikyā.
The *palāśa* tree is known as *viprapriyā*; *guḍūcī* is *jvarāri*.
In the case of white *kaṇṭakārī*, one should know it as *kapaṭeśvarī*.
*Paṭola* is *pāṇḍuphala*, and *śāliparṇī* is considered *sthirā*.
Gāyatrī is said to be the *khadira* tree; *ervāru* is the cucumber (*karkaṭī*). *Nīvāra* is wild rice (*araṇyaśāli*); *pārvatī* is the elephant pepper (*gajapippalī*).
*Devaputrī* is *spṛkkā*; and *devadāru* is the *aṅkola* tree.
They call the soapberry tree *prakīryaka*, and it is known as *dantī* and *keśaruhā*.
The mango is *sahakāra*, while the palmyra palm is to be known as *drumeśvara*.
The *coraka* plant is called *duṣputra*, and the *māḍa* is indeed *vitānaka*.
Māciṣā is said to be maṇḍaka; mārjārī is that which is produced from musk (mṛganābhi). Bījāmla is found in the tamarind (tintiḍīka), while sakṛtphalā is in the plantain (kadalī).
Jartila is the wild sesame, and tārkṣyaśaila is rasāñjana.
*Kalinda* refers to the *vibhītaka* tree; *pāṭalā* should be known as *śāli* rice;
*raṅgamātṛ* refers to lac; and *agnijvālā* refers to *dhātakī*. *Bhasmagarbhā* occurs in the *tiniśa* tree; *madhukarkaṭī* is found in the *madhūlī* plant.

*Sitaguñjā* refers to *kākapīlu*, while *guḍūcī* is found in *candrā*. *Naṭa* occurs in the *aśoka* tree, and *phalaṣāḍava* is used for the *dāḍima* (pomegranate). *Palaṅkaṣā* refers to *niṣpāva*, while *kalaśī* is *pṛśniparṇikā*.
*Dīrghaśūka* is for *rājānna*; *jaraṇa* is for black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*).
*Piṅgā* is for turmeric (*haridrā*), and *yava* is known for white-awned barley (*śvetaśūka*). *Tribīja* is for *śyāmāka*, while *tuvarī* is known for *āḍhakī*.
In wheat, *mṛdu* is said to be the best; likewise, *karalā* and *tripuṭā*.
In green mung beans (*harimudga*), *rājānna* with short grains is the best;
in wild mung beans (*vanamudga*), there is *makuṣṭa*; and in *makuṣṭha*, there is *kṛmīlaka*.
*Kṛṣṇa* refers to the *kāśmīra* tree; *viṣatindu* refers to the poison-tree (*viṣadruma*).
*Pattraka* is said to be the *palāśa*, and *nyagrodha* is known as *rohiṇa*. *Rasaphala* is the coconut (*nārikela*), while *śambara* is the *tāla* palm.

The *vikaṅkata* is known for its soft fruit; the *kesara* is remembered as the *bakula*. *Śephālī*, *sindhuvāra*, and *matsyākṣa* are synonyms for *hilamocikā*. *Vāstuka* is the white *cillī*, while *vellikā* is the *upodakī*.
In the case of the *ārāmavallikā*, the root-sprout is well-known;
*makaranda* refers to the nectar of flowers, while *sumanā* is recorded as the name for the jasmine (*jāti*).
In the case of the *āmrātaka*, it is *pītanaka*; and in the case of honey, it is known as *puṣpāsava*.
*Mṛdu* is said to be *kanyā*, and likewise *jīvaka* is *jīvā*. *Guḍūcī* is [used] for *chinnā*, and *śatāvarī* for *nārāyaṇī*.
*Bastakarṇī* is [used] for *sarja*, and likewise *bilvaka* for *śalāṭu*.
Within the *sarja* group, there is *aśvakarṇa*; *gokarṇī* is in the *samadhu-rasa* group;
they call *kṛṣṇa* and *nīlāñjana* [the same]; *ākhukarṇī* is *śambarī*.
*Durgā* is *śyāmayakṣī*, and *bhūta* is *mustā*; then *durgraha* is [the same].
Apāmārga is [the name] for *raktā*, while *śaṭa* is likewise for *mañjiṣṭhā*. *Brahmajā* and *brāhmī* are for *dhustūra*, and *gandharva* is recorded as being for the *kokila*.
*Saraṭī* is for *durārohā*, and *tarvaṭa* is recorded as being for *bāhulī*.
Sarṣapa is indeed durādharṣa; likewise, hrīvera is bālaka.
Haimavatī is alparasā, and bhiṣaṅmātā is āṭarūṣaka. Brahmaputrī is bhārgī, and hastiparṇī is karkaṭī.
*Tulasī* is known as *bahumañjarī*, and *kaṭabhī* is remembered as *gardabhī*. *Kacchughna* is in *havuṣā*, while *śālmalī* is in the *yamadruma*.
*Sūkṣmailā* is in *koraṅgī*, and *dhūmapattrikā* is in *gandhāḍhyā*.
*Śailajā* is found in *gajapippalī*; *kṣīriṇī*, however, is *kuṭumbinī*.
*Trāyantī* and *kaṭī* are recorded as names for *devabalā*, while *khadira* is known as *rajanī*.
*Indīvarā* is [a name] for *karambhā*, and *indīvara* is recorded as the name for the lotus root (*kanda*).
In *puṣpa* there is *rājakanyā*, and likewise *tagara* in *pārthiva*.
In *sāgara* there is *ratnagarbha*, while the earth (*medinī*) is *ratnagarbhā*.
In *suvarṇa* one should know *kāñcana*, while *hemadugdhā* is *kāñcanī*.
In *prasāriṇī* there is *rājabalā*; in camphor, *himavāluka*;
they say "hima" refers to camphor; *gośīrṣa* is known as sandalwood (*candana*).
*Brahmadāru* is known in *phañjī*, and *paṇyandhā* is known as *paṇadhā*.

*Vatsādanī* is used for *guḍūcī*, while *somavallī* and *antravallikā* are synonyms for *nadyāmra*. *Samaṣṭhila* refers to *rajani*, and the wise state that *kālameṣī* is known as *dugdhārha*; furthermore, *palāṇḍu* is said to be *tilaka* and *dīpana*.
*Mocā* is declared to be *hastiviṣāṇaka*, while *padmā* is remembered for *bhārgī*. *Śīrṇadala* is likewise stated here for *nimba*, and *dhānyarāja* is [found] in *yava*.
In the *Rājanighaṇṭu*,

in the section on words with single meanings and so forth (*Ekārthādivarga*), among those with two meanings (*Dvyarthāḥ*): they declare that *saurāṣṭrī* means both "delight" (*rucide*) and "joining together" (*saṃdhāna*).

*Palāśikā*, *śaṭī*, and *lākṣā* denote the lac insect; *kitava* and *coraka* denote the rogue or thief. *Balākā* and *barhiṇa* are proclaimed as names for the peacock, as is *meghānanda*. *Ākāśa*, *abhraka*, and *gagana* denote the sky; *jalūkā* denotes the leech, and *matkuṇa* denotes the bedbug. *Asra* denotes blood.
The word *nāsa* refers to the nose and a constellation; *nāḍī* refers to the kola plant; *kaṇā* refers to the *śuṇḍika* plant;
*jvaraghna* refers to the *chinnavāstūka* plant; and *lalanā* refers to both *cāra* and *sarja*. (RājN 24.3) Furthermore, *kumārī* preceded by *nāga* refers to both *mañjiṣṭhā* and *guḍūcī*.

*Saptaparṇa* is said to be *mudgara* and *saptacchada*. *Kṛtrimaka* refers to *viḍa* salt, glass, and the *pākya* variety of *viḍa* salt derived from barley. *Kulaka* is said to be a type of snake and the *paṭola* plant.
In the Vāstuka plant, she is to be known as Cakravartinī;
she is declared to be Madhurā in the Jīvaka plant, and likewise remembered in the Medā.
She is proclaimed as Karkandhū in the Badara and the Pūtimāruta.
*Vāsantī* refers to the female cuckoo, while *dantyāpuṣpa* is said to be [the plant] *citraka*.
*Candrābja* refers to the blue lotus (*utpala*), and *kṛkara* to both *kuṣṭha* and *cavya*. *Capalā* denotes both wine and *māgadhī*, while *kṣamā* refers to both the earth and the *khadira* tree.
Sindhupuṣpa is in the Kadamba and the Bakula; then Lomaśā is in Kākolī and Vacā; Sūkṣmailā and Indravāruṇī [are likewise there]. Rajñī 24.9:
Aindrī is in Godāvarī, and Rocanā is in Gautamī.
*Kusumbha* refers to both the wild safflower and *kausumbha*; *kusumāñjana* refers to *śaṭī*, *gandhaniśā*, *coraka*, and *karkaṭī*.
Furthermore, *śatāhvā* refers to *devadālī*, *trapusī*, and *śatāvarī*.
*Miśi* is known as *tutthanīlinī*, as well as *sūkṣmailā*;
*vitunnaka* is [found] in *bhūdhātrī*, and likewise *kustumbarī* is well-known.
*Barhis* refers to *darbha* grass and the peacock; *plava* refers to the *plakṣa* tree and the monkey.
Ākhuparṇī is known to be in Sutaśreṇī as well as in Pratyakśreṇī. Aṃśuka is mentioned in Vastre and Tamālapattra;
likewise, Vajra is found in Darbha, Kuśika, Kaṅgu, and Dhānya-priyaṅguka.
*Kaṅguraṅgāravallī* refers to *phañjī*, *hastikarañja*, and *vakrapuṣpa*; *śvapucchaka* refers to *agasti* and *palāśa*. *Cillī* refers to *māṣaparṇī*, *śunaḥpuccha*, *śākala*, and *udhra*.
Alternatively, [the term] *indravāruṇī* refers to *śakrāhva* and *indrayava*;
*kākabhāṇḍī* is known as *kākatuṇḍī*; [it is also found] in *hastikarañjaka*, *dīrghāṅkuśī*, and *palāśa*. Furthermore, *yājñika* and *vidārikā* [are also included].
*Kāśmarya* is known as *śṛgālī*, *ṭeṇṭī*, and *mṛgadhūrtaka*;
*bhallūka* is known as *rudantī*, while *gokṣura* is *caṇapattra*.
*Kaṭukā* and *gajapippalī* are both known as *śakulādanī*. (RājNī 24.18)

*Manthānaka* is declared [to mean] *rājavṛkṣa*; *tṛṇādhipa* [means] *madana*; likewise, *kuṭila* means *tagara*, and then *raktikā*. *Rājikā* refers to both *guñjā* and *piśuna*, as well as *kuṅkuma*.
Then there is *tagara*, *yavāhvā* (barley), *yavakṣāra* (barley alkali), and *yavāsikā*.
*Aṅkura* and *odana* are both called *kūra*; likewise for the flowers of *dantī* and *madhuka*.
*Madhupuṣpa* is *śophaghnī*, as are *śāliparṇī* and *punarnavā*.
*Bālapattra* refers to *yavāsa*, *khadira*, and *bālaka*.
*Udīcya* is in the northern region; *kapi* refers to *kīśa* and *turuṣka*;
*sīrī* refers to *lāṅgalī* and *darbha*; and *pragraha* refers to the aquatic *vetasa*.
Vyādhighāta is cloves; śrīgandha is divine sandalwood.
They call svādukaṇṭaka by the names gokṣura and vikaṅkata;
yavaphala is the seed of bamboo; and dhānyamārka is vatsaka.
Devapriya is *agastya*; *vacā* is *śvetādipiccharī*.
*Gṛñjana* is said to be *golomyā*, and *laśuna* is the round-rooted [garlic]. *Kuṅkuma* is *rāmaṭha*; *bāhli* is *balā*; and *odanī* is *āmodanī*.
*Mahāsamaṅgā* is known as *aiśvaryā*; *jaṭā* is recorded in *jaṭāmāṃsī*. *Kastūrī* is proclaimed to be in *mṛganābhi*, and also in *dhustūra*.
*Godhāpadī* is known by the wise as both *haṃsapādī* and *musalī*.
*Tapasvī* refers to *hiṅgupattrī*, *prakīrya*, silver, and pearl;
*tāra* is said to be *māṣaparṇī* and *liṅgī*; and *svayambhuva* is said to be *kastūrī*, *rāmaṭha*, and the filaments of a lotus (*abjakesara*). (RājNī 24.27)
They say *puṃnāga* refers to the *tuṅga* tree, and [the suffix] *tri* is used for the two [types of] *vṛddhi* and *viśeṣa*. *Masūra* also [denotes] *viśvā*, as well as *śuṇṭhī* and *prativiṣā*.
*Śrīgandha* refers to *gandhapāṣāṇa* and *gandhasāra*, as well as *picchila*.

*Śālmalī* and *śiṃśapā* are called *vāsā*, while *bṛhatī* is known by the name *hiṃsrikā*. The word *markaṭa* is renowned for both *ajamodā* and the forest-dweller (the monkey). *Lāṅgalī* refers to *guḍūcī*, while *viśalyā* and *tejinī* [are synonyms].
*Tejovatī* refers to *mūrvā*, *cāṅgerī*, and *loṇaśāka*.
*Loṇikā* also denotes oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), sesame dregs, and turuṣka.
*Bṛhatī* refers to the eggplant (*vṛntāka*) and the *vārttākī* which bears fruit constantly.
In the *udumbara* tree, the *bilva* tree, the *lajjā* and *khadira* trees;
in the *khadira*, in sea salt (*sāmudra-lavaṇa*), and in sea-foam (*abdhi-phena*);
in the *granthila*, the *gokṣura*, the *bilva*, the *kaṭukā*, and in fish-bile.
*Matsyapitta* is [the bile] of fish; *rajanī* refers to both *haridrā* and that called *nīlikā*;
*miśreyaka* and *muralī* are [synonyms for] *vātapattra*; *mustaka* is [also known as] *abda*;
*puṣkara* is considered to be both *abhraka* and the white lotus.
*Tuṇḍikā* is praised for *tuṇḍikerī*, *kārpāsa*, and *tuṇḍikā*;
*dhūrta* for *dhustūra* and *viḍa*; and *vṛkṣadhūpa* is proclaimed for *śrīveṣṭa*, *sūcipattraka*, *himāṃśu*, and *karpūra*.

*Jātīphala* refers to *śailūṣa* and *śrīphala*; *sitāvarī* refers to *sūcipattra*, *vākucī*, sugar, and *gaṇḍadūrvā*. *Matsyaṇḍikā* refers to *drākṣā* (grape); *carā* and *tāpasapriyā* refer to the year. 24.37–38.
Phañjī and vokaḍī are said to be synonyms for ajāntrī;
arkāvarta, arka, and sūrya are synonyms; and peya is recorded as being used for milk and water.
Karpūra, cukraka, and candra are synonyms; and kṣaudra, tāpya, and mākṣika are synonyms.
*Mañjiṣṭhā*, *tagara*, *bhaṇḍī*, *uccaṭā*, *guñjā*, and *mustā*;
*suvarcala* refers to *mātuliṅga* and *rucaka*;
while *suvarcalā* refers to *arkāvarta*, *maṇḍūkī*, *hrīvera*, and *picumarda*.
*Nimba* is [known] as *saptalā*, while *saptalā* is *navamallikā*.
*Lāṅgalī* and *gajapippalī* are likewise known as *vahniśikhā*. *Jyotiṣmatī* is *kākajaṅghā* and also *pārāvatapadī*.
Durālabhā, yavāsa, and yāsa are considered kṣuraka;
gokṣura, kokilākṣa, kṣura, and gokaṇṭaka are also kṣura;
and puṣkara and palāśa are proclaimed as the best among milky plants (kṣīraśreṣṭha).
*Soma* refers to *dhānyābhra* (mica), *soma*, *priyā* (a type of plant), and among women, a beloved wife;
*munidru* refers to *ghaṇṭuka* and *agastya*; furthermore, *amṛṇāla* refers to *uśīraka*, *lāmajjaka*, *brahmavṛkṣa*, *raktāgastya*, and *palāśaka*.
*Vaṭa* and *plakṣa* are synonyms for the *śṛṅgī* tree; *kāntāra* refers to both a forest and a bamboo thicket.
*Bhūtṛṇa* and *dhānyaka* refer to the same plant; *chattra* refers to radish and the root of the *śigru* tree;
*mūlaka* refers to radish; and *yamānī* refers to both *dīpikā* and *bastamoda*.
Elavāluka and karkaṭa; vāluka and kṣīrabhūruha; copper and udumbara; then bhūrja and indrāśravaṇī. Rīti refers to brass and *puṣpāñjana*; rīti also denotes a minister, a counselor, and a rogue.
In *cāṇākā*, *mūlaka*, and *miśra*, there are rice grains; then in *arka* and *sārivā*; in *āsphotā*, *parjanya*, *vṛṣṭi*, and *dāruharidrā*;
in *lakuca*, *cukra*, and *vāstūka*; and then in *likuca*—these are considered the qualities. (Rajni 24.49–50)
*Dūrvā* is *māṃsarohiṇī*, while *sātalā* is also *māṃsarohiṇī*. Both [names] apply to *carmakaṣā*; *nīvāra* is *piṇḍakarburā*. *Munipriya* is [found] in *varā*, while *guḍūcī* is in *viḍaṅga*.
The word *rasa* refers to mercury (*pārada*) and borax (*bola*); *rasa* also denotes quicksilver (*pārada*) and leather (*carman*).
*Bhallūka* refers to a dog and a bear; *nalinī* refers to a lotus plant and an elephant (*ibhī*).
The two words *pravara* and *ārūka* are well known as designations for the *kiṃśuka* tree. (RājNī 24.52–53)
*Citrika* refers to *methikā* seeds or to *jyotiṣka* in the rainy season;
*trāyamāṇā* refers to *anyapuṣṭī*, while *methikā* and *citramūla* are [also its names]. *Vallarī* refers to the *dhustūra* plant or to a young elephant.
Elā is found in *truṭi* and *nīlikā*; *śikhaṇḍī* is in *mayūraka*, *suvarṇayūthikā*, *kārava*, and *rucaka*. That which is called black salt (*kṛṣṇalavaṇa*) is also in *dāḍima* and *kapittha*.
*Kucaphala* is known as a superior vegetable, as is *kuṣmāṇḍaka*;
*kaliṅga* is likewise known, and then *khaga* refers to both wind and a bird.
*Dhanurvakṣa* is [found] on the Dhanvana mountain, and it is also called *bhallāta*.
Gheṭuka is khaḍgaśimbī, and pṛthuśimbī is cetanā. Pathyāruṣka is known as nicula, and aśoka is vañjula.
Kapikacchu is apāmārga, and markaṭī is anyapakṣiṇī.
Bhāradvājī is found in wild cotton and also in guggulu;
pura is said to be in dahana and aguru; then jatupattrikā is in kṣudrāśmabheda and aṅgerī; atasī is in śāliparṇikā.
The *kumbhī* plant may have a single root, as may the *pāṭalī* and the *droṇapuṣpa*. The *vārāhī*, *harikrāntā*, and *viṣṇukrāntā* are considered synonymous.
The term *sāraṅga* refers to the *cātaka* bird, while *raṅku* refers to the deer; *śaṅkha* denotes that which is produced in water, and *nakha* denotes the claw.

*Māṃsala* is said to be [a name] for the fruit of the *vṛntāka* and the *kaliṅgaka*; *niṣpattrikā*, *vaṃśāgra*, and *karīra* are proclaimed as synonyms; furthermore, *māṣaparṇī*, *guñjā*, *kāmbhojī*, and *pūtanā* [are synonyms]. *Rājñī* 24.63.

The wise know *gandhamāṃsī* as *harītakī*, *citrāṅga* as the *mleccha* and *tāla* trees, and *madana* as the *aṅkolaka* and *gandhotkaṭa*. Furthermore, *bhasmagarbha* is proclaimed to be the *tiniśa* and the *śiṃśapā* tree.
*Samīraṇa* is known by physicians as a term for wind and for *marudgada*;
*kṣīra* is used for milk and for *tavakṣīra*; *kṣavathu* refers to sneezing and coughing;
and *kurava* is recorded as a specific type of white *mandāraka* flower.

*Suṣavī* is known for both *kaṭuhuñcī* and large cumin (*sthūlajīraka*). *Kaṇṭakī* is said to refer to *khadira* and eggplant (*vṛntāka*). Furthermore, *nīlikā* refers to *sinduvāra* and the blue jay (*pika*), while *kokilā* likewise refers to the blue jay.
*Kokilākṣa* is [the name] for *gāndhārī*, and it is also used for *patrī* and *yavāsaka*.
*Cakrāṅgī* is proclaimed to be for *rohiṇī* and *mañjiṣṭhā*.
*Masūrā* is said to refer to *trivṛtā* as well as a specific type of grain.
Girija is said to be red ochre (gairika), while śilājatu is highly praised. Candrikā is proclaimed to be both candrakānta and nirguṇḍī;
phañjī is found in yojanabalā, and nīlikā is likewise in bhārgī.

*Mṛgākṣī* refers to the *śrīphalī* fruit; *mṛgākṣī* also denotes the *dhātrikā* fruit. Furthermore, *khyātāmṛtaphala* refers to the *śyāmekṣu* and the *kokilākṣaka*. Regarding *ikṣuraka*, they call it *vakraśalyā* and *kaṭubimbī*.

The term *kartarī* is well-known by the wise for *dantyantara*, *vibhāṇḍī*, and *abhayā*; likewise, it is declared for *harītakī* and *amṛṇālī*. Furthermore, the best of physicians recognize *bhrāmarī* as referring to *jantukā* and *jananī*.
*Gorasa* refers to cow's milk; *gavya* refers to products derived from a cow; *kārpāsya* refers to cotton; *cavya* and *cavyaka* refer to the same medicinal plant.
*Gorocanā* and *rocanā* are well-known terms for gallstone (bezoar); *vaṃśarocanā* refers to bamboo manna.
*Piṅgalā* is proclaimed as a name for the *jyotiṣmatī* plant and for a particular species of bird.
Amṛtā is proclaimed in the case of śāliparṇī, while sudhā is celebrated for pārada and rasāñjana; rasarāja is likewise designated for vallīkarañja,
sitapāṭalā, kuberanetrā, and jaṭāmāṃsī.
Māṃsī is [found] in Rudantī; lavaṇa is [found] in the two earth-born [substances]; and that which is called romaka is indeed found in kānta, ayas, and aśman.
(Rājanighaṇṭu, Ekārthādivarga, Tryarthāḥ 24.77)
*Vāsantī* is used for *śatapattra* (the hundred-petaled white lotus) and *mādhavī*;
*kaṭabhī* is recorded as a name for *jyotiṣmatī*, *kiṇihī*, and *supuṣpī*.
*Punarnavā* and *indragopa* are known as *varṣābhū*, while *dardura* refers to the frog.

*Sukumāra*, however, refers to *śyāmāka*, *campaka*, and likewise *kṣavaka*. *Sprkkā* is known as *sukumārā*; *nepālī* is considered to be *mālatī*. *Mahābalā*, *gavākṣī*, *girikarṇī*, and *gavādanī* [are synonyms].
*Ariṣṭa* refers to a type of buttermilk, as well as to the *nimba* tree and garlic;
likewise, *kaṭukā*, bamboo, *dūrvā* grass, *śataparvā*, and *kiṃśuka*;
*jyotiṣmatī*, *palāśa*, *nandīvṛkṣa*, and *lāṅgalī*.
It is recommended for *halinī*, *gajapippalī*, and coconut;
for *kadamba*, the jasmine called *mallikā*, and *śirīṣa*—the round-flowered variety—for *girikarṇī*, *indravāruṇī*, *piṇḍī*, and *gavādanī*. (Rājñī 25.5–6)
Śirīṣa, madhuka, and dantī; madhupuṣpa and vañjula; aśoka and bheriṇī; nicula and then nākulī;
sarpākṣī and sitakṣudrā; yavatiktā and then dardura.

The word *bhallātaka* is praised when applied to the *ṛṣabhaka* plant and to a bull; *mayūraka* occurs in the sense of *methikā* and *citraka*; and the term *śikhī* applies to the *kadalī* plant and *ajamodā*.
Similarly, the designation *hastī* is used for an elephant and the *kadala* fruit. (Rājani 25.8–9)
Amoghā is found in *padmabheda*, *pāṭalī*, and *vilaṅga*.
*Kulmāṣa* is well-known in *kāñjika*, bamboo, and fragrant garlands (*gandhamālya*).
*Sāmāyā* is recorded as being in *mahiṣīvallī*, *brāhmī*, and *hemanta*.
*Tṛṇarājaka* occurs in the sense of bamboo, coconut, and palmyra;
*ghana* refers to nut-grass (*mustā*), mica, and cloud; and *pitṛpriya* is well known as a name for the Agasti plant, the Bhr̥ṅgarāja, and the Kālaśāka herb.
*Dantaśaṭha* is used for *cāṅgerī*, *jambīra*, and *kapittha*;
*dahana* is said to refer to *aruṣkara*, *vṛścikālī*, and *citraka*;
and *balā* is recorded as being used for *viḍaṅga*, *jayantī*, and *moṭā*.
In the *āmrātaka*, the *śirīṣa*, and the *plakṣa* tree, as well as in the *kapītana*; in the *kuṭaja*, the *huñcī*, the *kāravallī*, the *kāṇḍīra*, and the *cīrapadma*;
in the *yavāsa*, the *kṣudrakhadira*, and the *kārpāsa*—these are the trees born of the Maruts.
*Samudrāntā* refers to *spṛkkā*, *kārpāsa*, and *yavāsaka*;
*maṇḍūkaparṇī* refers to *maṇḍūkī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *ādityakāntā*. *Ṛṣabha* is known as *vāsā* (the plant), while *vṛṣa* is traditionally used for a bull.

*Cāmpeya* is said to refer to the *campaka* flower, while *kiñjalka* refers to the *nāgakesara*. *Uśīra*, *lavaṅga*, and *śrīkhaṇḍa* are synonyms for *vārisambhava*. *Palita* is well known as a term for *śailaja*, for *śyāma*, and for white hair.
*Kunduruka* is known as a variety of incense, as *śallakī*, and as a type of grass;
*hiṅgupattrī* is [a synonym for] *pṛthvīkā*; *sthūlailā* is considered a bud;
*śatapattra* refers to a royal parrot, a lotus, and a specific flower.
*Nyagrodha* is recorded as being used for *akhuparṇī*, *viṣaparṇī*, and the banyan tree (*vaṭa*).
*Kṣudrāgnimantha* is [used] for *tarkārī* and *jīmūta*, and *agnimanthaka*.
*Śvetā* is proclaimed to be used for silver (*raupya*), *mīnāṇḍī*, and sugar (*sitā*).
*Somavalka* refers to the *rīṭhā*, the *kadara*, and the *kṛṣṇagarbhaka*;
*śaileyaka* is called *śilāhvā*, as well as *kunaṭī* and *śilājatu*.
*Kṛṣṇavṛntikā* refers to the *pāṭalā*, the *māṣaparṇī*, and the *kāśmarī*.
One *pala* each is prescribed for *jaṭāmāṃsī*, meat, and lac.
*Samaṅgā*, *raktapādī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *balā* are prescribed.
*Bhallātaka*, the *bilva* tree, and *pārtha* are prescribed as *vīrataru*.

Duḥsparśā, kaṇṭakārī, kapikacchu, and durālabhā are synonyms for vatsādanyā; likewise, guḍūcī, tārkṣī, and gajapippalī are synonyms for it. Āmaṇḍa, puṣkara, and kañja are said to be synonyms for padmapattra.
*Kāleyaka* is used for *dārvī*, saffron, and yellow sandalwood;
*tilaparṇikā* is used for *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *ajagandha*, and *śrīveṣṭa*.
*Kramuka* is known to denote *lodhra*, betel nut, and cotton.
Pippalī is found in yūthikā, and mādhavī in jīraka;
ajamodā is in śatāhvā, and miśi is indeed śatāvarī. Trapusī is karkaṭī, and likewise tausī is vanakarkaṭī.
*Kustumburī* and *bhūdhātrī* are recorded as synonyms for *dhānya*, such as rice (*vrīhi*) and other grains.
*Trapusī* and *devadālī* are recorded as synonyms for *ghoṭikā* and *śaphalā*.
*Taṇḍulīyaka* and *yavatiktā* are synonyms for the words *śaśāṇḍulī* and *abda*, among others.
*Suradāru* refers to both *gandha* and *badhvā*. *Gandhamādinī* is found in *caṇḍā*.
*Kokilākṣaka* occurs in *śyāma*, *ikṣuka*, and *kṣuraka*, as well as in *kākākṣa*.
*Varāṅga* is praised for its application to the head, the private parts, and the skin.
*Śvetakiṇihī*, *kaṭabhī*, and *girikarṇikā* are [synonyms] for *karṇī*;
likewise, *pataṅga* refers to *arka*, *madhūka*, and *paṭṭarañjanaka*.
*Drākṣā* is [a synonym] for *śatavīryā*, and *dūrvā* is [a synonym] for *śatāvarī*.

Ginger, *prativiṣā*, and *viśvā* are recommended for *śatāvarī*; likewise, *jayā*, turmeric, and *vijayā* are praised for *jayantī*. For *kacchurā*, *durālambhā*, *svayaṃguptā*, and *yavāsaka* are used.

They declare that *puṇḍrekṣu*, *godhūma*, and *rasāla* [are synonyms]; furthermore, *drākṣā* is said to be *rasālā*. And it is stated by the best of physicians that *vacā*, *śvetakṣīriṇī*, and *lomaśā* are remembered as synonyms for *haimavatī*.
*Śrīphala* refers to the *bilva*, the *dhātrī* fruit, and the fresh, glossy *śrīphala*. *Kamala* is known as a specific bird and the *sārasa*.
*Chinnaruhā* is the *tilaka*, while *suṣavī* would be the *ketakī*. (Rājñī 25.37)
The word *vaṃśa* is recorded as referring to the *sarja* tree, a bamboo, and a lineage;
*viṣa* is traditionally known to mean water, aconite (*vatsanābha*), and a serpent.
*Sthūlakanda* may be *mukhālu*, while *śūraṇa* is the elephant-yam (*hastikandaka*).
Āmrātaka is also called pītanaka and amlikā; palāśikā is another name for it. Viṣadoḍyā is used for mahānimba, and viṣamuṣṭika for madana.
Tagara is said to be kuṅkuma, and śaṭha is recorded as a name for dhustūra.
*Kapittha* refers to the *svarṇayūthī* tree; *puṇḍraka* denotes the *kuṣmāṇḍa*, the *nāgapuṣpaka*, the *tilaka*, the *atimukta*, and a variety of sugarcane;
while *vāruṇī* refers to the *ākhoṭa* tree, and *carmavādinī* to the *gavākṣī*.
In *toyavallī*, *kāraṇḍīra* flows with great milk like nectar;
on the earth, *pṛthvī*, *punarnavā*, *medā*, and *dhāriṇī* are praised.
In *mucukunda*, *jayāpuṣpa*, *gaṇerī*, and *harivallabhā* [are likewise effective].

*Kāmuka* refers to the *laghukāśmarī* tree; *kaiḍarya* refers to another species of *karañja*; *śikhariṇī* refers to a variety of grape, as well as *nevālī* and a type of curd. *Kuṭaja* and *indrayava* are said to be [synonyms for] *puṣpa*, *kāsīsa*, and *vatsaka*.
*Madhu* is said to be in honey and certain types of liquor; it is also recorded as *madhuyaṣṭī* (licorice). *Nīlakaṇṭha* refers to the sparrow and the peacock.
*Śoṇita* is in saffron and blood; it is also known as *raktagandha*.
*Tarkārī* is in *devadālī*, and *araṇyā* is in the circle of fire (*vahnimaṇḍala*).
*Vasaryā* is in *vṛścika*, while *kākabandhyā* and *sakṛtprajā* are in *kaṭvaṅgī* and *kaṭabhī*. *Dadhipuṣpikā* is in *paṭolī*. (Rājñī 25.47)
One speaks of *suvarṇa* in reference to the thorn-apple (*dhustūra*), the filament (*kesara*), and gold. *Vāruṇī* refers to turmeric (*haridrā*) and the resin *kaṇaguggulu*.
*Śūkarī* refers to the female hog (*vārāhī*), the porpoise (*śiśumāri*), and a type of tuber.
It is designated as *mahākanda* by those proficient in the meaning of the medical scriptures (*vaidyaśāstra*) when it occurs among onions, garlic, and the root known as *cāṇakya*;
it is also found in iron, wild plantain, and the small stone-breaker (*laghupāṣāṇabheda*).
And regarding these three, Girijā is prescribed by the best of physicians:
Jaraṇa is [used] for Kāsamarde, while Rāmaṭha is for Kṛṣṇajīraka;
that [Girijā] brings about pacification, and it is highly praised in the case of Tīkṣṇa and Tagara.

*Durālabhā* may be used for *kapikacchuka*, as well as for *śikhari*. *Durabhigrahā* is [also] so called. *Mahāsamaṅgā* and *bahuputrikā* are synonyms; it is *sārivā* in the case of *phaṇijihvikā*. (Rājanighaṇṭu 25.53)
In the section on words with one meaning and so forth,
those with four meanings:
*mocikā* refers to both the *amlikā* (tamarind) and the *cāṅgerī* (sorrel), as well as the *āmraciñcā* (a type of mango).
In the *Vayaḥsthā* [chapter], *Kākolyau*, *Dārvī*, and *Somavallarī* are mentioned;
in the *Jantukā* and *Putradātrī*, as well as the *Ṣaṭpadī*, *Bhramarī*, and the two types of *tvac*;
and *Bhramarī*, *Cāraka*, and the *Vaidyaśāstra* are recorded in the *Āyuṣmatī*.
Abhayā, cirbhiṭā, bandhyā, karkoṭī, and mṛgādanī—
these four are declared by the best of physicians to be synonyms for pathyā.
Kuṣṭha, kunduruka, nimba, rājaka, and rājabhadraka [are synonyms for kuṣṭha].
*Kaṭaka*, *kācaka*, *loha*, and *tilaka* are synonyms for *gandhabhedaka*.
Furthermore, *matsyākhya*, *mahārāṣṭrī*, and *kākamācī* are used;
and *brahmamaṇḍūkikā* is said to be *matsyākṣī*.
*Naktañcara* refers to a bat, *kauśika*, *balguja*, a small drum (*duṇḍubha*), or a city (*pura*).
*Śiphā*, *jagandhā*, *kāravya*, *methikā*, and *ajamodikā* [are synonyms].
*Hari* is known to denote a lion (*pañcāsya*), a monkey (*markaṭa*), a horse (*aśva*), and a frog (*maṇḍūka*).
Śyāmālaṅkā is found in Tripuṭā; sthūlailā is vṛttamallikā. Loha is in iron and bronze, as well as in black iron and aguru. Kharjūrī is in coconut; tāla is in palm; and durāruhā is in bamboo.
*Śuṇṭhī*, *marica*, *pippalī*, *kaṇāmūla*, and *ṣaḍūṣaṇa*;
likewise *agni*, *tvaruṣkara*, *jāra*, *nimbuka*, and *citraka*.
*Bhūtāṅkuśa* is found in *apāmārga*, as well as *sukumāra* and *rājikā*.
Regarding the skin and the strength of the eyes, it has been declared therein by the best of physicians:
*śamī*, *haridrā*, *vṛddhi*, *lakṣmī*, *padmacāriṇī*, *jambūkī*, *somamatsyākṣī*, *kroḍī*, and *brāhmī* are thus proclaimed. (Rajñī 26.10–11)
*Mārkava* refers to *bhrāmara* and *bhṛṅga*; *tvac* refers to a specific type of bird.
*Rocana* occurs in *dāḍimaka*, *jambha*, *nimba*, and *pūraka*.
*Puṇḍarīka* refers to the white lotus (*sitābja*), *damana*, *vyāghra*, and a type of disease.
Jalajā is found in pearls, conch shells, salt, alkaline substances, and cloves;
vandhyākarkoṭakī, bṛhatī, and another variety of lakṣmaṇā are proclaimed as the four plants that grant sons and bestow progeny.
Uśīra, gṛñjana, madhupuṣpa, and vañjula; dīrghapattra and ketakī; kanyā and dīrghapattrikā;
vāsanta and rucaka; plakṣa and devasarṣapa in Kaliṅga.

*Dīrghamūlā* is known by the wise as *lāmajjaka*, *yāsa*, *vellantara*, and *śaṭha*; likewise, it is found in *śāliparṇī*. *Rāmā*, *trāyamāṇā*, *kanyā*, *śoka*, and *sātalā* are synonyms for *dīrghamūlā*.

*Amṛtā* is used for *vedanākṣāra*, *sudhā*, poison, the porpoise (*śiśumāra*), the female boar (*vārāhī*), the male boar (*śūkara*), and the cloud (*ghana*). *Vārāhī* refers to the *vañjula* tree, *kāsa*, and the *nādeyī* or aquatic *vetasa*.

The word *śārada* refers to the *bakula* tree, the *rāṣṭrī* plant, *sārivā*, and black *mudga* beans; it is also dear to women in the sense of "beloved. The word *kāśmīra* refers to saffron (*kuṅkuma*), the region of Kashmir (*deśa*), the lotus (*pauṣkara*), and musk (*mṛganābhija*).
*Kesara* refers to the *bakula*, gold, the filament of a lotus, and green vitriol (*kasīsa*).
*Jambīra* may denote the *maruvaka* and the cluster of the two types of *arjuna*.
*Vasuka* denotes *vasurāja*, the sun, black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*), and *punarnavā*.
The *lakṣmaṇā* plant grows among the *japā*, *nṛkanda*, *akṣudrā*, and *mucukunda* flowers.
The *harṣaṇī* grows among the *sārasa*, the *kāmin* among the *cakra* and *pārāvata*,
and the *bahuprajā* among the *mūṣaka*, *kukkuṭa*, *krauñca*, and *vṛścika*.
Goat’s horn combined with mañjiṣṭhā,
karkaṭaśṛṅgikā combined with prativiṣā, and likewise śṛṅgī are highly recommended.
Surasa, tulasī, brāhmī, nirguṇḍī, and kaṇaguggulu [are also used].
In the *Cīnā*, *Kārabalī*, *vacā*, and *lavaṇa* it is called *paṭu*;
likewise, in the *pāṭalī*, *śyāmā*, *kiṇihī*, and *tāmravallī*,
as well as the *jīvantikā* and *tāmrapuṣpī*, these names have been declared by those learned in the scriptures.
Hiṅgula, kuṅkuma, raktamasa, and padmaka are said [to be synonyms];
likewise dugdhī, goḍura, bhūpalāśa, kākolī, and dugdhaphenaka;
as well as musalī, svarṇulī, kaṇṭakārī, and indravāruṇī.
In the *Hemapuṣpī*, it has been declared by those expert in the knowledge of various meanings:
"In the *Niśā*, the *Nīlinī*, the *Haridrā*, and the *Alaktaka*, the wise call it *Rajanī* in the *Āyurvedas*. (Rajñī 26.28–29)
*Rājanighaṇṭu*, *Ekārthādivarga*, Section on Fivefold Synonyms:
*ajamoda*, *ajagandhā*, *śikhaṇḍī*, and *kokilākṣaka*.
Apāmārga—these five are designated by the term "mayūra.
Kadalī, śālmalī, mocā, nīlī, and likewise śobhāñjana; among these five, the best of physicians apply the name "mocā" specifically to the mocā plant.
Surabhi, śallakī, voka, kadamba, campaka, surā, yayo, darbha,
and haridrā are purifiers; so too are hijjala, tila, yamānī,
jīraka, modā, abjā, and raktacitraka.
And *nimbu*— these five are thus declared to be the *dīpyakas*.
*Kapikacchū*, *kovidāra*, *pannaga*, *kṛtamālaka*,
and likewise *chinnaruhā*— these are remembered as the five *kuṇḍalīs*.
Śalāṭu, agnimantha, kṣudrāgnimathana, kāśmīrī, and śiṃśapā— these, along with śrīparṇī, are remembered as the fivefold [group]. Mahāsamaṅgā, vandākā, jatukā, and amṛtasravā.

These five, including *mahāmedā*, are to be known by the wise as growing on trees. The term *kapilā* is recorded by the learned in five senses: in a particular type of cow, in a female deer, in the *śiṃśapā* tree, in the substance called *reṇukā*, and in a different kind of metal.
*Kākolyau* refers to the two types of *kākolī*, as well as *pathyā* and *bahumañjarī*.
*Vyāla* refers to the leopard, tiger, lion, rogue elephant, and so forth.
*Vṛntāka* refers to the eggplant (*anyavāruṇī*), the small gourd (*kṣudrā*), and that which is called *cirbhiṭa*.
In these five— the *liṅginī* included— it should be known by the wise that the results are manifold. Indeed,
the term *barbara* is declared by those learned in the scriptures to refer to *hiṅgu*, *bālā*, *bhāraṅgī*, yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*), and both black and white *arjaka*.
*Ugragandhā* is prescribed for *yamānī*, *ajamodā*, *vacā*, *dīpyaka*, and redless garlic (*araktalaśuna*)— thus in these five. *Sahadevī* is declared to be present in *mahābalā* and *nīlinī*.
Vatsādanī, devasahā, and pippalī are recorded as the five [names] for jyotiṣmatī; likewise, vāyasī is used in five ways for kākatuṇḍī, kākamācī, kākajaṅghā,
and kākī.
Liṅginī, svarṇajīvantī, raudrī, and likewise nākulī, as well as bandhyākarkoṭakī, are proclaimed to be in the [direction] of Īśvarī.
In the [direction] of Vasantadūtī, there are gaṇikārikā, āmra, vāsantikā, pāṭala, and kokila.
Vatsādanī, vākucikā, guḍūcī, saumā, and samaṇḍūkikasomavallī;
cakrī, nakhāntara, koka, dadrughna, and tiniśa;
khara, sindhuja, tilaka, dhātrī, pārada, and ṭaṅkaṇa are synonyms for śiva (mercury).

The wise call *kanaka* the names for the *jātī*, *surīrī*, *kaṭutumbinī*, *chuchundarī*, *reṇu*, *rasā*, *ajaputrī*, gold, as well as *guggulu*, *kesara*, and the rat *ākhū-śaṭha*. (Rājanighaṇṭu 27.18)
The group of six with a single meaning consists of *bṛhadbalā*, *varī*, *tālī*, *kaṭukā*, *ativiṣā*, and *kākolī*;
these are declared to be the group of six for *vīrā*. (Rajni 28.1)
Sātalā, kṣīrakākolī, vibhāṇḍī,
ajaśṛṅgikā, kuñjara, and dardura are proclaimed as the six-horned [herbs].
Nīladūrvā, niśāhva, rocanā, and harītakī;
Bahupuṣpī is recorded by the best of physicians as one of these six [plants] in the Śivā group.
Nimba, kharjūrī, tālīsa, marica, vṛttamūlaka,
and palāṇḍu— these six are proclaimed as those known by the name nimba.
Mūrvā, spṛkkā, sahadevā, devadroṇī, and keśara—
these six are proclaimed as the "devī" (divine) plants, dedicated to the Sun.
The Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Danta, Sarpa, and Khaga likewise [are the six classes].
These are always proclaimed by the wise using the terms *dvija* and *dvijanman*.
Furthermore, *gavādanī*, *dūrvā*, *gaṇḍadūrvā*, *hastinī*, *pratīcī*,
and *madirā*— these six are highly esteemed as belonging to the western quarter (*vāruṇī*).
Hapuṣā, pītanirguṇḍī, viṣṇukrāntā, jayantikā,
śitādrikarṇī, and śaṅkhinī— these six are the aparājitās. Also, kumārī, varāhī, vandhyākarkoṭakī, and mṛdu.
Sthūlailā, sthalaparṇī, and the six maidens (ṣaṭkanyāḥ) are the young girls (kumārikāḥ).
Regarding the seed-tree, the elephant, lead, nāgakesara,
poison, and the serpent— these are also known as the "six-fold hymn" (ṣaṭsūkta) and the "serpent" (nāga).
Sūkṣmailā, mahārāṣṭrī, matsyākṣī, kākamācikā, gaṇḍadūrvā,
and gaṇḍūkī are said to be the six types of matsyādanī.
[The six types of] māṇa are kaliṅga, kośāmra, śalya, kāka, and dhūrtaka.
And Madana is also proclaimed; these six are thus enumerated.
Doḍī, Guḍūcī, Medā, Kākolī, Hariṇī, and Jīvantī—these six are declared by the best of physicians to be the varieties of Jīvantī.
Indeed, *dhūmrāṭa* and *bhṛṅgī*, as well as the fleshy parts of *plakṣa*, *śirīṣa*, and *kuṭaja*;
*kuliṅga*, *drākṣā*, *dūrvā*, *jaraṇā*, *kaṇā*, that which is called *kṛṣṇā*, *vākucikā*, and *kaṭu*. (Rājanighaṇṭu 28.14)
Ekārthādivarga: The Sevenfold Meanings.
Regarding the *bhadrā* plant, the best of physicians have declared that there are seven [synonyms]: *balā*, *nīlī*, *dantī*, *kāśmarī*, *sārivā*, *śvetādrikarṇī*, and *gaurī*. (Rajni 29.1)
Mañjiṣṭhā, kaṭukā, pathyā, kāśmarī, candravallabhā, vandāka, and rajanī are known as the seven [herbs] for Rohiṇī.
Dhātrī is used for Bahuphalā; chardinī is kākamācikā.
Kāmbhojī, śaśāṇḍūlī, kaṭuhuñcī, and vālukī; maṇḍūkī, brahmajā, śaṅkhapuṣpī, jyotiṣmatī, muni,
viṣṇukrāntā, and white vacā— these seven are considered pure (medhyā).
Ākhukarṇī, sutaśreṇī, indrāhvā,
kaliṅgaka, gaṇḍadūrvā, and gavākṣī— these are on one side of Citrā;
rāsnā, pāṭhā, priyaṅgu, sitakṣudrā, and harītakī [are on the other].
Śreyasī, samproktā, ambaṣṭhā, and gajapippalī are thus declared [synonyms]. (Rājanighaṇṭu,
Ekārthādivarga, Aṣṭārthāḥ 29.6)
Vijayā, the pair of Kāñcanas, Mañjiṣṭhā, and likewise Vacā;
there should also be Śvetanirguṇḍī, Jayantī, Kāñjikā, and Abhayā;
Eraṇḍa, Nadyāmra, Latā, Karañja, Brahmadaṇḍī, Panasa, and Kusumbha.

Gokṣura, kaṇṭaphala, and dhūrta—these eight are declared by physicians [to be auspicious]. (Rājñī 30.2) In the case of gold, *kapiccha*, curd, coconut, *jīvaka*, as well as *sthalapadmaka*, *mayūraketu*, and *madhūka*—these eight they proclaim to be auspicious. (Rājñī 30.3)
In the *Rājanighaṇṭu*,
in the section on words with a single meaning (*Ekārthādivarga*), under the category of nine meanings (*Navārthāḥ*):
"vātāri" [is used] for *jatukā*, *bhallyā*, *nīla*, and *davañjaya*.
The *ṭendu*, *kāmaṇḍu*, *bhārgī*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *śūrāṇa* are recorded [in this context].
*Dhātrī*, *guḍūcī*, *rāsnā*, the two kinds of *dūrvā*, *harītakī*, *liṅginī*, *tuvarī*, liquor, and *dhīmatā* constitute the nine medicinal herbs (*navauṣadhī*). (Rajni 31.1–2)
Brāhmī, Varāhī, Laśunī, Viṣa, Śuklakanda and others, Sitakaṇṭakārī, Bhūmyāhulī, Aparājitā, and Śuṇḍī— among these, there shall be the great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadhī). *Rājanighaṇṭu*, 31.3.
Ekārthādivarga, Ten Meanings:
In the *Sitā* lexicon, *vākucī*, *dūrvā*, *madya*, *dhātrī*, *kuṭumbinī*, *candrikā*, *priyā*, *piṅgā*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *tejinī* share the same meanings. (Rajni 32.1)
Rājanighaṇṭu,
Section on Synonyms and so forth,
Eleven Meanings.
Abhramāṃsī, tulasī, haridrā, tāla, as well as rocanā and gold;
janapriyā, yojanavallikā, and mallikā—these are for Gaurī.
Dūrvā, niśā, ṛddhi, vacā, and priyā; that [plant] māṣaparṇī, śimi, and rocanā—these are for Rājñī.
Trāyantikā, jīvanikā, mahābalā, and maṅgalyakā are called by the name *candramā*.
Priyaṅgu, chinnā, trivṛtā, kaṇāhvayā, vandāka, dūrvā, tulasī,
nīlinī, durgā, khaga, kasturikṛṣṇasārivā, śyāmā, and mahīndu are declared as such by the best of physicians.

Having reflected thus, the physician who possesses great devotion should examine this section, which is complete with a collection of groups of names for various single and multiple substances; then, he himself should determine the applications appropriate to the specific context.

(Rajni 33.4) He who is the sole one among the wise, he who is not clever among the two Aśvins, he who is not clever among the three-eyed one, and he who is the five-faced conqueror of the six enemies by name—[he is the one].
This twenty-third great chapter, beginning with "Ekārtha," which serves as the crest-jewel of the *Nāmaracanā*, has been completed together with this present work. 33.5.
